# Ashgill, After Midnight

## I. The Coup

On the morning her father lost the company, Maud Fenwick was in the ladies' toilets on the fourteenth floor, practising a smile.

She had practised it all week. It was the smile for the shareholders' meeting, meant to say *continuity* and *confidence* and *nothing to see here*. When she came out with it fixed in place, the boardroom doors were already shut, and through the glass she could see her uncle Gordon on his feet at the head of the table. Her father sat very still at the side of the room, with his hands flat on a folder, like a man who has just been told the price of something and is trying not to show he can't afford it.

It took forty minutes. The vote was nine to four. By lunchtime the brass letters in reception still said FENWICK & CO., but they meant something different.

Peter Fenwick did not make a scene. He wasn't the kind of man who made scenes, which, Maud thought later, was probably how his brother had managed it. He shook hands with the board. He took his coat from the stand. In the lift he said to her, "Well. I always did say I'd like to see more of the hills," and then he laughed, and the laugh went wrong in the middle.

He was gone within a month: north to a valley in the fells called Ashgill, where his mother had been born and where nobody had ever heard of a quarterly forecast. He wrote to Maud once a week, real letters, in fountain pen. The letters were full of sheep and weather and someone called Ewan, who had a radio transmitter.

Maud stayed. Gordon kept her on, at first, because firing her would have looked bad. And there was Cass.

Cass was Gordon's daughter: Maud's cousin, a year younger, her nearest friend since they were small enough to share a bath. Cass had sat in the boardroom on the day of the vote and voted against her own father. Nobody had ever forgiven her for it, least of all Gordon. She didn't care.

"He wants me to choose," Cass said, in the flat they had shared since university, with her feet on the coffee table and a glass of wine balanced on her stomach. "Him or you. As if that's a choice."

"He's your father."

"He's a man who stole his brother's company by phoning round the board at eleven o'clock at night. You're my cousin." Cass took a long drink. "That isn't a contest."

---

Maud lasted until the company's centenary gala, at the end of October.

It was held in a converted warehouse on the river. There were ice sculptures and a string quartet, and Gordon made a speech about *family values* that made Maud grip her glass so hard the stem cracked. Afterwards, at the edge of the room, she watched him take apart a junior catering assistant who had spilled a tray of champagne near his shoes. He did it quietly, pleasantly, in front of everyone. The girl was perhaps nineteen. Her face had gone the colour of the tablecloths.

Then one of the waiters put down his tray and walked over.

He was tall and thin, with dark hair that needed cutting and a borrowed-looking white jacket. Maud never knew exactly what he said, because he said it as quietly as Gordon had. But she saw Gordon's face change. She saw the girl stop crying. And she saw the waiter take off his white jacket, fold it neatly over the back of a chair, and walk towards the door.

She caught up with him outside, by the river, in the rain.

"That was either very brave or very stupid," she said.

He looked at her. He had a nice face, she thought: ordinary and open, the sort of face that hadn't learned yet to hide anything. "Probably both," he said. "I needed that job." He frowned. "Do you work for him?"

"Sort of. He's my uncle."

"Oh." He went red. "God. Sorry."

"Don't be." To her own surprise, she laughed. "Nobody's spoken to him like that since he was eleven. What did you tell him?"

"That my dad ran a bakery for thirty years and never once talked to anyone like that, and that he'd have been ashamed to." He shrugged. "Then I told him what I thought of his speech. The family values bit."

They stood under the warehouse awning for ten minutes while the rain came down on the river. He told her his name was Kit Loxley. His father had died in the spring and left the bakery to his two sons. His older brother Neville had somehow ended up with all of it, by a process involving solicitors that Kit didn't fully understand. Kit had been waiting tables ever since. He didn't say any of this bitterly. He said it as if it was weather.

When he had to go, she took a business card out of her bag, wrote her personal number on the back, and gave it to him.

"In case you need a reference," she said. "From someone who saw you do it."

He put it in his shirt pocket. Then he walked off into the rain, and the card went through the wash two days later and came out as pulp. He didn't ring. She didn't know why. She found she minded far more than she had any reason to.

A week later Gordon called her into his office and told her, pleasantly, that he thought she would be happier somewhere else.

"You were seen leaving the gala," he said. "With that waiter. Talking to the press, for all I know."

"I wasn't talking to the press."

"I don't think," said Gordon gently, "that I can take the risk." He smiled. "You're too much like your father, Maud. People feel sorry for you. It's bad for discipline."

She was packed by Friday. Cass was packed by Friday too.

"Don't," Maud said. "He'll cut you off."

"He's welcome to." Cass zipped up her suitcase and sat on it. "Where are we going?"

"North," said Maud. "Dad's got a transmitter."

## II. Ashgill

Ashgill was three hours north of anywhere. You reached it by a road that climbed over a high pass, with snow poles marking the edges for the winter. Then it dropped down into a long green valley with a river in the bottom, and stone walls running up the fellsides like lines on a hand. There was a pub called the Fleece, a shop that was also the post office, a church, a primary school with eleven children, and about four thousand sheep.

There was no mobile signal. There was a single internet cable that went down whenever it rained, which was often.

And there was Radio Ashgill, 97.1 FM, broadcasting from a portakabin behind the Fleece.

Peter Fenwick had not started it. It had been going, after a fashion, since the 1980s, run by a series of retired schoolteachers and enthusiasts. When he arrived it was down to four hours a week and a transmitter held together with gaffer tape. But he had put money into it, and time, and all the energy that had once gone into Fenwick & Co. Now it broadcast twenty-four hours a day, to an audience of perhaps three thousand people scattered across the fells, mostly farmers, and mostly at night.

"Lambing," Peter explained, the first evening, at the Fleece. He looked ten years younger than he had in the lift. He had a beard now and a thick jumper with a hole in one elbow, and he laughed easily. "Calving. Snow. Long nights in the barn with a ewe that won't get on with it. They're all up at three in the morning, alone, waiting. And they want to hear a voice."

"Whose voice?"

"Well. That's the problem." He looked at her sideways over his pint. "Ewan does midnight to six, but Ewan's a sound engineer, not a presenter. He plays records and doesn't talk, which is fine for an hour and depressing for six. We need somebody who'll talk to them."

"Dad."

"You were always good at talking."

"I was good at talking to *shareholders*."

"Same thing," said Peter. "Just with more sheep."

---

Ewan turned out to be a long, grey, bony man in his sixties who had once been a radio reporter in Beirut and Sarajevo and Grozny, and who now lived alone in a caravan beside the transmitter mast on the hill behind the village. He looked at Maud the way he looked at most things: patiently, a little sadly, as if he had already seen how this would end and was too polite to say.

"You'll want a name," he said, showing her round the studio. It was a desk, two microphones, a mixing board older than she was, and a window looking out over the dark valley. "Not your own. People talk differently when they don't know who they're talking to. So do you."

"Like a disguise."

"Like a mask." He adjusted a dial on the board. "In my experience, a mask is the only way most people ever tell the truth."

She thought about it for a long time. Then, on her first night, at one minute past midnight, she leaned into the microphone. She pitched her voice lower and slower than her own, and Ewan ran it through a compressor that gave it a dark, close, smoky edge, like somebody talking right next to your ear.

"Good morning, Ashgill," she said. "This is Gale. It's one minute past midnight, it's minus two on the tops, and I'm here until the sun comes up. If you're awake, I'm awake. The lines are open."

Nobody rang the first night. On the second night a farmer called Alf rang about a dead ewe and talked for forty minutes. On the third night, four people rang.

By December, Gale had become the most famous person in Ashgill that nobody had ever seen.

## III. The Bunkhouse

Kit Loxley arrived in Ashgill in the first week of December, in a borrowed car with a cracked windscreen. In the passenger seat was a seventy-nine-year-old man called Sam Daly, who had worked in the Loxley bakery since before Kit was born and had followed him out of it.

Neville had come round to the flat in November. He wasn't drunk and he wasn't angry; he was calm, which was worse. He explained that the bakery was in difficulties, that Kit's position was *untenable*, and that he would be grateful if Kit would sign some papers. When Kit refused, Neville sighed, said he had hoped to do this nicely, and left. The next day Kit's landlord gave him notice. The day after that, someone put a brick through the windscreen of his car.

"He wants you gone," Sam said. They were sitting in the bakery's back room at four in the morning, the only place Kit knew he could find the old man. "Your brother. He wants you a long way off, where you can't make trouble about the will." He reached into his apron and took out an envelope, thick with notes. "There's eleven hundred pounds. It was for my funeral. I'd rather spend it on a living Loxley than a dead Daly."

"Sam, I can't."

"You can, and you will, and you'll take me with you." Sam's face was set. "I'm not staying here to be shouted at by Neville. I knew your father forty years. He'd have wanted me to keep an eye on you." He stood up, with difficulty. "My sister had a cottage up in the fells, years ago. Ashgill. She's dead now, but there was a bunkhouse up the valley that used to take walkers cheap in winter. We'll go there."

They had very nearly not made it. The car died at the top of the pass, in the dark, in a blizzard. Sam had been coughing for two days. Kit left him wrapped in both their coats and walked down into the valley, two miles through the snow, towards the only light he could see. It was a portakabin behind a pub, with a red bulb over the door that said ON AIR.

He banged on the door until a big, bearded man in a holey jumper opened it.

"There's an old man in a car on the pass," Kit said. "He's sick. I need help. I'll pay. I'll do anything."

Peter Fenwick looked at him for a moment. Then he reached for his coat.

"You don't need to pay," he said. "This isn't that kind of place."

---

They got Sam down with the Fleece's Land Rover, and the doctor came over from the next valley in the morning and said it was a chest infection and he'd do. Peter found them two beds in the old walkers' bunkhouse up the valley. He found Kit work, too: mending walls, driving the shop's van round the farms, sweeping out the portakabin, which was what he was doing on the night of the fifteenth of December when Ewan came out of the studio, sat down on an upturned crate, and began to talk.

Kit never knew what started it. Possibly nothing. Ewan was like that: he went quiet for days, and then he would talk for an hour without stopping, as if something inside had come loose.

"I've got a box of tapes in there," Ewan said, nodding at the studio. "Thirty years of callers. I've kept them all. Do you want to know what's on them?"

Kit, who had learned that you didn't stop Ewan once he started, leaned on his broom.

"A boy," said Ewan. "Seven years old, 1994. Rings in at two in the morning to ask if the moon follows the car or if it just looks like it does. Then, a few years later, the same boy. Fourteen. Rings to request a song for a girl at school. He's so frightened his voice keeps cracking. Then he's twenty-three, and he rings at four in the morning because he's in the lambing shed alone and his first wife has just left, and he wants to know if anyone else is up. Then he's thirty-five, and his father's dying, and he doesn't say that. He talks about the weather for half an hour. Then he's fifty and he rings to complain about the council." Ewan smiled faintly. "Then he's sixty-eight, and he rings to say he's selling the farm, and is there anyone left who remembers his dad."

He stood up, stiffly.

"Then one night he doesn't ring. And that's it. That's all of it. You pick up the phone at the start and you put it down at the end, and in between you say the same five or six things that everybody says." He looked at Kit with those patient, sad eyes. "Everybody thinks they're the first person who's ever been in love. They're not. You're not. You're just the latest caller."

"How do you know I'm in love?"

"You've been writing on the backs of the shop's delivery notes for a week," said Ewan. "And you keep looking at the phone."

## IV. The Caller

It was true. He had been writing poems.

They were bad poems. He knew they were bad. But he had met a woman once, for ten minutes, under an awning, in the rain, and she had laughed when he told her what he'd said to her uncle. She had written her number on the back of a card, and he had put the card through the wash. He had stood in the launderette staring at the grey pulp in his shirt pocket, unable to believe he could have been so stupid. He had tried to ring her company switchboard, but she had already gone, and they wouldn't say where.

He didn't know her surname. He only knew she was called Maud, because she'd said so, and that her uncle was the kind of man whose name was on a building.

So he wrote poems. He wrote them about her eyes, and her laugh, and the rain. And on the night of the eighteenth of December, after the pub shut, with Sam asleep in the bunk below him, he took the bunkhouse phone into the boot room, rang the number for Radio Ashgill, and asked if he could read one out.

---

In the studio, Maud nearly dropped her coffee.

She knew his voice at once. It was the second word. He said *hello* and then *I*, and the *I* was the same *I* that had said *I needed that job* under the awning by the river. She looked through the glass at Ewan on the other side. Ewan raised one grey eyebrow.

She leaned into the microphone. Her heart was going very fast. The compressor took her voice and made it Gale's: slow and low and smoky, nothing like her own.

"Go ahead, caller," said Gale. "What's your name?"

"Kit. Er. I'm up at the bunkhouse. I just wondered — I've written something. For someone. I don't know where she is. I thought maybe, if I read it out, somehow — I know that's stupid."

"It's not stupid," said Gale. "Read it."

He read it. It was about a woman's eyes, which were compared to the river, and to stars, and to a lamp in a window. It was, Maud thought, quite possibly the worst poem she had ever heard. When he finished, there was a long silence on the line.

"Kit," said Gale. "Can I be honest with you?"

"Yes."

"That's a terrible poem."

Through the glass, she saw Ewan put his face in his hands. On the line there was a pause, and then, unexpectedly, Kit laughed.

"Yeah," he said. "I know."

"Six different things about her eyes. What colour are they?"

Another pause. "I don't actually know. It was dark. It was raining."

"Then why are you writing about them?" said Gale. "Tell me something real. Tell me what she *said*."

So he told her. He told her about the gala, and the waiter's jacket, and the awning, and the rain on the river. He told her that the woman had said *that was either very brave or very stupid*, and that she'd laughed, and that he'd wanted to make her laugh again more than he'd wanted anything for a long time.

Maud listened to her own words coming back to her down a phone line from a boot room two miles up the valley. She found she had to stop and look out of the window at the dark for a moment before she could speak.

"Kit," said Gale, finally, "that's a much better poem."

## V. Lessons

He rang the next night, and the night after that. By Christmas it had become a regular thing, the bunkhouse caller and Gale. Half of Ashgill was staying up past midnight to listen.

He didn't recognise her. She was almost sure of it. The compressor helped, and the lowered voice, and the simple impossibility of it: he had no idea she was within a hundred miles. And there was something else as well. On air, as Gale, she found she could say things she would never have dared to say in her own voice. It was as Ewan had told her. The mask let her tell the truth.

"Here's what I think," Gale said, on the twenty-third, at half past two in the morning. "You're not in love with her. You're in love with ten minutes in the rain."

"That's not fair."

"Isn't it? You've built a whole woman out of ten minutes. She laughs at the right moments, and she's brave, and she's kind to waiters. That's lovely. But what about when she's in a foul mood because her father's lost everything, and she snaps at you for no reason? What about when she's wrong, and won't admit it? What about when she's so frightened of getting hurt that she'd rather pretend to be someone else entirely than tell you how she feels?"

There was a silence on the line.

"That's quite specific," Kit said.

Through the glass, Ewan was grinning, which he never did. Maud glared at him.

"I'm just saying," said Gale, "the real person is going to be much more difficult than the woman in your poems. And much more interesting. If you're going to love somebody, love the actual one. Not the one you've made up."

"So how do I do that?" Kit said. "If I can't find her?"

Maud took a breath.

"Practise," said Gale. "On me."

---

It became a game, and then something more than a game.

*Pretend I'm her*, Gale said. *Tell me what you'd say.* And Kit, at two in the morning, in the boot room of the bunkhouse, told her: haltingly at first, then more easily. He talked about the bakery, and his father, who had got up at three every morning for thirty years and never once complained. He talked about Neville, and how he still didn't hate him, and didn't understand why not. He talked about Sam, and the eleven hundred pounds for the funeral. He asked her questions, and she answered as Gale, but the answers were Maud's: about her father, and the lift, and the laugh that went wrong in the middle.

He said *I'd want to know what she's frightened of*. He said *I'd want to make her breakfast. Not a big breakfast. Just toast. Every day. For years.*

And Gale said, *That's not a poem, Kit.* And he said, *No. I know. It's better.*

"You're cruel to him," Cass said, on Christmas Eve, in the cottage Peter had rented for the three of them. She was lying on the hearthrug with a mince pie, watching Maud stare at the fire. "You know that? You're making that poor boy fall in love with you twice."

"I'm not making him do anything."

"You're sitting in a box every night, wearing a fake voice, teaching him how to love you. And you won't tell him it's you."

"I can't." Maud pulled her knees up. "If I tell him now, it'll be — it'll be the woman in the rain. The poem. I want him to know who I actually am first. I want him to have heard me say the worst things." She put her forehead on her knees. "And I'm frightened, Cass. That's the honest truth. As Gale, I can say anything. As me, I don't know if I can say anything at all."

Cass was quiet for a moment.

"You know," she said, "for somebody who keeps telling him to love the real person, you're quite keen on hiding her."

## VI. The Shepherd

There were other callers.

There was Alf, and his dead ewes. There was a woman in Kirkby who rang at four every morning to say she couldn't sleep, and then never said why. And there was Dougie Pratt, who farmed twelve hundred acres of fellside alone at the head of the valley. Dougie was thirty-four, enormous and shy, and in love, hopelessly and publicly, with a woman called Fen Garside, who ran the riding stables at the bottom of the dale and would not look at him.

"She says I smell of sheep," Dougie told Gale, sorrowfully, at three in the morning, on Boxing Day. "Which is fair. I do."

"Does she say anything else?"

"She says she's not going to marry a farmer and spend her life up a hill. She says she's going to marry somebody *interesting*." Dougie sighed down the line. It sounded like a cow lowing. "I'm not interesting. I've got sheep."

"Dougie," said Gale. "You're one of the most interesting people I've spoken to in my life."

The trouble was that Fen Garside was listening.

She rang the next night. She was furious. She said Gale had no business encouraging Dougie Pratt, who had no idea what a woman wanted, and that it was humiliating to have your private life discussed on the radio in front of four thousand sheep. She talked for twenty minutes, and towards the end her voice changed. She said that Gale was the only person in Ashgill who seemed to understand anything at all. She said she thought she'd like to meet her. She said she'd been listening every night, to the bunkhouse boy and the way Gale talked to him, and that she couldn't sleep for thinking about that voice.

Through the glass, Ewan had stopped grinning and was looking at Maud with real alarm.

"Oh, no," said Maud, off air, with the microphone muted. "Oh, no, no, no."

---

It came to a head on New Year's Eve, in the Fleece. Maud was at the bar with Cass when Fen Garside walked in, scanned the room, and came straight up to them. Ashgill was a very small place. Everyone knew by now who Peter Fenwick's daughter was, and everyone was beginning to guess what she did at night.

"It's you," Fen said. "Isn't it. You're Gale."

There didn't seem any point denying it.

Fen stared at her for a long time. Then, slowly, she went scarlet.

"I said some things," she said. "On the phone."

"I know," said Maud. "I'm sorry. I should have told you. I shouldn't have let you go on." She hesitated. "Can I say something? As me, not as her?"

Fen nodded stiffly.

"You keep saying you want somebody interesting," Maud said. "I've talked to Dougie Pratt every night for six weeks. He's delivered four hundred lambs on his own in the dark. He reads astronomy books in the tractor cab. He knows the name of every star you can see from the top of Ashgill Fell, and he's never told anyone, because he thinks they'll laugh at him." She took a breath. "He's not boring, Fen. He's just shy. You've never actually listened to him."

Fen said nothing. But two nights later, at a quarter to four in the morning, she rang the station.

"Is Dougie Pratt listening?" she said, very fast, before she could change her mind. "Because if he is, I want him to come down and tell me about the stars."

On the other side of the glass, Ewan let out a long breath, reached into his jacket, and passed Maud a five-pound note. They had had a bet.

## VII. The Pass

On the fourth of January, in a blizzard, Neville Loxley tried to drive over the pass into Ashgill.

He had come to find his brother. Afterwards, he could never fully explain why. He told himself it was about the papers: Kit had to sign them, and he'd heard from somebody who'd heard from somebody that Kit was up in the fells. But that wasn't quite it. He'd been sleeping badly since November. The bakery was losing money in a way he couldn't understand. The old staff had all gone, the bread had stopped tasting right, and late at night in the empty flat above the shop, he had begun to hear his father's voice.

His car went off the road just below the summit, where the snow poles had blown flat. It went down a short slope on its side and came to rest against a wall, its headlights pointing up into the falling snow.

Kit, driving the shop van back from a late delivery to the farms on the other side, saw the lights.

He didn't know whose car it was. He climbed down the slope in the dark with a torch and a tyre lever. He smashed the side window, cut his arm to the elbow doing it, and pulled the driver out through the gap. Then he dragged him up the slope to the van with his blood soaking into the snow. It was only when they were both in the cab, with the heater roaring and the man coughing and shaking beside him, that Kit looked at his face properly in the cab light and saw that it was his brother.

They sat there for a long time, not saying anything.

"Why?" said Neville at last. His voice was cracked. "You didn't know it was me. But if you had. Would you have done it?"

Kit thought about it honestly. He looked down at his arm, which had begun to throb.

"Yes," he said. "Dad would have."

Neville put his face in his hands and began, terribly, to cry.

---

Maud heard about it at seven the next morning, at the end of her shift. Neville Loxley came into the portakabin with snow on his shoulders and a borrowed coat over his own torn one. He looked pale and much younger than she had expected. He was carrying a bloodstained handkerchief.

"I'm looking for Gale," he said. "My brother said I'd find her here. He's at the doctor's in Kirkby having his arm stitched. Twenty-two stitches. He asked me to tell you he won't be able to call tonight, and to give you this." He held up the handkerchief. "He said you'd understand. I don't."

Maud took the handkerchief. It was stiff with dried blood. She didn't trust her voice. She found she had sat down without meaning to.

Behind her, Cass, who had come to bring her a bacon sandwich, looked at Neville Loxley with an expression Maud had never seen on her cousin's face before.

"You'd better sit down too," Cass said to him. "You look awful. There's tea."

He sat down. She made him tea. Within ten minutes they were talking as if they had known each other for years. Within an hour, Maud, who was watching them across the portakabin through a fog of exhaustion and fear for Kit's arm, knew that something irreversible had happened. Cass was laughing in a way she hadn't laughed since the boardroom. Neville Loxley was looking at her as though he had come up out of deep water.

"Oh, for God's sake," Maud said to Ewan, very quietly.

Ewan only smiled. "It's the valley," he said. "It does it to people. You come up here with nothing, and you find out who you are."

## VIII. The Uncle

Gordon Fenwick came over the pass on the sixth of January, in a rented four-by-four, to bring his daughter home.

He had heard about Neville Loxley, and that Cass was planning to marry him. He'd heard about Peter, too, and the radio station, and the fact that half his own senior staff seemed to have started streaming something called *Gale After Midnight* on their phones at work, where they shouldn't have been able to get it at all. He was not used to being unheard of, or laughed at. And under all of it, though he never once admitted it to himself, was the fact that he was lonely. He had a company with his name on the building and an office on the fourteenth floor, and not one single person who rang him at night.

The snow came down hard on the summit. He got the four-by-four as far as the Fleece and no further. The road out was closed behind him. He took a room at the inn and sat in it, furious, with no phone signal, no internet, nothing to read but a leaflet about lambing and an old radio on the bedside table.

At midnight, with nothing else to do, he switched it on.

---

It was the last night. Maud had decided. She had sat up all afternoon in the cottage with Cass, and Peter, and Ewan, who had come down from his caravan specially. They had made a plan.

At one minute past midnight, she leaned into the microphone.

"Good morning, Ashgill," said Gale. "It's one minute past midnight on the seventh of January. It's minus eight on the tops, and the road over the pass is closed. So whoever you are, wherever you are, you're stuck here with us tonight. The lines are open."

They rang. Alf rang about his ewes. Dougie Pratt and Fen Garside rang together, giggling, from the stables, to say they were getting married in the spring, and that Gale had to come. The woman in Kirkby rang and said, for the first time, why she couldn't sleep. Gale listened to her for twenty minutes and told her it wasn't her fault. Neville Loxley rang, and then put Cass on. Cass said, "Dad, if you're listening — and I know you are, because the Fleece has a radio in every room — come down to the portakabin. Please. I want you to meet somebody."

And then, at two in the morning, Kit rang. His arm was strapped up. His voice was tired.

"Gale," he said. "I can't do this anymore."

"Do what?"

"Practise." He sounded exhausted. "I've been practising on you for a month. Pretending you're her. And I've been thinking about it, lying in the bunkhouse with my arm hurting, and I don't think I'm pretending anymore. I think I'm in love with *you*. And I don't even know what you look like. I don't know your name. I only know what you're like at two in the morning." He paused. "Which is maybe the only thing that matters."

Maud closed her eyes. On the other side of the glass, Ewan's hand rested on the compressor.

"Kit," she said. "Where are you?"

"Outside," he said. "I'm in the car park. I'm looking at your red light."

Maud nodded to Ewan. He reached out and switched the compressor off.

She took a breath and leaned into the microphone. She spoke in her own voice, the one she had used under an awning by the river ten weeks ago, and hadn't used on air once since.

"That was either very brave," she said, "or very stupid."

Out in the car park, through the window of the portakabin, she saw a tall thin figure with a strapped-up arm go completely still in the snow.

## IX. Midwinter

Afterwards, nobody in Ashgill could quite agree on what happened next. Most of them were listening on the radio, and the radio, for once, went silent: Gale had left the microphone open and walked out of the studio. All anyone could hear for nearly ten minutes was the hum of the transmitter, the wind, and, very faintly, through the open door of the portakabin, two voices in the snow.

Then Ewan, who had been a professional for forty years, leaned over and put on a record.

---

Gordon Fenwick came down to the portakabin at a quarter to three in the morning. He had a coat over his pyjamas. He stood in the doorway with snow on his shoulders and looked at the people inside.

There was his daughter, holding hands with a young man he had never met. There was his niece, on a plastic chair, holding hands with a different young man, whose arm was in a sling. There was a weathered grey stranger at the mixing desk. And there was his brother, Peter, in a jumper with a hole in it, holding a thermos flask of tea.

He looked at them all. He opened his mouth to say the thing he had come to say. Nothing came out.

"Gordon," said Peter. "Come in. You're letting the cold in."

Gordon came in. He sat down on the edge of the desk. He took the cup of tea his brother gave him and held it in both hands without drinking it.

"I heard all of it," he said finally. "The woman in Kirkby. The farmer. The boy." He looked at Kit. "You're the waiter."

"Yes."

"You told me I should be ashamed of myself."

"Yes," said Kit. "Sorry."

"Don't be." Gordon looked down at his tea. "It's been a long time since anyone told me anything." He was quiet for a while. When he spoke again, his voice had gone very small. "I sat in that room with no phone. And for three hours I listened to people ringing each other in the dark. Just to say they were awake. And I thought, if I rang that number, there's not one person on this earth who'd want to hear from me." He looked up at his brother. "Is that what it's been like for you? Up here?"

"No," said Peter gently. "It's been the opposite."

---

They talked until the sun came up. Gordon said he would give the company back. Peter said he didn't want it. They argued about it. It was the first proper argument they'd had since they were boys, and by the end of it they were both laughing. Gordon would stay on, in the end, but with a new board, and with Peter's name back on the letterhead and Peter's vote on every decision. Peter would stay in Ashgill.

"Somebody's got to run the station," he said. "And Maud's going to be busy."

"Doing what?" said Maud.

Her father smiled at her, and then at Kit, who had not let go of her hand in four hours.

"Making toast," he said. "Every day. For years."

## X. Gale

They were married in the spring, all three couples, in the little church at Ashgill, on the same day, because Dougie Pratt said it would save on cake. Neville baked the cake anyway: four tiers, with the bakery's old recipe that his father had written down and Sam Daly had kept in his apron for forty years. Sam gave both Loxley brothers away, very slowly, on two sticks, and wept the whole way down the aisle.

Ewan didn't come to the service. He sent a card that said *I hope it lasts. Most things don't. But some do.* On the morning of the wedding, they found him up on the hill beside his caravan, under the transmitter mast, looking out over the valley.

"You could come back," Peter said to him. "To the city. Gordon would give you a job tomorrow. A proper one. Real money."

Ewan shook his head.

"I've been to the city," he said. "I've been everywhere. Somebody's got to stay up here with the transmitter, for the ones who ring at three in the morning." He looked down at the church, at the people coming out of it into the sunlight. "Go on. Go and be happy. I'll keep the lights on."

---

That night, at one minute past midnight, Radio Ashgill came on air as usual.

"Good morning, Ashgill," said a voice: a woman's voice, a little hoarse after a long day of laughing, warm and close and quite unmistakably her own. "This is Gale. Or — well, it's Maud, actually. I suppose you all know that by now. It's one minute past midnight, it's five degrees on the tops, and I'm going to be here until the sun comes up. Same as always."

She paused. Through the glass, Ewan raised his grey eyebrow at her.

"I wanted to say something," she said, "before the lines open. I spent a long time in this box pretending to be somebody else. I thought it was the only way I could tell the truth. And it was, for a while. You need a mask sometimes, when the world takes everything off you. It gives you room to find out what's left underneath." She smiled. "But it turns out what's left underneath is just — me. Bad-tempered at four in the morning. Wrong about things and won't admit it. Frightened of getting hurt. A bit of a show-off, if I'm honest. And the thing I learned, sitting up here in the dark with all of you, is that's enough. That's actually all anybody wants: someone real on the other end of the line."

She leaned closer to the microphone.

"So if you're awake," she said, "I'm awake. Whoever you are, whatever you sound like, however bad your poems are. You don't have to be anyone else. The lines are open."

And out across the dark fells, in lambing sheds and farmhouse kitchens and cold cabs, one by one, the phones began to ring.

19. AS YOU LIKE IT

1. Title of the Work
The Edge of the Emberwood

2. Creative Work

The neon-drenched spires of the Upper Sectors had always felt less like a home to Kaelen and more like a glittering cage. For twenty years, he had operated under the thumb of his elder brother, Valerius, the CEO of Aegis Dynamics. Valerius had kept Kaelen in the windowless sub-levels of the company, utilizing his architectural genius while stripping his name from every patent, ensuring Kaelen remained entirely dependent on his meager corporate rations. But when Valerius’s paranoia reached its zenith—manifesting in an order for the corporate enforcers to permanently "liquidate" his younger brother's assets and his life—Kaelen fled.

He did not run to the neighboring megacities. He fled outward, beyond the synthetic barriers, into the Emberwood.

The Emberwood was a massive, untamed expanse of bioluminescent flora and jagged canyons, a place the city authorities deemed a toxic wasteland. Yet, as Kaelen stumbled through the dense, glowing foliage, his lungs burning with un-scrubbed air, he found it to be the exact opposite. The air was sharp and cold, biting at his exposed skin, but it was the first honest thing he had felt in years. The wind did not flatter him; the towering, moss-draped ironwoods did not plot against him.

He was not alone in his exile. The Emberwood was a haven for the discarded. Deep in the valleys, Kaelen encountered a loose commune of refugees led by a former magistrate, a man who had traded his velvet robes for woven bark and claimed he preferred the sting of the winter rain to the smiles of politicians.

In his newfound freedom, Kaelen found himself consumed not by bitterness, but by an irrational, blooming hope. He spent his days exploring the ancient groves and his nights carving fragments of poetry into the hardened resin of the trees. He wrote of a world rebuilt on empathy, and he wrote of Lyra, the magistrate’s fiery, sharp-witted daughter whom he had briefly met before the city’s collapse. He did not know that Lyra was already in the woods.

Fleeing her own arranged corporate marriage, Lyra had cut her hair, strapped a scavenger’s rig to her chest, and taken the name 'Leo.' She navigated the forest with a hardened exterior, adopting the swagger of a mercenary to ward off thieves. When she stumbled upon Kaelen’s carvings, she felt a mixture of profound warmth and deep irritation. The verses were hopelessly idealistic, bleeding with a naive romanticism that the brutal world outside rarely rewarded.

When she finally cornered him near a rushing stream, she maintained her disguise. Her voice was pitched low, her posture combative.

"You're the fool scarring the timber with these utopian fantasies," Lyra said, leaning against a boulder.

Kaelen looked up, wiping dirt from his brow. "I am carving what I believe. If the wood minds, it hasn't told me."

"It's a sickness," Lyra scoffed, stepping closer. "This belief that love and poetry can survive the rot of the world. You’re infected with hope. I know the symptoms. If you come to my camp every day, I can cure you of it. I’ll play the part of this perfect world you dream of, and I will mock you, disappoint you, and break your promises until you see reason."

Kaelen smiled, an expression that seemed to finally fit the contours of his weathered face. "I don't want to be cured, Leo. But I will come to your camp."

For weeks, under the golden canopy of the Emberwood, they engaged in a relentless, sharp-tongued dance. Lyra, protected by the armor of her false identity, pushed Kaelen to his limits, deconstructing his naive philosophies and forcing him to build stronger, more resilient truths. In return, Kaelen’s unwavering kindness began to chip away at the cynical walls she had built to survive the city. In the wild, stripped of their names and their systemic inheritances, they were forging something violently real.

But the city rarely lets its prisoners go without a fight.

Kaelen was charting a new water source when he heard the mechanical shriek. He rushed through the underbrush to find a man pinned to the earth by a rogue, feral security drone—a jagged amalgamation of spinning blades and rusted plating left over from the border wars.

The man screaming beneath it was Valerius.

Kaelen froze in the shadows. His brother was dressed in torn executive fabrics, having clearly ventured into the woods to finish the assassination himself, only to fall prey to the ruins of his own company's technology. All Kaelen had to do was turn his back. The woods would consume the man who had tried to erase him, and Kaelen would be entirely free.

The drone raised a heavy, hydraulic scythe.

With a roar that tore his throat, Kaelen lunged. He drove his climbing axe into the drone’s optical sensor, grappling with the heavy machinery. Metal tore into his shoulder, burning like white fire, but Kaelen held fast, leveraging his weight to shatter the drone’s power core. The machine sparked, shuddered, and died in the mud.

Bleeding and breathless, Kaelen collapsed onto the forest floor. Valerius scrambled backward, eyes wide with a terror that slowly melted into absolute disbelief. He looked at the smoking wreckage, and then at the brother he had hunted.

"Why?" Valerius whispered, his voice stripped of all its corporate command, trembling like a child's. "I came to kill you."

"Because out here," Kaelen gasped, clutching his bleeding shoulder, "we are what we do, not what we are born to. And I am not a killer."

Valerius fell to his knees in the damp soil. The towering, silent trees seemed to press in on him, ancient and indifferent to his wealth, his titles, and his paranoia. For the first time in his life, the armor of his ambition cracked, and he wept. He wept for the years he had wasted building cages, and for the brother who had just reached through the bars to pull him out.

When Kaelen finally limped back to the camp, supported by the trembling, humbled weight of his older brother, Lyra dropped her scavenger's rig and ran to him. She didn't speak with the gruff cadence of 'Leo' anymore. The disguise was no longer necessary. The forest had burned away everything they used to be, leaving only the truth of who they had chosen to become.

The city of Bellwether had been built in a place where the river did not wish it to exist.
For two hundred years, its inhabitants had argued with the water. They had raised walls, driven steel into mud, constructed pumping stations, and taught their children to regard the broad gray river as an obedient feature of the landscape. The river, having no interest in their opinions, continued its ancient business of seeking the lowest ground.
Elias Venn understood the river better than most people.
He was thirty-two, a municipal risk analyst, and the sort of man who could look at a map of a neighborhood and see not houses but probabilities. Where others saw a school, he saw an evacuation radius. Where they saw a retirement home, he saw ninety-seven vulnerable occupants and a transportation delay of fourteen minutes.
He considered this ability a form of moral clarity.
Numbers, he believed, had a virtue human beings lacked: they could not be persuaded by affection.
This conviction had grown stronger during the three years of his mother's illness. He had watched medical decisions turn upon sentimental hesitation, administrative confusion, and the cowardice of professionals who would rather preserve their reputations than speak an unpleasant truth.
His mother had died in a hospital where four departments had debated her care.
Afterward, Elias abandoned the notion that goodness depended upon kindness. Kindness was too vague, too easily manipulated, too often employed as an excuse for doing nothing.
Goodness, he decided, required calculation.
He wrote this conclusion in a notebook he kept beside his bed:
An action cannot be judged by its appearance. Only its consequences reveal its value.
The sentence pleased him. It possessed the completeness of a mathematical proof.
Then came the autumn storms.
For eleven days, rain moved across Bellwether in nearly continuous sheets. The river climbed its concrete embankments. Beneath the eastern districts, the ancient drainage tunnels began to fill.
The municipal emergency office operated from a low building beside the railway station, where tired engineers studied colored screens and drank coffee that had acquired the bitterness of medicine.
On the twelfth morning, Elias discovered a structural fault in the floodgate beneath the industrial quarter.
Gate Seven, built during the last expansion of the river defenses, had developed a dangerous distortion. If the pressure continued to increase, the gate might collapse and release a surge through the underground channels.
The potential consequences were enormous.
He calculated eighteen thousand residents in the threatened districts. There were three hospitals, two schools, and a transportation terminal within the projected flood zone.
There was, however, another possibility.
If a secondary spillway were opened before the gate failed, the river could be directed into the low-lying neighborhood of Ash Row. The diverted water would destroy buildings, but it would relieve enough pressure to protect the greater city.
Ash Row contained four hundred and twelve residents.

Elias listened through the glass partition.
One wanted another inspection. Another wanted to consult the regional government. The third insisted that public panic could prove more dangerous than the water.

The official investigation began two days after the flood.
