Instead, he purchased an abandoned warehouse near the southern riverbank.
The building had once belonged to the foundry where the protests had begun.
Its windows were broken, its brickwork blackened, and its roof dangerously weakened.
Many officials considered the site unsuitable for a work of national importance.
Elias considered it essential.
He spent three years transforming the warehouse.
The building contained a central hall, several small chambers, workshops, classrooms, and a public archive where recorded voices could be preserved.
He refused to name it after himself.
He also refused to dedicate it to any government, political party, or benefactor.
At the entrance he placed a simple inscription:
Everyone has a life that cannot be heard from the outside.
The opening ceremony attracted a smaller crowd than the authorities had expected.
There were no military bands, no triumphal speeches, and no elaborate decorations.
Elias invited workers, teachers, shopkeepers, children, and residents from every district.
He asked them to bring stories.
Some arrived carrying photographs.
Others brought letters, songs, or objects whose significance would have been invisible to strangers.
An elderly woman brought a small coat.
Elias recognized her before she recognized him.
She was the woman he had encountered outside the foundry during the uprising.
Her son had never returned.
She had preserved his coat for more than twenty years.
When she entered the central hall, Elias approached her.
"I remember you," he said.
She studied his face.
"Yes. You were the architect."
"I was."
"You promised to ask about my son."
"I did."
"And?"
He swallowed.
"I found nothing."
She looked down at the coat.
For a moment he feared that she would turn away.
Instead, she asked, "May I tell people about him?"
"That is why this place exists."
She stood in the center of the hall.
Her hands trembled.
At first she spoke so quietly that Elias, standing near the entrance, could scarcely distinguish the words.
Then the building carried her voice.
She described her son's childhood, his impatience, his foolish jokes, his habit of leaving books open beside his bed.
She spoke of his work at the foundry.
She spoke of the morning he disappeared.
She did not ask the audience to admire him.
She asked only that they know he had existed.
When she finished, the room remained silent.
A young man approached and placed a chair beside her.
Another brought water.
No one applauded.
Elias thought of the unknown singer in the northern harbor, of Mara's insistence that profound things often occurred in small rooms, and of Samuel Orr's warning that a single note could never become a song by itself.
He sat among the audience.
For the first time at the opening of one of his buildings, he did not feel compelled to explain what he had made.
The voices were explanation enough.
Over the following months, the hall developed a life beyond anything Elias had imagined.
Children used its rooms for performances. Workers gathered there to discuss conditions at the factories. Families recorded memories for descendants not yet born.
Arguments occurred.
Friendships formed.
Some meetings ended in bitterness.
Others produced reconciliation.
Elias learned that no building, however carefully designed, could guarantee wisdom or kindness.
He also learned that the possibility of being heard did not ensure that others would agree.
Yet these discoveries no longer troubled him as they once would have.
He had abandoned the ambition to create perfection.
He wanted only to make room for human imperfection without surrendering the hope of understanding.
One evening, a young apprentice named Nora approached him.
She was seventeen and worked in the hall's recording workshop.
"Master Vale," she asked, "how do you know when something you've made is good?"
Elias looked at the instruments scattered across her workbench.
"Does it do what you intended?"
"Sometimes."
"Does it help anyone?"
"I think so."
"Then you're beginning well."
She frowned.
"But how do you know when it's great?"
He considered this.
At her age, he would have answered with confidence. He might have spoken of originality, beauty, courage, or the triumph of imagination over convention.
Now he found himself reluctant.
"Perhaps," he said, "you don't."
"Then why spend your whole life trying?"
He looked through the open doorway.
In the central hall, several children were arranging chairs for a storytelling evening. An old man was teaching a girl how to repair a damaged recording cylinder. Beyond them, the river moved beneath the evening light.
"Because sometimes the work itself becomes a way of loving the world."
Nora seemed dissatisfied.
"That isn't much of an answer."
"No," Elias admitted. "But it's the best one I have."
Epilogue: What Remains
Elias Vale died in his seventy-first year, during a winter unusually severe even by Bellwether's standards.
His death occasioned substantial public mourning.
Newspapers described him as a visionary whose discoveries had transformed acoustic architecture.
Government officials praised his contribution to national culture.
A committee proposed erecting a statue in the northern square.
The proposal was eventually abandoned when the committee failed to agree upon the appropriate expression for his face.
Some wanted him represented as a commanding genius.
Others preferred a thoughtful scholar.
A few insisted that his rebellious reputation demanded a more dramatic pose.
Nora, by then director of the hall, suggested that the money be used to repair the roof.
Her proposal prevailed.
Among Elias's belongings, she discovered a small wooden box containing his father's photograph, several letters from Mara, a worn notebook, and a tuning fork made from blue metal.
The notebook contained sketches for buildings he had never constructed.
Some were magnificent.
Others were absurd.
On the final page he had written a few sentences in an unsteady hand.
When I was a child, I believed the world concealed a voice that would reveal its meaning if I listened carefully enough.
When I was young, I believed I had been chosen to give that voice a form.
Later, I believed that truth could be built into stone, and that a sufficiently beautiful structure might persuade human beings to become better than they were.
I was mistaken in all these beliefs, though none was entirely useless.
The world does not possess a single voice. It contains innumerable voices, some gentle, some cruel, many contradictory, and most too easily forgotten.
If I have accomplished anything, perhaps it is that I have made a little more space for them.
Nora closed the notebook.
That evening, she carried the blue tuning fork into the central hall.
A group of children had gathered to rehearse a play.
Their voices rose and fell in disorderly excitement. Someone laughed. Someone protested an unfair assignment of roles. A boy dropped a wooden chair, producing a tremendous crash.
Nora stood at the entrance and listened.
She thought of Elias as a frightened child beneath his mother's staircase, searching the sounds of an empty house for the father he had lost.
She thought of the young dreamer who had imagined buildings capable of transforming humanity.
She thought of the exile who had discovered that the greatest human experiences often remained hidden in ordinary lives.
Then she struck the tuning fork.
Its clear note trembled through the hall.
For a moment the children fell silent.
The sound grew faint.
Soon it could no longer be distinguished from the breathing of the room.
"Again!" one of the children cried.
Nora smiled.
She handed the instrument to the smallest girl.
"Here," she said. "You try."
The child struck it.
The note returned, bright and delicate.
Then the others gathered around, each waiting for a turn.
Outside, the bells of Bellwether began announcing the hour.
The river continued its passage toward the sea.
The building held the children's voices without possessing them.
And in that place, where so many lives had briefly met, something of Elias Vale's long and unfinished dream continued—not as a monument to the man who had imagined it, but as a living work that no single person could ever complete.
The End
texts.Claude:
8. MY LIFE

# Leitmotif

*A novel in two voices*

---

## PREFATORY NOTE

*Jonah Reyes's memoir, which he called* My Own Account*, was found among his papers after his death. It was handwritten in eleven black notebooks and never finished. It is printed here as he left it. Between his chapters are letters, emails and voice-message transcripts by his wife, Marisol Ferrer, which she gave permission to include. She asked that nothing in either be corrected.*

---

## I. FROM *MY OWN ACCOUNT*

I was born in Stockton, California, on the ninth of March 1976, in the back bedroom of a rented house on Wilson Way that smelled of tomato canneries, three weeks before my father walked out. I have always believed the timing was significant. I came into the world at the exact moment a man left it, at least the part of it I would live in. It seems to me now that I have spent my whole life trying to fill the silence he left behind.

My mother worked nights at the county hospital, emptying bedpans. In the evenings I was left with our downstairs neighbour, Mr Alcaraz, a retired bandleader from Guadalajara with a gold tooth and a broken upright piano. He played boleros on it with one finger missing from his left hand, singing along in a voice like a wet road. He was the first person who ever told me I was special. He said it when I was five, after he caught me picking out, on his broken piano, the melody of a song I had heard on the radio that morning. I played it in the right key, with both hands, and added a bass line nobody had taught me.

"*Mijo*," he said, and put his eight-fingered hand on my head. "God has put something in you. You must never let anyone take it out."

I have never forgotten those words. I mention them here because I have been accused, by many people and at many times, of selfishness. I want it understood from the start that I never once thought of what I carried as mine. It was given to me, the way a debt is given to an heir. Everything I did afterwards, including the things I am least proud of, I did in its service.

---

At fourteen I heard my first orchestra. It was the Stockton Symphony in a school gymnasium, playing a cut-down version of a symphony by a nineteenth-century composer whose name I will not write here. I have since come to despise most of what he stood for. But I sat on a folding chair at the back of that gymnasium, with the basketball hoops folded up into the ceiling above me, and something happened to me that has happened only three or four times in my life. The world came apart at the seams, and through the gap I saw what lay behind it.

I went home that night and told my mother I was going to be a composer. She was asleep on the sofa in her hospital scrubs, too tired to take them off.

"That's nice, honey," she said, without opening her eyes. "Is there any money in it?"

There isn't. I have been explaining that to people ever since.

---

## II. MARISOL

*Email, from Marisol Ferrer to her sister Inés, Madrid, 14 October 1999*

Inés,

I've met someone. Don't laugh. I know what I said after Raúl.

He's American. A composer. He's twenty-three, a year younger than me, and he's in Berlin on a tiny scholarship that ran out in August. He's living in a sublet in Kreuzberg with no heating, and he spends all day and most of the night writing music on a keyboard plugged into headphones so the neighbours won't complain. He's thin. He doesn't eat. He talks faster than anyone I've ever met, about everything: music, politics, philosophy, the end of the world. He told me on our second date that he's writing a piece that will take twelve hours to perform and change the way people listen. He said it as if he were telling me the time.

I laughed. He didn't. He looked at me as if I'd hit him. And then he played me eight minutes of it on his laptop, in a café on the Oranienstraße. It's called *The River Cycle*. Inés, I cried. In public. In front of the waiter. I've never heard anything like it. I don't know how to describe it. It sounds like the inside of your own chest.

I know what you're going to say. Artists. Poor. American. I know. I'm an actress with three lines on a German TV hospital drama. I know all about poor.

But you should see the way he listens. He listens to everything — traffic, birds, the U-Bahn, people arguing in the street — as if it were all music, and he's the only person who can hear it. When he looks at you, you feel like you're the only thing in the room.

I don't know. Maybe it's nothing. Write soon.

M.

---

## III. FROM *MY OWN ACCOUNT*

I met Marisol at a party in a squat in Friedrichshain in September 1999. She was standing by the window, smoking, looking bored. She was the most beautiful woman in the room and seemed entirely unaware of it. That was her great gift and also, I came to understand, her great limitation. She was a gifted actress, more gifted than she ever realised, but she was never willing to give herself to it completely. She always held something back for a life beyond the stage: a home, a garden, children, ordinary happiness.

I have never been capable of holding anything back. I believe this was the source of every difficulty between us, and also of everything good.

I will not pretend I loved her from the beginning. I'm not sure I understood then what love was. What I felt, standing beside her at that window, was something closer to recognition. She was the first person I had met in Berlin who seemed to understand, without being told, that there were more important things than comfort. I was wrong about that, of course. But it was a very beautiful mistake, and I've never regretted it.

We were married the following May at the Standesamt in Kreuzberg. My best man was a Turkish drummer called Emre, who I owed four hundred marks. Marisol's sister came from Madrid and wept throughout, not entirely from happiness. We spent our wedding night in my unheated sublet. In the morning I played Marisol the first act of *The River Cycle*, which I had just finished. It was the best wedding present I could give her. She told me later it was the moment she knew what she had married. I have always taken this as a compliment.

---

## IV. MARISOL

*Voice message (transcribed), Marisol to Inés, 3 February 2001*

Inés, it's me. Sorry, it's late. I just — I need to talk to someone.

We have to leave Berlin. Tonight. Jonah owes the landlord eleven months' rent, and the man came round this afternoon with two friends and said he'd have the police on us by Monday if we didn't pay. Jonah also owes Emre, and the man at the music shop for the keyboard, and some woman in Neukölln he borrowed money from for copying the parts for that concert in November — the one where nobody came. I didn't even know about half of it until today. He keeps it all in his head. He says money's not real, it's just a story people agree to tell each other, and the music is the only thing that's real.

Anyway. There's a bus to Paris at eleven from Zoo station. Emre's cousin is driving us there in his van with the keyboard and the scores, because Jonah won't leave without the scores, obviously. Obviously. We've got three hundred euros. We're leaving the furniture. I'm leaving my winter coat because it doesn't fit in the bag with the score of the second act.

I'm not crying. I'm fine. I'm just tired. I had a callback on Thursday for a theatre thing at the Volksbühne, a real part, a real one, and now I'll miss it.

He says Paris is where things happen. He says there are people there who'll understand what he's doing.

I hope he's right. I really hope he's right.

Okay. I have to go. Emre's cousin is here. Love you. I'll call from Paris.

---

## V. FROM *MY OWN ACCOUNT*

The night of our flight from Berlin is one I have always remembered with a strange kind of joy.

We crossed the city in Emre's cousin's van in a snowstorm, with the keyboard strapped to the roof and four hundred pages of score in a plastic crate between my knees. Marisol sat beside me, silent and pale, holding my hand. At the bus station, our pursuers (for so I thought of them, though in fact the landlord had no idea we were leaving) seemed to be everywhere. I saw them in every shadow, every policeman, every man in a dark coat. Our bus left forty minutes late. We sat at the back in the dark while it crawled out through the suburbs in the snow, and I felt, for the first time in my life, completely free.

I think this was when I understood something about my own nature that I've never been able to explain to anyone. I am at my best, as an artist, in flight: with nothing, owing everyone, in the dark, going somewhere new. Comfort kills me. Security kills me. A fixed address, a regular salary, a house with furniture in it — I have tried all of these at various times for Marisol's sake, and each time I felt the music in me begin to go quiet, the way a river goes quiet under ice.

Somewhere around Hanover, at three in the morning, the bus stopped at a service station. Marisol was asleep against the window. I got out and stood in the snow under the orange lights, and the whole opening of the third act of *The River Cycle* came to me at once, complete. A storm at sea, a ship running before the wind, sailors singing. I wrote it down on the back of a fuel receipt with a borrowed pen, and when I got back on the bus I was weeping. I've never been so happy.

It is my greatest regret that I couldn't make Marisol understand that night. She woke up when I got back on the bus, saw me crying, and thought I was sad.

---

## VI. MARISOL

*Letter, Marisol to Inés, Paris, 22 November 2002 (handwritten)*

Dear Inés,

Thank you for the money. I won't tell him where it came from. He'd be furious. Or worse, he wouldn't be, and he'd just spend it on music paper.

You asked what our life is like here. I'll try to tell you honestly.

We live on the sixth floor of a building in the 19th arrondissement, in one room under the roof, with a sloping ceiling that Jonah hits his head on twice a day. There's a gas ring, a sink, a mattress on the floor and the keyboard. There's no toilet. It's on the landing, shared with four other rooms. In the winter the water in the sink freezes. Jonah wears his coat and fingerless gloves when he composes, and I wear two jumpers and my coat in bed.

He earns money arranging music, if you can call it that. He does library tracks for a company in the 9th that sells background music for TV shows and adverts and supermarkets. *Upbeat corporate. Romantic piano. Tense thriller.* He gets thirty euros a track. He can do six in a day if he doesn't sleep. He hates it more than I've ever seen him hate anything. Sometimes he comes back from delivering them and lies face down on the mattress for an hour without speaking. Once he said, into the pillow, "I'm selling my blood, Mari. I'm opening my veins and selling it by the litre so the supermarkets can play it over the frozen peas."

I've been doing some dubbing work, Spanish voices for French cartoons, and a bit of waitressing in a tapas bar in the Marais. It pays the rent, mostly.

The rest of the time, every hour he isn't selling his blood, he works on the *Cycle*. He's finished the first two acts now. Six hours of music. He's sent it to every opera house and festival in Europe. Eleven of them have sent it back. The others haven't answered.

I know you think I should leave him. I know Mamá does. I've thought about it, Inés. I have. Some nights, lying awake in the cold, listening to him playing very softly through the headphones, I've thought about it very seriously.

But then he takes the headphones off and puts them on my head and says, "Listen to this, Mari, just this bit, tell me if it works." And I listen, and it's the most beautiful thing I've ever heard. And I know that whatever else happens, I'm the first person in the world to hear it. Nobody else has ever heard this. It's been inside him, and now it's inside me.

I don't know how to explain that to you. I don't know if it's enough. But it's something.

Your loving sister,
M.

---

## VII. FROM *MY OWN ACCOUNT*

The Paris years were the hardest of my life and the most important. I will not dwell on the material privations. They have been much exaggerated by people who wish to make me a martyr, and by others who wish to make Marisol one. We were poor, it's true. We were often hungry. But every artist worth anything has been poor and hungry at some point, and I believe it was necessary. Hunger clarifies. It strips away everything that isn't essential. In Paris I learned exactly what was essential to me, and I've never forgotten it since.

What I want to record here instead is a single encounter, because it changed the course of my life.

In the spring of 2004, a critic from *Le Monde* came to hear a concert performance of the first act at a tiny church in Belleville. We had organised it ourselves, Marisol and I, with eleven unpaid musicians from the conservatoire and a choir of retired postal workers. Thirty-one people came. Half of them were the musicians' parents. The critic left at the interval. I thought it was a disaster.

Three weeks later he published a review. It wasn't long. It said that he had heard, in a draughty church in the 19th arrondissement, the work of a young American he had never heard of, which was either the most pretentious thing he had ever sat through or the beginning of something that would be talked about in fifty years. He couldn't yet decide which. He recommended that his readers go and find out for themselves.

That review changed everything. Within a month I had a publisher, an agent, and a commission from a festival in Lisbon for the complete *River Cycle*, all four acts, to be premiered in the summer of 2009. They gave me an advance. It was more money than I had ever seen in my life. Marisol wept when she saw the cheque. I think it was the first time in five years she had wept from happiness.

I spent most of it within a year. I don't apologise for this. I needed a proper studio. I needed proper instruments, proper software, proper speakers. I needed to hear the music as it would really sound. The flat in the 11th, with a separate room for my work, was a necessity, not a luxury. So was the piano. Marisol never understood this. She wanted us to put the money in a bank, buy a small apartment, and "be safe", as she always said. I tried to explain to her that safety was the one thing an artist could never afford.

---

## VIII. MARISOL

*Email, Marisol to Inés, Lisbon, 30 June 2009*

Inés,

It's done. It happened. Last night. All four acts. Twelve hours and forty minutes, with three intervals, starting at four in the afternoon and finishing at a quarter to five this morning, as the sun came up over the Tagus. They opened the big doors at the back of the hall for the last act so the audience could see the river.

Two thousand people. Half of them left before the end. The other half stood up and shouted for twenty-five minutes. I've never seen anything like it. Old men crying. Young people in the aisles hugging each other. A woman I'd never met grabbed me by both arms in the foyer and shouted at me in Portuguese for about two minutes, and then kissed me on both cheeks and ran away. I have no idea what she said.

Jonah stood on the stage at the end with the conductor and the singers, in the grey morning light, and he didn't bow. He just stood there with his arms hanging down, looking out at the audience, at the river, at the sun coming up, as if he didn't know where he was. Then he looked for me in the crowd and found me, in the sixth row, and he smiled. Inés, he looked about fourteen years old.

I keep thinking about Paris. The frozen sink. The library tracks. The thirty-one people in the church in Belleville. I keep thinking, it was worth it. It was all worth it. I was right to stay.

I'm so happy I can hardly type.

M.

P.S. The reviews this morning are mostly wonderful. One of them calls him "a genius and a monster". I asked him which one he thinks he is. He laughed and said, "Can't I be both?"

---

## IX. FROM *MY OWN ACCOUNT*

There is a great deal of nonsense written about artists and politics. Most of it is written by people who have never had to choose between them. I want to set down plainly what happened in Istanbul in 2013, because it has been much misrepresented, by my enemies and also by my admirers.

I went to Istanbul in May of that year to write the music for a new production at a theatre in Beyoğlu, near Taksim Square. I had been there a fortnight when the protests began in Gezi Park. At first it was a few dozen people camping out to stop the trees being cut down. Within a week it was hundreds of thousands, and the whole centre of the city was in revolt.

I didn't go there intending to take part. I went there to write music. But I'm not capable of standing on the edge of something like that and watching it. I've never been capable of watching anything. On the third night, I took a portable keyboard and an amplifier into the park and played. I played for eleven hours, through the tear gas and the water cannon. I improvised on themes from *The River Cycle* and on Turkish folk songs the protesters taught me, while thousands of people sang around me in the dark. It was, I think, the greatest performance of my life. Nobody recorded it. Nobody even knew my name. I was just a foreigner with a keyboard under a plane tree.

I didn't think of it as politics. I thought of it as music doing what music is supposed to do: making people feel, for a few hours, that they are not alone, that the world could be different, that something new is possible. I believed then that art and revolution were the same thing, two expressions of the same longing. I still believe it, though I have since learned how high the price can be.

The price, in this case, was that my name was given to the police by somebody at the theatre. My visa was revoked. I had to leave the country in forty-eight hours, by night, on a ferry to Greece, with nothing but my laptop and the clothes I was wearing. The production was cancelled. I never got paid.

But I had sung with a hundred thousand people under the plane trees of Gezi Park, and I would not trade those eleven hours for anything I own.

---

## X. MARISOL

*Voice message (transcribed), Marisol to Inés, Lisbon, 12 June 2013*

He's on a ferry to Lesbos. He just called me from the ferry. No passport stamp, no luggage, no money. He sounded so happy, Inés. He sounded happier than he's sounded in years.

The theatre in Istanbul wants its advance back. All of it. Forty thousand euros. Which he's spent, obviously. On the studio here, the new speakers, the trip to Vienna in March to hear that orchestra he was obsessed with. And the lawyer he hired last year to sue the festival in Munich over that thing with the programme notes. He spent all of it. So now we owe forty thousand euros to a theatre in Istanbul, on top of everything else.

And I've just been offered a part. A real part. The lead in a new Portuguese film, a proper film, by a director people have heard of. Shooting in September in the Alentejo. Three months. It's the best thing that's ever happened to me professionally. It's the first time in fourteen years that anyone has offered me something that wasn't a nurse with three lines or a cartoon squirrel.

And I don't know if I can take it, because if I take it, who's going to deal with the lawyers and the theatre and the bank and the landlord? He won't. He'll be in Greece, or Vienna, or God knows where. Writing music. Singing under trees.

Sorry. I'm sorry. I'm just tired.

I'm going to take it. I've decided. I'm going to take the part.

---

## XI. FROM *MY OWN ACCOUNT*

I come now to the most difficult part of this account. I have thought for a long time about whether to include it. I've decided I must, because to leave it out would be to lie, and I have tried in these pages, whatever else I have done, never to lie.

In the winter of 2014 I spent three months in Geneva, at the invitation of a foundation run by the widow of a pharmaceutical magnate, a woman of great wealth and great sensitivity. She had heard *The River Cycle* in Lisbon and wanted to support my next work. She gave me a house on the lake, a monthly stipend, and complete freedom.

Her daughter-in-law, Anouk, was twenty-nine. She was a cellist, trained at the Paris Conservatoire, married to the widow's son, a banker, a decent man with no interest in music. Anouk had given up her career for the marriage and was dying of it, slowly, the way a plant dies in a room without windows. She came to the house on the lake to play through my sketches for the new work. She understood them, as no one had ever understood my music before, not even Marisol. She heard what I was trying to do before I had finished doing it. She finished my phrases for me on her cello, in the cold blue light off the lake, and I felt the music in me break open like ice in spring.

I won't describe what happened between us. It belongs to us. I will only say that by the end of February we had decided to leave together. Leave Geneva, her husband, Marisol, everything. We would go somewhere new, Japan perhaps, or Chile, and live entirely for music. Love, in the sense the world gives that word, was the least of it. We would create something no one had ever created before.

I wrote to Marisol from Geneva. I told her the truth. I told her I was grateful for everything she had done, for every sacrifice she had made, and that I would always love her, but that I had to follow where the music led. I told her I hoped, one day, she would understand.

Anouk's husband found the letters three days before we were due to leave. There was a scene, which I won't describe. Anouk's mother-in-law, my benefactor, withdrew the stipend and asked me to leave the house. Anouk, under pressure from her family that I can only guess at, sent me a message saying that she couldn't go through with it. She was sorry. She had been mistaken. She asked me never to contact her again.

I was alone in Geneva in March, with no money, no house, no Anouk and no Marisol. I spent three days in a cheap hotel near the station, unable to work, unable to sleep, unable to think. On the fourth morning, Marisol's sister called me.

---

## XII. MARISOL

*Letter, Marisol to Jonah, Lisbon, 28 February 2014 (handwritten; found among his papers, folded inside the eighth notebook)*

Jonah,

I got your letter.

I've read it eleven times now. I've decided not to tear it up. I'm going to keep it, because I want to remember, if I ever forget, exactly how you write when you're telling someone you're leaving them. It's very beautiful. You should be proud of it. It reads like the libretto of an opera.

I'm not going to beg you to come back. I'm not going to scream, or cry, or threaten you, or tell you what you owe me, though God knows, Jonah, you owe me a great deal. I'm too tired for any of that. Fourteen years too tired.

I just want to tell you one thing. I want you to hear it, even if you never answer.

You've always said that I didn't understand. That I wanted safety, and comfort, and a house with furniture in it, and that I couldn't understand what it's like to carry something inside you that's bigger than you are, something that has to come out whatever the cost. You've said it so often that I almost believed it.

But I do understand, Jonah. I understand it better than anyone in the world. Because I've watched you pay the cost for fourteen years, and I've watched who you made pay it with you. It wasn't just me. It was Emre and his four hundred marks. It was the woman in Neukölln who lent us money for the copying. It was the eleven musicians in the church in Belleville who never got paid, and the man at the music shop, and the theatre in Istanbul, and my sister, and now this poor girl in Geneva and her husband. All of them. You've always said the music is the only thing that's real, and everything else is just a story people agree to tell each other. But we're real too, Jonah. All of us. The people you leave behind in the snow at three in the morning are real.

I've rented a flat. It's in Alfama, on the hill, with a view of the river. It has two rooms, one of them very quiet. I'm going to be filming in the Alentejo until May, so I won't be there much. But I'll leave a key with the woman downstairs.

## XIII. FROM *MY OWN ACCOUNT*

I arrived in Lisbon on the twentieth of March 2014, on a night train from Geneva by way of Madrid, with my laptop, a suitcase and the sketches for the new work.

She had had it moved from the studio in the 11th in Paris, which I'd assumed long since repossessed. She had paid for it herself, out of what she'd earned from the film. There was a note on the music stand. It said only: *Eat something.*

I didn't eat. I sat at the piano all night and played, very softly, so as not to wake the neighbours, and watched the lights on the Tagus.

I have been asked many times, by many people, whether I felt guilt. I want to answer that question here, honestly, once and for all.

Yes. I felt it. I have always felt it. I've felt it every day of my life since the night I fled Berlin in the snow. But I've never allowed it to stop me, and I don't believe I should have. Guilt is a feeling. The music is a duty. When the two have come into conflict, as they have so many times, I have always chosen the duty. That is who I am. I don't ask anyone to forgive me for it. I only ask them to listen to the music and decide whether it was worth it.

Marisol came back from the Alentejo in May. She stood in the doorway of the second room and looked at me at the piano for a long time, without saying anything. Then she came in and sat beside me on the bench.

"Play me what you've written," she said.

I played her the new work. All of it, what there was: forty minutes. When I'd finished she sat for a long time with her eyes closed.

"It's the best thing you've ever done," she said at last.

"I know," I said.

Neither of us said anything about Geneva. We never did, in all the years that followed. I took her silence as forgiveness. I see now, writing this, that it may have been something else.

---

## XIV. MARISOL

*Afterword, written by Marisol Ferrer for the first publication of* My Own Account*, Lisbon, 2031*

Jonah died in the spring of 2029, at the piano in the second room of the flat in Alfama. He was working on the last act of a new opera, which he never finished. He was fifty-three. His heart had been bad for years, and he never once did what the doctors told him. I found him in the morning with his head on the keys and his pencil still in his hand.

I've been asked many times, by many people, to write about him. I've always said no. This is the only thing I will ever write, and I'll keep it short.

You'll have read his account by now. You'll have noticed, I'm sure, what's missing from it. He tells you about the night he fled Berlin in the snow, and the music that came to him at three in the morning in a service station near Hanover. He doesn't tell you that I left my winter coat behind, or that I missed the only real audition I had in five years. He tells you about the eleven hours under the plane trees in Gezi Park. He doesn't tell you about the forty thousand euros, or the film I nearly didn't make. He tells you about the girl in Geneva and the music that broke open in him like spring ice. He doesn't tell you about the key I left downstairs.

I don't say this to accuse him. He's beyond accusation now, and I'm too old for it. I say it because this is what an artist's life looks like from the inside. They see only the music. Everything else, every person, every debt, every cost, falls away into the dark at the edge of the stage. That's not cruelty. I used to think it was, but it's not. It's a kind of blindness, the price they pay for seeing one thing so brightly.

The people at the edge of the stage pay a price too. That's all I want to say. We pay it quietly, and nobody writes it down.

People ask me whether it was worth it. They ask me whether I regret staying.

I have thought about it for a very long time. I've thought about it in the frozen room in Paris, and in the sixth row in Lisbon at five in the morning watching the sun come up over the river, and in the flat in Alfama with his head on the keys.

The honest answer is that I don't know. I'll never know. I gave him thirty years of my life. I gave up most of my own work for his. He gave me a great deal of pain and a great deal of joy, and the music. The music is extraordinary. I've never heard anything like it, and I don't expect I ever will. Whenever I hear it, I'm back in that café on the Oranienstraße, twenty-four years old, crying in front of a waiter, feeling something open inside my chest that's never closed since.

Was it worth it? I don't know. But I was the first person in the world to hear it. Before anyone else, before the critics and the festivals and the two thousand people in Lisbon, it was inside him, and then it was inside me.

That's something. I've decided, finally, that it's enough.

*M.F.*

While his masters droned on about the rigid mathematics of counterpoint and the dry grammar of classical forms, Julian’s mind was a tempest of romantic rebellion. He sought the **sublime and the terrifying**, chasing the intoxicating high of an art that could bypass the intellect and strike directly at the soul. When the academies failed him, he sought his education in the chaotic, destructive vortex of the city's underworld.

The turning point arrived on a night of utter despair, when he found himself holding the very last coin of a pension fund entrusted to him by his desperate family. He staked it not just as a wager, but as a gamble on his very existence; to lose meant a flight into the unknown, a permanent exile from everything he loved. When the cards turned in his favor, multiplying his wealth until his debts were eradicated, a profound, almost holy peace washed over him, convincing him that divine providence had stood by his side to pull him from the abyss. He walked out into the dawn a resurrected man, forever cured of the vice, his chaotic energies now violently and irrevocably channeled back into his music.

Yet, the pursuit of grand artistic visions required survival in a world that traded in cold coin. It was here, amidst the tawdry illusions of the stage, that he met Clara.

Clara was a creature of striking beauty and serene composure, a beacon of pragmatic stability in his tumultuous life. Born into crushing poverty, her entire existence was a calculated maneuver to secure a comfortable independence, free from the artistic idealism that she viewed as a frivolous luxury. She possessed no inherent passion for the theater; it was merely a marketplace where her beauty could secure her survival. To Julian, whose soul was a perpetually burning furnace of artistic ambition, her calm, motherly tolerance was a desperately needed anchor. He mistook her quiet pragmatism for a deep, unspoken understanding.

Their union was a collision of opposing universes. Julian dragged her to the altar on a freezing November morning, his mind fractured by a terrifying dual vision: one part of him soaring toward a sunlit dream, the other paralyzed by a dark, inexplicable dread. When his uncompromising artistic standards clashed with the petty realities of theater management, resulting in lost wages and mounting debts, Clara’s resentment grew. She could not comprehend his refusal to compromise; he could not fathom her willingness to smile at wealthy, untalented patrons to secure their daily bread. The very tranquility that had once drawn him to her mutated into a suffocating wall of misunderstanding, trapping the visionary artist in a domestic cage where the pursuit of the infinite was constantly interrupted by the brutal, agonizing demands of the mundane.

"No."
"What, then?"
He looked uncomfortable.
"To have dinner."
She was so surprised by his plainness that she laughed.
"That is a rather mysterious purpose."
"I could invent a more elaborate one if you prefer."
"Please don't."
"Then will you come?"
She studied him.
The Adrian Mercer she had first met would never have exposed himself to the possibility of a refusal without carefully securing some advantage.
The man before her appeared to have no defense against one.
"Yes," she said.
His relief was immediate and unmistakable.
It pleased her more than she expected.
Their friendship developed without the approval of Bellwether, which considered friendship between an unmarried man and woman to be merely an engagement that had not yet received adequate publicity.
Mrs. Vale was delighted.
June was suspicious.
Ruth was amused.
"You appear to like him," Ruth told Clara.
"I respect him."
"How terrible."
"I also enjoy his company."
"An increasingly serious condition."
Clara sighed.
"Must every feeling have an official name?"
"No. But feelings denied names have a habit of making fools of the people who possess them."
Clara thought about this.
Then she asked Ruth a question she had been avoiding.
"Do you believe people can really change?"
Ruth set down her teacup.
"Not into entirely different people. But I believe they can become more truthful versions of themselves."
"And how can one know whether the change is real?"
"By watching what they do when it costs them something."
Clara remembered Adrian standing before the planning committee and acknowledging the foundation's responsibility.
She remembered him listening to Thomas Bell describe the water entering his workshop.
She remembered the careful way he had revised his proposals.
Then she remembered her own delight in discovering his faults.
She began to wonder whether changing her opinion of Adrian would be enough.
Perhaps she would also have to change the person who had formed it.
Chapter Six: A Public Mistake
The opportunity came sooner than she wished.
In May, a confidential memorandum appeared in the local newspaper.
It claimed that the Harrow Foundation intended to sell part of the revised development to a private investment company.
The report suggested that the cooperative market might eventually be converted into high-rent commercial property.
The town was furious.
Clara felt a familiar anger rise within her.
For several hours, she believed she had been deceived.
Then Adrian telephoned.
"I assume you've seen the article."
"Yes."
"The memorandum is genuine."
Clara closed her eyes.
"But it describes an option we rejected three months ago."
"Then why wasn't that made clear?"
"Because someone removed the first page and the date."
"Who?"
"I don't know."
She hesitated.
"Can you prove the proposal was rejected?"
"Yes. The committee minutes record the decision."
"Then release them."
"I intend to."
"Today?"
"Today."
He paused.
"Clara, I know what this looks like."
She remembered the first reception, the model with its missing houses, and the pleasure of condemning him.
"Yes," she said. "I do too."
"And what do you think?"
She looked at the newspaper spread across her desk.
"I think I need to see the complete document."
For a moment there was silence.
Then Adrian said softly, "Thank you."
But the damage had already spread.
At an evening gathering of residents, Clara was asked whether she believed the foundation could be trusted.
She rose slowly.
A dozen people were watching her.
Six months earlier, she would have known exactly what to say.
Now she felt the weight of what she did not know.
"The memorandum is real," she began, "but incomplete. The foundation says the proposal was rejected. The committee records should establish whether that's true."
Someone called out, "So you're defending Mercer now?"
"No," Clara replied. "I'm defending the need to establish facts before we condemn someone."
A woman near the front shook her head.
"That's convenient, now that you're friends."
The accusation struck painfully.
Clara understood why it had been made.
She also understood that it was not entirely unjust to question whether affection might influence her judgment.
"You're right to ask whether my friendship affects me," she said. "It might. That's why the evidence matters more than my opinion."
A murmur moved through the room.
She continued.
"I criticized the original development because it ignored the people who would live with its consequences. I still believe that criticism was justified. But I also accused people of motives I could not prove. I mistook certainty for honesty. Those are not the same things."
Her voice trembled slightly.
"I would rather be embarrassed by changing my mind than comforted by defending an accusation that turns out to be false."
She sat down.
The room remained quiet.
The following morning, the full committee records were published.
They confirmed that the private sale had been considered and rejected.
Clara felt relief, but it was different from the triumph she had experienced when the drainage survey proved her right.
She no longer felt that another person's error had made her larger.
Nor that her own uncertainty had made her smaller.
The distinction seemed important.
That afternoon, Adrian arrived at the archive.
"I heard about the meeting," he said.
"Bellwether has never been particularly successful at keeping conversations private."
"You didn't have to speak for me."
"I didn't."
He smiled.
"No. I suppose you didn't."
She looked at him across the long reading table.
"I was afraid I would believe the worst of you simply because I had believed it before."
"And did you?"
"For a few hours."
"Then I am grateful you gave me a few more."
She laughed.
He stepped closer.
"Clara, there's something I ought to tell you."
She felt a sudden nervousness.
"You're about to say something important."
"I hope so."
"Then perhaps you should sit down."
"I'd rather stand."
"Very well."
He seemed to struggle with several possible sentences, rejecting each before it could be spoken.
Finally, he said, "When I first met you, I thought you were arrogant."
"How charming."
"And I thought you enjoyed humiliating people."
"Less charming."
"Some of the time, I was right."
Clara raised her eyebrows.
"This is an extraordinarily poor beginning."
"I know."
He took a breath.
"But you made me question things I had accepted without thought. You were willing to confront me when nearly everyone else preferred to flatter me. And later, when I began to understand my mistakes, you allowed me to be more than the person who made them."
His voice softened.
"I have come to love the way you see the world, even when I wish you would look at it less fiercely."
Clara could not speak.
He continued.
"I don't know whether you feel anything similar. I only know that I have grown tired of pretending my reasons for coming here concern old documents."
The room seemed very still.
Clara looked at the shelves, the long windows, the sunlight falling across the floor.
For years, she had relied upon language as a shield.
Now every clever sentence appeared insufficient.
At last, she said, "I thought you were arrogant too."
"I was."
"And rather cold."
"That also."
"And I was certain I could never like you."
He looked at her with an expression she had not seen before.
"Was that judgment mistaken?"
"Entirely."
He took her hand.
Neither made any promise.
Neither demanded one.
For the moment, the simple admission was enough.
Chapter Seven: The River's Second Course
Summer brought the completion of the first drainage works.
The old channel was reopened beneath a public garden, and the water that had once threatened Sparrow Lane found a safer route toward the river.
The workshop roofs were repaired.
The bakery received new foundations.
A small public square replaced an abandoned storage yard, and the residents chose the trees themselves.
Not everyone was satisfied.
Victor Ames continued to complain that the work had taken too long, though he eventually secured a transport contract for the revised development.
Thomas Bell insisted that the compensation paperwork was unnecessarily complicated.
Naomi argued that the cooperative market's governing board needed more places reserved for small businesses.
Clara supported her.
Adrian agreed, though he insisted they examine the proposed structure carefully.
Their arguments continued.
This no longer surprised anyone.
The exhibition opened in September.
It was titled The River We Built Around.
There were maps showing the town's transformation, photographs of vanished streets, letters from factory workers, records of floods, and recordings of residents describing their lives.
At Clara's insistence, one room was devoted to decisions the town had made badly.
She had expected objections.
Instead, visitors spent more time there than anywhere else.
An elderly man stood before a photograph of the demolished north railway district and pointed to a small window.
"My mother lived in that room," he told a child beside him.
"Why did they pull it down?"
"They thought something better should be there."
"Was it better?"
The old man considered.
"Not for her."
The child looked at the photograph for a long time.
Clara, watching from a distance, felt that the exhibition had achieved something more valuable than admiration.
It had made room for a question.
That evening, after the last visitor had gone, she found Adrian beside a display of the original flood survey.
"Are you satisfied?" he asked.
"Mostly."
"An extravagant endorsement."
"The lettering on the final panel is too small."
"I'll alert the authorities."
"And the lighting could be improved."
"Naturally."
She smiled.
He took her hand.
They walked outside toward the river.
The western sky had turned the color of faded copper. Evening lamps shone along the new promenade, and beyond them the older streets continued their irregular passage uphill.
Clara watched the water flowing beneath the pedestrian bridge.
"When I was younger," she said, "I thought loving someone meant finding a person who would never disappoint me."
"And now?"
"Now I think disappointment is inevitable. What matters is what happens afterward."
Adrian looked at her.
"That sounds rather unromantic."
"I've been accused of worse."
He leaned against the railing.
"I once believed respect was something people owed me because of my position. Now I suspect it is something one can receive only by accepting that others owe no such thing."
Clara laughed.
"We have become terribly serious."
"Have we?"
"Yes. We used to insult one another with much greater elegance."
"I might still manage it."
"Please try."
He looked toward the archive.
"Your exhibition contains a remarkable quantity of information. It is unfortunate that its creator remains so reluctant to admit how much she doesn't know."
Clara turned toward him.
"And its principal supporter remains astonishingly pleased whenever he discovers that humility has made him admirable."
He smiled.
They stood together in the gathering dusk.
Then Adrian spoke.
"I've been offered a position in London."
The words surprised her.
"For how long?"
"Indefinitely."
"Will you take it?"
"I haven't decided."
She waited.
"I wanted to ask what you thought."
Clara looked back at the water.
Months earlier, she might have interpreted the question as an invitation to surrender her own life to his.
Or as proof that he expected her to accompany him.
Or as a test designed to determine how much she valued him.
Now she simply asked, "Do you want to go?"
"Part of me does. The work would be interesting. But I have responsibilities here, and I'm beginning to understand what they are."
"Then you should decide what matters most."
"And you?"
"What about me?"
"Would you consider living in London?"
She thought of the archive, the familiar streets, her mother and sister, the community she had come to know more deeply than before.
"I don't know," she said.
He nodded.
"That's fair."
"I might want to. Someday. But I couldn't promise it now."
"I wouldn't ask you to."
She watched him carefully.
"Would you be disappointed if I stayed?"
"Yes."
"And would you resent me?"
"No."
The simplicity of the answer moved her.
She rested her hand against his arm.
"I love you," she said.
It was the first time she had spoken the words aloud.
His face changed, not dramatically, but with the quiet astonishment of someone receiving something he had not believed he could claim.
"I love you too."
They stood together while the river carried the last light downstream.
Nothing was settled.
There were careers to consider, families to disappoint, practical difficulties to negotiate, and arguments they had not yet imagined.
But neither believed that love required the surrender of judgment.
Nor that independence required the refusal of love.
And because they had learned to question the stories they told about one another, they were finally able to begin a story together.
Epilogue: What Remains Unfinished
Three years later, Bellwether had acquired new buildings, several new businesses, and an almost entirely new collection of complaints.
The cooperative market was flourishing, although its members disagreed vigorously about opening hours.
The riverfront garden had become a favorite place for children, elderly residents, and people who wished to appear occupied while observing their neighbors.
The archive received more visitors than at any previous time in its history.
Clara divided her working year between Bellwether and London, where she had accepted a position advising a preservation trust.
Adrian had declined the permanent London appointment but traveled frequently to oversee development projects that required both financial experience and the patience to endure public scrutiny.
They had married quietly the previous autumn.
Mrs. Vale had initially objected to the small ceremony, then informed everyone that its modesty had been entirely her idea.
June composed a short piece of music for the occasion and afterward declared that marriage had improved her sister's disposition only slightly.
Ruth predicted that the couple would enjoy a long and argumentative happiness.
She was correct.
They disagreed about money, books, furniture, travel, and the proper temperature of the bedroom.
Clara maintained that Adrian's habit of arranging objects symmetrically suggested a dangerous desire to govern the universe.
Adrian maintained that Clara's habit of leaving books in every room suggested she was conducting a campaign against usable surfaces.
Neither found these differences particularly alarming.
One rainy Sunday, they visited Bellwether and walked down Sparrow Lane.
Thomas Bell had retired.
Naomi now managed the workshop, which had expanded into the neighboring premises.
A sign above the door read:
BELL & DAUGHTER — REPAIRS, RESTORATION, AND OTHER IMPROBABLE RECOVERIES.
Clara stopped to admire it.
"That last phrase is excellent."
"Your contribution?"
"Naomi's."
"I should have known. Yours would have been longer."
Clara gave him a look of affectionate disapproval.
They continued toward the bridge.
The rain had strengthened, and the river ran high, but the reopened drainage channel carried the overflow safely through the gardens.
Beside the water stood a plaque recording the history of the works.
It named the engineers, the residents' committee, the archive, the construction teams, and the organizations that had funded the project.
Clara read it.
"There's something missing."
Adrian leaned closer.
"What?"
"The first meeting."
"An omission for which future generations may be grateful."
"Without that meeting, none of this might have happened."
"Without your questioning the plans, certainly."
"And without your willingness to change them."
He looked at the plaque.
"Then perhaps it tells the truth rather well. No one person deserves all the credit."
Clara considered this.
Once, she would have found such a statement merely sensible.
Now she understood how difficult it could be to live by.
They crossed the bridge as the rain softened.
On the opposite bank, a group of children had gathered around a puddle. One little girl was attempting to build a bridge of stones while two boys explained, with great confidence, why her design could not succeed.
She ignored them.
Clara watched in amusement.
"She seems very sure of herself."
Adrian studied the uneven construction.
"She may be wrong."
"Perhaps."
The girl placed a final stone.
Water slipped beneath the small bridge. She stepped across it triumphantly.
One of the boys followed.
The other crouched beside the stream and began adjusting the stones to make them more secure.
Clara smiled.
"Or perhaps she was right."
"About some things."
Adrian offered her his hand.
She took it.
Ahead of them, the path divided around a stand of young willow trees before joining again farther along the river.
They chose neither branch immediately.
Instead, they stood for a moment watching the water, each aware of how much of the world remained beyond the reach of judgment.
They had once mistaken confidence for wisdom, restraint for superiority, anger for principle, and certainty for truth.
They had learned that affection could make a person blind, but so could resentment.
That wealth could conceal weakness, while hardship did not guarantee virtue.
That good intentions mattered, though consequences mattered too.
Above all, they had learned that another human being could never be understood completely through one injury, one kindness, one rumor, or one fortunate act.
To love someone was not to pronounce a final verdict upon them.
It was to remain willing to discover who they were becoming.
The rain stopped.
Sunlight appeared briefly between the clouds.
And together, with no certainty about everything the years would bring, Clara and Adrian continued along the river, carrying their imperfect understanding of one another into a future neither could have planned alone.
The End
