9. Pride and Prejudice

# The Second Look

## I.

The first thing Dr Imogen Ashcombe ever said about me, I wasn't supposed to hear.

It was at the St Aldric's Hospital winter fundraiser, in a hired ballroom in a hotel near Liverpool Street, the sort of place with chandeliers and waiters who look at your shoes. I was there because my brother Femi was there. Femi was there because he was a cardiac nurse at St Aldric's and had won two free tickets in the staff raffle. My mother had then refused to let him take anyone but a sibling, "so that people can see what a good family you come from." She meant so that some unmarried doctor might fall in love with him across a crowded room. My mother has believed for eleven years that a doctor in the family would solve every problem we have, including the damp in the back bedroom.

I'm a paramedic. I've been one for nine years, out of Deptford station. In my mother's eyes this makes me nearly a doctor, in the way a minicab is nearly a Rolls-Royce.

So I was standing by a pillar in a borrowed suit, holding a glass of warm prosecco and watching my brother fall in love. That part, at least, was going to plan. Within twenty minutes of arriving, Femi had been introduced to Dr Clara Hale, a new cardiology registrar with red hair and a laugh like a dropped tray of cutlery. Within forty minutes they were dancing. By the hour mark they were sitting together at a table in the corner, heads bent, talking about something that made Femi go pink to the ears, which I'd never seen happen in thirty-four years.

I was pleased for him. I was also bored, and my feet hurt, and I'd come off a twelve-hour night shift that morning and slept four hours. I was looking for somewhere to put down my prosecco when I heard Clara's voice behind the pillar.

"Imo, please. Just dance with somebody. You're frightening the waiters."

"I don't dance at these things. You know I don't."

The second voice was low and cool and perfectly clipped, the kind of voice that has never once had to repeat itself.

"Then talk to someone. Femi's brother's on his own over there. Danny. He's a paramedic. He's very funny."

There was a pause. I didn't move.

"He's a paramedic who thinks he's funny," said the cool voice. "I've met hundreds. They bring me patients at three in the morning with handover notes written on a glove, and then they tell me a joke about it." Another pause. "He's perfectly pleasant-looking, Clara, I'm sure. But I've been on my feet since five, and I'm not going to spend my one evening off making conversation with someone because his brother's dancing with you."

I put my prosecco down on the tray of a passing waiter and stepped round the pillar.

She was taller than I'd expected, and older, maybe thirty-eight or forty. She had dark hair pulled back hard, a black dress that probably cost more than my car, and a face that might have been beautiful if it had ever, even once, relaxed. Clara saw me first and went scarlet. The cool woman turned and looked at me with no change of expression at all.

"Evening," I said. "I'm the funny paramedic. I'd tell you a joke, but I can see you've heard them all."

Clara made a small noise like a kettle. Dr Imogen Ashcombe looked at me for exactly as long as it took to decide I wasn't worth looking at any longer.

"Good evening," she said, and walked away across the ballroom.

I told the story at least nine times over the next fortnight, at the station and the pub and Sunday lunch at my mother's. It got better every time. By the ninth telling, she had a monocle. My mother said that's what happens to women who spend too long at university. My brother Tobi said she sounded fit. My youngest brother Kunle, who is nineteen and has never in his life said anything that wasn't designed to cause trouble, said she sounded like exactly my type, and we were in the car park outside the Co-op before my mother stopped shouting.

I found out later that she was a consultant cardiothoracic surgeon, one of the best in London, with a waiting list eleven months long. Her father had been a High Court judge. She'd grown up in a house in Northumberland with its own name and a wall round it. She had a reputation on the wards for being brilliant, cold, rude to registrars and unbearable to anyone who got a drug dose wrong.

Fine, I thought. I knew exactly who she was. I'd met hundreds of her.

## II.

I met her properly six weeks later, at three in the morning, in resus at St Aldric's.

We'd brought in a sixty-two-year-old bus driver called Mr Adeyemi, who had collapsed at the wheel of an empty night bus on the Old Kent Road. My crewmate Sal and I had worked on him in the back of the ambulance for nineteen minutes. We'd shocked him twice and got him back once, and we'd done everything right. I knew we'd done everything right. And when we came through the doors at a run with the trolley, there she was, in green scrubs, with her hair under a cap. She'd been called down from theatre because the cardiac registrar was stuck with another case.

I gave her the handover. I gave it well, fast and clear, in order, the way I'd done it a thousand times.

She listened without looking at me. Then she said, "Your rhythm strip's incomplete. There's a gap between the second shock and arrival. What happened in that gap?"

"We were moving him from the bus to the vehicle. There was no room to—"

"So you don't know what his rhythm was for three minutes."

"I know he had a pulse. I checked it myself."

"You checked a pulse in a moving bus at three in the morning." She was already turning away to the patient. "Thank you. That's all."

I stood in the corridor outside resus afterwards with my hands shaking. Sal had to take the keys off me because I wanted to drive the ambulance into the car park wall.

Mr Adeyemi lived. I found out a week later. She'd taken him straight to theatre and spent six hours on him. He went home to Catford in time for his granddaughter's christening. I was glad. Of course I was glad.

But I didn't forget the gap in the rhythm strip, or the way she'd said *thank you, that's all*, as if I were the man who'd brought the sandwiches.

## III.

Femi and Clara were serious by February. My mother had started referring to Clara as "my daughter the doctor" to the women at church, which was premature. Clara, who was from a big, loud, chaotic family in Leeds and therefore entirely unafraid of mine, thought it was hilarious.

Imogen Ashcombe was Clara's oldest friend. They'd been at medical school together, and Clara loved her loyally and without much evidence, as far as I could see, that the love was returned. So Imogen was around. She came to a dinner Clara threw in March, in a flat in Bermondsey, and sat in the corner and said nine words all evening, four of which were "no, thank you, I'm driving." She came to Femi's birthday drinks in a pub in Peckham and stood at the bar looking at the sticky carpet as if it had personally offended her. Every time I looked up, she seemed to be looking at me, not with interest but with a kind of examining attention, as if she were trying to work out what was wrong with me.

"She fancies you," said Clara, three drinks in.

"She thinks I'm an infection."

"That's how she looks at people she fancies. I've known her twenty years. She did that to a man at medical school for a whole term. He thought she was going to report him for something."

"Did she ever do anything about it?"

"No," said Clara. "She never does. She thinks wanting things is a weakness." She drained her glass. "Her dad was like that. Never said anything nice to anyone. She worshipped him."

I didn't believe a word of it. And then, at the end of March, I met Marcus Vale, and I stopped thinking about whether Imogen Ashcombe fancied me and started thinking about something else.

## IV.

Marcus was an anaesthetist, a locum, picking up shifts at St Aldric's and two other London hospitals while he "sorted things out." He was thirty-six, easy, handsome in a slightly worn way, and brilliant company. He told stories at the bar at the Ivy House in Nunhead that made the whole room laugh. He remembered everybody's name. He asked about my job, and actually listened to the answer, and told me paramedics were the real heroes of the NHS. I'm ashamed of how much I liked that.

He'd trained at the same hospital in Newcastle as Imogen Ashcombe, he said, at the same time. Her father had been on the board.

"She was the golden girl," he said, turning his pint slowly on the bar. "The judge's daughter. Everybody knew she'd be a consultant by thirty-five. I was the boy from the estate in Gateshead on a scholarship. We were friends, sort of, for a while." He smiled ruefully. "Then I made a mistake. A small one. A drug chart, a dose written down wrong at the end of a thirty-hour shift. Nobody was hurt. But Imogen saw it. She went straight to her father, and her father went to the board, and within a month I was out. No reference, no training post. I've been a locum ever since, eleven years, picking up scraps."

"Christ," I said.

"It's fine." He shrugged. "It's how that world works. People like her never make mistakes, you see. Or if they do, nobody writes them down."

I believed him. I believed every word. It fitted everything I already knew about her: the gap in the rhythm strip, the sticky carpet, *thank you, that's all*. It never once occurred to me to ask myself why a man would tell a near-stranger in a pub the worst thing that had ever happened to him, on the second evening they'd met.

## V.

My best friend since primary school is called Shirin Moradi. She's a pharmacist at a Boots in Lewisham, the cleverest person I know and the least sentimental. In April she married a man called Gerald Pike.

I'd like to be fair to Gerald. He's not a bad man. He's a senior operations manager in the trust that runs St Aldric's. He talks about "throughput" and "patient flow optimisation" at dinner parties, and he once explained to me for forty minutes, at a barbecue, why ambulances were a "legacy delivery model." He had a pension, a new-build house in Orpington, and a car with heated seats. He proposed to Shirin after four months, at a Harvester, and she said yes.

"Don't," she said, when I opened my mouth on the phone. "Don't, Danny. I'm thirty-three. I've got thirty-one thousand pounds of student debt and a rented room in Catford with a landlord who keeps trying to come in without knocking. Gerald's kind. He's boring, but he's kind, and he wants children, and he'll never cheat on me because it wouldn't occur to him. I'm not you. I can't afford to wait for somebody who makes me laugh."

"You could—"

"I could what? Hold out for love? On a pharmacist's salary in London?" She laughed, not happily. "That's a luxury, Danny. It's for people with family money, or people who don't mind being alone forever. I'm neither."

I went to the wedding in Orpington and smiled for the photographs. Afterwards, at the reception in a function room above a golf club, I stood on the terrace with a warm beer and watched Shirin dance with Gerald, and felt something I couldn't name. It was grief, partly. Partly it was the horrible suspicion that she might be the sensible one, and I might be the fool.

Imogen Ashcombe was at the wedding.

It turned out Gerald reported, three rungs down, to the clinical director of cardiothoracic surgery at St Aldric's, who was Imogen. He had invited her out of something between deference and terror, and she had come out of something I couldn't work out at all. She sat at the end of the top table in a navy dress, looking out of place, being very polite to Gerald's mother. Gerald spent the speeches thanking her for her "visionary clinical leadership" in a voice that trembled with feeling.

At ten o'clock, while I was on the terrace, she came out and stood beside me.

She didn't say anything for a long time. Below us on the dark golf course a sprinkler was ticking round. Then she said, very fast, without looking at me, "I want to ask you to have dinner with me."

I actually thought I'd misheard.

"I've tried not to," she went on, in the same fast, flat voice, like someone reading out a list of complications before surgery. "For three months. I want you to know that. I know it's ridiculous. I know we have nothing in common. I know your family—" She stopped. "Your mother told Clara's mother in front of me at Femi's birthday that she's been praying for him to marry a doctor since he was twenty-three. Your youngest brother was sick in the pub toilet at eight o'clock. You make jokes about everything, including things that shouldn't be joked about, and your handover notes are adequate at best. I'm forty. I've never in my life done anything I couldn't justify on paper." She turned, at last, and looked at me. Her face was white. "I can't justify this. I've tried. I want to have dinner with you anyway."

I don't know what I'd have said if she'd stopped there. I think about it sometimes. But she'd said *your family*, and *your youngest brother*, and *adequate at best*. Six months of every story I'd told about her rose up in my chest like boiling water.

"No," I said.

She didn't move.

"You want to know why?" I said. "I'll tell you why. Because you've just told me, in the same breath as asking me out, that my family's an embarrassment and my brother's a drunk and I'm not good enough at my job. Because you treat everyone who isn't a consultant like the help. Because Clara told me last month that Femi's devastated and she doesn't know why, and that she's been having doubts since the night you told her he seemed 'unserious', and that his family were obviously 'pushing'. You did that. You broke them up, and you didn't even think about it. And because of Marcus Vale."

That one landed. I saw it. Something went across her face very fast.

"What about Marcus Vale?"

"I know what you did to him. In Newcastle. One mistake at the end of a thirty-hour shift, and you went to Daddy and finished his career." I put my beer down on the wall. "So, no. Thanks. I'd rather eat at a Harvester with Gerald."

She stood there for a long moment in the light from the function room, perfectly still. When she spoke, her voice was very quiet.

"Thank you," she said. "That's very clear."

And she walked back inside.

## VI.

The email arrived at 3:47 the next morning. I read it on my phone in the cab of the ambulance at the station, on a break between jobs, with Sal asleep beside me.

> *Danny,*
>
> *Don't worry. I'm not writing to repeat anything I said last night. I won't embarrass either of us that way again. But you accused me of two things, and I find I can't leave them without an answer. Read this or delete it. It doesn't much matter.*
>
> *Your brother and Clara. Yes, I said something to her. I'm not going to pretend otherwise. I've known Clara for twenty years. I've watched her fall in love four times, each time with a man who wasn't half as serious about it as she was, and each time I've picked up the pieces. I watched your brother carefully for three months. He's quiet. He's gentle. He's very reserved. I've seen him with her at three dinners and a birthday party and I never once saw him show anything at all. I didn't know him. I didn't know your family. I heard your mother at the birthday and drew a conclusion. It may have been the wrong one. I told Clara to be careful. That's all. If I was wrong, I'm sorry, and I'll tell her so. But I did it to protect her, not to hurt him.*
>
> *Marcus Vale. I'm going to tell you something I've told perhaps four people in my life. I'd be grateful if you didn't repeat it.*
>
> *There was a drug chart in Newcastle. That part's true. But it wasn't one mistake at the end of a long shift. It was eleven months of mistakes. Controlled drugs signed out and not given, morphine and fentanyl, always on his shifts, always for patients too sick or too sedated to complain. I didn't notice. A ward pharmacist did. By then a seventy-one-year-old woman on a surgical ward had been given half the analgesia she was written up for, for nine days after an operation, because the other half was going into Marcus. She was in agony for nine days. She thought she was dying. She told her daughter the hospital was punishing her for something.*
>
> *I didn't go to my father. My father was dead. He'd died six months before. I went to the clinical director, as I was supposed to, with the pharmacist, and the evidence. Marcus was given every chance. He was offered treatment, a supported return to work, and confidentiality. He took none of it. He left before the hearing and has worked as a locum ever since, moving every few months, which is why he's never been caught again.*
>
> *That's not why I hate him, though. I hate him because the year before all this, when my sister Lottie was seventeen and I was working ninety hours a week, he spent the summer at our house in Northumberland as my friend. And he told her he was in love with her. He told her she was the only person who understood him. He told her to keep it secret from me because I'd never understand. He asked her for money, from a trust my father had left her, to "start a new life" for the two of them. She very nearly gave it to him. She found out what he was only because I found the messages. She was seventeen. She still won't talk about it.*
>
> *That's all. You can check any of it. The NMC and GMC records are public, though his case was closed when he left. Clara knows about Lottie. Ask her.*
>
> *I'm sorry I said what I said about your family. You were right that it was unforgivable. I'm not going to ask you to forgive it.*
>
> *I.A.*

I read it three times. Then I sat in the dark cab of the ambulance with the phone in my lap and Sal snoring beside me, and the radio crackling, and felt the whole of the last six months turn over and show me its underside.

I checked. Of course I checked. I'm a paramedic; checking is the job. The professional register said what she'd said it would. I rang Clara, and Clara went silent on the phone for a long time and then said, "She told you about Lottie? God. She's never told anyone about Lottie."

I thought about Marcus at the bar of the Ivy House, turning his pint slowly, telling a stranger the worst thing that had ever happened to him on the second evening they'd met. I thought about how much I'd liked being called a hero. I thought about the gap in Mr Adeyemi's rhythm strip, and the fact that she'd been right about it. I'd checked a pulse in a moving bus at three in the morning with my hands shaking, and I hadn't known, and I'd been too proud to say so. I thought about my nine retellings of the night at the fundraiser, the monocle, the laughter round the table at Sunday lunch.

All my life I'd been proud of reading people fast. It was half of what made me good at my job. Thirty seconds through a front door and I'd know who was lying, who was drunk, who was frightened, who was going to swing for me. I'd been so proud of it that it had never once occurred to me how often I might be wrong.

I'd looked at her once, at a party, through a pillar, and decided everything. I'd never looked again.

## VII.

In July I went to Northumberland for my cousin Ade's wedding, in Alnwick. My aunt Funmi, my mother's younger sister, had moved up there twenty years ago with a Geordie husband and never looked back. She was the only member of my family with a gift for silence, and I'd always loved her for it.

On the Sunday after the wedding, Aunt Funmi wanted to go to a free heart health screening at a village hall on the coast, twelve miles north, because her husband had high blood pressure and wouldn't go to the GP. I drove them. It was a small grey stone village above a long beach, with a pub, a church and a lifeboat station. There was a queue outside the village hall: farmers, fishermen, old women in rain jackets, a man with a sheepdog.

Inside, behind a trestle table with a portable ECG machine, sat Dr Imogen Ashcombe in jeans and an old jumper, listening to an elderly fisherman's chest.

I stopped in the doorway. She looked up. For a moment neither of us moved.

Then she said, "Mr Okoro," quite calmly, as if we'd met at the shops. "Is this your family?"

I introduced them. She was courteous to my aunt, more than courteous. She spent twenty minutes with my uncle, explained his blood pressure readings in words he understood, and booked him into a clinic in Alnwick for the following week. When he started being defensive, as he always does with doctors, she laughed — I'd never heard her laugh — and said something to him about the Newcastle United back four that made him laugh too.

Outside, while my aunt and uncle went to look at the lifeboat, I stood in the car park with a woman from the village who was handing out leaflets.

"She does this every month," the woman said, nodding at the hall. "Has done for ten years. Comes up from London on the Friday night train and does the whole coast on the Saturday and Sunday. Seven villages. No charge. Her father grew up in the house up there." She pointed up the hill to a big grey house behind a wall, half hidden by trees. "Our lifeboat coxswain had a heart attack on the beach four years ago. She was the one who found it on the screening the month before, sent him in. Saved his life." She looked at me with frank curiosity. "You know her, do you?"

"I thought I did," I said.

Imogen came out at four, when the queue was done, and found me still standing there. We walked down to the beach together, without either of us suggesting it. The tide was out and the sand went on for miles. The wind was cold off the North Sea, even in July.

"I read your email," I said, eventually.

"I assumed you had."

"I checked everything in it."

"I assumed that too." She almost smiled. "You're a paramedic."

We walked a bit further. A dog ran past us after a gull.

"I was wrong," I said. "About Marcus. About you. About a lot of things. I'd decided who you were in about four seconds, behind a pillar, and then I spent six months making every single thing you did fit the story." I made myself keep going. "I've always been proud of how fast I can read people. Turns out I was just proud."

She stopped walking and looked out at the sea.

"I was wrong too," she said. "About Femi. About your family." She was quiet for a moment. "I went home after Shirin's wedding and I couldn't sleep. I kept thinking about what you'd said. That I treat everyone who isn't a consultant like the help. I wanted it not to be true. I spent a week thinking about everything I'd said to every registrar and nurse and porter and paramedic for fifteen years." She laughed, a small, unhappy sound. "It was a very long week."

"And?"

"And I rang Clara and told her I'd been wrong about Femi. That I'd mistaken shyness for indifference, because I'm shy myself, and I've never let anyone see it." She glanced at me. "They're back together. Did you know?"

"I didn't."

"Since last Thursday. She's taking him to Leeds to meet her mother."

We stood there on the sand with the wind in our faces. Up the hill, behind the trees, the grey house sat behind its wall.

"I'm sorry," I said. "For what I said at the wedding."

"I'm sorry for what I said first," said Imogen.

## VIII.

Kunle disappeared in August.

He'd met Marcus Vale at a party in Peckham in June. I found that out later. Of course he had. Marcus had been in and out of our part of south London all summer, picking up locum shifts, and it would have taken him about four minutes to work out who Kunle was. Nineteen, bored, beautiful, desperate for something to happen to him, my little brother would have been the easiest mark in the world. By August Marcus had told him about a job, a "medical wellness retreat" in Ibiza, run by a friend, which needed someone young and photogenic to do the social media. There'd be good money, sunshine and parties. Kunle should keep it from the family, because they'd never understand.

He left on a Tuesday with a backpack, a one-way flight, and nine hundred pounds he'd taken from my mother's savings tin in the kitchen. He left a note on the fridge that said *don't worry I'm fine back soon*.

My mother went to bed and didn't get up for three days. Femi and I rang everyone. We rang the police, who said he was nineteen and could go where he liked. We rang the Foreign Office, who said the same thing more politely. By the following Monday we'd had one message from Kunle, a photograph of a swimming pool, and then nothing.

On the Tuesday, Imogen rang me.

I'd told her about Kunle the Friday before, without really meaning to. We'd been on the phone about something else. We'd started talking on the phone since Northumberland, late at night, after our shifts, about nothing in particular. It just came out. She'd gone very quiet on the line when I said the name Marcus Vale.

"I've found him," she said. "Kunle. He's in a flat in San Antonio with four other kids Marcus recruited. The 'retreat' doesn't exist. Marcus took their money for 'accommodation' and 'training' and he's been gone for a week. They've got no money, no return flights, and the landlord's threatening to call the police." There was a pause. "Kunle's fine. Frightened. A bit thin. But fine."

"How do you—"

"I know some people. Doctors talk." She said it very drily. "I've booked him a flight home tomorrow. Gatwick, four fifteen. Someone will put him on the plane."

"Imogen. I can't — the money—"

"It's done," she said. "Don't."

Kunle came through the arrivals gate at Gatwick the next afternoon with his backpack and a sunburn, and walked straight into our mother's arms and burst into tears like a five-year-old. In the car home, sitting in the back with his face against the window, he said quietly, "That doctor came. The posh one. She flew out on Monday night. She sorted the landlord. She got the other kids home too. She paid for everything." He was silent a while. "She told me not to tell you."

I pulled over on the hard shoulder of the M23 and sat with my hands on the wheel. My mother said, "Danny? Danny, what's wrong?" I didn't answer for a long time.

## IX.

Her mother came to see me at the ambulance station in September.

I knew who she was the moment she walked into the crew room. She had the same face as Imogen, thirty years further on and much harder, and the same voice. She was perhaps seventy, in a camel coat, with a walking stick she didn't seem to need. Lady Ashcombe, the High Court judge's widow, magistrate, governor of three charitable trusts. Sal took one look at her and found something urgent to do in the garage.

"Mr Okoro," she said. She didn't sit down. "I understand you've been seeing my daughter."

"I've been talking to her on the phone," I said. "Mostly about work."

"Don't be impertinent. I'm not a fool." She looked round the crew room: the battered sofa, the kettle, the rota on the wall, the half-eaten packet of Hobnobs. "I'll be brief. Imogen is forty years old. She is one of the finest surgeons in this country. She has a reputation, a position, and responsibilities that you cannot possibly appreciate. She has, it seems, formed some kind of attachment to you. I'm sure you're a perfectly competent ambulance man. I'm told your family is very lively." She said the word as if it tasted of something. "But I want you to understand that whatever this is, it cannot go anywhere. She would be laughed at. You would be laughed at. And she has been foolish once before, with a man from the wrong sort of background, and it nearly destroyed her sister."

I felt the old heat rise in my chest, the heat from the terrace at Shirin's wedding. I let it come, and then, for the first time in my life, I let it go.

"Marcus Vale," I said, "was not a problem because of his background, Lady Ashcombe. He was a problem because he was a liar and a thief who hurt people. My brother found that out last month. Your daughter flew to Ibiza to get him home, and didn't tell anyone, and paid for it herself." I looked at her. "I don't know where this is going. Honestly, I don't. But I'm not going to promise you anything about it. That's between me and Imogen."

She stared at me for a long moment. Then she turned without a word and walked out of the crew room. Through the window I watched her get into the back of a black car waiting in the station forecourt.

Sal came back in from the garage.

"Who was that?" he said.

"Future mother-in-law," I said. "Possibly."

He looked at me as though I'd lost my mind. I thought I possibly had.

## X.

She was waiting outside the station at the end of my night shift a week later, at seven in the morning, leaning against the wall in a long grey coat with two coffees in a cardboard tray.

"My mother told me she came to see you," she said. "She told me what you said. She said it was the most impertinent thing anyone had said to her since 1974." Imogen handed me a coffee. "I think it's the first time I've ever seen her impressed."

We walked down to the river at Deptford, along the path past the old shipyards, in the grey early light. The tide was coming in. A rowing eight went past, the cox shouting.

"I asked you to dinner once," she said, after a while. "On a terrace in Orpington. It was the worst-phrased request in history."

"It was pretty bad."

"I listed everything wrong with your family before I got to the point."

"And my handover notes."

"Your handover notes are actually fine," she said. "I lied. I was frightened. I've been frightened of you since the fundraiser. You looked at me as if you could see straight through me, and I didn't know what you'd find."

"I couldn't see anything," I said. "I just thought I could. That was the problem."

We stopped at the railing. Across the water, Canary Wharf caught the first sun. She turned the coffee cup in her hands.

"I'm going to ask again," she said. "Properly, this time, with no list. Will you have dinner with me, Danny? Not a gala. Not a wedding. Just dinner. Somewhere with sticky carpets, if you like."

I looked at her: her careful, guarded, frightened face, which had never in its life been allowed to show what it felt, and was trying now.

"Yes," I said.

She let out a breath I think she'd been holding since April. And then Dr Imogen Ashcombe, consultant cardiothoracic surgeon, judge's daughter, the most terrifying woman at St Aldric's, put down her coffee on the railing, took my face in her cold hands and kissed me. It was seven fifteen in the morning, by the Thames at Deptford, in front of a rowing eight and two joggers and a man walking a Staffie. The cox shouted something that was probably rude.

---

We've been married four years now. My mother tells the women at church that her son married a surgeon. She leaves out that I'm still a paramedic, and that Imogen is the one who sits through Sunday lunch being shouted at about the damp in the back bedroom. Kunle's at college doing a sports science course and says Imogen is "actually all right, for someone that posh." Femi and Clara have twin girls. Shirin had a little boy last year and says Gerald is a wonderful father. Watching him at the christening, walking up and down with the baby on his shoulder explaining patient flow to it in a low soothing voice, I believed her.

I still read people fast. It's still half of what makes me good at the job. But I've learned to do one thing more, and I try to teach it to every new paramedic who comes through Deptford. Whatever you see the first time you walk through a door, make yourself look again before you decide. The first look tells you what you expect to see, mostly. The second one is where the truth starts.

The radiator in the corner of Clara’s cramped apartment hissed, a frantic, rhythmic sputtering that did nothing to chase the damp chill from the Boston evening. She stood motionless by the window, the city lights bleeding into indistinct streaks against the rain-lashed glass. In her hands, she clutched the heavy, cream-colored envelope Julian Hayes had thrust at her on the stone steps of the library only an hour before.

His face—usually a flawless, impenetrable mask of Beacon Hill superiority—had been startlingly pale. The rigid posture she had always interpreted as aristocratic disdain had instead resembled the brittle tension of a man bracing for a fatal blow. He had not lingered to debate her. He had simply handed her the letter, his eyes dark with a stormy, bruised intensity, and walked away into the deluge.

Clara broke the wax seal, her fingers trembling. She expected a defense of his arrogance, a patronizing justification for why he had so ruthlessly engineered the separation of her sister, Nora, from his wealthy, amiable cousin, David. She expected him to double down on his contempt for Clara’s working-class family, their loud debates, their frayed cuffs, their unapologetic ambition.

Instead, the severe, aggressive strokes of his black ink offered no apologies, only a brutal, blinding illumination.

*I do not write this to ask for a forgiveness you have already made clear I do not deserve,* the letter began, the words scoring the thick paper. *I write because my character, whatever its flaws, cannot bear the specific weight of the crimes you assigned to it tonight. You accused me of destroying David’s happiness out of malice. You accused me of ruining Elias Vance out of jealousy. You are a woman who prides herself on her immaculate perception of the world, Clara. Now, I ask you to perceive the truth.*

Clara’s breath hitched as her eyes darted across the pages. Julian stripped away the polite fictions of their social circles. He detailed the night of the winter gala—not with the haughty judgment she had assumed, but with the cold, clinical terror of a guardian. He hadn't separated David and Nora because Nora was poor. He had intervened because he had watched Clara's mother openly bargaining over David’s inheritance with a society reporter, while Nora herself remained entirely passive, offering no sign that she viewed David as anything more than a convenient escape from poverty. Julian had acted to save a naive man from what looked, in every measurable way, like a financial trap.

**It was a staggering blow to Clara's pride, but it was merely the prelude.**

When Julian’s letter shifted to Elias Vance, the charming, tragic academic whom Clara had championed as a martyr of the Hayes family’s cruelty, the ink seemed to press even harder into the page. Elias had not been denied his rightful tenure out of spite. Julian outlined, with devastating precision and verifiable dates, how Elias had systematically embezzled from the university’s endowment, gambling the funds away in underground parlors. Worse still, when Julian’s father had quietly dismissed Elias to save him from prison, Elias had retaliated by attempting to manipulate Julian’s fragile, grieving younger sister into an elopement, hoping to extort a permanent settlement from the family estate.

The pages slipped from Clara’s hands, fluttering like wounded birds to the scuffed hardwood floor.

She backed away from them, her chest tight, the oxygen in the room suddenly thin. The silence of the apartment roared in her ears. She had been so fiercely certain. She had built a towering monument to her own intellect, convinced that her outsider status gave her a flawless, piercing vision into the hypocrisies of the elite. She had looked at Julian’s quiet reserve and seen only a tyrant. She had looked at Elias’s practiced, sorrowful smile and seen a kindred spirit, a victim.

**Her intellect had been nothing more than a fortress built to protect her own insecurities.**

Clara sank onto the edge of her unmade bed, pressing her palms against her eyes. The charm she had so readily consumed from Elias was a hollow architecture, designed specifically to flatter her ego and weaponize her resentment. And Julian—the man she had scorched with her righteous indignation, the man she had called inhuman and cruel—had borne her insults in silence to protect his sister’s reputation. He had absorbed Clara's hatred rather than expose a teenage girl's vulnerability to the world.

A profound, sickening wave of shame washed over her, hot and suffocating. All her life, she had fought against the world’s prejudices, entirely blind to the fact that she was paralyzed by her own. She had judged a book not merely by its cover, but by the shadows her own mind had cast upon it. As the rain continued to beat against the glass, Clara stared at the fallen pages, knowing that the woman who had opened that envelope was gone, shattered entirely by the weight of a truth she had been too proud to see.

Des fils argentés commençaient à apparaître dans ses cheveux.
La vie lui avait offert d’autres amitiés, d’autres voyages et des joies qu’elle n’avait pas cru possibles après la mort de Gabriel.
Elle avait appris que continuer à vivre ne signifiait pas abandonner ceux qu’on avait perdus.
Au milieu du pont, elle s’arrêta à l’endroit où ils s’étaient tenus ensemble autrefois.
Une plaque discrète avait été fixée à la pierre.
Elle portait les noms des ouvriers morts pendant les travaux d'urgence, accompagnés de ceux des victimes de l'ancienne catastrophe.
Aucune famille n'y occupait une place privilégiée.
Élise posa la main sur la pierre froide.
Elle revit Gabriel tel qu’il était à vingt-trois ans, avec son carnet usé et ses projets innombrables.
Elle se rappela une question qu’il lui avait posée lors d’une de leurs dernières promenades :
— Crois-tu que les hommes puissent un jour apprendre à ne plus se haïr pour des choses qu’ils n’ont pas vécues ?
Elle avait répondu qu’elle l’espérait.
À présent, elle savait que l’espoir ne suffisait pas.
Il fallait des actes, des renoncements, des vérités pénibles et cette décision quotidienne de ne pas faire payer aux vivants les blessures des morts.
Elle contempla l'eau.
Le fleuve emportait les feuilles, les reflets et les dernières couleurs du jour. Il ne distinguait ni les riches des pauvres, ni les innocents des coupables, ni les maisons de ceux qui s'aimaient de celles de ceux qui se détestaient.
Il suivait sa course.
Derrière Élise, des pas résonnèrent.
Deux jeunes gens traversaient le pont, leurs mains étroitement unies.
Ils riaient de quelque chose qu’elle n’entendit pas.
La jeune femme portait un bouquet de fleurs sauvages. Son compagnon s’arrêta pour retirer de ses cheveux une feuille que le vent y avait déposée.
Le geste était si simple qu’Élise sentit soudain les larmes lui monter aux yeux.
Ils passèrent près d’elle sans connaître son histoire.
Ils ignoraient qui avait aimé sur ce pont, qui y avait attendu, qui avait souffert pour qu’il soit de nouveau ouvert.
Ils n'avaient pas besoin de le savoir.
Leur bonheur n’avait aucune dette à acquitter.
Il leur appartenait.
Élise les regarda s’éloigner vers l’autre rive.
Pendant longtemps, elle avait cru que le destin se présentait comme une puissance étrangère, décidant à l’avance de la joie et du malheur des hommes.
Elle comprenait désormais que les tragédies étaient parfois préparées par des générations de petites décisions auxquelles personne n’avait voulu donner leur véritable nom.
La peur.
L’orgueil.
Le silence.
Et pourtant, ces mêmes générations pouvaient aussi préparer autre chose.
Un passage.
Une parole.
Une confiance offerte à celui qu’on avait appris à craindre.
Le jour s’effaçait derrière les collines.
Sur les deux rives, les fenêtres s’allumaient.
Élise ferma les yeux un instant.
Elle ne demanda plus au passé de lui rendre ce qu’il lui avait pris.
Elle lui demanda seulement de ne pas être oublié.
Puis elle reprit sa marche.
Au-dessous d’elle, l’Aulne continuait de couler, indifférent aux noms que les hommes donnaient à leurs douleurs.
Et, sur le pont, il n’y avait plus deux villes.
Il n’y en avait qu’une.
Fin.

10. Roméo et Juliette

# L'Été des cendres

## I. La source

Il existe, au-dessus du village de Saint-Aurel, dans les collines de garrigue qui séparent la plaine du Languedoc des premiers contreforts des Cévennes, une source qu'on appelle la Font du Loup. Elle sort d'une fente dans le calcaire, au pied d'un chêne vert si vieux que personne au village ne se souvient de l'avoir vu jeune. Elle coule dans un bassin de pierre sèche, puis se perd dans une rigole qui descend entre les vignes. Elle n'a jamais tari. Même en 1976, même en 2003, quand les puits de la plaine crachaient de la boue et que les rivières n'étaient plus que des lits de cailloux blancs, la Font du Loup donnait encore son filet d'eau froide, à peine plus gros qu'un doigt.

C'est pour elle que les Cabanel et les Marty se haïssent depuis quatre-vingt-dix ans.

L'histoire, chacun la raconte à sa manière. Chez les Cabanel, on dit qu'en 1934 le vieux Marius Marty a déplacé de nuit les bornes du cadastre, de dix mètres, pour mettre la source de son côté. Chez les Marty, on dit que c'est Achille Cabanel qui a corrompu le géomètre, et que les bornes n'ont jamais bougé. Ce qui est sûr, c'est qu'il y a eu un procès, puis un deuxième, puis un troisième. Qu'un soir de juillet 1951, au bal de la Saint-Roch, un Cabanel a cassé la mâchoire d'un Marty avec une bouteille. Qu'en 1962, pendant la grande sécheresse, on a retrouvé le jeune Paul Cabanel noyé dans le bassin de la source, et que personne n'a jamais su s'il était tombé ou si on l'y avait poussé. Que depuis ce jour-là, les deux familles ne se parlent plus, ne se saluent plus, ne s'assoient plus à la même table au café de la place, et ne vendent même plus leur vin à la même coopérative.

Les vignes des Cabanel occupent le versant est de la colline. Celles des Marty, le versant ouest. Entre les deux, au sommet, il y a la source, le chêne vert, et une clôture de barbelés rouillés que chaque famille accuse l'autre d'avoir posée.

Au printemps 2022, Lou Cabanel avait dix-neuf ans. Elle ne s'était jamais approchée de cette clôture à moins de cent mètres.

## II. La fête

Il n'avait pas plu depuis le mois de février. En juin, les ceps commençaient à jaunir sur les terrasses les plus hautes, et l'on parlait au café d'arrêtés préfectoraux, de restrictions d'eau, de vendanges en août. La garrigue craquait sous les pas comme du papier. Les pompiers du canton avaient déjà éteint trois départs de feu le long de la départementale. Le soir, quand le vent du nord se levait, il apportait une odeur sèche de thym chauffé et de résine, et les vieux levaient le nez en silence.

La fête votive de Saint-Aurel a lieu le dernier week-end de juin. Il y a des taureaux lâchés dans les rues le samedi après-midi, une course de vachettes dans les arènes de planches montées sur le parking de la coopérative, et un bal le soir sur la place, sous les platanes, avec un orchestre de reprises qui vient de Lodève. Les Cabanel occupent les tables de gauche, devant la boulangerie. Les Marty, celles de droite, devant le tabac. Entre les deux, la piste de danse, où les jeunes des deux familles ont appris dès l'enfance à ne jamais se frôler.

Lou n'aimait pas la fête. Elle était rentrée de Montpellier deux semaines plus tôt, après sa deuxième année de licence d'agronomie, pour aider son père aux vignes pendant l'été. Elle avait passé l'après-midi à regarder son cousin Bastien et ses copains courir devant les taureaux en hurlant. Le soir, assise à la table familiale, elle écoutait son oncle expliquer pour la centième fois que les Marty pompaient la nappe en secret, qu'ils avaient creusé un forage illégal sous leur cave, que c'était pour ça que la source baissait.

« Elle ne baisse pas, la source, dit Lou. C'est la sécheresse. Tout baisse. »

Son oncle la regarda comme si elle avait juré à la messe.

« Ça, c'est ce qu'on t'apprend à Montpellier ? »

Elle se leva, prit son verre, et alla s'asseoir seule sur le muret de la fontaine, au fond de la place, là où la lumière des guirlandes n'arrivait plus. C'est là qu'il la trouva.

Il s'assit à l'autre bout du muret sans rien dire. Il avait à peu près son âge, des cheveux bruns coupés trop court, une chemise blanche froissée, et un gobelet de bière tiède qu'il ne buvait pas. Il regardait la piste, lui aussi, où les couples tournaient sous les platanes au son d'une chanson de Goldman massacrée par l'orchestre.

« Ils jouent faux, dit-il au bout d'un moment.

— Ils jouent faux depuis 1998, dit Lou. C'est la tradition. »

Il rit. C'était un rire bref et surpris, comme s'il ne s'attendait pas à rire ce soir-là. Elle le regarda mieux. Elle ne le connaissait pas. Ou plutôt, elle avait l'impression vague de l'avoir déjà vu, de loin, sans jamais l'avoir regardé.

Ils parlèrent. De l'orchestre, d'abord, puis de la sécheresse, des vignes qui grillaient, de la fac. Il faisait un BTS de viticulture à Montpellier lui aussi, à Agro, de l'autre côté de la ville. De ce qu'ils feraient plus tard. Lui voulait planter des cépages qui résistent à la chaleur, des variétés grecques, siciliennes, qu'on n'avait jamais vues dans la région. Elle voulait travailler sur l'eau, la façon de la garder dans les sols, de la partager. Ils parlèrent une heure sans voir le temps passer, et quand l'orchestre attaqua un slow, il se leva et lui tendit la main sans rien dire. Elle la prit.

Ils dansèrent au fond de la place, dans l'ombre, loin des guirlandes. Elle sentait son cœur battre contre sa joue à travers la chemise blanche. Quand la chanson finit, il ne la lâcha pas tout de suite.

« Je m'appelle Théo, dit-il.

— Lou. »

Une voix cria quelque chose depuis les tables de droite. Il tourna la tête, et elle vit son visage changer.

« Théo ! Théo Marty ! Qu'est-ce que tu fous là-bas ? »

Elle le lâcha comme si elle s'était brûlée.

Il la regarda. Il avait compris aussi. Elle le vit dans ses yeux, la même stupeur, le même vertige. Pendant une seconde, ni l'un ni l'autre ne bougea. Puis il recula d'un pas, et un autre, sans la quitter des yeux, et disparut dans la foule vers les tables de droite.

Lou rentra à pied par le chemin des vignes, seule, à deux heures du matin, sous un ciel sans lune et sans nuages. La garrigue sentait la poussière chaude. Elle pensait : *un Marty. De tous les garçons du canton, un Marty.* Elle pensait aussi, et c'était plus effrayant encore : *ça ne change rien. Ça ne change absolument rien.*

## III. La clôture

Il l'attendait le lendemain soir, à la clôture.

Elle ne savait pas pourquoi elle y était montée. Elle s'était dit qu'elle allait voir l'état des vignes du haut. Elle s'était dit qu'elle voulait voir la source, qu'elle n'avait pas vue depuis l'enfance. Elle s'était dit beaucoup de choses en grimpant le sentier de cailloux blancs dans la chaleur du soir, et aucune n'était vraie. Quand elle arriva au sommet, il était là, de l'autre côté des barbelés, assis contre le tronc du chêne vert, les pieds dans le bassin de pierre.

« Je savais que tu viendrais, dit-il.

— Tu ne savais rien du tout.

— Non, avoua-t-il. J'espérais. »

Elle s'arrêta à deux mètres de la clôture. Entre eux, les barbelés rouillés brillaient dans la dernière lumière.

« Tu sais ce que ma famille dirait, si elle me voyait ici ? dit-elle.

— La même chose que la mienne. »

Il se leva, enjamba le bassin, et s'approcha de la clôture jusqu'à la toucher. Il était si près qu'elle voyait les grains de poussière sur ses cils.

« Je n'ai pas dormi, dit-il. Toute la nuit. J'ai pensé à ton nom. J'ai essayé de le détester. Je n'y arrive pas. » Il eut un sourire triste. « Mon grand-père dit que les Cabanel ont tué notre source. Que vous l'avez volée, que vous l'avez empoisonnée, que vous avez noyé un des vôtres dedans pour nous faire accuser. Il me le répète depuis que j'ai cinq ans. Et je te regarde, et je ne vois aucun Cabanel. Je vois juste toi. »

Lou posa la main sur le fil de fer entre deux pointes. Le métal était encore chaud du soleil.

« Cette clôture, dit-elle, elle n'est à personne. Personne ne sait qui l'a posée. Mon père dit que c'est ton grand-père. Ton grand-père doit dire que c'est le mien. » Elle serra le fil. « On se bat depuis quatre-vingt-dix ans pour un filet d'eau gros comme un doigt, et personne ne se souvient même pourquoi. »

Il posa sa main sur la sienne, de l'autre côté du fil.

Ils restèrent là jusqu'à la nuit, sans franchir la clôture, debout de part et d'autre des barbelés, à parler tout bas. Le filet de la source chantait dans le bassin. Les étoiles sortaient une à une au-dessus de la garrigue. Quand elle redescendit vers la maison, à minuit passé, elle avait les mains écorchées par le fer et ne s'en était pas aperçue.

## IV. Fernand

Il fallait quelqu'un. Ils le comprirent très vite.

Dans un village de six cents habitants, deux jeunes gens de familles ennemies ne peuvent pas se voir longtemps sans que quelqu'un le remarque. Il fallait un lieu, un messager, un allié. Ce fut Théo qui pensa à Fernand.

Fernand Roux avait quatre-vingt-un ans. Il avait été instituteur à Saint-Aurel pendant trente-sept ans. Il avait appris à lire à la moitié du village, Cabanel et Marty confondus, et il était sans doute le seul homme de la commune que les deux familles respectaient encore. Depuis sa retraite, il vivait seul dans une capitelle restaurée à flanc de colline, une de ces vieilles cabanes de berger en pierre sèche, rondes, coiffées d'une voûte d'encorbellement, qu'on trouve partout dans la garrigue. Il y élevait des abeilles. Il y lisait Montaigne et Giono. Il descendait au village deux fois par semaine pour acheter son pain et jouer aux boules, et il avait l'habitude de dire, en riant, que la seule chose plus têtue qu'une abeille, c'était un vigneron de Saint-Aurel.

Il les reçut un soir de juillet, assis sur le banc de pierre devant sa capitelle, au milieu du bourdonnement des ruches. Il écouta tout sans rien dire. Puis il resta longtemps à regarder la vallée.

« Vous savez qui était Paul Cabanel ? demanda-t-il enfin. Celui qu'on a retrouvé dans la source en 62 ? »

Ils secouèrent la tête.

« C'était mon meilleur ami. On avait dix-neuf ans. Il était amoureux d'une Marty, Hélène, la grand-tante de Théo. Personne ne le savait, sauf moi. Ils se retrouvaient à la source, la nuit. C'était le seul endroit où personne ne venait. » Il se tut un moment. « Le soir où il est mort, il y avait eu une bagarre au café. Son frère et le frère d'Hélène. Pour une histoire d'arrosage, de tour d'eau, je ne sais plus. Paul est monté à la source pour la voir, pour lui dire qu'il fallait partir, tous les deux, quitter le village. Il faisait nuit. Il n'y avait pas de lune. Je crois qu'il a glissé sur les pierres du bassin. Je l'ai toujours cru. Mais les deux familles ont décidé que c'était l'autre qui l'avait tué, et elles le croient encore. Et Hélène est partie à Paris l'année suivante, et elle n'est jamais revenue. »

Il regarda Lou, puis Théo.

« Soixante ans, dit-il doucement. Soixante ans de haine sur une nuit sans lune et des pierres mouillées. »

Il accepta de les aider. La capitelle devint leur refuge. Ils s'y retrouvaient le soir, quand Fernand descendait au village, ou la nuit, quand il dormait dans sa chaise longue sous le mûrier. Ils y parlaient des heures, de tout et de rien, de l'avenir surtout, de la vie qu'ils auraient ailleurs. Ils iraient à Montpellier. Ils trouveraient du travail. Ils planteraient un jour, quelque part, une vigne qui serait à eux, qui n'aurait pas de nom de famille, pas de procès, pas de bornes déplacées.

« Il faut que vous leur parliez, leur disait Fernand. À vos parents. Pas tout de suite, mais avant la rentrée. Il faut que ça sorte. Les secrets, dans ce village, ça finit toujours par tuer quelqu'un. »

Ils promettaient. Ils remettaient. L'été était si long, si chaud, si immobile, qu'il semblait ne jamais devoir finir.

## V. Samir

Le 14 août, il y avait un concours de pétanque à la fête du village voisin de Montbazin, et Théo y alla avec son meilleur ami, Samir.

Samir Belkacem était le fils du garagiste de Saint-Aurel. Il avait grandi entre les deux familles sans appartenir à aucune, et cela lui donnait une liberté que Théo lui avait toujours enviée. Il était drôle, insolent, rapide, incapable de se taire. Il appelait les Cabanel « les Capulet » et les Marty « les Montaigu », depuis qu'il avait vu le film en classe de troisième, et il riait de toute cette histoire avec une gaieté qui scandalisait les anciens. Il était le seul à qui Théo avait parlé de Lou.

« T'es fou, avait dit Samir, cette nuit-là, assis sur le capot de sa vieille Clio. Complètement fou. » Puis il avait souri, de son grand sourire de travers. « Mais c'est le premier truc intelligent que je t'entends dire depuis le collège. »

À Montbazin, sur la place, entre deux parties de boules, ils tombèrent sur Bastien Cabanel et trois de ses copains.

Bastien avait vingt-trois ans. Il était le cousin de Lou, le fils de son oncle, et il portait la haine de la famille comme d'autres portent une médaille. Il avait bu. Il avait entendu des rumeurs. Quelqu'un avait vu la voiture de Théo garée sur le chemin de la capitelle, un soir, à côté de la vieille 205 de Lou. Il s'approcha de Théo avec ce sourire mauvais que tout le village connaissait.

« Alors, Marty. Il paraît que tu traînes dans la garrigue la nuit ? »

Théo ne répondit pas. Il ne voulait pas se battre. Il pensait à Lou. Il pensait : *si je frappe son cousin, elle ne me le pardonnera jamais.* Il baissa les yeux, et se tourna pour partir.

Ce fut Samir qui répondit.

Il dit quelque chose de drôle et de cruel sur la famille Cabanel, sur l'intelligence de Bastien, sur ce que les taureaux de la fête pensaient de lui. Les copains de Bastien rirent malgré eux. Bastien devint blanc. Il y eut une bousculade, des cris, une table renversée, des boules de pétanque qui roulèrent sur le gravier. Samir tomba en arrière contre le rebord de pierre de la fontaine.

Il ne se releva pas.

Les pompiers arrivèrent en onze minutes. Ils ne purent rien faire. Fracture du crâne, dit plus tard le rapport du légiste. Une malchance, un mauvais angle, une seconde.

Théo était à genoux sur le gravier, la tête de Samir sur ses cuisses, quand Bastien et ses copains montèrent en courant dans leur pick-up. Il les entendit démarrer. Il vit les phares s'éloigner sur la route des vignes, vers Saint-Aurel.

Il se leva, couvert du sang de son ami, monta dans sa voiture, et les suivit.

## VI. Le feu

Ce qui se passa ensuite sur la route des vignes, la gendarmerie mit trois mois à le reconstituer, et ne le reconstitua jamais tout à fait.

On sait que la poursuite dura neuf kilomètres, sur une petite route étroite entre les vignes, à plus de cent vingt kilomètres à l'heure. On sait que dans le virage du Mas Blanc, à deux kilomètres de Saint-Aurel, le pick-up de Bastien quitta la chaussée, fit trois tonneaux dans un fossé et s'immobilisa sur le toit dans la garrigue. On sait que les trois passagers furent éjectés et survécurent, et que Bastien, qui conduisait, resta coincé dans la cabine. On sait que le réservoir prit feu. On sait que Théo arriva trente secondes plus tard, s'arrêta, courut vers le pick-up, essaya d'ouvrir la portière, et se brûla les deux mains jusqu'au coude en tirant dessus. On sait qu'il ne réussit pas.

On sait que le vent du nord soufflait ce soir-là à soixante kilomètres à l'heure. On sait que la garrigue n'avait pas reçu une goutte de pluie depuis six mois.

À vingt-deux heures quarante, le feu du pick-up atteignit les premiers chênes kermès au bord du fossé. À vingt-deux heures cinquante, il courait dans la colline. À vingt-trois heures quinze, il avait passé la crête et descendait vers Saint-Aurel sur un front de deux kilomètres, poussé par le vent, dans un grondement que les habitants du village ont tous décrit, plus tard, de la même façon : le bruit d'un train qui ne s'arrête jamais.

---

Lou était chez elle quand on vint annoncer la mort de Bastien.

Elle entendit sa tante hurler dans la cour. Elle entendit son oncle, la voix brisée, répéter le nom de Théo Marty, encore et encore, comme une malédiction. Il l'avait poursuivi, il l'avait poussé dans le fossé, il l'avait regardé brûler. Les gendarmes le cherchaient. Il avait disparu dans la colline, à pied, dans la fumée. Par la fenêtre de sa chambre, elle voyait la lueur orange monter derrière la crête, vers le nord, et les premières flammes passer sur le ciel noir comme une ligne d'écriture.

Elle ne savait pas ce qui s'était passé. Elle ne savait pas pour Samir. Elle savait seulement que son cousin était mort, que la colline brûlait, et qu'on accusait Théo.

Et elle savait où il était allé.

Elle prit son téléphone. Elle appela Théo. Messagerie. Elle l'appela encore. Messagerie. Elle appela Fernand. Ça sonna longtemps, longtemps, et enfin il décrocha.

« Il est ici, dit Fernand. Il est arrivé il y a vingt minutes. Il a les mains brûlées. Il dit qu'il n'a pas poussé Bastien, qu'il a essayé de le sortir. Il dit que Samir est mort. » La voix du vieil homme tremblait. « Lou, écoute-moi. Le feu vient vers nous. Les pompiers vont évacuer toute la colline. Je vais l'emmener à la route de Lodève par le vieux chemin des bergers, à l'ouest, c'est le seul passage. Ne viens pas. Tu m'entends ? Ne viens surtout pas. Reste au village. Je t'appelle dès qu'on est à la route.

— Je viens.

— Lou, non ! Le feu est entre toi et nous. Tu ne passeras pas. Reste là. Je te le jure, je t'appelle dans une heure. Fais-moi confiance. »

Elle raccrocha. Elle resta debout au milieu de sa chambre, le téléphone à la main, à regarder la lueur derrière la crête. Puis, une heure plus tard, comme promis, le téléphone sonna.

Ce n'était pas Fernand. C'était un message automatique de l'opérateur : *Votre correspondant n'est pas joignable. Service temporairement indisponible dans votre zone.*

Le feu venait de passer sur le relais téléphonique du Puech d'Auriol. Pendant les quatorze heures suivantes, il n'y eut plus aucun réseau sur toute la commune de Saint-Aurel.

## VII. Le chemin des bergers

Elle ne sut jamais combien de temps elle attendit. Une heure, deux heures, peut-être plus. Les sirènes passaient sans arrêt dans la rue. Des gens couraient sur la place avec des valises. Les gendarmes frappaient aux portes pour évacuer les maisons du haut du village. Son père chargeait des affaires dans la camionnette en criant son nom. Elle ne répondait pas. Elle regardait son téléphone mort et la lueur rouge, et elle pensait à Fernand, quatre-vingt-un ans, sur le vieux chemin des bergers, avec un garçon aux mains brûlées, dans la fumée.

Un pompier entra dans la cuisine, noir de suie, et parla à son père à voix basse. Elle saisit trois mots : *capitelle*, *Roux*, *trop tard*.

Elle n'attendit pas d'entendre la suite.

Elle sortit par la porte de derrière, traversa le jardin en courant, sauta le muret, et monta vers la colline par le sentier de cailloux blancs, celui de la source. Elle ne savait pas ce qu'elle allait faire. Elle savait seulement qu'elle ne pouvait pas rester en bas à attendre, une heure de plus, que quelqu'un lui dise qu'il était mort.

---

Ce qu'elle ne savait pas, et qu'elle n'apprit que trois jours plus tard, c'est ce que le pompier avait dit à son père.

Il avait dit : *Ils ont trouvé le vieux Roux sur le chemin des bergers. Il était tombé. Une crise cardiaque, sans doute, avec la fumée et l'effort. Le garçon le portait sur son dos quand les gars de la colonne l'ont trouvé. Ils ont réussi à les sortir tous les deux à temps. Le vieux est vivant. Mais le garçon s'est échappé. Il a dit qu'il devait retourner chercher quelqu'un. Il a dit qu'il y avait une fille, là-haut, à la source. Il est reparti dans la fumée avant qu'on puisse l'arrêter. C'est trop tard pour lui.*

Théo était remonté vers la Font du Loup parce qu'il était sûr qu'elle y viendrait. Lou montait vers la Font du Loup parce qu'elle était sûre qu'il y serait.

## VIII. La Font du Loup

Elle arriva au sommet à deux heures du matin.

Le feu était passé sur le versant ouest, celui des Marty, une heure plus tôt. Il avait laissé derrière lui une étendue noire et fumante, piquée de braises, où les souches des vieux ceps rougeoyaient encore comme des yeux. Le vent avait tourné. Le front était maintenant loin vers le sud, une longue ligne orange qui descendait vers la plaine. Mais sur la crête, autour de la source, les flammes avaient laissé un cercle étrange, presque intact. Le chêne vert était roussi d'un côté seulement. Le bassin de pierre sèche, plein de cendres, laissait encore échapper son filet d'eau. Et la clôture de barbelés avait fondu par endroits sous la chaleur, si bien qu'elle pendait maintenant en lambeaux tordus entre les piquets noircis.

Il était là. Assis contre le chêne vert, du côté des Cabanel, les pieds dans l'eau du bassin, comme le premier soir.

Elle courut vers lui en criant son nom. Elle trébucha sur les pierres chaudes, se releva, enjamba les débris de la clôture sans même s'en apercevoir, et tomba à genoux à côté de lui.

Il avait les yeux ouverts. Il la regarda, et elle vit qu'il la reconnaissait. Il essaya de sourire. Ses mains, enveloppées de bandes de tissu déchirées dans sa chemise, reposaient sur ses genoux. Il respirait mal, avec un bruit rauque, terrible, qu'elle avait appris en cours de secourisme à la fac. Fumée. Brûlure des voies respiratoires. Trop de temps dans la colline.

« Je savais que tu viendrais, dit-il, d'une voix qui n'était plus qu'un souffle.

— Tu ne savais rien du tout. »

Il rit, ou essaya, et le rire se transforma en toux. Elle prit sa tête contre elle. Elle se pencha vers le bassin, mit de l'eau dans ses mains et la lui fit boire, goutte à goutte, l'eau froide de la Font du Loup, celle qui n'avait jamais tari. Il but. Il ferma les yeux.

« Je n'ai pas tué Bastien, murmura-t-il. Il faut que tu le saches. J'ai essayé de le sortir. La portière... »

Il ne finit pas.

« Je sais, dit-elle. Je sais. »

Elle le garda contre elle jusqu'à l'aube. Elle lui parla tout le temps. Elle lui parla de la vigne qu'ils planteraient un jour, des cépages grecs et siciliens qui résistent à la chaleur, de la petite maison qu'ils auraient, sans nom de famille sur la boîte aux lettres. Elle ne savait pas s'il l'entendait. Le filet d'eau chantait dans le bassin de cendres. Au-dessus de la garrigue noire, les étoiles pâlissaient une à une.

À un moment, peu avant le jour, elle s'aperçut qu'il ne respirait plus.

Les pompiers les trouvèrent à six heures, en remontant la crête. Elle était assise contre le chêne vert, du côté des Cabanel, avec Théo Marty dans les bras, et elle ne voulait pas le lâcher. Il fallut trois hommes pour lui faire desserrer les doigts.

## IX. Les cendres

Le feu de Saint-Aurel brûla trois mille deux cents hectares de garrigue et de vignes en dix-sept heures. Il détruisit onze maisons, deux caves coopératives et la totalité des vignes des familles Cabanel et Marty, sur les deux versants de la colline. Il tua deux personnes : Bastien Cabanel, vingt-trois ans, et Théo Marty, vingt ans. Il s'arrêta au matin du 15 août, sur la route de Lodève, devant une ligne de canadairs. Puis, enfin, après six mois sans une goutte, il plut.

Fernand Roux survécut. Il passa trois semaines à l'hôpital de Montpellier, et c'est lui qui raconta tout, aux gendarmes d'abord, puis aux deux familles réunies pour la première fois depuis soixante ans dans une même pièce, la petite salle des fêtes de la mairie, l'une à gauche, l'autre à droite, comme à la fête votive. Il raconta l'été, la clôture, la capitelle. Il raconta la bagarre de Montbazin, la mort de Samir, la poursuite sur la route des vignes. Il raconta comment Théo avait essayé d'arracher la portière en flammes du pick-up de Bastien, et comment il l'avait ensuite porté, lui, Fernand, sur son dos, dans la fumée, sur le chemin des bergers, avant de retourner chercher Lou. Il raconta Paul et Hélène, en 1962, la nuit sans lune et les pierres mouillées.

Quand il eut fini, personne ne parla pendant longtemps.

Puis le grand-père de Théo, Émile Marty, quatre-vingt-sept ans, celui qui avait répété toute sa vie que les Cabanel avaient volé la source, se leva. Il traversa la salle en s'appuyant sur sa canne, très lentement, jusqu'aux chaises de gauche, et s'arrêta devant le père de Bastien. Les deux hommes se regardèrent. L'un venait de perdre son fils, l'autre son petit-fils, la même nuit, dans le même feu, sur la même colline.

« Mon frère Henri a posé cette clôture, dit Émile Marty. En 1963. Après la mort de votre Paul. Je l'ai aidé. On avait peur que vous veniez venger votre frère à la source. » Sa voix tremblait. « Je ne l'ai jamais dit à personne. J'avais honte. Et puis, avec les années, j'ai fini par croire que c'était vous. »

Le père de Bastien ne répondit pas. Il regardait ses mains. Puis, au bout d'un temps qui sembla très long à tous ceux qui étaient dans la salle, il se leva à son tour et prit la main du vieil homme dans la sienne.

## X. La vigne

On n'a jamais reconstruit la clôture.

Au printemps suivant, les deux familles, qui n'avaient plus de vignes ni l'une ni l'autre, firent une chose que personne à Saint-Aurel n'aurait cru possible. Elles mirent leurs terres en commun, sur les deux versants de la colline, pour créer un domaine unique, une coopérative à deux familles, gérée ensemble. Il fallut un an de réunions chez le notaire, beaucoup de cris et quelques larmes. On l'appela le Domaine de la Font du Loup. On décida que l'eau de la source serait partagée par moitié, selon un tour d'arrosage affiché sur la porte de la mairie, et que personne n'aurait jamais le droit de la clore.

Lou Cabanel n'est pas retournée à Montpellier cette année-là. Elle est restée au village. Elle a planté, sur la terrasse la plus haute, juste sous le chêne vert, du côté qui avait été celui des Marty, une petite parcelle d'une vigne que personne dans la région n'avait jamais vue : de l'assyrtiko de Santorin et du nero d'Avola de Sicile, deux cépages qui supportent la chaleur et la sécheresse, et qui donnent du raisin même quand il ne pleut pas pendant six mois. Il lui a fallu trois ans pour trouver les plants. Elle en a parlé à Fernand, qui a pleuré.

La parcelle est petite : quelques rangs à peine, entre les pierres noircies que le temps blanchit peu à peu. Il n'y a pas de nom dessus, pas de panneau. Mais les gens du village savent. Les jeunes y montent parfois, le soir, à la fin de l'été, quand la chaleur tombe et que le vent sent le thym. Ils s'assoient contre le chêne vert, les pieds dans le bassin de pierre, et écoutent le filet d'eau qui chante. Quelqu'un leur a raconté l'histoire, ou une version de l'histoire, celle qu'on raconte maintenant à Saint-Aurel, qui change un peu chaque fois, comme toutes les histoires.

Fernand est mort l'hiver dernier, à quatre-vingt-quatre ans, dans sa capitelle, au milieu de ses abeilles. Avant de mourir, il a dit à Lou une chose qu'elle n'a pas oubliée.

« Ce n'est pas l'amour qui les a tués, tes deux garçons, dit-il. Ni le feu. Ni la malchance. C'est la haine des autres, celle qu'on leur avait donnée en héritage, comme une vieille maison dont personne ne veut mais que personne n'ose vendre. L'amour, lui, c'est la seule chose dans toute cette histoire qui ait réussi à franchir la clôture. »

Lou a cinquante rangs de vigne maintenant, et une petite fille de deux ans qu'elle a eue avec un garçon de Lodève, gentil et patient, qui sait qu'elle a aimé quelqu'un d'autre avant lui et ne lui en veut pas. Elle s'appelle Hélène. Le soir, en été, Lou la porte jusqu'à la source, et la laisse mettre les mains dans l'eau froide. L'enfant rit. Le chêne vert, roussi d'un seul côté, repousse lentement. Et en bas, sur les deux versants de la colline, à perte de vue, la vigne a reverdi.

Mais le temps d'Horlogia ne pardonne pas. Leurs rencontres secrètes, dans les catacombes de la ville, devinrent le seul repère de leurs existences. Ils rêvaient d'une fuite, d'un monde où un Vasseur pourrait aimer une Morvan sans que le sang ne soit exigé en tribut.

Plutôt que d'accepter un mariage arrangé par son père avec un riche marchand de cuivre, Liana se tourna vers un vieil alchimiste. Elle avala un élixir paralysant, conçu pour simuler un arrêt cardiaque, espérant qu'une fois dans le caveau familial, Élias viendrait la secourir pour fuir la cité.

Le message, hélas, se perdit dans la tempête de neige qui s'abattit sur les montagnes environnantes. Élias ne reçut que la rumeur de la mort de sa bien-aimée. Fou de douleur, il força les portes du cimetière d'Horlogia, s'introduisit dans le caveau des Morvan et, face au corps pâle de Liana, brisa le cadran de sa propre vie en buvant un poison foudroyant.

Liana s'éveilla quelques minutes plus tard, le goût de la liberté sur les lèvres, pour trouver l'immobilité glacée de son amant contre elle. Le cri qu'elle poussa déchira la nuit et brisa les horloges de la grand-place. Elle ne chercha pas de poison. Le lendemain, les patriarches Vasseur et Morvan se tinrent face à face dans la crypte. # The Architecture of Small Mercies

An Original Novel

## Chapter One: The House Above the River

On the morning they lost their house, Clara Vale discovered that grief could be measured in ordinary things: the number of cups remaining in a cupboard, the weight of a key, the pale rectangle on a wall where a painting had hung for twenty-three years.

Her younger sister, Iris, stood at the drawing-room window, watching rain stitch the garden into a thousand trembling pieces.

“They cannot make us leave,” Iris said.

“They can. The sale is final.”

“But Father built this place.”

“He borrowed against it.”

“He loved it.”

Clara folded a linen tablecloth into a cardboard box. “Both things can be true.”

The house stood above the River Arlen, a long, weather-beaten structure with narrow windows and a conservatory whose glass roof had leaked every winter since Clara could remember. Their father, a celebrated architect whose reputation had survived considerably longer than his financial judgment, had designed it before either daughter was born.

To Iris, the house was a living creature. Every room possessed a temperament; every staircase preserved the sound of childhood footsteps. The east-facing studio was their father's mind made visible, crowded with architectural drawings, chipped plaster models, and books whose margins contained arguments with authors long dead.

To Clara, the house was all these things and also a financial catastrophe.

When their father died in February, she had discovered unpaid loans, deferred taxes, and a succession of courteous letters that became less courteous as the months passed. The family home had been mortgaged three times. Its eventual sale would cover most of the debt but leave their mother and the two sisters with little more than an inheritance of furniture.

Their mother, who had spent thirty years believing that elegance was a form of security, received the news with a bewilderment that Clara found more painful than anger.

“But we have always managed,” she said.

Clara did not reply that they had managed largely because nobody had yet insisted on being paid.

By April, arrangements had been made for the family to move into a modest apartment in Bellwether, a former industrial town two hours west of the capital. Clara had accepted a position at the municipal planning office, where she would assess applications for building repairs and supervise a restoration project in the old river district.

Iris, twenty-four and recently graduated from music college, regarded the move as an exile.

“I could stay here,” she suggested one evening. “There must be something I could do.”

“There is. You could help us begin again.”

“That sounds like something people say when they have stopped believing in anything beautiful.”

Clara looked up from her accounts.

“Iris, I believe in beautiful things. I simply prefer them with working plumbing.”

Her sister turned away, wounded less by the words than by their calmness.

Clara felt the familiar tightening in her chest. She wished she could speak as Iris did, without measuring every sentence against its probable consequence. She wished, sometimes, that someone else would count the money, arrange the transport, answer the creditors, and remember which medicine their mother needed before breakfast.

Instead, she returned to the accounts.

The next morning, a letter arrived from Julian Mercer, the solicitor managing their father's estate.

He had written several times already, always with exactness and unfailing courtesy. This letter contained the final settlement figures and a brief personal note.

I hope the arrangements in Bellwether will allow you some peace. Your father spoke often of your judgment. I think he understood its value, even when he found it inconvenient.

Clara read the final sentence twice.

She had known Julian for three years. He had sometimes visited their father to discuss contracts, and he had remained afterward for tea. He was neither remarkable in appearance nor especially impressive in conversation, but he listened with an attentiveness that made his silences companionable.

During her father's last illness, he had driven Clara to the hospital on several occasions. Once, when she had been too exhausted to speak, he had bought her a sandwich and left it beside her without comment.

She had never forgotten that small kindness.

Nor had she forgotten the evening when he had nearly said something important, then stopped himself.

Since the funeral, his correspondence had become formal.

Clara folded the letter and placed it with the others.

Iris, watching from the doorway, said, “You are in love with him.”

Clara closed the drawer.

“You have an extraordinary talent for drawing conclusions from furniture.”

“You put his letters in the top drawer.”

“I put electricity bills there too.”

“Then perhaps you love the electricity company.”

Clara smiled despite herself.

But when Iris had gone, she reopened the drawer and touched the envelope.

She knew Julian's father, a prominent businessman, expected his son to marry a woman with wealth and advantageous connections. She also knew Julian had recently begun spending more time in the capital.

What she did not know was whether his reserve concealed a struggle or an absence of feeling.

She preferred uncertainty to an answer she might regret demanding.

Outside, the river flowed beneath the darkening sky, indifferent to deeds, signatures, and the little ceremonies by which human beings convinced themselves that anything belonged to them forever.

## Chapter Two: A Town of Unfinished Things

Bellwether had once manufactured clocks.

Its factories were closed now, and the great brick buildings along the river stood empty, their windows broken or boarded over. Yet the town retained a peculiar stubbornness. Flowers grew through cracks in the pavement. The old public market opened every Saturday beneath a patched iron roof. On summer evenings, children played in streets where delivery trucks had once carried machinery to the railway.

The Vales' apartment occupied the second floor of a narrow building overlooking the market square.

Their mother disliked the stairs, the kitchen, and the view of the bakery's exhaust vent.

Iris disliked everything.

Clara, however, discovered that the apartment received morning sunlight, that its roof did not leak, and that the landlord repaired a faulty tap within twenty-four hours.

She considered these advantages substantial.

Her work concerned the rehabilitation of the river district. The municipality had acquired several abandoned industrial buildings and hoped to convert them into housing, workshops, and public spaces.

The largest of these, the Meridian Works, contained an extraordinary central hall beneath a roof of iron and glass. Although rust had spread across its beams, Clara could still see the intelligence of its original construction.

One afternoon, as she stood beneath the roof examining a cracked support, someone called from the far end of the hall.

“You ought not to stand there without a helmet.”

She turned.

A man approached carrying a canvas tool bag. He was tall, broad-shouldered, and dressed in clothes that suggested he had come directly from some practical and disagreeable task.

“I have a helmet,” Clara said.

“Where?”

“In my office.”

“That is a considerable distance from your head.”

She looked at him with irritation, then noticed the loose section of metal hanging above her.

She stepped aside.

“Thank you.”

“You're welcome. I'm Daniel Rowan.”

“Clara Vale.”

“I know. The new restoration officer.”

“And you?”

“I repair things that people have decided are beyond repair.”

“An ambitious profession.”

“Mostly an underpaid one.”

He was a structural engineer employed by a local preservation trust. Over the following weeks, they met frequently at the Meridian Works, sometimes by arrangement and sometimes because they were both unwilling to abandon an argument.

Daniel believed the building could be saved.

Clara believed it could be saved only if the municipality secured additional funding, replaced several load-bearing supports, and abandoned the more extravagant elements of the proposed design.

“You are determined to make this project less interesting,” Daniel complained.

One afternoon he introduced her to a woman selling flowers.

“This is Mrs. Arden,” he said. “She knows everything worth knowing about Bellwether.”

“And several things that aren't worth knowing,” Mrs. Arden added.

She was a large, energetic widow with white hair and an appetite for conversation that appeared unaffected by the absence of listeners.

Within ten minutes, Clara learned that Daniel had once been engaged, that the engagement had ended unhappily, and that he had subsequently turned down a lucrative position abroad.

Daniel stood beside them, looking resigned.

“Mrs. Arden,” he said, “perhaps Miss Vale would also like to buy some flowers.”
