The official investigation blamed Rusk.
Documents bearing his signature showed that he had approved inferior materials. Witnesses claimed that he had dismissed warnings from workmen. The company books indicated that money intended for repairs had disappeared.
Rusk denied everything.
Nobody believed him.
When Elias first saw the man, he was sitting alone in a corner of the hotel dining room.
Rusk was broad-shouldered, with a heavy face and eyes that seemed perpetually exhausted. His hands lay on the table beside an untouched plate.
The other diners avoided his corner.
Elias took his supper across from him.
"Seat taken?"
Rusk looked up.
"No."
Elias sat down.
For several minutes they ate in silence.
Then Rusk said, "You're the fellow who pulled that wagon free."
"I helped."
"Daniel Mercer says you understand machinery."
"A little."
"Would you understand a reservoir?"
"Depends what was wrong with it."
Rusk laid down his fork.
"That's what I've been trying to find out."
Elias met his eyes.
"Folks say you already know."
A shadow crossed the older man's face.
"Yes," he said. "They do."
"Are they right?"
Rusk looked toward the window, where the last sunlight lay across the street.
"No."
There was no anger in his voice.
That interested Elias more than anger would have.
"Then why don't you prove it?"
"I've spent six months trying."
"And?"
"Every document I find condemns me. Every witness remembers something I didn't say. Every question I ask makes me look more guilty."
He leaned forward.
"Tell me something, Mr. Vane. How does a man defend himself when every piece of evidence against him appears to be genuine?"
Elias became very still.
"You haven't told me your name," Rusk observed.
Elias looked down at his hands.
"No," he said quietly. "I haven't."
Outside, the church bell began to ring.
Seven slow strokes echoed over the town.
Rusk rose.
"Those bells used to mark the end of the working day," he said. "Now they ring for the dead."
He left his supper unfinished.
Elias remained at the table long after the room emptied.
He had come to Bellwether seeking one particular man.
Instead, he had found another man whose life was being destroyed by something that resembled the truth.
He wondered whether the resemblance was an accident.
Chapter Three: What the Water Concealed
The following morning, Daniel Mercer found Elias examining the foundations of the old pumping station.
The building stood a mile upstream, abandoned after the reservoir disaster. Rust streaked its corrugated roof, and weeds grew between its stone steps.
Daniel approached cautiously.
"You've got a habit of being places you shouldn't."
"So I've been told."
"What are you doing?"
"Looking."
"At what?"
"Things folks stopped looking at."
Daniel folded his arms.
"That station hasn't worked since the flood."
"Why not?"
"Equipment's ruined."
"All of it?"
"Most."
Elias knelt beside a section of pipe protruding from the ground.
Its flange was bright beneath a thin covering of dirt.
Someone had recently removed the bolts.
He touched the exposed metal.
"Interesting."
Daniel frowned.
"What is?"
"Nothing stays unused forever. Especially when there's money in making it useful again."
The young man followed his gaze.
Then his expression changed.
"My father worked here."
Elias looked up.
"Did he?"
"He was one of the men killed in the flood."
For a moment neither spoke.
Daniel stared toward the mountains.
"He warned Mr. Rusk about the reservoir wall. I know he did."
"How?"
"He wrote it in his notebook."
"You still have it?"
Daniel hesitated.
"Yes."
"May I see it?"
"No."
The answer came so quickly that Elias almost smiled.
"Fair enough."
Daniel turned away, then stopped.
"Why are you asking these questions?"
"Because something doesn't fit."
"What?"
Elias stood.
"The water."
Daniel stared at him.
Elias pointed toward the mountains.
"When that wall failed, where did the flood go?"
"Down the eastern channel."
"All of it?"
"Most of it."
"And the western farms?"
"They were nearly dry."
Elias looked toward the distant fields.
"Then why did somebody spend money repairing the western sluice gate three weeks before the disaster?"
Daniel's face lost its color.
"How do you know they did?"
"Fresh bolts. New timber. Tool marks under old mud."
He brushed dust from his hands.
"Somebody wanted that gate ready."
Daniel looked toward the pumping station.
Then he whispered, "But the western gate was supposed to be permanently closed."
"Supposed to be," Elias agreed.
Far above them, the mountains stood motionless beneath the morning sun.
Somewhere among those slopes, the river continued its ancient journey toward the valley.
And Elias began to suspect that the flood had not been merely a failure of stone and timber.
It had been directed.
Chapter Four: The Price of Being Believed
By evening, the town knew that Elias Vane had been asking questions about the reservoir.
By midnight, someone had searched his hotel room.
Nothing valuable was taken.
His saddlebag lay open.
His clothes had been scattered.
And on his pillow rested a folded paper.
Elias opened it.
Inside was a single sentence:
The river has already buried seven. Don't make it eight.
He read the warning twice.
Then he carried it downstairs and placed it on the hotel counter.
The proprietor, a nervous man named Wilkes, stared at the paper.
"Lord Almighty."
"Recognize the handwriting?"
"No."
"Know who was in my room?"
"No."
Elias regarded him.
Wilkes swallowed.
"Listen, mister. I got a wife and two children."
"So do lots of people."
"I don't want trouble."
"Neither do I."
"Then why are you bringing it here?"
Elias folded the paper.
"Because trouble came looking for me first."
He went outside.
The night was cold and clear.
Across the street, a lantern burned in Samuel Rusk's office.
Elias crossed to it and knocked.
Rusk opened the door carrying a revolver.
"You're becoming unpopular," he said.
"So I've noticed."
"Come in."
The office contained shelves of engineering manuals, survey maps, and boxes of records. A large drawing of the reservoir hung behind the desk.
Elias examined it.
"Who supervised construction after the company dismissed you?"
Rusk frowned.
"I wasn't dismissed."
"Then who took over?"
"Mr. Harrow's men."
Elias looked at him.
"The gentleman who owns the mill?"
"And half the other businesses in town."
"Does he own the water company?"
"Controlling interest."
"Who profited when the eastern farms were destroyed?"
Rusk stood very still.
Then he said, "Harrow bought the land."
"All of it?"
"Nearly."
"For what?"
"He says he intends to extend the railway."
Elias turned toward the reservoir drawing.
"And where would the new railway pass?"
Rusk approached the map.
His finger traced the eastern valley.
Slowly, his hand began to tremble.
"Through the ruined farms."
"At what price did he buy them?"
"A fraction of what they were worth."
Elias nodded.
"There's your reason."
Rusk shook his head.
"That doesn't prove he caused the flood."
"No."
"And Harrow has the documents. Every one of them."
"Then we'll need something he hasn't got."
Rusk laughed bitterly.
"What would that be?"
Elias looked toward the window.
"Water doesn't sign papers," he said. "But it leaves marks."
Chapter Five: A Name From the Past
Three days later, Elias discovered why Mr. Harrow's face had seemed familiar.
The discovery came in the general store.
He was purchasing coffee when a man entered carrying a bundle of newspapers from the southbound stage.
The proprietor spread them across the counter.
Elias glanced at the nearest paper.
A small article described the reopening of an abandoned silver mine in the southern territories.
Beneath it was a photograph.
Three men stood before a wooden building.
One was Mr. Harrow.
Another was a prosperous-looking stranger named Jonathan Pike.
The third was Elias's older brother, Nathaniel Vane.
Elias felt the room narrow around him.
For eleven months, he had searched for Nathaniel.
Once they had worked together at a silver mine beyond the state line. Nathaniel managed the company's accounts while Elias maintained its machinery.
When a shipment of silver vanished, documents bearing Elias's signature appeared in the company records.
Witnesses remembered seeing him near the locked storeroom.
The company accused him of theft.
A warrant followed.
Nathaniel disappeared with the missing silver.
And Elias became a fugitive.
He knew his brother had arranged it. He had found the account books, seen the altered figures, recognized Nathaniel's handwriting.
But the originals were gone.
Everything that remained pointed toward Elias.
Now his brother's face stared up from a newspaper in Bellwether.
Beneath the photograph was the caption:
Regional Investors Announce New Mining Partnership.
Mr. Harrow was not merely a mill owner.
He was a man who dealt with Nathaniel Vane.
Elias bought the newspaper.
When he turned around, Daniel Mercer was standing in the doorway.
"You look like you've seen a ghost."
"Something close."
Daniel glanced at the photograph.
"That's Mr. Harrow."
"Know the other two?"
"No."
Elias folded the paper.
"Then maybe it's time you did."
They walked together toward the river.
For the first time since arriving in Bellwether, Elias told someone his full story.
Daniel listened without interruption.
When Elias finished, the young man stared at the moving water.
"So you're wanted."
"Yes."
"For something you didn't do."
"That's right."
"And you expect me to believe you?"
"No."
The answer surprised Daniel.
Elias leaned against the railing.
"I expect you to remember what happened to your father. And to ask yourself whether a piece of paper can be true simply because somebody important says it is."
Daniel remained silent.
Then he said, "What if you're lying?"
"Then you'll have to find that out."
The young man looked across the bridge.
"My father used to say that courage wasn't being certain you were right."
"What was it?"
"Being willing to find out you were wrong."
Elias smiled sadly.
"Sounds like he was a better man than most."
Daniel took a folded notebook from his coat.
"Here," he said.
It was his father's notebook.
Chapter Six: The Secret of the Western Gate
The notebook contained measurements, dates, sketches, and calculations written in a precise hand.
Most pages described ordinary maintenance.
But near the end, Elias found a series of entries concerning the western sluice gate.
Three weeks before the flood, Daniel's father had recorded unusual activity at the abandoned pumping station.
New machinery had arrived at night.
Workers unknown to him had entered through the western service road.
And a private order from the company's directors had prohibited inspection.
Beneath these notes stood one final observation:
The western channel is being prepared for a release far greater than normal operation requires. I have requested an explanation. No answer has been given.
The entry was dated four days before the disaster.
The following page was blank.
Elias closed the notebook.
"Your father knew."
Daniel nodded.
"Can we prove it?"
"We can prove somebody intended to use the western gate."
"But the flood went east."
"Exactly."
Daniel stared.
"I don't understand."
Elias spread a survey map on the table.
"Suppose you wanted to weaken the eastern wall without leaving signs of an explosion. You could change the flow behind it. Force the water to strike a foundation never designed for that pressure."
Daniel leaned closer.
"By opening the western gate?"
"Not exactly. By reversing the pressure through the service channel. The pumping station could do that if the valves were changed."
"Wouldn't the machinery break?"
"Probably."
"Then we'd find the damage."
Elias smiled.
"Now you're thinking."
They went to the pumping station before dawn.
Inside, beneath a layer of dust, Elias found what he needed.
The machinery had been dismantled.
But one enormous iron coupling remained.
Its teeth were broken, not by ordinary wear but by a sudden force in the wrong direction.
More importantly, someone had tried to conceal the damage beneath fresh mortar.
Daniel ran his fingers over the shattered metal.
"Can this prove what happened?"
"It can prove the machinery was operated against its design."
"Can it prove who ordered it?"
"No."
Daniel's shoulders sank.
Elias glanced toward the entrance.
"Not yet."
Footsteps sounded outside.
Both men turned.
Three strangers appeared in the doorway.
The foremost carried a shotgun.
"Morning, gentlemen," he said.
Elias looked at the weapon.
"Seems like it is."
"Mr. Harrow wants a word."
"Does he?"
"He does."
Elias moved slowly toward the wall, where an old iron lever protruded from the machinery.
"Then he ought to come ask for himself."
The stranger raised the shotgun.
"Don't make this difficult."
Elias sighed.
"I've had a difficult year."
His hand closed around the lever.
He pulled.
With a tremendous crash, a suspended section of rusted pipe dropped between the men and the doorway.
The shotgun fired.
Pellets tore through the wall.
Daniel sprang toward a side exit.
Elias followed.
They escaped through a drainage tunnel, crawling through mud and darkness until they emerged beneath a stand of willow trees.
Behind them, angry voices echoed from the station.
Daniel lay on the ground, gasping.
"Are you insane?"
"Not generally."
"They could have killed us."
"Yes."
"Then why did you go in there?"
Elias wiped mud from his face.
"Because now we know something else."
"What?"
"Harrow is frightened."
Chapter Seven: The Town Meeting
The council assembled at noon in the old courthouse.
Mr. Harrow presided from a high-backed chair.
Samuel Rusk stood before the gathering while nearly two hundred townspeople crowded the benches.
Elias entered through the rear door.
Conversation ceased.
Harrow's eyes narrowed.
"You have no business here."
"Seems to be plenty of business."
"This meeting concerns the management of the reservoir."
"Then I'm in the right place."
The mayor rose.
"Mr. Vane, you are not a resident of Bellwether."
"No, sir."
"Then what standing have you?"
Elias unfolded the newspaper he had purchased.
"Perhaps Mr. Harrow could tell you."
He laid the photograph on the council table.
Harrow glanced at it.
His expression did not change.
"I know those gentlemen."
"I expect you do."
"What of it?"
"One of them is my brother."
A murmur moved through the room.
Elias continued.
"His name is Nathaniel Vane. He's wanted for questioning in connection with a silver theft that was blamed on me."
Harrow smiled thinly.
"An extraordinary accusation."
"Not as extraordinary as what happened to the reservoir."
The mayor struck his gavel.
"Keep to the matter before the council."
Elias nodded.
"Gladly."
He displayed the damaged coupling and Daniel Mercer's notebook.
He explained the altered valves, the concealed repairs, and the unnatural pressure that could have undermined the eastern retaining wall.
The townspeople listened.
When he finished, Harrow rose.
"An impressive performance," he said. "But where is your proof that I directed any of this?"
Elias looked at him.
"I haven't shown it yet."
Harrow laughed.
"Then perhaps you should."
"Perhaps I should."
Elias reached into his coat.
A man near the side door suddenly shouted.
"He's armed!"
The room erupted.
A constable drew his revolver.
Another man rushed toward Elias.
But Elias withdrew only a folded telegram.
He held it above his head.
"This arrived from the railway office this morning."
Harrow's smile vanished.
Elias opened it.
"Mr. Harrow, I sent a message to your business partner two days ago. I used your name. I told him the pumping station records had been recovered, and I asked whether the original instructions should be destroyed."
The old man's face turned gray.
"That's a lie."
"Then explain why the reply gives instructions for destroying them."
The room fell silent.
Elias read the message.
It referred to the concealed repairs, the pressure alteration, and the destruction of the eastern wall. It instructed Harrow to remove the original company directives before the next inspection.
At its conclusion stood the signature:
N. Vane.
Harrow lunged for the paper.
Elias stepped aside.
The council constable seized the older man's arm.
For the first time, Mr. Harrow appeared genuinely afraid.
Then he began to laugh.
"Do you think that proves anything? A telegram? A book? A broken piece of iron?"
His voice rose.
"You think the world is governed by truth? It is governed by the people who possess the documents, the machinery, the banks, and the land!"
Nobody answered.
Harrow pointed at Elias.
"That man is a thief! There is a warrant for him! Search him!"
The constable looked uncertainly toward the mayor.
Elias remained motionless.
"He's right," he said.
The room stirred.
"There is a warrant."
He drew a folded wanted notice from his pocket.
"My brother made sure of it."
He looked at the crowd.
"Maybe you'll decide I'm guilty. Maybe you'll decide Samuel Rusk is guilty. But before you do, ask yourselves why the same man who bought the ruined farms also ordered the machinery altered. Ask why workers were forbidden to inspect the station. Ask why seven people died while a few men grew rich."
Daniel stepped forward.
"And ask why my father was silenced when he tried to warn them."
His voice shook, but he continued.
"My father wrote those notes. I know his handwriting. He died believing somebody would listen."
Across the room, an elderly farmer stood.
"My daughter died in that flood."
Another man rose.
"My land was bought for almost nothing."
A third spoke.
"I worked on that western gate. We were told to keep quiet."
Soon the room was filled with voices.
Harrow backed toward the door.
But the townspeople no longer moved aside for him.
Chapter Eight: The Man Behind the Papers
The confrontation in the courthouse might have ended everything had Nathaniel Vane not arrived that evening.
He came in a hired carriage, wearing a dark suit and a fine hat, with a leather valise resting beside him.
He had heard of the inquiry.
He had also received Harrow's frantic message.
Elias was waiting at the railway platform.
For a moment, the brothers simply stared at one another.
Nathaniel was older by six years. His face had grown fuller, and his hair had begun to thin, but his eyes remained as cold and watchful as Elias remembered.
"You look terrible," Nathaniel said.
"You look prosperous."
"I work hard."
"So did the men who died at the reservoir."
Nathaniel's expression stiffened.
"I don't know what you've been told."
"Enough."
"Then you'll know I can make your troubles disappear."
Elias glanced at the valise.
"What's in there?"
"Money."
"How much?"
"Enough for you to start again somewhere else."
Elias looked beyond the platform toward the mountains.
"Funny thing about starting again," he said. "You can't do it while the old life is still following you."
Nathaniel lowered his voice.
"Listen carefully. Those people in town don't care about justice. They care about someone to blame. Today it's Harrow. Tomorrow it may be you."
"Probably."
"You could leave tonight."
"I could."
"Then take the money."
Elias shook his head.
Nathaniel's face hardened.
"You always did have a talent for making yourself miserable."
"Maybe."
"You think a confession will save you? You think telling the truth changes what people believe?"
Elias stepped closer.
"No. I think telling the truth gives them a chance to change."
Nathaniel looked at him with contempt.
Then his right hand moved toward his coat.
Elias caught his wrist.
The two brothers struggled beside the platform railing.
Nathaniel struck him across the face.
Elias staggered, but held fast.
A pistol fell from Nathaniel's coat and clattered onto the boards.
The stationmaster shouted.
Two railway guards rushed forward.
Within moments, Nathaniel lay pinned against the platform.
His valise burst open.
Bundles of currency spilled across the boards.
Among them lay company seals, forged contracts, and the original reservoir directives.
Nathaniel had carried the evidence because he trusted nobody else to destroy it.
Elias knelt beside the scattered papers.
He picked up one bearing his own name.
The forged authorization for the stolen silver.
For eleven months, that piece of paper had governed his life.
He turned it over.
On the reverse, Nathaniel had written several calculations in his own unmistakable hand.
Elias stared at them.
Then he began to laugh.
Not with amusement.
Not with triumph.
But with the exhausted disbelief of a man who had traveled too far in pursuit of something that had been lying in another man's pocket all along.
Nathaniel looked up from the platform.
"You've destroyed us both."
Elias folded the paper carefully.
"No," he said. "You've only run out of places to hide."
Chapter Nine: The Weight of a Verdict
The investigation lasted through the winter.
Harrow was charged with arranging the deliberate weakening of the reservoir wall. Nathaniel was charged with fraud, conspiracy, and the earlier theft.
Several company officials confessed to lesser offenses.
The original documents, recovered from Nathaniel's valise, confirmed that the alterations had been ordered to ruin the eastern farmland and make its purchase cheaper.
Samuel Rusk was cleared of wrongdoing.
But his vindication did not restore what he had lost.
The dead remained dead.
The ruined farms remained ruined.
And the town that had condemned him could not undo six months of cruelty with a few apologies.
On a cold February morning, Rusk stood beside the river with Elias.
"I thought I'd feel better," he admitted.
"About what?"
"Being proved innocent."
Elias watched ice drift slowly along the bank.
"Don't you?"
"Some."
Rusk picked up a pebble and threw it into the water.
"But I've spent so much time wanting people to believe me that I forgot what it would feel like when they finally did."
Elias said nothing.
Rusk continued.
"Yesterday the mayor offered to make me superintendent again."
"Will you take it?"
"I don't know."
"Why not?"
"Because I don't know if I can trust them."
Elias nodded.
Rusk turned toward him.
"How did you learn to trust anyone after what your brother did?"
The question hung between them.
Elias thought of Nathaniel.
He thought of the long road, the sleepless nights, and the faces of strangers who had looked at a wanted notice and seen only a criminal.
Then he thought of Daniel Mercer handing over his father's notebook.
Of Samuel Rusk offering him a seat at his table.
Of the townspeople who had finally found the courage to speak.
"I haven't learned it completely," he said.
Rusk smiled faintly.
"Neither have I."
They stood together while the river carried the winter ice toward the distant plains.
Chapter Ten: The Bridge in Spring
When spring came, the river rose again.
Snow melted in the upper mountains, and the streams swelled with cold, green water.
Bellwether began rebuilding.
The eastern farms were restored through a fund established from the assets seized from Harrow and his accomplices.
The old pumping station was dismantled.
A new reservoir committee was formed, with elected representatives from the farms, mills, and town.
Samuel Rusk accepted the position of chief engineer, but only after insisting that all inspection records remain open to the public.
Daniel Mercer became his assistant.
And Elias Vane, whose innocence had finally been established in the silver theft, prepared to leave.
He had stayed longer than intended.
Long enough to see winter disappear.
Long enough to become familiar with the faces on the street.
Long enough that the hotel proprietor no longer looked nervous when he entered the dining room.
On the morning of his departure, Daniel found him beside the bridge.
The young man carried a small wooden box.
"Mr. Rusk wanted you to have this."
Elias opened it.
Inside lay a brass compass.
Its lid bore a simple inscription:
For the man who showed us where to look.
Elias turned it in his hands.
"Tell him thank you."
"He said you'd say that."
Daniel smiled.
"Will you come back?"
Elias looked downriver.
"Maybe."
"Where will you go?"
"West, I reckon."
"Why?"
Elias considered the question.
For nearly a year, every journey had been shaped by pursuit.
He had ridden to find Nathaniel.
To clear his name.
To recover a past he could not bear to abandon.
Now there was no one left to chase.
No accusation left to answer.
No hidden document waiting to be discovered.
Yet the road remained.
And beyond it were places he had never seen.
"I don't know," he admitted.
Daniel laughed.
"That's not much of a plan."
"No."
Elias mounted his horse.
"But it's the first one I've had in a long time that belongs entirely to me."
He touched the brim of his hat.
Daniel stepped aside.
The horse carried Elias slowly across the bridge, its hooves striking the new planks with a steady wooden rhythm.
Halfway across, he stopped.
The river moved beneath him, bright in the morning sun.
Its water carried silt from the mountains, branches from distant forests, and the fragments of a winter that was ending.
Once, that same river had been turned into an instrument of destruction.
Once, its course had been altered by men who believed they could shape the land, the law, and the truth to suit themselves.
But the river had preserved evidence of what had been done.
In broken iron.
In scarred stone.
In the memories of those who had survived.
And when the truth had finally emerged, it had not returned the dead or repaired every injury.
It had done something smaller, and perhaps more necessary.
It had made it possible for the living to begin again.
Elias looked back.
Daniel raised one hand.
The town stood beyond him, its rooftops shining in the sunlight.
For a moment, Elias felt the strange weight of belonging somewhere.
He had spent so many months fleeing the judgment of strangers that he had almost forgotten what it meant to be welcomed.
He returned Daniel's wave.
Then he rode on.
Beyond Bellwether, the road climbed through green hills toward the western mountains.
The air smelled of thawing earth and young grass.
A hawk circled overhead.
Somewhere in the distance, a meadowlark began to sing.
Elias took the brass compass from his pocket.
The needle trembled.
Then it settled toward the north.
He smiled and closed the lid.
For the first time in many months, he did not need a compass to tell him where he belonged.
He belonged wherever he could travel without fear of the truth catching up with him.
And so he rode west, carrying neither a false name nor a borrowed purpose, while the morning opened before him like a country that had not yet been mapped.
Epilogue: What Remains
Years afterward, the people of Bellwether told many stories about the stranger who had come to their town.
Some said he had been a famous detective.
Others claimed he was a former outlaw who had turned against his companions.
A few insisted he had once been a government agent.
The stories grew stranger with each telling.
But Samuel Rusk never corrected them.
When visitors asked about Elias Vane, he simply directed them to the bridge.
There, fixed to one of the new stone supports, was a small brass plate.
It bore neither a name nor a date.
Only these words:
What is believed may be false.
What is hidden may be found.
And justice begins when someone dares to question.
The river flowed beneath the inscription through summer heat and winter frost.
Children played along its banks.
Farmers crossed its bridge.
Travelers stopped to water their horses.
Most never noticed the plaque.
Those who did sometimes paused to read it.
Then they continued on their way.
And the river, indifferent to praise and accusation alike, carried its water onward beneath the open sky.
The End

12. Sonny

# Firestick

## I.

The horse was trying to kill a man when Jess Calder drove into Mirrabool, and nobody seemed especially surprised about it.

It was a little after eleven on a Saturday morning in January, forty-four degrees in the shade, though there wasn't much shade. Mirrabool was one street, eight hundred metres long, laid down on the red plain of western Queensland as if someone had dropped it from a height and couldn't be bothered to pick it up again. There was a pub, the Royal, with an iron verandah. There was a police station, a fibro box with a flagpole and a dead garden. There were a general store, a stock and station agency, a closed bank, a community hall, a racecourse with no rails, and a set of saleyards at the far end, where about forty people were leaning on the rails watching a grey-and-white brumby try to put a young stockman through the fence.

Jess pulled her old Land Cruiser in under a pepper tree, turned off the engine, and sat for a moment with her hands on the wheel.

She hadn't meant to stop here. She'd meant to fill up with diesel and keep going west, as she'd been doing for eleven days now, ever since she'd read the email on her phone in a roadhouse outside Dubbo. She'd read it twice, then switched the phone off, taken out the SIM card, and dropped it in the roadhouse bin. But the horse caught her eye, and she'd been looking at horses all her life, and she couldn't make herself look away.

It was a grey, flecked with white like ash on a dying fire, about fifteen hands, compact and deep-chested. It moved like nothing she'd seen in years. As she watched, it bucked twice, high and twisting, then dropped its shoulder and spun on its hindquarters in a full circle so fast that the rider's hat flew off. Then it planted its forefeet and stopped dead. The rider went forward over its neck, hit the red dirt, and rolled. The horse wheeled and came down at him with both front hooves. Two men jumped the rails with ropes, and the rider scrambled under the fence, and for a moment there was a lot of dust and shouting.

When it cleared, the grey stood alone in the middle of the yard, sides heaving, ears flat, eyes rolling white, daring anyone else to try.

Jess got out of the Land Cruiser.

"What do they call him?" she asked the nearest man on the rail, an old drover in a stained Akubra with a rollie stuck to his lip.

He looked at her sideways. "Firestick," he said. "Officially. That young fella in the dust there's calling him something else."

The young fella was limping out through the gate, holding his shoulder. He was about twenty-two, red-faced, furious, with a split lip.

"That your horse?" Jess asked him.

"Not on your life," he said. "If he was mine I'd have shot him a month ago and sold him to the knackery in pieces."

"Mind if I have a go?"

He looked at her properly for the first time: a woman of twenty-six or so, wiry, with short hair, burnt brown arms, faded jeans and riding boots worn through at the heel. Something like a grin went across his split lip.

"Go for your life," he said. "Fifty bucks says you don't last as long as I did."

"I haven't got fifty bucks to lose," said Jess. "But I'll ride him for nothing, if the owner says yes."

---

The owner was standing a little apart from the others, at the far end of the rail, in a sweat-darkened blue shirt with a Queensland Police patch on the shoulder. He was about fifty, heavy-set and quiet, with grey stubble and a face like a dry creek bed. He'd watched the young stockman get thrown without any change of expression. When Jess asked, he looked at her for a long time.

"He'll kill you," he said.

"He might," Jess agreed.

He shrugged. "Your funeral."

Jess felt the hair rise on the back of her neck as she walked towards the gate, and it wasn't the horse. It was the patch on the man's shoulder. Somewhere in a database in Sydney, eleven days ago, a warrant had been issued for the arrest of Jessica Anne Calder. Twenty-six, horse breaker, last known address Scone, New South Wales, wanted for theft of forty-one thousand dollars from the Brennan Racing stables, where she had been employed as a track rider. She hadn't taken a cent. But the money had gone out of the stable's account through her login, on her shift, and the cash withdrawals had been made by someone wearing her jacket and her cap. And her half-brother Dean, who had got her the job and knew her passwords and borrowed her jacket that week, had vanished three days before the police came.

She didn't know if the warrant had reached Queensland yet. She didn't know if this quiet sergeant leaning on the saleyard rail had already seen her photograph. She walked into the yard anyway, because the horse was there, and she'd never once in her life been able to walk away from a horse like that.

They'd blindfolded him with a hessian bag to get the saddle back on. Jess checked the girth, swung up, settled her boots in the irons, and nodded. The men pulled the bag away and jumped clear.

Nothing happened.

The grey stood perfectly still under her. He turned his head, quite calmly, and looked round at the men on the rail as if wondering what all the fuss was about. Jess sat still. She didn't touch him with her heels. She waited, and leaned forward, and put her hand flat on his neck under the mane, where the skin was hot and wet and trembling.

"All right, mate," she said quietly. "Let's see what you've got."

The grey exploded.

## II.

She stayed on for four minutes and nineteen seconds. The young stockman, whose name was Lachie Byrne, timed it on his phone and showed her afterwards.

She remembered very little of it. She remembered the sky and the red ground changing places, again and again. She remembered the horse spinning beneath her like a top, bucking with his back arched so high she felt her spine compress, then racing flat out for the far fence and digging in his forefeet at the last instant to send her over his head. She stayed on. She remembered the noise from the rail growing, until forty people were roaring.

And she remembered the moment, near the end, when the grey ran at the fence again and, instead of stopping, threw himself down sideways against it on purpose, to crush her leg between his body and the rails. She got her foot out of the iron just in time, rolled over his belly and came up on her knees in the dust with blood running into her eye from a cut on her eyebrow, where a hoof had grazed her.

Men were climbing the rails with ropes.

"Leave him!" she shouted. "I've got him."

The grey scrambled up. Jess was on him again before he'd found his feet. This time she didn't wait for him to tire. She rode him hard, coldly, deliberately, giving him nothing, asking for everything, until he'd tried every trick he had twice over, and then a third time, and finally had nothing left. He stood in the middle of the yard, head down, flanks heaving, coated in red dust and sweat, beaten.

Jess slid off. Her legs nearly went from under her. She walked round to his head and stood in front of him, and after a long moment he lifted his head and looked at her, and blew out through his nose.

"You're not a firestick," she told him, wiping blood from her eye. "You're a bushfire. Who owns this horse? I want to buy him."

The sergeant came through the gate. Up close he was bigger than she'd thought, and older. His eyes were pale grey and very tired.

"Ray Hollis," he said. "I own him. And he's not for sale."

"Everything's for sale."

"Not for money." He looked round. Jess followed his gaze. The forty people on the rail were leaving, all at once, without a word, walking away in twos and threes, back up the street towards the pub. Within a minute the saleyard was empty except for Lachie Byrne, nursing his shoulder by the gate.

Hollis watched them go with no expression at all.

"I'm not very popular round here at the moment," he said. "You might have noticed." He turned back to her. "I can't ride that horse. Never have been able to. I'll give him to you, papers and all, if you'll do something for me first."

"What?"

"Stay a month. Work for me. Be my eyes in this town, because nobody will talk to me anymore." He looked at the cut over her eye. "You'll probably end up hurt. Maybe worse. But you'll get the horse."

## III.

The station was hot and dim and smelled of dust and old coffee. Hollis pulled down a venetian blind against the glare, sat behind a desk heaped with paper, and pushed a bottle of water across to her.

"They're saying I'm in with the duffers," he said.

Jess knew the word. In this country cattle thieves had been called duffers for a hundred and fifty years.

"Are you?"

"No." He said it quietly. His hand, flat on the desk, closed slowly into a fist until the knuckles went white. "But if I heard the evidence against anyone else, I'd believe it."

He told her. Over eighteen months, more than nine hundred head of cattle had gone missing from stations in the Mirrabool district, worth over a million dollars. They vanished from remote back paddocks at night, in trucks, across country, without a trace. The thieves were good. They knew which bores were unwatched, which gates were unlocked, which station managers were away at the races. And they always seemed to know where the police would be.

Then the evidence against Hollis had started to pile up. His police ute was seen near the boundary of Coolibah Downs on a night when two hundred head went missing. He said he'd been called out to a car crash on the highway, but there was no record of the call. In October a station hand found forty stolen steers in a disused yard on an old block called Hollis's Bore, which had belonged to his late father. He hadn't been out there in years, he said. Cattle with their ear tags cut out, and an altered brand. And in the shed beside the yard, a set of homemade branding irons and an old police-issue jacket with his name on the inside of the collar.

"I gave that jacket to the op shop in Longreach two years ago," Hollis said. "Nobody believes me."

"So they think you're tipping off the duffers."

"They think I *am* the duffers, half of them." He rubbed his face. "The graziers have hired a private investigator out of Brisbane. Somebody's written to the commissioner. Bill Calloway at Coolibah Downs, who's been my mate for twenty years, crossed the street last week rather than say g'day. And anyone who works with me, people think they're in on it too. My last constable transferred out in November because someone put a brick through his windscreen."

Jess turned the water bottle round and round in her hands.

"So when you hire me," she said slowly, "people think I'm one of your gang."

"Probably."

"And if I'm actually one of the duffers' people, come to plant more evidence?"

Hollis looked at her with those pale, tired eyes.

"Then I'll arrest you," he said, "and you'll never see that horse again."

Jess thought about it. She thought about the email in the roadhouse outside Dubbo. She thought about Dean, somewhere out here in this enormous red country, with forty-one thousand dollars that weren't his, and her name on the warrant. And she thought about Hollis's knuckles going white on the desk.

All her life she'd watched horses, and men around horses. She'd learned that people lie with their faces, their voices and their eyes, and much less often with their hands. Her grandfather had taught her that, on his station near Tambo, before he died and Dean sold everything. *Watch the hands, Jessie. A horse can't lie to you, and a man's hands mostly can't either.*

"All right," she said. "A month."

## IV.

She went to the Royal that afternoon, because a pub is where a town keeps its secrets.

It was dim and cool after the street, with a ceiling fan turning slowly overhead, a cricket match on the television above the bar and a few flies circling the beer taps. The publican was a big bald woman called Shaz who looked at the cut on Jess's eyebrow and silently pushed a bag of ice across the bar. Lachie Byrne was at a corner table with his arm in a makeshift sling. At the table beside him sat four men who were so clearly brothers that they might have come out of the same mould at slightly different temperatures.

Jess looked at them, and went cold all over.

She knew them. Three years ago, at the horse sales in Roma, she'd seen them selling a truckload of brumbies with papers that didn't add up. Dean had been with them, drinking with them, laughing, slapping the eldest on the back. When she'd asked Dean about them afterwards, he'd said they were business contacts and told her to mind her own.

They looked at her now with no sign of recognition at all. She'd had long hair then, and they'd barely glanced at her. She'd only been Dean's little half-sister, holding a lead rope in the background.

"Shout the bar," she told Shaz, and put a fifty on the counter, the last fifty she had. "I'm Jess. Sergeant Hollis's new offsider. First town I've ever been in where anyone thought I'd stop trouble rather than start it."

There was silence. The brothers looked at each other. Then Lachie Byrne grinned through his split lip.

"Put your money away," he said. "I'll shout. You rode that bastard horse. I've never seen anything like it."

"Where you from?" said one of the brothers abruptly. He was the eldest, maybe thirty-five, with a scar through his left eyebrow and small, pale, watchful eyes.

"Here and there," said Jess. "Right now I'm working for the police. So I reckon I'm the one asking the questions."

"You won't last a week," said another brother into his beer.

"Why's that?"

"Hollis'll get you into trouble," said a third. "And if he doesn't—"

"Someone else will," said Lachie, still grinning. "Duffing's a touchy subject round here. People reckon it's coming out of the police station. You thinking of taking up duffing yourself?"

"No," said Jess. "I've been accused of enough lately."

The four brothers got up together. The eldest looked at her a moment longer than the others.

"See you round," he said. "Maybe."

When they'd gone, Jess turned to Lachie.

"Who are they?"

"The Voss boys," said Lachie. "Gary, Kev, Mick and Darren. Came up from the Darling Downs couple of years back and bought Willara, out on the Thomson. Run three thousand head between them. They lost two hundred head to the duffers last year. Hit them pretty hard." He looked at her curiously. "Why?"

"No reason," said Jess. She sat down at his table. "Tell me what you know about Hollis."

So he told her. It was mostly what Hollis had told her himself: the ute near Coolibah Downs, the steers at Hollis's Bore, the jacket. Then he told her something new.

"The Voss boys had a station hand," he said. "Craig Mulvey. They let him go last winter, and he came into town and got a job helping Hollis out, unofficial, like. Two weeks later Hollis arrested him for belting a girl at the B&S ball in Longreach, and Mulvey left the district. The girl backed Hollis's story. But afterwards the Voss boys said they'd fired Mulvey on purpose, so he'd get in with Hollis and find out if he was crooked. And they said Mulvey had texted them, right before he was arrested, saying he'd found proof."

"Did anyone see the text?"

"Gary says he deleted it by accident." Lachie shrugged. "But it looked bad. Real bad. It's always something with Hollis, you know? Never quite enough to charge him with. But always something."

Jess thought about it.

"Lachie," she said. "Do you know where Firestick came from? Before Hollis had him?"

"No idea. Why?"

She leaned back in her chair and spoke, quite loudly, so the whole pub could hear. Shaz was behind the bar, two old drovers were by the window, a young couple were at the pool table, and the door to the beer garden was open, where the Voss boys had gone.

"Because I think I know where he was stolen from," she said. "And I reckon I know where the missing cattle are, too. Give me a week and I'll have names for you."

## V.

Somebody tried to run her down that night.

She was walking back from the pub to the police house at the end of the street, where Hollis had given her a room. It was nearly midnight, very dark, with no street lights. A ute came out of the side road by the closed bank with no headlights, fast, straight at her. She threw herself sideways into the stormwater drain and felt the wind of it go past. By the time she'd scrambled out, it was gone up the highway towards the Thomson River, a dark shape against the stars, its engine fading.

She stood in the empty street, brushing red dust off her jeans, her heart going like a hammer, and thought: *now I'm sure. Now it's just a matter of which thing I said frightened them.* Was it the cattle, or was it the horse?

---

When she got back to the police house, her swag had been opened.

It was neat work. Someone had come in through the back door, which she'd left unlocked because nobody locked their doors in Mirrabool. They'd unrolled her swag on the bed, gone through her saddlebags, and rolled it up again almost exactly as she'd left it. Almost exactly. Jess had packed swags for twenty years, and there was a fold in the canvas that wasn't hers.

She unrolled it. At the bottom of the left saddlebag, under her spare socks, she found a plastic bread bag with eleven yellow plastic ear tags in it.

They were NLIS tags, the national livestock identification tags every beast in Australia has to wear in its ear by law. Each carried a unique number registered to a property. These eleven had been cut out of the ears of eleven cattle with pliers or snips. Jess turned on the bedside lamp and looked at the numbers. She didn't need to check the database to know they'd come from Coolibah Downs, from Bill Calloway's missing steers.

If anybody found these in her saddlebag, she was finished. So was Hollis, the man who'd hired her. *Look what we found on his new offsider. Proof.*

She sat on the bed and thought for a long time. Then she took a closer look at the tags under the lamp.

Each one had been cut out of the ear in the same way, a rough U shape. On every tag, at the bottom of the U, there was a small, sharp notch in the plastic, the same shape each time. It looked like a tiny arrowhead. Whoever had cut these tags out had used a pair of snips with a chip in one of the blades.

Jess had seen that notch before. That afternoon at the saleyards, before she rode Firestick, she'd walked along the pens looking at cattle out of habit, the way she always did. In the end pen there'd been a draft of thirty Brahman-cross steers waiting for Monday's truck, tagged and branded and properly papered. A sign on the gate said WILLARA — VOSS BROS. Three of those steers had had their tags replaced recently. The old tags had been cut out and new ones put in, which happens sometimes when a tag fails. The old ear wounds were still raw. In each one, at the bottom of the U-shaped cut, the healing flesh showed a small, sharp arrowhead notch.

Jess put the eleven tags back in the bread bag. She took a pad of paper from Hollis's kitchen drawer and wrote for nearly an hour. Then she folded what she'd written into an envelope and put it in the bread bag with the tags. She put the bread bag back exactly where she'd found it, at the bottom of her left saddlebag, under her spare socks. She rolled the swag up again, leaving the fold just as the stranger had left it.

Then she went out to the yard where Firestick stood dozing under the pepper tree, saddled him in the dark, and rode out of town towards the Thomson River, by starlight.

## VI.

Hollis was waiting when she rode back in at dawn. He was standing on the station verandah in yesterday's shirt with a mug of coffee, looking as if he hadn't slept.

"Where've you been?"

"Willara," said Jess, sliding off Firestick. Her legs were stiff; she'd ridden forty kilometres in the dark. "The Voss place. There's a set of yards in a gully on the back of it, on the river, behind a ridge where you can't see them from the road. They're new. Built last year, I'd say. There's three hundred and ten head of cattle in them, all with their tags cut out and fresh brands over the old ones. I counted twice." She drank from the water bag on her saddle. "There's a cattle truck parked behind the shed with interstate plates. I'd say they're moving them across the border into the Territory this week."

Hollis stared at her.

"You're sure?"

"I took photos." She held out her phone, the cheap prepaid one she'd bought in Bourke after she threw the other away. "There's something else. Someone broke into your house last night and planted eleven of Bill Calloway's ear tags in my saddlebag."

Hollis went very still.

"And somebody," Jess added, "has nicked your .308 out of the gun safe."

He turned and went into the station. She heard the safe door clang. When he came back his face was grey.

"The graziers are meeting at the hall at seven tonight," he said. "About the duffing. They didn't invite me." He looked at her. "Someone's going to stand up at that meeting and say they know who the duffers are. Then someone's going to search your gear and find those tags, and then they'll come for me."

"Probably," said Jess.

"You need to leave. Now. Take the horse and go. I mean it. This is going to get ugly, and it's not your fight."

Jess looked at him: a big, tired, grey-faced man, standing on the verandah of a fibro police station in the middle of a red plain, with the whole town against him, telling a stranger to save herself.

"It is my fight, actually," she said. "More than you know." She handed him her phone. "Ring someone in Longreach you trust. Not the local blokes; someone outside the district. Get them out to Willara with a truck and a couple of stock inspectors at seven tonight, while everyone's at the meeting. Send them the photos. Tell them to look for the yards in the gully behind the ridge."

"And you?"

"I'm going to the meeting," said Jess. "I'm not invited either. But my grandfather always said, waiting to be invited is a good way to miss the party."

## VII.

The Mirrabool Community Hall was a long tin shed with a stage at one end and a portrait of the Queen at the other that nobody had got round to replacing. By seven o'clock it was full: graziers, station managers, stockmen and their wives, sitting on plastic chairs or leaning on the walls with stubbies in their hands. The ceiling fans did nothing against the heat. The Voss brothers sat together in the second row. Lachie Byrne leaned against the back wall with his arm still in its sling. Bill Calloway of Coolibah Downs, a huge red-faced man of sixty, stood on the stage beside a whiteboard.

The room went quiet when Jess walked in.

"You've got a nerve," said Calloway, from the stage.

"So I've been told," said Jess. She walked down the middle aisle, between the plastic chairs. She could feel every eye on her. Her hands were steady. "I heard you're offering twenty thousand dollars to anyone who can name the duffers and prove it."

"That's right."

"I can name them," said Jess. "Four names. That's five thousand a name. Good money."

There was a stir round the hall. In the second row, Gary Voss shifted in his seat.

"Then name them," said Calloway.

"In a minute," said Jess. "First I want to say something about Ray Hollis."

"Here we go," said someone at the back.

"He hired me yesterday," said Jess. "I've known him twenty-four hours. I don't know him at all, really. But I'll tell you what I do know. Last night someone tried to run me down in the main street with their lights off, after I said in the pub that I knew where the cattle were. And last night, someone broke into Hollis's house and stole his rifle out of the safe. Then they put something in my swag that they wanted found."

Gary Voss was on his feet.

"She's lying!" he shouted. "She's covering for Hollis! Bill, search her gear. Search it right now. I'll bet you anything she's got something in there. She's one of them. She rode in yesterday out of nowhere, and suddenly she's Hollis's best mate. Search her swag and you'll see."

The hall erupted. Calloway was shouting for order. Two men from the back pushed out of the door and ran. Jess's swag was in the back of Hollis's ute, parked outside. She'd made sure of that. They came back two minutes later with her saddlebags and threw them on the trestle table in front of the stage.

Gary Voss was there before anyone else. He tore open the left saddlebag, dug through the socks, and pulled out the plastic bread bag. He held it up so the whole hall could see the yellow tags inside.

"There!" he shouted. "Calloway tags! Bill, those are *your* tags, off your steers! Proof! She's in it with Hollis, the both of them—"

"There's an envelope in there too," said Jess quietly. "Gary, why don't you give it to Mr Calloway? Let him read it out."

Voss looked down. He saw the envelope among the tags. Something flickered across his face. For half a second, Jess thought he was going to put it in his pocket. But the whole hall was watching. Calloway had already stepped down off the stage and held out his hand. Slowly, Gary Voss handed it over.

Calloway tore it open and read it. He read it again. His big red face changed colour, slowly, from red to white.

"Read it out, Bill," somebody said.

He cleared his throat.

"*To whoever finds this,*" he read. "*These eleven ear tags were put in my saddlebag last night by someone who wanted them found. Look at them closely. Every one has been cut out with the same pair of snips, which have a chip in one blade. It leaves a little arrowhead-shaped notch at the bottom of the cut. If you go down to the saleyards and look in the end pen, at the Willara steers waiting for Monday's truck, you'll find three with their tags recently replaced. The old cuts in their ears have the same arrowhead notch. Whoever cut out these tags also cut out those.*"

The hall was silent. Calloway went on reading, his voice getting quieter.

"*There are three hundred and ten more stolen cattle in a set of hidden yards on the back of Willara, in the gully behind the ridge on the Thomson. Stock inspectors from Longreach should be there right now. And whoever took Sergeant Hollis's rifle last night, I'd check under the seat of the Voss brothers' white Hilux.*"

Gary Voss was already moving towards the side door.

He didn't make it. Lachie Byrne was standing by that door with his arm in a sling. He stepped across it and stood there, grinning through his split lip, and didn't move. Behind Gary, half the hall was on its feet. Jess saw Kev Voss reaching inside his shirt, and four stockmen landed on him before he got there.

And at that moment, through the open main doors of the hall, came the sound of tyres on gravel and the blue flash of police lights. Ray Hollis walked into the hall in his sweat-darkened shirt. Behind him came two uniformed officers from Longreach and a stock inspector in a hi-vis vest, holding up a phone.

"Three hundred and ten head," said the stock inspector into the silence. "On the back of Willara, in a gully. Tags out, brands altered. And a truck with interstate plates." He looked at the Voss brothers. "And a .308 rifle under the seat of a white Hilux in the yard, registered to Sergeant Hollis."

## VIII.

Afterwards, when the Voss brothers had been taken away in the back of the Longreach police wagon, the hall slowly emptied. Bill Calloway came over to Ray Hollis, his huge face red again, and held out his hand.

"Ray," he said. "I've been a bloody fool. I said things I'll regret till I die. If anyone in this district ever says a word against you again, they'll answer to me."

Hollis looked at the hand for a long moment. Then he took it.

Calloway turned to Jess.

"Twenty thousand," he said. "You've earned it. And a job at Coolibah if you want one. I need people who can think."

"No, thanks," said Jess. "I'm moving on."

"Where to?"

She didn't answer. Hollis was watching her. After a moment he took an envelope out of his shirt pocket. It was a plain white envelope with the Queensland Police crest on it.

"This came through on the fax this morning," he said. "From New South Wales." He held it out. "I haven't read it. Not a word."

Jess took it slowly. She didn't open it. She didn't need to.

"There's no hurry," said Hollis. "Take your time."

---

She told Lachie Byrne, later that night, on the verandah of the Royal, with a beer in her hand and Firestick tied to the hitching rail below, dozing in the starlight.

She told him about Dean. Her half-brother, eight years older, wild and charming and always broke, who had got her the job at the Brennan stables in Scone because he knew the head trainer. Dean had known her passwords because she'd never thought to change them, and he'd borrowed her jacket that week because it was cold. She told him about the forty-one thousand dollars, the CCTV footage of a figure in her jacket and cap at an ATM in Muswellbrook at two in the morning, and the police at her door. Dean had gone three days before.

"He sold Firestick, too," she said. "Three years ago. To the Voss brothers, at Roma. Kev Voss told the Longreach cops tonight, trying to save his own skin. Firestick was my grandfather's horse. Born on his station near Tambo. Granddad died, and Dean got the station in the will, and he sold everything off to pay his debts. I was nineteen. I never knew what happened to Firestick. The Vosses sold him on to some bloke in Barcaldine, who sold him to Hollis." She looked down at the grey horse dozing by the rail. "He didn't know me yesterday, when I got on him. Or maybe he did. I don't know. Maybe that's why he tried so hard to get me off."

Lachie was quiet for a long time.

"And Dean?" he said at last.

"The Vosses said he's in Mount Isa," said Jess. "Working the mines. They've been in touch." She finished her beer. "That's where I'm going."

"And then what?"

Jess looked out at the dark red plain, going on and on under the stars, all the way to the Northern Territory.

"Then I'm going to find him," she said. "And I'm going to bring him back to Scone, and make him tell the truth. However long it takes."

Lachie grinned through his split lip.

"Glad I'm not him," he said. "You need anything? Food? Water? Money?"

"I've got twenty thousand dollars of Bill Calloway's," said Jess, "and the best horse in Queensland. I reckon I'm right."

---

She left at first light, with the Land Cruiser loaded and Firestick in the horse float behind it. As she pulled out from under the pepper tree, the grey kicked the side of the float so hard the whole rig shuddered on the road.

Ray Hollis stood on the verandah of the police station with his coffee and watched her go. Lachie Byrne stood beside him with his arm in its sling.

"There's a warrant out for her," said Hollis quietly. "In New South Wales. Forty-one thousand dollars."

Lachie looked at him.

"You going to do anything about it?"

Hollis watched the dust of the Land Cruiser drifting away up the highway towards Mount Isa, red in the low gold light.

"I've been on the wrong end of evidence that looked good," he said. "Two days ago this whole town would have hanged me on it." He finished his coffee. "Anyway, I haven't read the fax."

Lachie grinned. He rubbed his shoulder, where Firestick had thrown him into the saleyard fence the morning before.

"Well," he said. "If whoever's after her ever catches up, they'll have to get past that horse first. And I reckon they're welcome to try."

With a final, sickening lurch, the mech initiated a localized pulse-wave, severing the neural link and violently ejecting the pilot onto the grated floor. The crowd winced collectively as the man scrambled away, clutching his bleeding temples.

**"Intricate feedback loop,"** Kaelen murmured to a soot-stained mechanic gripping the safety rail. **"Looks like it’s overcompensating on the lateral thrusters."**

The mechanic spat a wad of synthetic resin into the dark. "Its designation is Unit 4, but the boys call it the Widowmaker. Core’s corrupted. Nobody can synchronize with it."

Kaelen dropped his stim-stick and crushed it beneath his boot. He had a long, bloody search ahead of him for the former partner who had framed him for the orbital station collapse, and navigating the fringe worlds required armor that could hit back. He vaulted over the safety rail, his boots clanging against the deck. He ignored the muttered warnings from the crowd, approaching the violently humming machine.

He didn't fight the connection when he strapped in. Instead of forcing the neuro-link to submit to his baseline rhythm, Kaelen let the machine’s chaotic, frantic data-stream wash over him. The *Wraith* bucked, its hydraulic limbs snapping out in a lethal dance meant to crush the user against the bay walls, but Kaelen moved with it. He endured the searing pain of the feedback loop, compensating for its digital rage with cold, calculated micro-adjustments. He pushed the machine to its absolute thermal limit, letting it exhaust its erratic energy until its servos whined in defeat and the massive chassis settled into a heavy, synchronized hum beneath his fingertips.

When Kaelen popped the canopy and climbed down, his nose was bleeding, but the machine stood docile and primed at his back.

A man in a worn, high-collar Enforcer’s coat stepped from the shadows of the gantry. The brass insignia on his lapel was heavily tarnished. "I own that rig," the Enforcer said, his voice like grinding tectonic plates. "And I need a deputy who can handle themselves. The pay is terrible, and the life expectancy is roughly a week."

Kaelen wiped the blood from his upper lip, recognizing the tension in the man's jaw. This was Chief Inspector Vance, a man currently drowning in rumors of syndicate collusion. The colony whispered that Vance was allowing the local drifter clans to siphon the isotope shipments, effectively bleeding Acheron dry.

"I’ve been shot at before," Kaelen replied smoothly.

"They'll tell you I'm taking a cut of the stolen shipments," Vance said, his eyes hard and unblinking. "The evidence is damning. Even I’d believe it if I were them. The drifters raided Sector 4 yesterday, and my customized plasma-carbine was found at the scene. Someone is building a cage around me, and I need a man on the outside to find the lock."

Kaelen spent the afternoon in the colony’s neon-drenched cantina, loudly buying rounds of synthetic gin for the very drifter clan suspected of the raids. He played the part of the arrogant, oblivious newcomer, boasting about his new position and heavily implying he knew exactly where the missing isotopes were hidden. He watched the clan leader’s eyes narrow, noting the subtle shift in the room's atmospheric tension.

An hour later, as Kaelen stood by the reinforced permaglass window overlooking the mining trench, a blinding flash of blue energy erupted from the dark alleyway outside.

The heavy permaglass shattered inward. Kaelen collapsed instantly, hitting the floor amid a shower of synthetic shards. Panic consumed the cantina. The clan leader smirked, stepping forward to declare that the corrupt Enforcer's new puppet had been eliminated, pulling a forged data-pad from Kaelen's motionless coat to 'prove' the extortion racket.

**"The tragic thing about plasma weaponry,"** Kaelen’s voice echoed calmly from the floor, **"is how easily the magnetic containment field can be inverted if you pack the barrel with a little thermal putty."**

Kaelen rolled to his feet, dusting glass from his shoulder, an archaic kinetic pistol already drawn and leveled at the clan leader.

Outside, a series of panicked shouts confirmed that the assassin in the alley was currently missing most of his right arm from the explosive backfire of Vance’s stolen rifle. Kaelen had found the weapon an hour prior, recognized the trap meant to frame Vance for his murder, and quietly sabotaged it before stepping into the crosshairs to bait the true thieves into the light.

When Vance arrived to arrest the bleeding saboteur and the stunned clan leader, he offered Kaelen a permanent badge and a cleared record in Acheron. Kaelen simply handed him the badge back.

"I've got a score to settle in the upper sectors," Kaelen said, walking back toward the maintenance bay where the *Wraith* was waiting in the dark. "But keep the skies clear, Inspector. You never know what's going to fall through."

Four fingers.

Ada studied the disorder.
"They were looking for something specific."

"Possibly."

He looked frightened.

"I haven't done anything wrong," he said.

"The flood files aren't in storage. They're in Mr. Harrow's private office."

"He says they're being reviewed before digitization."

A second channel had been constructed beneath the chemical warehouse.
It connected directly to a large underground storage chamber.

"September 1996."
Two years before the flood.
The surveyor's authorization was printed at the bottom.
E. Vale.
Eleanor had approved the map.
Ada studied it for a long time.
"She wasn't simply investigating what happened," she said.

"She was trying to understand what she helped make possible."
