16. THE HAND IN THE DARK

# The Hand on the Stair

## PART ONE: THE HOUSE

### I.

Strathmoy House stands on a shelf of land above the Moy Water, in the glen of the same name, forty miles north-west of Inverness. On a dry afternoon in September, with the heather turned to rust on the hills and the river low and amber over its stones, it looks like the kind of house people buy postcards of. Its grey harled walls have a round tower at the north-east corner and a crow-stepped gable at either end. Behind it, across the stable yard, stand the white-washed buildings of the Strathmoy Distillery, with their pagoda roof and the faint sweet smell of malt that hangs over the whole glen like weather.

The Strachan family has owned both since 1821.

There's a version of that history printed on the back of every bottle of Strathmoy single malt. It's about Alasdair Strachan, a "visionary" who saw the purity of the Moy Water and the richness of the barley on the haughlands and founded "a whisky of character, built to last." There's another version, which isn't printed anywhere, but which everyone in the glen knows. In it, Alasdair Strachan was the factor of the Earl of Moy, and in the spring of 1819 he cleared every family off the glen to make room for sheep. There were forty-one households. Most were burned out of their houses in the night, so they couldn't come back. An old woman called Mairead Ross refused to leave her house at Achnamoy, and Alasdair Strachan had it fired with her inside. She came out alive, they say, with her hair on fire. Before they dragged her down to the ships at Lochinver, she stood in the road in front of him and told him in Gaelic that what he built on the ashes of her house would be cleared in its turn, by its own hand. Then she spat in the road.

Two years later he bought the land from the bankrupt Earl and built his distillery on the site of Achnamoy.

Two hundred years on, the Strachans had made a great deal of money from the Moy Water and the haughland barley, and almost nobody now remembered Mairead Ross. But on the stone lintel over the door of the tower, very worn, you could still read the words Alasdair Strachan had had carved there in 1824, on the advice of a minister: *QUOD SEMINAS, METES.* What you sow, you shall reap.

The family had always told visitors it was a reference to barley.

---

In the autumn of 2019, the head of the family was Sir Hector Strachan, eighty-one, a former chairman of the Scotch Whisky Association, a widower, and frail. He spent most of his days in the library with the newspapers and a decanter, looking out at the hills. The house was really run by his sister, Miss Isobel Strachan. She was seventy-four, unmarried, tall, raw-boned and formidable, and she had never lived anywhere else. She was an elder of the kirk, a Justice of the Peace, and the chairwoman of every committee in the glen. She believed in duty, plain food, early rising, and the family. She had raised her nephew Euan, Sir Hector's only son, after his mother died when he was four.

Euan was thirty-four. He had been a delicate boy, with asthma and a weak heart, and was kept out of school sports, out of the army that his grandfather and great-grandfather had served in, and out of most things. He'd grown into a quiet, clever, intense young man, with the family's black eyebrows and narrow face. He ran the distillery's marketing from an office in Edinburgh, and was expected one day to run everything else. Two years earlier, at a whisky festival in Edinburgh, he had met Clara Fenn. She was twenty-seven, a brand consultant from London, blonde and quick and funny and restless. He married her within six months and brought her home to Strathmoy.

Clara hated it.

She didn't say so, at first. She tried. She redecorated two rooms of the west wing, gave dinner parties, invited her London friends up for shooting weekends, took over the distillery's Instagram, and turned the old maltings into an events space. But the glen was forty miles from the nearest cinema, with no mobile signal at the house and rain two hundred days a year. Miss Isobel ran it the way her grandmother had, and treated Clara with a cold, unfailing, devastating politeness. And Euan, whom Clara had married because he was gentle and attentive and adored her, turned out at Strathmoy to be someone else: quieter, more watchful, more and more absorbed in the house, the family, and the barrels. By the second autumn, the staff knew, and the glen knew, that the young Mrs Strachan was unhappy.

The staff knew a few other things too, but they kept them to themselves.

### II.

The housekeeper at Strathmoy was a widow called Morag Ross, fifty-two, careful and quiet, who had worked in the house for twenty-six years. She lived in a flat over the old coach house with her daughter Kirsty.

Kirsty was twenty-three. She had grown up at Strathmoy, the housekeeper's child, running in and out of the kitchens and the stable yard. She'd gone to Aberdeen University on a scholarship, the first in her family to go, and studied history. She'd come back to the glen that summer, with a first-class degree and no job, to help her mother and think about what to do next. She was tall and dark, with the grave grey eyes of the Rosses, and a stillness about her that made people lower their voices.

She had been in love with Euan Strachan since she was fourteen. Nobody knew this except her mother. Morag knew everything, and said nothing, and had once, when Kirsty was seventeen, taken her by both shoulders in the coach-house kitchen. "That family," she'd said, "has taken enough from ours. Don't you give them anything more."

Kirsty hadn't listened, of course. For one summer, the summer she was twenty-one and Euan was thirty-two and not yet married, they'd walked the hills together in the long evenings. He had talked to her about books and history and the glen, as nobody else at Strathmoy ever had. Then, in the autumn, he'd gone to the festival in Edinburgh and come back engaged. He had never once mentioned that summer to her since.

She did not hate Clara. She tried very hard not to think about Clara at all.

---

On the evening of Friday the twentieth of September, there were fourteen people at dinner in the long dining room at Strathmoy. Sir Hector and Miss Isobel were there, and Euan. There was the head distiller and his wife, the minister, and a whisky writer from Glasgow with his partner. There were four of Clara's London friends, up for the last weekend of the stalking season. And there was a man called Tom Ferrie, an old school friend of Euan's from Edinburgh, a television producer making a documentary series about Highland distilleries. He'd been staying in the house for a fortnight, filming.

Clara was not at dinner. She had a migraine, she'd told Miss Isobel at six o'clock. She was going to lie down in her room in the tower with the lights off, and asked not to be disturbed by anyone until morning.

At twenty to nine, halfway through the main course, a scream rang out from upstairs.

It came down through the old house, through the stone stairwell of the tower and along the gallery and down the main stair to the dining room. It was a woman's scream, high and terrible, cut off short. Then there was a long, sliding crash, like something heavy falling down a flight of stone steps.

Everyone at the table was on their feet. Euan was first out of the door, white-faced, shouting his wife's name. Tom Ferrie followed him, then the others. They ran along the gallery and through the low door into the tower and up the narrow spiral stair, the old turnpike stair of 1824, with its worn stone steps and iron hand-rope. At the bottom of the top flight, on the landing outside the tower bedroom, in the dark, they found Clara Strachan lying crumpled against the wall in her nightdress, with her neck at an angle that told everyone there was nothing to be done.

The light on the stair was off. When someone found the switch, they saw that the bedroom door above was open, the room dark beyond it.

Euan knelt beside his wife and gathered her into his arms. He didn't speak or cry. Then, as the others crowded the landing behind him, he made a strange choking sound, and fell sideways against the wall, and slid down it, unconscious.

His heart. They'd always known it was weak.

### III.

Detective Chief Inspector Graham Kerr of the Major Investigation Team in Inverness arrived at Strathmoy at a quarter past eleven that night. He was a large, red-faced, impatient man of fifty-five, twenty-eight years in the job, with a reputation for getting results quickly and a strong dislike of country-house money.

Within forty-eight hours, he believed he knew what had happened.

The pathologist said Clara Strachan had died from a broken neck sustained in a fall down the stone stair. But there was bruising on her upper arms, fresh and finger-shaped, consistent with being gripped hard, perhaps pushed. And there was a witness, of sorts. One of the London guests, a young woman, had gone up to her room on the first floor at about half past eight to fetch a cardigan. On her way back down, she'd seen someone on the gallery near the low door to the tower: a tall dark figure in the half-light, moving fast towards the back stairs. It was a woman, she thought. She hadn't thought anything of it at the time.

On the morning of the second day, Kerr's officers found a small silver brooch on the tower landing, in the gap between the wall and the iron hand-rope. It was shaped like a sprig of heather. Morag Ross, shown it in the housekeeper's room, went very pale and said nothing. Her daughter Kirsty, standing behind her, said quite calmly that it was hers. Her grandmother had given it to her when she went to university.

She had no explanation for how it came to be on the tower stair. She said she'd lost it some days before.

That afternoon a constable noticed that Kirsty Ross was wearing long sleeves, in a warm kitchen. When he asked her to roll them up, there were bruises round her right wrist. They were dark and fresh, the shape of fingers, clutched hard.

She wouldn't say how she got them. She wouldn't say anything at all.

By the evening, Kerr had found out the rest. The whole glen knew it, after all, and someone was bound to tell him. They told him about the summer two years ago, the long evenings on the hill, and the housekeeper's clever daughter who had loved the heir and been dropped for a blonde from London. He found out that Kirsty Ross had no alibi between eight and nine o'clock. She said she'd been in the flat over the coach house, alone, reading. But a groom crossing the stable yard at half past eight had seen the flat in darkness.

On the morning of the twenty-third of September, Kirsty Ross was arrested on suspicion of murder and taken to Inverness.

She said nothing in interview, nothing to the duty solicitor, and nothing to her mother. She sat in the cell in Burnett Road with her hands folded in her lap and her grey eyes on the wall, and did not speak.

## PART TWO: THE INVESTIGATOR

### IV.

Elspeth Moir had been a detective in Police Scotland and before that in Lothian and Borders for thirty-one years, the last nine as a detective superintendent running major investigations out of Edinburgh. She'd retired at fifty-five. She said it was because she was tired, which was true, but it wasn't all the truth. Since then she'd done some private work, mostly for defence solicitors: reviewing cases, re-examining evidence, finding the thing the original inquiry had missed. She was good at it. She was fifty-eight, small and grey and unremarkable to look at. She wore cardigans and reading glasses and could pass for a supply teacher or a church organist. That was useful.

Euan Strachan came to see her on the first of October, in her flat in Marchmont.

He'd been discharged from the Royal Infirmary in Edinburgh the day before, after eight days in the cardiac unit. He looked dreadful: grey-skinned, hollow-eyed, thinner than his photographs, moving slowly, like an old man. He sat in her front room overlooking the Meadows, holding a cup of tea he didn't drink. He told her, haltingly, in a quiet, educated voice, that he believed Kirsty Ross was innocent.

"I've known her since she was a child," he said. "She couldn't hurt anyone. She's not — it's not in her. And she had no reason to hurt Clara. I know what people are saying, about the summer before I married. I know what the police think. But it wasn't — it was a friendship. Nothing happened. Nothing that would make her—" He stopped, and put down the cup. "I want you to find out what really happened to my wife, Mrs Moir. Whatever it costs."

"What do you think happened?"

He was quiet a long time.

"I don't know," he said at last. "I've been lying in a hospital bed for eight days trying to think. All I know is it wasn't Kirsty." He hesitated. "There's one thing the police haven't paid attention to. I told DCI Kerr, and he wasn't interested. The light on the tower stair was off when we got there. And the bulb in it was new. I'd replaced it myself, two days before. Clara was afraid of that stair in the dark. She'd never have gone down it without the light on."

He looked at Elspeth with his dark, exhausted eyes.

"Someone turned it off," he said. "Someone was on that stair with her."

---

Elspeth took the case. She took most cases, if the money was right. But she would have taken this one for nothing, because she didn't like DCI Graham Kerr. She'd worked with him once, in 2009, on a case in Dingwall where he'd been very sure, very quickly, of the wrong man.

She drove north on the second of October and took a room at the hotel in the village at the foot of the glen. She spent three days reading everything. The defence solicitor had got her copies of the police file: the pathology report, the scene photographs, statements from all fourteen dinner guests and the eleven staff, the forensic reports on the brooch and the bruises, the timeline. She read them all twice. On the evening of the third day she sat in her room at the hotel with a glass of Strathmoy twelve-year-old, which she didn't much like, and a timeline drawn in pencil on the back of a menu. She looked at it for a long time.

The scream had been heard at twenty to nine, by all fourteen people in the dining room, and by two of the staff in the kitchen below. Every statement agreed on that. Several people had looked at their watches or phones. The minister had noted the time particularly, because he'd been about to leave for another engagement.

And yet.

The pathologist's report gave a window for the time of death, based on body temperature and the progress of rigor, of between seven-thirty and nine o'clock. That window comfortably included twenty to nine. But there was a note in it, near the end, that Kerr's team had apparently passed over. The blood that had pooled at the back of the head, from a small wound where it had struck the stone step, was described as "well clotted, with some separation of serum" when the first doctor arrived at five past nine. The doctor, a GP from the village, was quoted in a statement: "I remember thinking she'd been there longer than half an hour. But I'm not a forensic man."

Elspeth was not a forensic man either. But she had stood over more bodies than most GPs, and she knew how long blood took to do that.

She drew a small question mark beside *8.40* on her menu.

### V.

She went to see Kirsty Ross in HMP Inverness on the fifth of October.

The girl came into the visiting room in a grey prison sweatshirt, very thin and very straight. She sat down across the table, folded her hands, and looked at Elspeth with steady grey eyes, and said nothing at all.

Elspeth didn't ask her anything about the night of the twentieth. She'd learned long ago that the people who won't talk usually have a reason, and it's rarely the one you'd expect. Instead, she asked about the glen, and the house, and the history of the Rosses. She asked about Kirsty's degree. What had her dissertation been on?

For the first time something moved in the girl's face.

"The Clearances in Moy," she said quietly. "1814 to 1821."

"Including Achnamoy?"

Kirsty looked at her for a long moment. "Mairead Ross was my great-great-great-great-grandmother," she said. "She survived the ship. She came back to Sutherland in 1840. She's buried in Rogart." She paused. "Did you know that the distillery stands exactly on the site of her house? They found the hearthstone when they extended the stillhouse in 1962. It's built into the floor under Still Number Two. You can see it, if you know where to look."

"*Quod seminas, metes*," said Elspeth.

The girl almost smiled.

"Everybody in the glen knows what the Strachans sowed," she said. "They just don't say it at dinner."

Elspeth let the silence go on for a while. Then she leaned forward a little.

"Kirsty," she said gently. "I don't think you killed Clara Strachan. I think you went up that stair, for some reason of your own, and found something you weren't expecting. And whatever it was, you've decided it's better to go to prison for murder than tell anyone about it." She paused. "I'd like to know why. Not today. But I'd like you to think about it."

Kirsty's face didn't change. But her folded hands, on the table, tightened until the knuckles went white.

When Elspeth stood up to leave, the girl spoke, so quietly that she almost missed it.

"She was cold," Kirsty said. "When I touched her. She was already cold."

## PART THREE: THE STAIR

### VI.

Elspeth went back to Strathmoy on the eighth of October. Euan Strachan had asked her to stay at the house while she worked, and she accepted. She told herself it was practical. It was also, she admitted, because she wanted to watch them.

Miss Isobel received her in the library with the grave, ceremonious courtesy of a great lady in mourning, and asked whether the roads had been good. Sir Hector, in his chair by the window, smiled at her vaguely and asked if she was the new minister. Euan wasn't there. He'd gone to his doctor in Inverness, Miss Isobel said, and would be back for dinner. He was still very unwell. She was worried about him.

"He hasn't slept," she said, "since that night. He walks about the house at three in the morning. I hear him on the stairs." She looked out of the window at the hills. "He loved her very much, Mrs Moir. Whatever people in the glen may say. He was never the same, after he married. He was happy." She was quiet a moment. "Too happy, perhaps. The Strachans have never been good at happiness. We're not built for it."

That afternoon, while the house was quiet, Elspeth went up the tower stair alone.

It was a narrow stone spiral, steep and worn, winding up the inside of the round tower from the gallery on the first floor to the top room under the conical roof. That had been Clara's room. She'd chosen it, Miss Isobel said, for the view. Three turns of the stair, perhaps twenty-five steps. A thick iron rope, polished by two hundred years of hands, ran up the outer wall through iron staples. The light switch was at the bottom, by the low door from the gallery, with a second at the top, outside the bedroom. On the landing at the foot of the top flight, where Clara had been found, there was a narrow window slit, and a stone ledge under it.

Elspeth stood on the landing for a long time.

Then she climbed to the top and went into the bedroom.

It was a round room, quite small, with whitewashed walls and a big old bed facing the window. There was a view down the whole length of the glen to the river, and the distillery roofs, and the hills beyond. The police had been through it, of course. They'd taken the bedclothes, photographed everything, and dusted the door and the light switches. It was tidy now, cleaned and aired, as if nobody had ever slept there.

On the bedside table, beside a lamp, was a small, round, fabric-covered speaker, the kind that connects to a phone. It was the same kind Elspeth had seen in every room of the house. The whole of Strathmoy was wired for sound, Euan had told her on the way in, with some embarrassment. Clara had insisted on it, for her parties. You could play music in any room from your phone, or set it to play on a timer, as an alarm in the mornings.

Elspeth looked at the speaker for a long time.

Then she took out her phone and rang a young man she knew in the cybercrime unit at Gartcosh, who owed her a favour from 2016.

### VII.

It took him four days.

On the evening of the twelfth of October, Elspeth sat in her car in the lay-by at the foot of the glen, where there was one bar of signal. She listened to the young man from Gartcosh explain, slowly, because she wasn't technical, what he had found.

The speaker in Clara Strachan's bedroom was connected to the house's wireless network and to a single account on a music streaming service. The account kept a log. On the evening of the twentieth of September, the log showed that at 8:39 and forty seconds, the speaker in the tower bedroom had played a single audio file. It was not music. It was a sound file, nine seconds long, which had been uploaded to the account's private library at 3:14 in the morning on the eighteenth of September, two days before Clara died. It had been scheduled to play once, at 8:39 and forty seconds on the twentieth, through that speaker only, at maximum volume.

"What was the file?" said Elspeth.

There was a pause on the line.

"I'll send it to you," he said. "But — Elspeth. It's a woman screaming, and then something falling down stairs. Like a sound effect. It's from a library of sound effects you can buy online for films. Number 4417: *Female scream, fall, stone stairs, interior, reverberant.*" He paused again. "The account it was uploaded from is in the name of Euan Strachan."

Elspeth sat in her car in the dark for a long time, with the engine off and the rain running down the windscreen.

The scream at twenty to nine had never been Clara Strachan. Clara had already been dead, at the foot of the tower stair, for half an hour or more. She had already been cold when Kirsty Ross found her.

---

She went back up to the house. It was after ten. The ground floor was dark except for a light under the library door. She went quietly up the main stair, along the gallery, through the low door into the tower, and up the spiral, without turning on the light. She stopped on the landing where Clara had been found and stood there in the dark.

She tried to imagine it.

Kirsty Ross, for some reason of her own, climbs the tower stair in the dark at about half past eight. Perhaps she's going to talk to Clara. Perhaps she's going to have it out with her. Perhaps she's just going to look at the woman who took the thing she loved. She doesn't turn on the light, because she doesn't want to be seen. She feels her way up the stair, one hand on the iron rope. At the landing her foot touches something soft. She bends down in the dark, reaching out to see what it is.

And a hand comes up out of the dark and seizes her wrist.

Elspeth stood very still on the landing.

The pathologist's report said Clara Strachan had died of a broken neck. It didn't say she'd died instantly. A high fracture can kill at once, but a lower one sometimes takes longer. There can be minutes, even tens of minutes, of terrible half-consciousness, with the body paralysed and breath coming hard, but one hand still able to move, to clutch, to grab at the dark.

Kirsty Ross reaches down in the dark, and the dying woman, lying broken on the landing, grabs her wrist. She holds it, hard, for perhaps a few seconds, with all the strength she has left, and then lets go. In the struggle Kirsty's grandmother's brooch is pulled loose and falls behind the iron rope.

And then, a few minutes later, while Kirsty is still kneeling there in the dark, frozen with horror, perhaps feeling for a pulse, the speaker in the bedroom above her screams.

Elspeth closed her eyes.

What would you do? You're twenty-three, on your knees in the pitch dark on a stone stair, beside a woman who has just grabbed you and let go and lies still. And from the room above comes a scream so loud it fills the whole tower, and the sound of someone falling. What would you think? That someone else was there, in the dark, above you, that you weren't alone. You'd run. Down the stair, along the gallery, to the back stairs. You'd be seen, perhaps, by a guest fetching a cardigan. And then you'd sit in your dark flat over the coach house with your bruised wrist and say nothing. Not because you'd done anything, but because you'd been on that stair, in the dark, with the dead wife of the man you loved, and no one in the world would ever believe you hadn't.

And there was something else, Elspeth thought. There must be, or the girl would have spoken by now. Kirsty Ross wasn't a fool. She'd had three weeks in a cell to think about that night. She must have worked out what Elspeth had just worked out, that Clara was already cold before the scream. And if she knew that, then she knew the scream had been staged, and by whom. And she had chosen to keep silent.

*That family has taken enough from ours,* her mother had said. *Don't you give them anything more.*

But she had. She'd given them everything.

## PART FOUR: THE HAND

### VIII.

They sat down to dinner on the thirteenth of October in the long dining room: Sir Hector, Miss Isobel, Euan, Tom Ferrie, and Elspeth Moir. Tom had stayed on at Euan's request, to finish the documentary, he said. Elspeth had begun to think it was for other reasons.

It was a quiet meal. Sir Hector talked happily about a trout he'd caught in 1974. Miss Isobel answered him with patient kindness, as she'd answered him for years. Tom Ferrie drank more than he ate. Euan sat at the end of the table, grey and silent, watching Elspeth.

When the plates were cleared and the housekeeper had gone, Morag Ross, white-faced and silent too, Elspeth put down her napkin and said, to the table in general, "I know who killed Clara Strachan."

Sir Hector smiled vaguely and asked if there was any more of the claret. Miss Isobel went very still. Tom Ferrie put his glass down too hard and it slopped.

Euan Strachan didn't move.

"Kirsty Ross didn't kill her," said Elspeth. "I'm going to the procurator fiscal in the morning with evidence that proves it. Clara was already dead, at the foot of the tower stair, for some time before the scream you all heard at twenty to nine. The scream was a recording. It was played through the speaker in her bedroom, on a timer, at a moment when every person who might be suspected of hurting her was sitting at this table. It was scheduled two days before."

There was absolute silence in the dining room.

Then Tom Ferrie said hoarsely, "Who—"

"I think you know," said Elspeth quietly. "Or you've guessed. That's why you've stayed on, isn't it? Because you've been afraid ever since that night that something was wrong, and that it would come back to you."

Tom stared at her. His face had gone the colour of the tablecloth.

"Clara and I—" he began.

"I know," said Elspeth. "I've spoken to her London friends. And I've found the hotel in Inverness. You were together for eight months, weren't you? You were going to leave, both of you, after the documentary was finished. She was going to ask for a divorce." She turned her head. "And Euan knew."

Everyone looked at him.

He sat at the end of the long table with his hands flat on the white cloth, and his face did a strange thing. It seemed to fall in on itself, slowly, like a house whose foundations have gone.

"Yes," he said. "I knew."

### IX.

He talked for a long time. Elspeth didn't interrupt him. She'd learned that too, over thirty-one years: when someone finally begins to tell the truth, you let them.

He had found them in June, he said, quite by chance, in Edinburgh, coming out of a restaurant on Thistle Street when they were both supposed to be elsewhere. He'd seen them through the window of a taxi. He'd seen the way Clara looked at Tom, the way she'd once looked at him. He'd watched them all summer, saying nothing. He'd read her messages on her laptop. He'd followed them to the hotel in Inverness and sat in his car outside, in the rain, for four hours.

And something had happened to him in that car, he said. He couldn't explain it. It was as if a door had opened in the bottom of his mind, onto something very old and very cold, and he'd stepped through it, and the door had closed behind him.

"I'd spent my whole life being the weak one," he said. He was looking down at his hands on the tablecloth. "The sickly one. The one who couldn't go to the army or play rugby or do anything a Strachan was supposed to do. The one who had to be protected and looked after. Even Clara looked after me. That was what she loved, at first, I think. That I needed her." His voice was very flat. "And then she found someone who didn't need her at all. Tom, with his television programmes and his rugby blue and his laugh. Who'd always been better at everything than me, since we were eleven."

Tom Ferrie made a sound, but said nothing.

"I wanted him to suffer," Euan said. "That was the whole of it. I didn't — I'm not sure I wanted Clara dead. I'm not sure she was even really Clara any more, by then. Not the woman I married. Just a sort of — a betrayal with her face on. But Tom. I wanted Tom to lose everything. His career, his name, his freedom. The way I had."

He had planned it for six weeks. He had planned it carefully, alone, at three in the morning in his study, the way he'd once planned marketing campaigns. Clara would die on the tower stair, a fall in the dark, from a woman who was afraid of the dark. But the time of the fall would be fixed by the scream, at a moment when Euan himself was at dinner, surrounded by fourteen witnesses, and when Tom Ferrie wasn't. Tom always left the table after the main course to smoke on the terrace below the tower, where nobody could see him.

"And then I'd make sure someone found out about them," he said. "The affair, the hotel in Inverness, the messages. And the police would look at Tom. The lover who wanted out. Alone on the terrace below the tower at the very moment she fell, with no one to say where he was."

"But Tom didn't go out to smoke that night," said Elspeth quietly.

"No." Euan almost laughed. "For the first time in fifteen years, he didn't. He'd given up, he told me afterwards. That week. For her. Because she'd asked him to." He looked up at Tom across the table. "She'd asked you to stop smoking because she wanted you to live a long time. Did you know that's what she said? I read it in her messages, afterwards, in hospital. *I want you around for a long time, idiot.*"

Tom Ferrie put his face in his hands.

"And I'd done it at half past eight," said Euan. "Gone up the stair while everyone was going in to dinner, while Aunt Isobel was in the kitchen with Morag. It took — not long. I turned off the light on my way down. Then I came back and sat at the table. I made conversation about the price of barley. And at twenty to nine the speaker screamed, exactly on time, and I was the first one out of the door. I meant to be first up the stair, so that I'd be the one who found her, so nobody would see that she was already cold." He stopped. "And then I saw her on the landing, and I picked her up, and she was cold. And I'd thought I could do it. I'd thought she wasn't Clara any more. And she was. She was."

He was silent a long time.

"I didn't know about Kirsty," he said at last, very quietly. "I didn't know she'd been on the stair. When they arrested her — I lay in that hospital bed for eight days, thinking. I couldn't let it happen. Not to her. Not after—" He stopped again. "I thought, if I hire someone good, someone better than Kerr, they'll find the affair, and they'll look at Tom, and Kirsty will be freed. I gave you the light bulb. I thought it would point at someone on the stair. I thought it would point at him."

He looked at Elspeth with his exhausted dark eyes.

"How did you know?" he said. "What did I miss?"

"The blood," said Elspeth. "It had clotted too far. And the girl. She told me Clara was already cold when she touched her." She paused. "And the hand."

"What hand?"

"The bruises on Kirsty's wrist," said Elspeth gently. "DCI Kerr thought they were from a struggle with Clara. Then I thought they might have been your hand, holding her, on the stair. But they weren't, Euan. The forensic lab measured them last week. They're too small to be yours. They're the size of a woman's fingers." She looked at him steadily across the table. "Clara wasn't dead when you left her. She was dying. And when Kirsty came up the stair in the dark and bent over her, she reached up and took hold of her wrist. As hard as she could. I think she was trying to tell her something."

Euan Strachan stared at her.

"Kirsty knows," said Elspeth. "She's always known. I think Clara said your name. I think that's why she wouldn't speak. Not to save herself. To save you."

### X.

There's not much more to tell.

Euan Strachan didn't try to leave. He sat at the end of the long table after Elspeth had finished, with his head in his hands, while Tom Ferrie wept openly at the other end and Sir Hector asked, puzzled, in his gentle old voice, whether something was wrong. Miss Isobel sat very straight and still with her hands folded in her lap, as if in kirk, and looked at her nephew and said nothing.

Elspeth rang DCI Kerr from the telephone in the hall. He came out from Inverness himself, in the rain, at half past eleven. To his credit, when he'd listened to the young man from Gartcosh and looked at the forensic report on the bruises, he didn't argue. He arrested Euan Strachan in the library at five past one in the morning, with great courtesy. They took him away in the back of a car down the long drive, between the dark trees, with the rain coming down.

Kirsty Ross was released from HMP Inverness two days later, on the fifteenth of October. Elspeth drove her home to the glen. They didn't talk much on the way. As they turned up the drive towards the house, the girl spoke for the first time in forty miles.

"She said his name," she said, looking out of the window at the wet trees. "When she held my wrist. She said, *Euan*. That was all. And then she let go. I didn't know if she was asking for him or telling me." She was quiet a moment. "Then the speaker screamed, and I ran."

"And afterwards? When you worked it out?"

Kirsty didn't answer for a long time.

"My mother said that family had taken enough from ours," she said at last. "I thought, if I keep quiet, then at least they'll owe us something. That one of them, at least, will owe a Ross his life." She almost smiled. "That's stupid, isn't it? That's a stupid reason to go to prison."

"It's a very old reason," said Elspeth. "It's the oldest one there is."

---

Euan Strachan pleaded guilty to the murder of his wife at the High Court in Inverness in March 2020. He was sentenced to life, with a minimum of eighteen years. He didn't serve them. His heart had always been weak. He died in his cell at HMP Shotts in the winter of 2021, of a cardiac arrest, at the age of thirty-six. He'd left a letter for Kirsty Ross. She never told anyone what was in it.

Sir Hector Strachan died the following year without, as far as anyone could tell, ever understanding what had happened to his son.

Strathmoy Distillery was sold in 2023 to a Japanese drinks company, which kept the name and the stills and the Moy Water, and gave the family history on the back of the bottles a new, shorter version that didn't mention Alasdair Strachan at all. Strathmoy House was sold separately and became a hotel. The tower room has a view down the whole length of the glen, and guests are advised to use the lift.

Miss Isobel Strachan lives in a small cottage in the village at the foot of the glen. She's eighty now. She still goes to kirk every Sunday, still chairs the community council, still walks two miles every morning in all weathers along the river. People in the glen say she has never once spoken about what happened at Strathmoy, and that she carries it the way she carries everything, upright, without complaint, as a duty.

But Elspeth Moir, who drove north to see her once, in the summer of 2024, saw something that nobody in the glen seemed to know about. In the old kirkyard at Rogart, in Sutherland, forty miles away, there's a grave with a small grey stone, almost illegible now, marking the burial in 1851 of a woman called Mairead Ross. And on the grave, freshly laid, there was a bunch of white heather from the hills above Strathmoy.

The girl at the kirkyard gate said that an old lady came every month and brought it, and stood there a long time, and never said who she was.

Kirsty Ross teaches history now at the High School in Dingwall. In the autumn term she takes her senior pupils on a trip to Strathmoy. She shows them the place where Achnamoy once stood, and the hearthstone in the floor of the old stillhouse, which the Japanese company has kept and lit, with a small plaque. She tells them about the forty-one families, and the ship from Lochinver, and the old woman who came out of a burning house with her hair on fire and spat in the road.

And she shows them the words carved over the door of the tower, worn almost smooth by two hundred years of rain: *QUOD SEMINAS, METES.*

"It doesn't mean barley," she tells them. "It never did."

25. THE HAND IN THE DARK

1. Title of the Work
The Shadow of the Mill
2. Creative Work
Blackwood Mill stood in the narrow throat of the Pennine valley like a stone sentinel, weary from two centuries of grinding water and broken lives. It had been built on the brutal sweat of the desperate, its massive oak beams soaked in the invisible despair of the riots of 1812, when starving weavers had fought their iron-fisted masters for the right to live. Now, it wore the hollow masquerade of a modern country estate. **Houses, like the bloodlines of men, cannot outrun their ghosts; they merely disguise their decay beneath a veneer of modern elegance.** The polished parquet floors, the imported tapestries, and the brilliant electric chandeliers only served to emphasize the grim, waiting silence of the ancient stone.

To cross the threshold was to step out of the roaring, mechanized twentieth century and into a frozen epoch of shadowed history. Yet, the current inhabitants played at rural simplicity with all the careless arrogance of wealth. Silas Blackwood, the frail, scholarly descendant of the original mill owners, had brought his bride, Seraphina, away from the glittering jazz clubs of London to this damp, isolated valley. Seraphina was a creature of restless boredom and modern cynicisms, treating the brooding architecture as a mere backdrop for her relentless social ambitions. She filled the echoing halls with her metropolitan friends—a flock of bright, chattering interlopers who smoked Egyptian cigarettes and drank cocktails where men had once starved.

On a suffocating autumn evening, the incongruity of this new world reached its peak. The guests were gathered in the dining room, the heavy velvet curtains drawn tight against the creeping valley mist. At the head of the table, Colonel Vance—a man with sun-baked skin and eyes like chips of flint—leaned forward in the candlelight, recounting a gruesome tale of a jade idol he had unearthed in a forgotten Cambodian temple. He spoke of ancient greed, of a thief whose hand had been severed in the dark, and of a blind, groping vengeance that followed the stolen jade across the oceans. Seraphina laughed, a thin, glittering sound, and adjusted the magnificent Blackwood Sapphire at her throat—a stone with a history of betrayal as dark as the mill itself. She declared that antiquity was merely an excuse for bad manners, and, complaining of a sudden headache, excused herself to her upstairs suite, leaving the men to their cigars and their shadows.

The scream tore through the civilized murmur of the dining room only moments later—a raw, primal sound of absolute terror that stripped away the centuries in an instant.

Silas dropped his glass; the crystal shattered against the mahogany table like a pistol shot. The men scrambled wildly up the grand, curving staircase, their laughter dead on their lips. They found Seraphina sprawled on the Persian rug of the master bedroom. The bright, restless defiance had been violently driven from her staring eyes, and the legendary sapphire had been torn from her bleeding neck. There was no weapon, no footprint, no sign of a struggle. **Civilization had proven to be but a fragile crust over the boiling magma of human savagery.**

Inspector Thorne arrived from the village with the cold, unyielding efficiency of modern law. He was a man who believed only in tangible motives, utterly blind to the oppressive weight of the mill's history. He searched the room with clinical detachment and, beneath the edge of the heavy oak bed, discovered a small, carved wooden bobbin—a relic of the old hand-weavers. It belonged to Elara, the quiet village girl who arranged the estate's flowers and read poetry to Silas on the long, lonely winter afternoons. Thorne’s conclusion was swift and devastating: a secret passion, a lover’s jealous rage, a swift theft to disguise the true motive.

But Silas, sitting paralyzed in the ruined bedroom, knew the truth ran deeper and darker than the Inspector's neat theories. He looked at the empty velvet jewel case and the blood soaking into the antique rug. He knew that the past had merely reached out its withered hand to claim the present. The stolen sapphire, the framed village girl, the brutal, silent violence—it was the same ancient, grinding wheel of the mill, turning once more, crushing new lives with the same indifferent greed. **The actors had changed their garments and their vernacular, but the tragedy remained eternally the same.**

She looked up.
Her face was exactly as he remembered it.

A mother carrying a sleeping infant.
They all turned toward him.
They were Mara.
Or rather, they were the lives Mara might have lived.
Elias crossed the threshold.
The field smelled of rain and warm earth.
His sister approached him.
"You came," she said.
He wanted to embrace her, but something in her expression prevented him.
"How do I bring you back?"
"You cannot bring all of me back."
"Then choose one."
She smiled sadly.
"That is what they have been doing to everyone."
The other figures drifted among the apple trees.
Mara touched the telescope.

"Why didn't you tell me?"
"I tried."
Elias remembered the last conversation in his workshop.
Her anger.
His impatience.
The door closing.
"I should have listened," he said.

"I could have prevented this."
"Perhaps."
Her refusal to absolve him was strangely merciful.
It allowed the past to remain what it was.
Mara led him to the edge of the field.
Beyond the apple trees he could see an ocean.
Across its surface floated innumerable lights, each moving independently.
"Every light is a history," she said. "Every history contains people who believe they are living the only possible life."
"What happens when Orre finishes?"
"The machine will select one final version of everything. All contradictions will disappear. All uncertainties will be resolved."
"And the others?"
"They will become inaccessible. Not destroyed, perhaps, but separated forever."
Elias looked at the ocean.
"Can we stop him?"
Mara nodded toward the handless clock.
"That is why I sent it."
He removed the clock from his coat.
For the first time, its empty face showed a moving shadow.
It resembled the minute hand of an ordinary clock, though there was no hand to cast it.
"How does it work?" Elias asked.
"It does not measure time. It measures the distance between what has happened and what might still happen."
The shadow advanced.
"When it reaches the thirteenth hour, the machine will complete its work."
"What must I do?"
"Return the clock to the center of the chamber and let it stop."
"And then?"
"The discarded histories will become independent. No one will be able to choose a single future for the entire world."
Elias looked at her.
"Will you come home?"
Mara did not answer immediately.
The wind moved through the grass.
At last she said, "There is a version of me that never disappeared. She lives in Bellwether. She has a husband and two children, and she remembers you with affection."
"Where is she?"
"In a history that has not yet been allowed to exist."
"Can I find her?"
"Perhaps."
"And you?"
She looked toward the sea.
"I am here."
He wanted to protest.
He wanted to demand that some power restore the world he had known.
Instead, he understood something he had resisted for three years.
His love for Mara did not entitle him to choose her life.
He embraced her.
For a moment she was simply his sister, warm and breathing, with the familiar scent of rain in her hair.
Then the field began to fade.
Chapter Six: A World Without Certainty
When Elias returned to the chamber, Orre was standing before the suspended rings.
The miniature city had become almost perfectly white.
Its streets were empty.
No smoke rose from its chimneys.
No clouds crossed its sky.
Every building stood in harmonious proportion to every other.
The city looked magnificent.
It also looked dead.
"The process is nearly complete," Orre said.
Elias approached the machine.
"How many people have you erased?"
"None," Orre answered sharply. "I have corrected conditions that should never have existed."
"How many?"
The director was silent.
Elias raised the clock.
Orre's composure broke.
"Do you understand what you're about to do? You will restore disease, war, catastrophe, and every cruelty humanity has ever inflicted upon itself!"
"No," Elias replied. "I will restore the possibility that they may happen. And the possibility that we may prevent them."
"You would trade certainty for hope?"
"Hope has no meaning without uncertainty."
Orre moved toward him.
"Think of your sister."
"I am."
Elias placed the clock inside the pale sphere.
For one terrible instant, nothing happened.
Then the rings stopped.
The miniature city darkened.
A deep vibration passed through the floor.
All around the chamber, the doors began opening.
From one doorway came the smell of the sea.
From another, the sound of a violin.
From a third, the voices of people speaking a language Elias had never heard.
The chamber filled with wind.
The white city inside the sphere fractured into thousands of luminous fragments.
Orre staggered backward.
"No," he whispered. "You are destroying everything."
But Elias saw that the fragments were not falling.
They were moving outward, each carrying its own light.
The chamber expanded.
Its ceiling dissolved into darkness filled with distant, burning worlds.
For a moment Elias saw countless versions of himself.
One had become a physician.
Another was a beggar.
One had died in childhood.
One had married Ada.
One had betrayed Mara.
One had never known her.
And one stood alone before a silent clock, wondering whether any decision could ever be entirely right.
Then the lights separated.
The walls returned.
The machine collapsed inward with a faint metallic sigh.
Dr. Orre was gone.
Only his empty shoes remained on the stone floor.
Elias knelt beside them.
He felt no triumph.
He had expected the destruction of the machine to produce some magnificent revelation, some final certainty that he had acted correctly.
Instead, he felt only grief.
He had ended the power to perfect the world.
He had also ended the power to repair it by decree.
Outside, morning had begun.
Bellwether did not awaken as the same city.
Some streets had disappeared.
Others led into neighborhoods no living resident remembered.
A bridge stood over a river that had not existed the previous day.
Families discovered unfamiliar photographs in their homes.
Old friends met one another as strangers.
A few people remembered dying.
Others remembered lives they had never lived.
The newspapers described the disturbances as a temporary disorder of public records.
The government issued statements promising a full investigation.
But no explanation satisfied everyone.
Over the following months, Bellwether became less orderly.
Its public gardens grew wild in places.
Buildings required repairs that the municipality could no longer anticipate.
Occasionally a train was late.
Sometimes an official decision was foolish.
People argued about the past.
They fell in love with unsuitable partners.
They made promises they could not keep.
They began, once again, to live without guarantees.
Elias returned to his work at the museum.
He no longer attempted to make damaged objects look untouched by time.
A cracked vase remained visibly cracked.
A faded portrait retained its scars.
When visitors asked why the restorations were incomplete, he explained that a history without evidence of damage was not necessarily a truthful one.
Ada came to see him often.
She had begun hearing ordinary sounds again, though not consistently.
Sometimes she heard birdsong.
Sometimes only the movement of dust across the windowsill.
Once she heard a bell strike thirteen.
She smiled when she told him.
"Perhaps the clocks are learning to count differently."
Elias laughed.
It was the first time he had laughed without remembering immediately afterward that Mara was missing.
Chapter Seven: The Unfinished Room
A year after the collapse of the Continuity Project, Elias received a letter.
It was written on ordinary blue paper.
There was no return address.
Inside, a woman explained that she had found his name in an old family album.
She believed they might be related.
Her name was Mara Ellery.
She lived in a seaside town several days from Bellwether.
She had two children, a husband who repaired fishing boats, and a peculiar collection of brass telescopes.
Elias read the letter several times.
Then he folded it and placed it in his desk.
He did not answer immediately.
For three days he walked through the city, considering what he should say.
He did not know whether Mara Ellery was truly his sister, a different version of her, or a stranger whose life happened to resemble something he had lost.
He understood that he might never know.
On the fourth morning he wrote back.
He told her about the museum, about Ada, and about the city where clocks sometimes behaved strangely.
He did not tell her that he remembered her childhood.
He did not tell her about the vanished histories or the chamber beneath the museum.
He simply said that he would be glad to meet her.
That winter, Elias began renovating the empty room beside his study.
It was a narrow space with a window overlooking the western gardens.
For years he had used it to store damaged furniture and unfinished projects.
Now he cleared away the clutter.
He painted the walls a pale blue.
He placed a small writing desk beneath the window and repaired an old chair.
On a shelf he set the brass telescope Mara had loved as a child.
Ada watched him work.
"Who is the room for?" she asked.
"I don't know yet."
"Then why prepare it?"
Elias considered the question.
Outside, snow was falling over Bellwether.
The city looked peaceful beneath the white roofs, but he knew that beyond the windows people were quarreling, grieving, forgiving, hoping, and making choices whose consequences they could not foresee.
He looked around the room.
"Because someone may need it."
Ada nodded.
She understood.
On the final evening of the year, Elias remained at the museum long after the other employees had gone home.
He was examining a painting that had arrived without a title.
It depicted an enormous hall beneath a starless sky.
At the center stood an open doorway.
Beyond it was not darkness, but a field illuminated by morning sunlight.
A woman could be seen walking away through the grass.
Elias studied the painting carefully.
He could not determine whether it was old or new.
Its surface had the cracked texture of an antique, but the pigments were fresh.
On the back of the frame someone had written a sentence:
What remains unfinished is not necessarily broken.
He turned the painting toward the window.
The glass reflected his face.
For an instant he saw another figure standing behind him.
A tall man in a dark coat.
The stranger's features were indistinct, though Elias had the uncomfortable impression that the man was smiling.
He turned.
The room was empty.
When he looked at the painting again, the doorway in the picture had closed.
The woman was gone.
Elias felt the old terror moving through him.
For a moment he was tempted to search for the explanation, to examine the canvas, to pursue the mystery until he could no longer distinguish discovery from obsession.
Then he heard footsteps in the corridor.
Ada appeared at the door carrying two cups of tea.
"You've been here all evening," she said.
"I was examining something."
"Did you find what you were looking for?"
He looked back at the painting.
The doorway was open again.
Beyond it the morning field stretched peacefully into the distance.
"I don't think so," he said.
Ada handed him a cup.
"Then come home."
He covered the painting with a cloth and extinguished the lamp.
As they descended the museum staircase, the city clocks began to strike midnight.
One.
Two.
Three.
Elias counted them without intending to.
By the twelfth stroke they had reached the street.
He paused beneath a gas lamp and listened.
For a moment the city was silent.
Then somewhere far away, beyond the gardens and the river, another bell sounded.
Thirteen.
Ada looked at him.
"Did you hear that?"
"Yes."
"What do you think it means?"
Elias considered the question.
Once, he would have been unable to rest until he had discovered the answer. He would have searched old archives, interrogated strangers, and sacrificed every ordinary happiness to the possibility of acquiring some final, forbidden knowledge.
Now he watched the snow falling on the uneven pavement.
A child was laughing in a nearby house.
Someone was playing a piano badly, repeating the same difficult passage with increasing determination.
From an open bakery came the smell of fresh bread.
The world contained mysteries, but it also contained these small and irreplaceable things.
"I don't know," he answered.
Ada smiled and took his arm.
They walked home together.
Behind them, in the deserted museum, the painting remained beneath its cloth.
For the rest of the night nothing moved in the darkened galleries.
Nothing visible, at least.
And in the little blue room beside Elias's study, where no one yet lived, the winter wind stirred the curtains around the open window.
On the desk lay an unfinished letter.
Its final sentence had been written carefully, then crossed out, then written again.
It read:
There will always be a place for you here, if you choose to come.
Outside, the city continued its imperfect journey into tomorrow.
And tomorrow, for the first time in many years, belonged to no one.
The End
