18. The Man Who Was Thursday

# The Man Who Was Indigo

*A Nightmare in Seven Colours*

---

## I. THE TWO POETS OF WALTHAMSTOW

There is a suburb of London, at the far north-eastern end of the Victoria line, which has been fashionable for about eleven years and will stop being fashionable any minute now. It's called Walthamstow, and it's full of artists. That is, it's full of people who moved there because they couldn't afford Hackney, and who now spend a great deal of money on sourdough to show that they're artists. Its streets of Victorian terraces have been painted in the colours of sweets. Its old pubs have been turned into craft breweries, and its old factories into studios. Its old residents have been gently priced out to Chingford and replaced by people with tattoos of fern leaves.

It was in the back garden of one of these painted terraces, on a cold evening in the second week of December, at a party for the launch of a poetry pamphlet nobody would buy, that Felix Marlow met Lucy Thorne.

Lucy Thorne was the poet whose pamphlet was being launched. She was twenty-nine, very thin and very pale, with black hair cut in a jagged bob as if she'd done it herself with garden shears, which she had. She wore a long black coat and fingerless gloves, and she had a voice like a match being struck. Her pamphlet was called *Unlight*. All forty poems in it were about how civilisation was a lie, order was a prison, and the only honest thing a person could do was set fire to the whole rotten edifice and dance in the ashes. She read four of them by the light of a patio heater to an audience of thirty people holding paper cups of mulled wine. They applauded enthusiastically, because it was cold and they wanted to go inside.

Felix Marlow didn't applaud. He stood at the back by the recycling bins with his mulled wine and said, quite loudly, "Rubbish."

Thirty heads turned.

Felix Marlow was thirty-four. He was also a poet, though a very different kind, and nobody in Walthamstow took him seriously, which he rather enjoyed. He wrote poems about the things nobody else wrote poems about: bus timetables, traffic lights, the 6:42 from Walthamstow Central arriving exactly on time, the extraordinary miracle of the Northern line, the heroism of the man who reads the gas meter. His pamphlet, which nobody bought either, was called *Signal Failure Is a Sin*. He believed, passionately and without irony, that order was the most romantic thing in the world. He thought the true rebel was not the man who throws a brick through a window but the man who keeps the trains running. In his view, every morning that the lights came on in London was a small, unreported miracle, achieved against overwhelming odds by people nobody would ever thank.

"I beg your pardon?" said Lucy Thorne, across the garden, over the heads of the audience.

"I said, rubbish," said Felix pleasantly. "Lovely imagery. Good rhythm. Complete rubbish. Anyone can write about burning things down. A toddler can knock over a tower of bricks. It takes a poet to see the miracle that the bricks were stacked in the first place."

There was an argument. It went on, after the audience had gone inside to the warm, for two hours, by the light of the patio heater, in the cold. Lucy said order was a lie the powerful told the weak to keep them in line. Felix said disorder was a lie the bored told the comfortable to make them feel interesting. Lucy said the trains running on time was the sound of the chains rattling. Felix said a train running on time was the closest thing modern London had to a cathedral. Lucy said he was a coward hiding behind timetables. Felix said she was a tourist who'd never actually seen chaos, or she wouldn't romanticise it.

At about eleven o'clock Lucy suddenly stopped talking. She looked at him for a long time across the patio heater, with her pale face lit orange from below.

"You think I don't mean it," she said quietly. "You think it's all just poetry. Imagery. A pose."

"Isn't it?"

She smiled. It wasn't a pleasant smile.

"Come with me," she said, "and I'll show you whether I mean it."

## II. THE SECRET OF FELIX MARLOW

What Lucy Thorne didn't know, and what nobody in Walthamstow knew, was that Felix Marlow was a policeman.

It wasn't the ordinary kind. He'd never worn a uniform or arrested a shoplifter. He'd been recruited, eighteen months earlier, in circumstances so strange he still sometimes wondered whether he'd dreamed them.

He'd been sitting on a bench on the Embankment, late one night in June, writing a poem about the lights of the Hungerford Bridge, when a man sat down at the other end. It was a policeman, a sergeant in an old-fashioned tunic, with a dry, intelligent face. They'd started talking. The sergeant had asked him what he was writing, and Felix had told him, a little defensively. And the sergeant, instead of laughing, had nodded slowly and said, "You love it, don't you? All of it. The bridges and the lights and the timetables. You think it's holy."

"Yes," said Felix, surprised.

"Then you're exactly the man we need," said the sergeant. He took a card out of his tunic and handed it over. It was plain white, with no name on it, just an address in Whitehall and a time: three in the morning, that night.

Felix went. Of course he went.

The address was a door in a blank wall in a lane off Horse Guards Avenue, with no sign and no bell. It was unlocked. Inside was a corridor, and at the end of it a room that was completely dark, so dark Felix couldn't see his own hand. Out of the darkness, from somewhere ahead of him, a voice spoke. It was very deep, very calm, very large, and seemed to come from everywhere at once.

"Sit down," it said. "There's a chair to your left."

There was. He sat.

"You've been brought here," the voice said, "because we've heard you love order. Not the order of the powerful, which is just another kind of greed, but real order: the order that keeps the lights on and the trains running and the water coming out of the taps. The order millions of people depend on every day without ever seeing it. Is that right?"

"Yes," said Felix.

"Then you should know that there are people in this city who want to switch it off." The voice paused. "Not for money, or for any cause you'd recognise. For its own sake. Because they've looked at the miracle of a city of nine million people that somehow works, and decided it's a lie, and that the only honest thing is to stop it. They're not ordinary criminals. Ordinary criminals want something. These want nothing. That's what makes them dangerous. And the only people who can catch them are people who understand them. Philosophers. Poets. People who understand ideas well enough to know when an idea has become a weapon." The voice was quiet for a moment. "We're a very small department, Mr Marlow. We don't exist. We have no budget, no offices and no name. We'd like you to join us."

"Why me?"

"Because you're the only poet in London who thinks the 6:42 from Walthamstow is a sacred event," said the voice, and Felix could have sworn there was amusement in it. "We need someone who'll fight for it."

"Who are you?" said Felix, into the dark.

But there was no answer. When he groped for the door and stumbled out into the dawn in Horse Guards Avenue, there was a white card in his pocket that hadn't been there before, with a phone number and a single word: *Welcome*.

He'd done nothing since. He'd rung the number every month and been told, by a pleasant woman, to wait. He'd begun to think it was a joke, or a hallucination, or a very elaborate prank by someone at a poetry slam.

And now Lucy Thorne was taking his arm in a cold back garden in Walthamstow and saying, *Come with me, and I'll show you whether I mean it.*

## III. THE MAN WHO WAS INDIGO

She took him to a launderette.

It was on Hoe Street, between a vape shop and a closed-down Polish deli: the Sunlite Laundrette, open twenty-four hours, with a flickering sign and twelve washing machines and a smell of fabric softener and damp. At half past eleven on a Thursday night it was empty except for a very old man in a flat cap, sitting on the plastic bench under the fluorescent lights, watching a single load of towels go round.

Lucy nodded to the old man. He nodded back. She walked to the last machine on the left, number twelve, opened its door, reached inside, and did something Felix couldn't see. The whole bank of machines swung silently outwards like a door, revealing a narrow flight of concrete steps going down into the dark.

"After you," said Lucy.

---

At the bottom of the steps was a long, low room that had once been a cellar or an air-raid shelter, lit by candles in jam jars. There was a trestle table down the middle, set with paper plates and a cheap bottle of red wine. And there were eight chairs, seven of them occupied.

Lucy stopped in the doorway and Felix nearly walked into her.

"Comrades," she said, in a different voice, very formal. "I've brought someone. A candidate. For the vacant seat."

The seven people at the table turned and looked at him.

Felix understood afterwards that this was the moment he should have been afraid. He wasn't. He was too interested. They were the strangest group of people he'd ever seen in one room, and he'd been to the Edinburgh Fringe.

At the head of the table sat an enormous man. He was not fat exactly, but vast, broad, as if he'd been built to a larger scale than other people, with a great bald head, a huge pale face like the moon, and a white beard. He was dressed entirely in white: a white linen suit, white shirt, white shoes. He sat absolutely still, with his huge hands folded on the table, and looked at Felix with mild, amused, terrible eyes.

On either side of him were six others. A thin, nervous young man in a red jumper chewed his nails. A plump, cheerful middle-aged woman in an orange cardigan was knitting. An old man in a yellow raincoat had very thick glasses and a long grey beard and appeared to be asleep. A broad, sensible-looking man in a green Barbour jacket might have been a farmer, or a vet. A sharp-faced woman of about forty in a blue trouser suit typed on a laptop. And a very small, very old woman in violet, with a violet hat, smiled at everyone like a grandmother at a christening.

"These are the Spectrum," said Lucy softly, at Felix's elbow. "Red, Orange, Yellow, Green, Blue, and Violet. And White. White is the President. When all the colours are mixed together, they make white light. And when we're finished—" she smiled her unpleasant smile "—there won't be any light at all."

"What's the vacant seat?" said Felix.

"Indigo," said the enormous man in white. His voice was deep and calm and large, and seemed to come from everywhere at once, and Felix felt the hair rise on the back of his neck. "Our previous Indigo died last week. A sad accident, on the Northern line. We need a replacement. Miss Thorne tells me you're a poet who loves order." He smiled. "Perhaps you'd like to tell us why we should trust you?"

Felix looked at the seven faces in the candlelight. He looked at Lucy, at his elbow, pale and eager. And he took a deep breath.

"Because," he said, "I've spent my whole life pretending to love order. Writing poems about bus timetables and traffic lights. And all that time, I've secretly hated it. Every single bit of it. The way it closes round you like a glove. The way nine million people get up every morning and get on the same trains and go to the same offices and come home and do it all again, for ever, like ants. I wrote those poems because I wanted to understand the enemy. Now I understand it." He looked at White. "And I want to switch it off."

There was a long silence in the cellar.

Then White began, very slowly, to laugh. It was a vast, rolling, delighted laugh, like a storm coming in off the sea.

"Excellent," he said. "Excellent! Sit down, Indigo. Welcome to the Spectrum. On midwinter night, at midnight, the shortest night of the year, we're going to turn off the lights of London. All of them. For good." He beamed. "Have some wine."

## IV. THE TALE OF A DETECTIVE

Felix walked home through the empty streets of Walthamstow at two in the morning, with his heart pounding and his mind going round like the towels in the launderette.

Midwinter night was the twenty-first of December, nine days away. He had no idea how the Spectrum meant to turn off the lights of London. Nobody had said. The plan, White said, would be revealed to each colour separately, at the proper time. But he had seen their faces. He had seen White's terrible, amused, moon-like eyes. And he knew, as surely as he'd ever known anything, that the vast man in white meant every word.

He rang the number on the white card from the bus stop on Hoe Street. The pleasant woman answered on the first ring. He told her everything. There was a long pause.

"Thank you, Mr Marlow," said the pleasant woman at last. "That's extremely helpful. Please continue as you are. Attend their meetings. Find out what you can. Report back. And — Mr Marlow?"

"Yes?"

"Be very careful of the President," said the pleasant woman. "Nobody knows who he is. Nobody has ever found out. Several of our people have tried." Another pause. "None of them came back the same."

## V. THE UNACCOUNTABLE CONDUCT OF THE WOMAN IN VIOLET

The Spectrum met again on the Saturday, in the cellar under the launderette. White didn't come. He'd sent word that he was unavoidably detained. The six colours and Felix sat round the trestle table in the candlelight and discussed the plan, or rather, discussed it without discussing it, in the elaborate code Felix was beginning to recognise. There were references to "the big switch," "the north feed," and "the dark at the heart of the grid." Red chewed his nails. Orange knitted. Yellow slept. Green made notes in a small black book. Blue typed. And Violet smiled at everyone like a grandmother at a christening.

When the meeting broke up, at one in the morning, Felix went up the steps first and out into Hoe Street. Halfway to the bus stop he became aware that someone was following him.

He looked back. It was Violet, the little old woman in the violet hat, toddling after him along the wet pavement with surprising speed.

He walked faster. She walked faster. He turned down a side street. She turned after him. He began, absurdly, to run, along Orford Road, past the shuttered cafés and the dark boutiques, under the frosty streetlights. And the little old woman in violet ran after him, her violet hat bobbing, faster than he'd have believed possible. She ran faster than him, in fact, until he turned into the churchyard of St Mary's at the top of the hill, gasping. She caught him up among the gravestones and seized his arm in a grip like a steel trap.

"Stop running, you idiot," she hissed. "I'm on your side."

Felix stared down at her.

She let go of his arm, reached into her violet handbag and took out a small white card, plain, with no name on it, just a phone number and a single word: *Welcome*.

"Detective Inspector Margaret Pettigrew," she said, quite crisply, in a completely different voice from the cooing grandmother of the cellar. "Metropolitan Police, retired, and now with a department that doesn't exist. I've been Violet for fourteen months. I watched you come in on Thursday and nearly had a heart attack. You're the first new face in a year." She peered up at him in the frosty light. "You're one of us, aren't you? The man in the dark room. The voice."

"Yes," said Felix faintly.

"Thank God." She sat down heavily on a gravestone. "I thought I was the only one. I've been sitting in that cellar every Saturday for fourteen months, pretending to want to plunge London into darkness, surrounded by lunatics, completely alone. Do you know what that's like?"

"Not yet," said Felix.

"You will," said Detective Inspector Pettigrew grimly.

## VI. THE EXPOSURE

It happened again on the Monday.

Felix was sitting in a café on Hoe Street with a coffee and a notebook, trying to make sense of the code from the Saturday meeting, when the man in the green Barbour jacket, Green, sat down opposite him without being asked. He had a square, sensible, weathered face and steady grey eyes.

"You're the new Indigo," said Green. "The poet."

"Yes."

"And Violet's been following you." Green looked at him steadily. "I saw her run after you on Saturday. A woman of seventy-eight, running like a whippet. That's not a woman who wants to turn off London. That's a woman who's been to police training college." He leaned forward. "So which are you? Are you with her, or are you about to tell White?"

Felix looked at the steady grey eyes for a long moment. Then, slowly, he reached into his pocket and laid the white card on the table between them.

Green looked at it. Then he laughed, a short, astonished bark of a laugh, and took an identical white card out of his own jacket and laid it beside Felix's.

"Sergeant David Achebe," he said. "Counter-terrorism, on secondment. I've been Green for nine months. I thought I was the only one too."

---

By the following Thursday, there were five of them.

It happened bit by bit, over the next few days, in a series of revelations that grew more absurd each time, until Felix began to feel he was in a farce. Blue, the sharp-faced woman with the laptop, turned out to be a cybercrime analyst from GCHQ, sent in eleven months ago. Orange, the cheerful knitter, was a retired MI5 officer who'd been tracking the Spectrum since 2019. She'd been knitting, she told Felix proudly, a jumper with the entire membership list encoded in the pattern. Yellow, the old man in the raincoat who always seemed to be asleep, was a professor of philosophy at UCL who'd been recruited, like Felix, on a bench on the Embankment. He was never asleep, he said. He was listening. He had been listening, with his eyes closed, for two years.

Each of them had been recruited by a voice in a dark room. Each had been given a white card, with no name on it, and the word *Welcome*. And each had spent months sitting in the cellar under the launderette, alone, pretending to want to plunge London into darkness, surrounded, as they believed, by genuine fanatics. Each was utterly convinced that they were the only one fighting for the light.

"It's absurd," said Yellow, the professor, in a café in Walthamstow at midnight on the Thursday. The five of them had crammed into a corner booth. "It's like a farce. A very bad farce. We've all been sitting in that cellar every week, terrified of each other, and every single one of us—"

"Not every one," said Blue sharply. "Red. The nail-biter. We haven't found Red's card."

They looked at each other.

"And White," said Detective Inspector Pettigrew quietly. "Nobody's found anything about White. Nobody knows who he is. I've been trying for fourteen months." She shivered. "Every time I look at him, I feel as if he can see right through me. As if he knows everything I'm thinking. As if he's laughing."

"He is laughing," said Felix. "He laughed when I told him I wanted to switch off London. Like a storm coming in off the sea."

They sat in silence in the corner booth.

"Midwinter night is in four days," said Green finally. "Whatever White's planning, we have to stop it. Together."

## VII. THE CRIMINALS CHASE THE POLICE

On the twentieth of December, the night before midwinter, it all went wrong.

Red, the nail-biting young man, had vanished from the Saturday meeting. Red, they all agreed, must be the real fanatic. Red was the one they had to stop. So the five of them went to the address Blue had traced for him, a flat above a kebab shop in Leyton.

The flat was empty. On the table was a note, in Red's spidery handwriting:

*They know. All of you. Run.*

And from the street below came the sound of a crowd.

---

Felix never fully understood what happened that night. He tried to piece it together afterwards, and it never quite fitted. It was like the logic of a dream, where everything makes perfect sense at the time and none at all in the morning.

There was a crowd in the street below the kebab shop: a hundred people, two hundred, more. Ordinary people, it seemed, in coats and scarves and woolly hats, holding phones and torches. And they were looking up at the window, and they were angry. Someone had posted online, the professor said afterwards, white-faced, scrolling through his phone. Someone had posted pictures of the five of them, with their names, and the words *THESE ARE THE PEOPLE PLANNING TO BLACK OUT LONDON*. And within an hour, the whole of east London seemed to have come out to find them.

They ran.

They ran down the back stairs of the kebab shop and out through the yard. They ran along Leyton High Road with the crowd behind them, past the closed shops and the Christmas lights. They ran through the dark of Walthamstow Marshes in the frost, with torches bobbing behind them and voices shouting. They hid in a lock-keeper's hut on the River Lea while the crowd went past. They crept through the back streets of Clapton at three in the morning, and took the last night bus to Hackney, crouching below the windows. And everywhere they went, there seemed to be more people looking for them. People in pubs, at bus stops, on the platforms of the Overground. People looking at their phones, and then at the five of them, and then shouting.

"It's madness," gasped Green, at four in the morning, crouched with the others behind the bins in an alley off Mare Street, with the crowd's torches flickering at the end of the street. "We're the police. We're the ones trying to save them. And the whole city's chasing us as if we were the criminals."

"Isn't that always the way?" said the professor bitterly. "The world can't tell the difference between the people trying to save it and the people trying to destroy it. They look exactly the same from outside. Both go about in disguise. Both whisper in cellars. Both say they're doing it for the city's own good."

Felix crouched behind the bins in the cold, with his heart hammering, and looked up at the sky. Above the rooftops of Hackney, the sky was orange with the glow of the city. Nine million people, more or less, and every light still on.

And in the window of a flat across the street, three floors up, a figure was standing, looking down at them. It was vast, and broad, and dressed entirely in white. It was too dark to see its face. But Felix could have sworn it was laughing.

## VIII. THE PURSUIT OF THE PRESIDENT

At dawn on the twenty-first of December, midwinter day, the five of them stood in the deserted lane off Horse Guards Avenue, outside the door in the blank wall with no sign and no bell.

They had come there separately, it turned out. Each had decided, alone, in the last hour of the night, to go back to the place where it had started. They'd find the voice in the dark and demand to know what was going on. And they'd arrived at the door within five minutes of each other, haggard and filthy and frozen, and stared at each other in astonishment in the grey light.

The door was unlocked.

They went in together. They went down the corridor, into the dark room.

"Sit down," said the voice, out of the dark. "There are chairs."

There were. They sat.

"You've done very well," said the voice. It was deep and calm and very large, and seemed to come from everywhere at once, and it was full of something Felix couldn't name. It might have been amusement, or tenderness. "All of you. Better than I could have hoped. You've been very brave."

"Who are you?" said Detective Inspector Pettigrew. Her voice was shaking. "I've been asking that for fourteen months. Who are you?"

And the lights came on.

They were sitting in a small, bare, whitewashed room with five wooden chairs and a table. At the table, enormous, filling the room, his great bald head gleaming under the bulb, his white linen suit immaculate, his huge hands folded, his mild, amused, terrible eyes looking at each of them in turn, sat White.

Nobody spoke for a very long time.

"You," said Felix at last. "You're the voice in the dark. You recruited us. And you're the President. You recruited them." His voice rose. "You were on both sides. The whole time. You sent us into that cellar to fight you, and you were sitting at the head of the table, laughing at us."

"Yes," said White simply.

"*Why?*"

White didn't answer. He stood up. He was even more enormous standing than sitting, so large that his head brushed the ceiling. He opened the door at the back of the room, and through it, impossibly, there was not a corridor in Whitehall but a garden. A vast old garden at night, under a sky full of stars, with lanterns in the trees and bonfires on the lawns, and music, and hundreds of people dancing in fancy dress.

"Come," said White. "There's someone you need to meet."

## IX. THE SEVEN COLOURS

They followed him out into the garden, and none of them ever afterwards agreed on what they saw there.

Felix remembered lanterns of every colour hanging in great old trees. He remembered the smell of woodsmoke and mulled wine, and music from somewhere, an old song he half knew, and people dancing on the frosty grass. They wore costumes: a man dressed as a lighthouse, a woman dressed as a train, a child dressed as a traffic light, two old men dressed as the sun and the moon, waltzing together. He remembered that there were seven great chairs on a terrace at the end of the lawn. Six of them stood in a crescent, each draped in a different colour, red, orange, yellow, green, blue and violet, with a seventh in the middle, draped in white.

And he remembered that there was an eighth chair, at the end of the crescent, draped in a deep, dark, beautiful blue, the colour of the sky just before the stars come out. Indigo.

They sat down in the chairs, all six of them, and White in the middle. And as each of them sat, the crowd of dancers roared and cheered and threw their hats in the air, the way crowds greet kings.

In the red chair, at the far end of the crescent, Red was already sitting. He was the thin, nervous young man who chewed his nails. He looked up at them as they came, and smiled shyly, and held up a small white card, plain, with no name on it, just a phone number and the word *Welcome*.

"Police Constable Toby Okonkwo," he said. "Sorry about the note. I panicked."

---

They sat in the seven chairs in the starlit garden, with the dancers whirling below them, and nobody said anything for a long time.

Then White spoke. His voice was dreamy, as if he were continuing a conversation, not beginning one.

"I sent you out alone," he said. "Each of you. Into the dark. I gave you a voice and a card and a task, and then I left you there, for months, for years, among people you believed were your enemies. You sat at that table every week, terrified, alone, certain that you were the only person in the room who loved the light. And you never gave up. Not one of you. You held on to that love when the whole world seemed to be against you. When your friends thought you were mad, and the city chased you through the night, and the very people you were trying to save hunted you as criminals." He looked at each of them in turn. "You were never alone. Not for one minute. You were surrounded, the whole time, by people exactly like you, each one in the dark, each one holding on. You just couldn't see each other. Nobody ever can. That's the whole secret of the world."

"But why?" said Felix. "Why do it like that? Why make us suffer?"

White looked at him with his mild, amused, terrible eyes.

And before he could answer, someone else spoke.

## X. THE ACCUSER

"Yes," said Lucy Thorne. "Why?"

She was standing at the foot of the terrace, below the eight chairs, in her long black coat and fingerless gloves, with her jagged black hair and her pale face lit orange by the bonfires. Felix hadn't seen her come. Nobody had. She stood alone on the frosty grass, while the dancers drew back from her on every side, and looked up at the seven people in their coloured chairs.

"I'm the only one, aren't I?" she said quietly. "The only real one. The only one in that cellar who actually meant it. Who actually wanted to put the lights out." She laughed, a short, terrible sound. "Six police officers and a professor and me. And all this time I thought I was part of something. A movement. Comrades. I thought I wasn't alone."

Nobody said anything.

"You want to know why I wanted to put out the lights?" she went on, and her voice was shaking now. "Because I've never once been inside them. You lot, with your timetables and your traffic lights and your trains running on time. You've never been the person outside the window, looking in. I grew up in a flat in Tottenham with no heating and a mother who drank, and I watched those lights every night through the window. Nine million people, all lit up, all warm, all getting on their trains and going to their jobs. None of them ever once looked out and saw me. I wanted to put them out so that, just for one night, everyone would know what it's like in the dark."

She looked up at the seven chairs, at the colours glowing in the firelight.

"You've never suffered," she said. "Not one of you. You've been warm your whole lives, and safe, and you call that holy, and write poems about it. What do you know about the dark?"

There was a long silence in the garden.

Then Felix stood up from the indigo chair.

"I know," he said, "that I've sat in that cellar every Saturday for weeks, terrified, alone, certain that everyone around me wanted to destroy everything I love. And so has she." He nodded at Detective Inspector Pettigrew. "For fourteen months. And so has he, and she, and him." He looked along the crescent of chairs. "Each of us. Alone, in the dark, holding on to a light that nobody else could see. We've been chased through the city in the night by the very people we were trying to save. We've been called criminals and madmen. We haven't slept. We've been more frightened than I've ever been in my life."

He came down the steps of the terrace, slowly, until he was standing on the frosty grass in front of Lucy Thorne.

"You're right that we've been warm," he said. "You're right that we never looked out of the window. That's true, and I'm sorry. But we have been in the dark, Lucy. Not as long as you. Not as badly. But enough to know that it's not something you'd wish on anyone. Not even nine million strangers who never looked out of the window at you." He held out his hand. "Enough to know you shouldn't have been out there on your own."

Lucy Thorne stared at his outstretched hand.

Then, slowly, she looked past him, up at the vast figure in white sitting in the central chair, with his great bald head silver in the firelight.

"And you?" she said. "You sent them all out into the dark. You sat at the head of the table and laughed. You were on both sides. You made them suffer, and you made me believe I wasn't alone, and it was all a game to you." Her voice cracked. "Have you ever suffered? Have *you* ever been in the dark?"

White looked down at her for a very long time.

His great face was quite still, like the face of the moon. Then, slowly, it began to change. It grew, or seemed to grow, until it filled the whole sky. It wasn't frightening, but enormous, and very old, and very tired, and very sad, and very kind. And his voice, when it came, came from everywhere at once: the trees, the stars, the frozen grass under Felix's feet, the lights of the city glowing orange on the horizon.

"Every night," he said. "Every night, child, since the first light was ever lit. I have stood outside every window."

And everything went white.

## XI.

Felix Marlow woke on the top deck of the N73 night bus, going north up Kingsland Road at half past six in the morning, with his forehead pressed against the cold window.

The bus was nearly empty. A cleaner in a hi-vis vest was asleep at the front, and an old man with a newspaper sat near the stairs. And beside Felix, in the next seat, in a long black coat with her hands in her pockets, was Lucy Thorne. She was looking out of the window at the city going by in the grey midwinter dawn.

He stared at her. She turned and looked at him. Her pale face was tired and quite calm.

"You fell asleep," she said. "Somewhere around Dalston. You were talking. Something about colours." She looked back out of the window. "We've been arguing since the party. All night, in the pub on Hoe Street until they threw us out, and then the café, and then the bus. You said order was holy. I said it was a lie." She was quiet for a moment. "You said something about being in the dark. About not wishing it on anyone. It was the first thing you said all night that I didn't want to argue with."

Felix looked out of the window. They were coming up Stamford Hill. Below them the city was waking: lights coming on in kitchen windows, shopkeepers pulling up their shutters, the first buses passing the other way, people in coats and scarves waiting at the stops with their breath steaming. Nine million people, more or less, getting up on the shortest day of the year, in the dark, to go and do it all again.

"I had a dream," he said slowly. "A very strange dream."

"Was I in it?"

"Yes."

"Was I the villain?"

He thought about it.

"No," he said. "No, I don't think you were. I think you were the only one in it who was telling the truth."

Lucy Thorne looked at him for a long moment. Then something happened to her face that he hadn't seen all night. She smiled, a real smile, small and tired and surprised.

"Get off at Seven Sisters with me," she said. "There's a café that does a decent fry-up. I'll tell you about Tottenham. And then you can tell me about your bloody bus timetables, and why you think they're holy." She stood up as the bus slowed. "I'll probably still think you're wrong."

"Probably," said Felix.

They went down the stairs together and out into the cold. The sun was coming up behind the tower blocks of Tottenham, red and low and enormous. It was the first sunrise after the longest night of the year. On every side of them, all across the city, the lights were going out one by one in the windows. Nobody was switching them off. It was simply morning.

23. The Man Who Was Thursday

## 1. The Watchers of the Glass Spire

## 2. Creative Work

The fog of the lower districts did not roll; it drifted like an audited ledger, neat and grey, settling upon the cobbles of Thames-side with an accountant's precision.

Julian Vane adjusted his pince-nez. The lenses were tinted a faint, defensive amber—not to keep out the sun, for no sun had troubled London since the committee began its sittings in November, but to dull the aggressive clarity of the modern world. Around him, the gaslamps of the embankment hissed with a wet, flat sound, like geese in a pond.

A man was leaning against the granite parapet some twenty yards away. His coat was cut with the exaggerated swagger of the younger aesthetic set—long in the skirt, velvet-collared, and altogether too loud for an evening that smelled of wet soot and stale porter. Yet it was not the coat that drew Vane’s eye; it was the stillness. In a city of frantic clerks and desperate cabmen, the figure stood like a monument to an unemployed eternity.

Vane stepped closer, his heels clicking a sharp, syncopated rhythm against the stone.

"The wind," Vane remarked, pitching his voice to the flat register of a civil servant addressing a junior clerk, "is blowing from the Essex marshes. It carries a distinct flavour of turnips today."

The figure turned slowly. His face was thin, carved with the sharp planes of a hungry hawk, and his eyes burned with an interior combustion that owed nothing to common health. A shock of dark hair fell over his brow in a studied posture of rebellion.

"It carries the smell of decay," the stranger retorted, his voice rich and resonant, vibrating with the spurious theatre of the lecture-room. "And decay, my dear sir, is the only true progress left to us. I am Julian Gregory. I spend my afternoons proving that the state is an illegitimate fiction and my evenings demonstrating that morality is a provincial error."

"An ambitious programme," Vane murmured, inspecting his own gloved fingers. "And does it leave you any time for breakfast?"

Gregory narrowed his eyes, sensing the absence of proper terror. "You speak with the atrocious calm of a man who believes in timetables. You are one of them—one of the tidy ones who think that because a train leaves at nine-fifteen, the universe has a destination."

"The universe," Vane said mildly, "does me the honour of arriving at Victoria at ten past ten. It is a narrow view, perhaps, but it saves one from the inconvenience of infinity."

Gregory struck the stone balustrade with a fist encased in an iron ring. "Infinity is our birthright! We are the vanguard of the great unmaking! Look at that river—a sewer of conventional morality, hurrying down to wash the feet of a hypocritical empire. We are the ones who mean to dam it with fire!"

"A formidable enterprise," Vane observed, adjusting his amber glasses. "Though I should imagine the masonry required would strain the municipal budget. Will you take a chop at the 'Blue Boar'? My cousin in the Home Office allows me a modest account for the pacification of poets, and I find you are considerably cheaper than the Irish."

---

Three hours later, past a grease-stained kitchen and down a flight of brick stairs that smelled powerfully of damp cabbage and secret printing presses, Gregory unlocked a heavy iron door.

"You mock us," Gregory whispered, his theatrical arrogance curdling momentarily into genuine heat as he threw the portal wide. "You think we are a club of undergraduates with pocket-pistols. Step inside, Mr. Vane, and tell me if your Bradshaw can map this."

The room beyond was circular, walled entirely with grey slate shelves upon which sat rows of round, iron vessels resembling oversized plums—each tipped with a brass nipple. In the center stood a long oak table littered not with manifestos, but with cold mutton, crusts of dry bread, and several bottles of inferior claret. Five men sat around it. They did not look like the destroyers of empires; they looked like men who had spent twenty years trying to balance the accounts of a failing provincial drapery.

At the head of the table sat the Chairman.

He did not rise as they entered. Indeed, rising seemed a physical impossibility for a frame of such architectural immensity. He was simply *there*, like an iron safe dropped into the center of a vestry. His white hair was brushed straight back from a forehead broad enough to bear an inscription; his coat was strained across a chest that seemed built to contain a cathedral organ. Yet his eyes—small, bright, and utterly devoid of mischief—fixed upon Vane with the terrifying hospitality of an executioner offering a choice of blindfolds.

"Ah," the big man rumbled. The sound was like gravel shifting in the hold of a barge. "The gentleman from the Board of Works. Or is it the Board of Redemption? They use the same stationery."

Vane did not flinch. He pulled out an empty chair, dusted the seat with his handkerchief, and sat down with the air of an inspector checking the weights and measures in a Welsh butter-market.

"My name," said Vane, "is Gabriel Vane. I am an official of the second class, charged with the supervision of public drains and private delusions. I have come to inform you that your conspiracy is awkwardly placed."

A murmur went round the table. A thin, rat-faced man with spectacles so thick his eyes appeared like magnified beetles spat into his plate of mutton. "We have no conspiracy. We are the voice of the absolute negation."

"Quite so," Vane nodded sympathetically. "And yet, your Mr. Gregory here has neglected to grease the hinges of your slate-room door. A conspiracy that squeaks is a public nuisance. The constable on the beat has noted it twice this week."

The Chairman leaned forward. The oak table groaned beneath the sudden redistribution of weight. "And what does the constable propose to do, Mr. Vane? Arrest the Absolute?"

"He proposes," Vane said, lifting his glass of claret to the light and squinting through the amber tint, "to ignore you until such time as you interfere with the omnibus traffic. London is very tolerant of the apocalypse, provided it does not delay the fishmongers."

Gregory leapt up, his face purple. "We are not a municipal inconvenience! We are the lightning before the storm! We have sworn to dismantle the machinery of heaven and earth!"

"Just so," Vane sighed, setting his glass down with a tiny *clink*. "And that brings me to the core of our little conference. Who is to replace the machinery? If you dismantle the post office, how are my circulars regarding sewage rates to be delivered? Have you considered the administrative vacuum, Gregory? An anarchist without a filing system is merely a burglar with a grievance."

The Chairman let out a sound—not quite a laugh, more like the deflation of a monstrous bladder. "He asks for the filing system," the big man murmured, his massive head rolling toward the beetle-eyed secretary. "Hear him? The world is burning, and he wants a blue ribbon for the bundle of twigs."

"I want," Vane said, rising with a dry, parchment-like dignity, "to go home. My slippers are warming by a very respectable grate, and my cook has prepared a mutton chop that does not pretend to be an instrument of cosmic justice. Gentlemen, your meeting is adjourned by order of common sense."

Gregory snatched up a heavy iron paperweight. "You leave this room only when we permit it, Vane! You are our prisoner!"

Vane looked at the iron weight, then up at Gregory’s trembling fingers. "My dear boy," he said gently, "I am not your prisoner. I am simply the only person in this room who remembers what day of the week it is. It is Tuesday. On Tuesday, at nine o'clock, I inspect the gas meters in Soho. If I am not there, a very dull young man named Inspector Gorse will come down these stairs with six policemen and a crowbar—not because he hates your philosophy, Gregory, but because he hates paperwork."

He turned toward the door, nodding courteously to the mountain of white hair at the head of the table.

"Good evening, Mr... Chairman, is it? Or do you answer to a day of the week?"

The Chairman did not move. His vast face remained carved in that monumental ambiguity, neither smiling nor frowning, like an idol fished out of a muddy river.

"Call me Saturday," the big man said softly. "It is the day before everything stops."

---

Three weeks later, Vane found himself walking through the same gray drizzle, though the scene had shifted from the cellars of Chiswick to the heights of Hampstead Heath. The scrubby gorse bushes stood up like bristles on the hide of a sleeping beast, and the city below was nothing more than a smudge of purple coal-smoke pierced here and there by the needle of a spire.

He was not alone. Behind him, splashing through the yellow mud with an irregular, halting gait, came a figure wrapped in an oversized mackintosh, an old green umbrella tucked under one arm like a broken spar.

It was the beetle-eyed secretary—the one they called the Professor. He had vanished from the cellar three days after Vane’s visit, leaving behind nothing but a half-eaten loaf and a volume of Schopenhauer annotated with rude remarks about the parish rates.

"You're following me," Vane said without turning around.

"I am not following you," came the thin, rasping voice from behind. "I am merely retreating in the same direction. It is a very different geometric proposition."

Vane stopped and turned. The Professor’s face was even greyer than it had been underground; his spectacles were smeared with rain so that he looked quite blind.

"Well?" Vane asked. "Has the universe collapsed yet? Did Gregory blow up the gasworks?"

"Gregory," the Professor spat into the gorse, "is an actor who forgot his lines. He went to Paris to throw a bomb at a cab-horse and was arrested for not paying his cab fare. The revolution is currently detained at a police station in the Rue de Rivoli."

"And the Chairman?"

The Professor shrank back slightly, as if the name itself had a physical weight. "The Chairman... do you know who he is, Vane?"

"I take him to be a retired contractor with a turn for heavy melodrama," Vane said, though his amber-tinted spectacles hid a sudden, sharp twitch of his eyelid.

"He is everywhere," the Professor whispered, clutching the green umbrella until his knuckles shone like peeled almonds. "I took the night mail to Edinburgh last Tuesday. I sat alone in the compartment. At Berwick, an old gentleman in a plaid shawl got in. He looked at me, Vane. He had those great, blind, blue eyes. He didn't speak. He just sat there and knitted a gray woollen muffler until the train reached Waverley. When I got out, the muffler was on the seat. It had no beginning and no end. It was just a loop of gray wool that went on forever."

"A common enough defect in amateur knitting," Vane remarked, though his voice lacked its usual dry polish.

"And yesterday," the Professor continued, his voice rising to a reedy pip, "I went to the British Museum. In the Reading Room. I sat at desk J-4. I looked up. At desk K-4, right across the aisle, sat the Chairman. He was reading a government report on the drainage of the Lower Medway. He looked across the ink-pots at me and smiled—just with the left corner of his mouth. Then he ate a biscuit. It sounded like the crack of doom."

Vane looked down at the city below them. The smudge of London seemed less like a human habitation now and more like a great, grey web spun by some industrious and indifferent spider.

"My dear Professor," Vane said, and for the first time his voice dropped its bureaucratic shell, revealing something thin and cold beneath, "you are suffering from an excess of imagination. Life is not an allegory. It is simply a very long series of mornings."

"Is it?" the Professor sneered, stepping closer, his breath smelling of stale chicory. "Then tell me this, Mr. Vane—why did you join them?"

Vane stiffened. "I did not join them. I investigated them."

"Did you? I saw your card, Vane. The blue card from Scotland Yard. Issued six months before you ever walked into Saffron Park. You weren't sent to watch us. You were sent to *find* us. But who sent you? Who told you where the cellar was?"

Vane opened his mouth to speak—perhaps to cite the Commissioner, perhaps to mention some forgotten memorandum from the Home Secretary’s desk. But no words came. The yellow fog of the heath seemed to thicken between them, smelling faintly of turnip-tops and old iron.

"He made us all," the Professor whispered, his eyes glaring behind the thick, smeared glass. "Every man jack of us. Gregory the fool, myself the coward, you the dry-as-dust who thinks he can audit the infinite. He set us running in circles like clockwork mice, just to see whose spring would snap first. And now the key is winding down."

The Professor turned sharply on his heel and plunged off the path into the wet bracken, his green umbrella tucked under his arm like a lance. Vane watched him go until the mist swallowed the black shape of his coat.

---

That evening, Vane did not go to his lodgings. Instead, he took a hansom down to the Embankment, paying the driver twice his fare without looking at the coins.

The tide was out, leaving a broad, glistening belt of Thames mud exposed beneath the stone walls—a grey ribbon sown with the broken crockery and iron scrapings of a century. Sitting on a stone bench, half-obscured by the shadow of Cleopatra’s Needle, was a figure.

Even in the gathering dark, there was no mistaking the bulk of him. He sat with his hands resting on his knees, his massive head bowed slightly as if listening to the pulse of the river beneath the masonry.

Vane walked slowly across the gravel and sat down on the other end of the bench. For a long time neither spoke. The only sound was the distant clatter of a coal-wagon over the Waterloo Bridge and the lapping of the dark water against the wooden piles.

"The Professor has been talking," Vane said at last.

"He always talks too much," the big man rumbled. "A nervous organism. Needs more butter on his toast."

"He thinks you are God," Vane said, his voice level, stripped of all irony.

The Chairman turned his great white head. In the dim amber light of the gas-lamp across the road, his eyes looked enormous—not fierce, but impossibly ancient, like two wells carved into the chalk of the downs.

"And what do you think, Gabriel?"

"I think," Vane said, staring straight ahead at the black lane of the river, "that you are an intolerable nuisance. You have disrupted my filing system. You have made me doubt the utility of the parish rates. And you have filled my head with an absurd notion that behind every lamppost in Soho there sits an archangel with a very poor sense of humour."

The Chairman let out a low, rumbling chuckle that shook the damp stone beneath them. "And is the archangel so wrong? Look at the city, Vane. Millions of men, walking through the dark, each one carrying within him a secret rebellion against the stars. They build streets, they buy boots, they elect parish councils—and all the while, their hearts are screaming because the world will not stay still. Are they mad, or are you?"

"We are both mad," Vane said bitterly. "Only I have the decency to wear a collar and tie while I do it."

The Chairman stood up. To Vane, sitting there in the damp dusk, the man seemed to expand until his white head cut off the grey reaches of the evening sky, blotting out the stars one by one. Yet when he spoke, his voice was quite ordinary—the voice of an old man with a heavy coat standing by the water.

"Come along, Gabriel," the Chairman said, holding out a hand the size of a ham. "The mutton is on the table, and Gregory is downstairs trying to explain to a French gendarme why he stole a cab-horse. It is going to be a very long night."

Vane looked at the huge, extended hand. He hesitated—perhaps for three seconds, perhaps for an entire geological epoch. Then, with a short, dry sigh that sounded like the turning of a very old page, he placed his thin, clerk's fingers into the giant's palm.

"I suppose," Vane muttered, standing up and shaking the Thames mist from his skirts, "there will be tea?"

"Gallons of it," said Sunday, turning his face toward the lights of London. "And none of it audited."

The storm arrived three days later.

The records would be burned.
The passages would be sealed.
Mara and Ilyra would be sent to an isolated religious house where their accusations could never be heard.
He called the decision necessary.

Mara caught his arm.
"Stop!"
"They are lies!"
"Then let them be examined."
"They will destroy everything!"
"No," she answered. "The deeds have already done that. The papers only show what happened."
A fragment of the ceiling collapsed between them.
Mara was thrown against a cabinet.
Severin stumbled backwards.
The floor gave way beneath his feet.
He caught the edge of a broken stone and hung above the rushing water.
"Help me!" he cried.
Mara crawled towards him.
She stretched out her hand.
He stared at it in disbelief.
"After what I have done?"
"Take my hand!"
He hesitated.
Below him the river roared.
He looked beyond Mara towards the staircase, where the other prisoners were escaping.
"Promise me," he gasped, "that you will destroy the papers."
Mara's expression changed.
"I will not."
"Then you condemn me!"
"No. I am trying to save your life."
His fingers slipped.
"Promise!"
"Take my hand, Severin!"
For a heartbeat he seemed ready to accept it.
Then he reached instead for the bundle of documents floating beside him.
The stone broke beneath his weight.
He vanished into the darkness.
Mara remained kneeling at the edge until the water forced her to retreat.
The bell rang once more.
Then it fell silent.

The survivors escaped through an old passage leading to the riverbank.
By dawn the storm had weakened.
The monastery stood above them, its towers emerging from the pale mist.
The western wing had collapsed, but the chapel and the principal buildings remained intact.
When the provincial authorities arrived, they found enough surviving documents to begin an investigation.
The accusations extended beyond Severin.
Several officials had knowingly accepted false confessions. Wealthy patrons had paid for private punishments. Monks who suspected the truth had remained silent for fear of losing their positions.
Yet the inquiry also revealed men and women who had resisted.
Some had hidden food for prisoners.
Others had preserved fragments of documents.
One novice had kept a secret list of the missing, concealed beneath the cover of a prayer book.
The monastery had contained cruelty, cowardice, kindness, and courage beneath the same roof.
No single judgment could encompass every soul within it.
Mara testified before the provincial court.
She spoke of her father, the hidden chambers, the false confessions, and Severin's final refusal to surrender the records.
The magistrate asked whether she believed the former superior had been an evil man.
Mara considered the question for a long time.
"He was a man who committed terrible wrongs," she answered. "But I believe the greater danger was that he taught himself to call those wrongs virtues."
"And do you forgive him?"
"I do not know."
The magistrate frowned.
"Surely you have considered it."
"Every day. But I do not think forgiveness can be demanded as another form of obedience."
Her answer was entered into the official record.
No one attempted to alter it.

Seven years passed.
The House of the Last Light no longer belonged to the religious order that had governed it.
Its damaged western wing was rebuilt, but the underground cells were preserved.
They were opened to visitors.
The names of the prisoners were engraved upon the walls, including those whose fates could never be discovered.
Above the entrance, a simple inscription was placed:
No sanctuary is holy when it requires the silence of the suffering.
Mara became the keeper of the house.
She refused the title of superior.
Instead, those who lived and worked there formed a council. Its decisions were recorded, questioned, and reconsidered.
The building sheltered travellers, orphaned children, and those fleeing persecution.
No one was required to confess before receiving food.
No one was imprisoned for doubting the judgment of another.
The old library was restored.
Its doors remained open throughout the day.
Brother Lucan lived long enough to see the transformation. In his final years he taught the children to read, sometimes pausing over a difficult passage as though each word were a small debt he had finally been allowed to repay.
Ilyra became the keeper of the records.
She insisted that the history of the monastery should include not only its crimes, but also the names of those who had shown courage within it.
"Otherwise," she told Mara, "we shall allow cruelty to claim the whole of the past."
One autumn evening, a young boy asked Mara about the bell that hung in the courtyard.
It was old, darkened by centuries of weather, and cracked along one side.
"Why do we never ring it?" he asked.
"Because it was once used by people who were not allowed to leave."
"Was it a punishment?"
"No. At first it was meant to summon help."
"Did anyone come?"
"Not often enough."
The boy considered this.
"Then why keep it?"
Mara looked towards the mountains.
"Because a thing that failed in its purpose may still teach us what that purpose was."
The child placed his hand against the metal.
"Can we make it ring again?"
She smiled.
"Yes."
Together they drew the rope.
The bell gave a rough, imperfect sound.
It was not beautiful.
A crack disturbed its note, and the echo broke unevenly against the stone walls.
Yet people emerged from the library, the gardens, and the kitchens to discover what had happened.
They gathered beneath the bell.
Some laughed at its awkward voice.
Others listened in silence.
Mara watched them and remembered the chambers beneath the monastery, the imprisoned woman whispering through stone, and the man who had valued his innocence more than the lives of those who depended upon him.
She had once believed that goodness was a condition a person might achieve and thereafter possess.
Now she understood it differently.
Goodness was not a spotless garment, preserved by refusing to touch the wounded.
It was the willingness to recognize another person's suffering, to accept responsibility for one's own actions, and to choose compassion even when compassion demanded the surrender of pride.
The bell sounded again.
This time the children ran towards it.
Epilogue: The Last Confession
Many years after Severin's death, a sealed letter was discovered behind a panel in his former study.
The paper had yellowed, and its edges were damaged by damp.
It was written in his hand.
There was no date.
The letter contained only a few lines.
He had written that, as a young man, he once watched a servant punished for breaking a precious vessel. He knew the servant was innocent, for he himself had broken it.
He had remained silent.
The servant was dismissed.
For years Severin remembered the incident with shame. Eventually, however, he persuaded himself that his silence had been necessary to protect the reputation of the religious house.
Soon he came to believe that preserving the reputation of a sacred institution was itself an act of virtue.
Then he began to believe that protecting his own reputation served the same purpose.
At the bottom of the page, the handwriting became unsteady.
I have spent my life teaching others to confess. I do not know whether I have ever done so myself.
There was no signature.
Ilyra brought the letter to Mara, who was now old enough to see in its trembling sentences something she might once have overlooked.
Not innocence.
Not redemption.
But the brief appearance of a truth Severin had spent his life refusing to acknowledge.
"Shall we add it to the records?" Ilyra asked.
"Yes."
"Even though it may cause some people to pity him?"
Mara folded the letter carefully.
"Pity does not erase what he did."
"And hatred?"
"Neither does that."
They placed the letter beside the testimonies of the people who had suffered under his authority.
It was neither hidden nor elevated above the others.
That evening the wind moved through the monastery gardens, carrying the scent of wet leaves and approaching winter.
The children had gathered in the courtyard to ring the old bell.
Its uneven voice travelled across the valley, where the river still flowed between the cliffs.
Mara stood at the library window and listened.
Once, the monastery had demanded that every human weakness be concealed beneath an appearance of perfection.
Now its walls held the evidence of ordinary and imperfect lives, with their failures, courage, grief, and capacity for change.
She thought of the long years during which she had searched for some final explanation of Severin's cruelty.
The answer had proved both simpler and more frightening than she expected.
He had not become cruel because he lacked the language of goodness.
He had become cruel because he had mistaken that language for goodness itself.
Outside, the bell sounded a final time.
Its echo travelled beyond the monastery, across the river and into the mountains.
For a moment the valley seemed to answer.
Then the sound faded, leaving only the voices of the living.
And in that ordinary mingling of laughter, disagreement, sorrow, and affection, Mara found something greater than the perfection Severin had pursued.
Not a world without darkness.
But a world in which darkness no longer possessed the right to call itself light.
The End.
