23. The Odyssey

# The Net

*A story in twenty-four knots*

---

## I. THE WIFE

On the island of Lunhaw, in the Camotes Sea, between Cebu and Leyte, there's a woman who has been making the same fishing net for nineteen years.

Every morning, Pilar Santos opens her small sari-sari store at the top of the beach in the village of Kalubihan. She sells cigarettes, sachets of shampoo, cooking oil by the cup, Coke in glass bottles, prepaid phone credit, and fish crackers. Then she sits on a plastic stool behind the counter, under a faded Pepsi umbrella, with a great heap of nylon twine in her lap, and she ties knots.

It's a gill net, the kind her husband used to make, the kind his father made, and his father's father, back to the time before anyone wrote things down. You make a gill net one knot at a time with a wooden shuttle and a gauge: a knot, a mesh, a knot, a mesh, row after row, until it's a hundred metres long. A good netmaker can finish one in a month.

Pilar has been making hers since the April of 2005. It's never been finished.

That's because every night, after she's closed the store and her son has gone to bed, she sits alone in the dark by the window with a kerosene lamp. With a small sharp knife, very carefully, she cuts through the knots she tied that day and pulls the twine free, back to where it was the night before.

Nobody on the island knows this except her. They know only that Pilar Santos has been making a net for nineteen years. Most of them think she's a little crazy. Some think she's a saint. And the men who want her land think she's playing for time.

They're right.

---

Her husband's name was Eliseo Santos. Everyone called him Ely.

In 2005 he was thirty-one, the best fisherman on Lunhaw, and the cleverest man anyone on the island had ever known. He could mend an outboard motor with a hairpin. He could talk a fish into a net. And he could talk his way out of any trouble the island had to offer: barangay disputes, fights at the cockpit, the coast guard, the parish priest. People said he could have talked the devil out of his own tail. He had a laugh that carried across the bay, and a scar on his left thigh, long and white, from a marlin's bill when he was sixteen.

He also had debts. The fishing was dying around Lunhaw by 2005. The big commercial boats from Cebu with their fine-mesh nets had stripped the reefs, and the coral was bleaching. A man couldn't feed a family on what came out of the sea any more. So when an agent came over from Cebu City offering contracts for experienced fishermen on deep-sea tuna boats out of Taiwan, at four hundred dollars a month, two-year contracts, money sent home direct, Ely signed.

He kissed Pilar on the pier at Kalubihan on the ninth of April 2005, with their son Tomas, aged two, on her hip. He said, laughing, that he'd be home in two years with enough money to buy a proper boat, and they'd never be poor again. He told her to make a net while he was gone, so he'd have something to fish with when he came back.

She never heard from him again.

## II. THE SON

Tomas Santos was twenty-one in the spring of 2024. He had no memory of his father at all.

He had a photograph: a thin, laughing man with a moustache, squinting into the sun on the prow of a banca, holding up a grouper. He had the stories, a thousand of them, told by his mother and his grandmother and every old fisherman on the island. Ely and the marlin. Ely and the coast guard. Ely and the time he talked the bishop of Cebu into blessing the cockpit. And he had a gap, the shape of a man, in the middle of his life, that he'd been walking round since he could walk.

He'd finished school on the island and worked on the boats, what boats there were, and in the resort. He'd watched his mother sit under the Pepsi umbrella every day making her net. And he'd watched the men come.

They'd started coming about ten years before, when the first resort was built on the other side of the island. There were rich men from Cebu and Manila, and a Korean consortium, and the barangay captain's cousin, who had a construction company. They wanted the land: the three hectares of coconut and beach and mangrove at the north end of Kalubihan that had belonged to Ely's family for four generations, and that was now, legally, in a mess. Ely had never made a will. He'd never been declared dead. His wife couldn't sell, and nobody could buy. She could sign the papers to have him declared legally dead, which she was entitled to do after seven years. Then the land would be hers, and she could sell it for more money than anyone in Kalubihan had ever seen. They came to the store under the Pepsi umbrella and explained this to her, very patiently, again and again.

"He's dead, Ate Pilar," they said. "Nineteen years. You know he's dead. Let him go. Think of your son."

And Pilar would look up from her net, smile politely, and say she'd sign the papers when the net was finished.

By 2024 there were seven of them who came regularly. Chief among them was Antonio Lim, the barangay captain's nephew, forty-five, smooth and well-fed, with a gold watch and a white Hilux. His company wanted to build a hundred-room resort with a marina on Ely's three hectares. He'd let it be known, quite openly, that he would marry the widow Santos if necessary to get them. He came to the store every evening and sat on the plastic chair by the counter, drinking her Coke without paying for it, telling her she was still a beautiful woman, and that it was time.

The others ate at her table, slept in her late father-in-law's empty house, drank at the store, and helped themselves. They brought their friends. They talked about her husband as a joke. They told Tomas, laughing, that he was a man now, and should make his mother see sense.

In April 2024, nineteen years to the week after his father left, Tomas Santos decided he'd had enough. He took his savings, eleven thousand pesos, and the photograph. He took the ferry to Cebu City, to find out what had happened to Eliseo Santos.

## III. NOBODY

Here is what had happened to Eliseo Santos.

The agent in Cebu City had been a liar. That was the first thing. There were no two-year contracts and no four hundred dollars a month sent home direct. There was a flight to Kaohsiung on a tourist visa, a night in a locked room at the port with eleven other men, and then a long-line tuna boat called the *Hai Feng 7*. It was rusted and stinking, with a crew of twenty-two: Filipinos, Indonesians, Vietnamese, a couple of Burmese. It sailed south into the Pacific and didn't come back to port for three years.

The captain was a huge man from Fujian whom the crew called the One-Eyed, because he'd lost an eye to a snapped longline years before, and wore no patch, and didn't care who saw. He was the most frightening person Ely had ever met. He ran the *Hai Feng 7* the way a farmer runs a pig shed. The men worked twenty hours a day hauling longlines, slept four, ate rice and fish bait, and were beaten if they slowed down. Their passports were locked in the captain's cabin. Their wages, the agent's four hundred dollars, were "held back against expenses," which never ended. Men who got sick were left in their bunks. One of the Indonesian boys, eighteen, died of beriberi in the second year and was put over the side in a tarpaulin while the One-Eyed watched from the bridge, eating noodles.

Ely survived because he was clever.

He learned the captain's language, enough of it. He learned which officers could be bribed with cigarettes and which would report you. He mended the boat's ancient radio, the engine, and the freezer, and made himself too useful to beat. And he waited.

In the third year the *Hai Feng 7* put into Suva, in Fiji, for fuel and to offload catch to a refrigerated transport. The One-Eyed came down to the crew quarters in the night, drunk, and stood over Ely's bunk with a torch, and asked him his name.

"My name is Walang Tao," said Ely, in Tagalog. *Nobody.*

The One-Eyed laughed, and went away, and wrote it in the crew log.

At three in the morning, Ely and four others went over the side into the black water of Suva harbour. They swam half a mile to the docks. In the morning the One-Eyed went raging to the port police and reported deserters. When the police asked for their names, he looked in his log, and the first one said *Walang Tao*. When the Fijian officer, who had a Filipino wife, translated it for him, the whole police station laughed. The One-Eyed stood in the doorway, purple with rage, shouting that Nobody had robbed him, Nobody had escaped, Nobody must be found.

Nobody was never found.

## IV. THE ISLAND OF FORGETTING

For four years after that, Ely Santos didn't exist.

He had no passport, no papers, no money. He was an illegal in Fiji, a country he'd never heard of until he arrived. He worked where he could: on construction sites in Suva, on sugar plantations near Lautoka, on fishing boats out of Levuka, paid in cash, sleeping in barracks with other men who also didn't exist. He tried to get word home. He wrote letters that were never answered. He found out later that the agent in Cebu had given a false address on all his papers. He rang the only phone number on Lunhaw he remembered, the barangay hall, from a phone box in Suva, and got a recorded message in a language he didn't understand. The number had changed.

And then, on a small island in the Lau group, in the east of Fiji, where he'd gone to work on a copra plantation, he met Vasiti.

She was a widow, thirty-five, the daughter of the local chief, and she ran a small guesthouse for divers on a beach of white sand under coconut palms. It was the most beautiful place Ely had ever seen, more beautiful than Lunhaw. The reef there was still alive, still full of fish, as Lunhaw's had been when he was a boy. She took him in. She fed him and gave him work, mending the boats and guiding the divers, and then she gave him a room in her house, and then everything else.

"Stay," she said, after the first year, lying beside him under the mosquito net with the surf breathing on the reef. "Why go back? There's nothing for you there. They think you're dead. Your wife will have married again. Your son won't know you. Here you have everything. The sea, the fish, me. My father will give you land. You can be a man here, Ely, not a ghost. You can forget all of it. You can be happy."

And for a long time, he was.

He stayed on Vasiti's island for seven years. He learned to speak Fijian. He fished the living reef. He drank kava with the chief and his men in the evenings, and slept under the mosquito net with the surf on the reef, and was, in every way that anyone could see, a happy man. Vasiti's father gave him land. The village came to think of him as one of their own. Some days, for weeks at a time, he didn't think about Lunhaw at all.

But every evening, at sunset, he walked to the end of the beach alone and sat on a rock looking north-west, across six thousand kilometres of ocean, towards a place he couldn't see. And Vasiti, watching him from the door of the guesthouse, knew she was losing him, and had always been going to.

"What's there?" she asked him once, sitting beside him on the rock. "What's there that I can't give you?"

He thought about it for a long time.

"A net," he said at last. "My wife is making a net. I told her to, when I left. I want to see if she finished it."

Vasiti looked at him for a long time. Then she put her head on his shoulder and wept. The next morning she went to her father. Her father went to a cousin in Suva who worked for the government, and the cousin found a lawyer, and the lawyer found an official at the Philippine embassy who owed him a favour. And eleven months later, in the spring of 2024, a man called Eliseo Santos was issued an emergency travel document by the Philippine embassy in Suva, and a ticket home.

Vasiti took him to the boat herself. She didn't cry on the dock. She kissed him once, and gave him a carved wooden bowl her husband had made, and said, "Go and see your net."

## V. THE BEGGAR

Ely Santos came home to Lunhaw on the twenty-third of May 2024, on the afternoon ferry from Danao. He was fifty, and nobody knew him.

He'd changed. Nineteen years of the sea and the sun and the One-Eyed and the sugar fields had made an old man of him. He was thin and stooped, his face burned black and seamed like a dried riverbed, his hair and moustache gone white, with a limp from a winch accident on the *Hai Feng 7*. He wore a cheap shirt and a pair of old trousers, carried a plastic bag with everything he owned in it, and spoke Cebuano with a strange accent that he couldn't get rid of. He stood on the pier at Kalubihan where he'd kissed his wife goodbye, and looked up at the beach, the palm trees, the store with the faded Pepsi umbrella. Under it sat a grey-haired woman with a great heap of nylon twine in her lap, tying knots.

He didn't go to her.

He'd thought about this moment for nineteen years, and in the end, he didn't go to her. He didn't know what he'd find. He didn't know who she was now, or who was in her house, or whether she'd married again, or whether his son was alive. He'd learned, on the *Hai Feng 7* and in the barracks of Suva and the cane fields of Lautoka, that a man who walks into a strange place and tells the truth about himself is a fool. So he walked up the beach past the store, limping, with his plastic bag, and nobody looked at him twice. He was just an old man, a beggar perhaps, off the ferry.

He walked to the old house of Ka Emong, the swineherd, at the top of the village, who had been his father's friend.

Ka Emong was eighty-one, nearly blind, and kept pigs in a pen behind his house, as he had for sixty years. He gave the old stranger a bowl of rice and a fried fish and a place to sleep on the porch, as anyone on Lunhaw would. And over the rice, not knowing who he was talking to, he told the stranger everything.

He told him about Ely Santos, the best fisherman on the island, who'd gone away to Taiwan nineteen years ago and never come back. He told him about Pilar, who'd waited, and waited, and was still waiting. He told him about the net she'd been making for nineteen years, which was never finished. He told him about the men who came for the land, Antonio Lim and the others, who ate at her table and drank her Coke and slept in her father-in-law's house, and laughed at her husband's memory, and wanted her to sign the papers. And about the son, Tomas, who'd gone to Cebu City a month ago to find out what had happened to his father.

"They're going to make her sign," said Ka Emong, squinting into the dark. "Antonio Lim's got the barangay captain on his side, and a judge in Cebu. They're saying if she doesn't sign by the fiesta, they'll go to court and have Ely declared dead anyway, and then the land goes to auction for the debts, and Lim buys it for nothing." He shook his head. "The fiesta's in nine days. Poor Pilar. Poor Ely. He was a good man. A clever man. If he was here, he'd talk them all into the sea."

Ely sat on the porch in the dark and said nothing for a long time. Then he asked, "And the son? The boy?"

"Coming home," said Ka Emong. "Tomorrow. On the morning boat. He rang. He didn't find anything."

## VI. THE SON AND THE FATHER

Tomas Santos came home on the morning ferry on the twenty-fourth of May with nothing.

He'd spent a month in Cebu City and then in Manila, going from office to office: the Philippine Overseas Employment Administration, the Department of Foreign Affairs, the Coast Guard, a dozen NGOs that worked with trafficked seafarers. He'd found the agent's office in Cebu, long closed, and the name of the boat, the *Hai Feng 7*, in an old report by an NGO in Taiwan on forced labour in the tuna fleets. He'd found a list of crew names from 2005 to 2008, partial, incomplete. His father's name was on it, and then, in 2008, it wasn't. The NGO said the *Hai Feng 7* had been seized by the Fijian authorities in 2012 for illegal fishing and broken up for scrap. It had no records of the crew. His father had simply gone.

He came up the beach from the pier, tired and dusty, and went up the path to the top of the village, to Ka Emong's house, because he couldn't yet face his mother. On the porch, an old man was sitting, a stranger, thin and stooped and burned black, mending a broken fishing line with his fingers.

The old man looked up at him.

Tomas didn't know him. How could he? He had no memory of his father at all, only a photograph of a thin laughing man with a moustache on the prow of a banca. This old man had a white moustache and a face like a dried riverbed and the eyes of someone who had seen terrible things.

But the old man looked at Tomas for a long time, and his face did something strange. It seemed to fall in, and then fill up again, like the tide.

"Sit down, son," he said, in Cebuano, with a strange accent. "Ka Emong's gone to feed the pigs. Sit with me a while."

Tomas sat. He couldn't have said why.

They talked, the old stranger and the young man, on Ka Emong's porch, for an hour. Tomas told him, he didn't know why, about Cebu, Manila, the *Hai Feng 7*, the crew list, and the name that disappeared in 2008. The old man listened with his eyes closed. Then, when Tomas had finished, he opened his eyes and said, very quietly, "In 2008, in Suva harbour, five men went over the side of the *Hai Feng 7* at three in the morning and swam to the docks. When the captain reported them to the police, the first name in his log was *Walang Tao*."

Tomas stared at him.

"It was a joke," said the old man. "The captain asked me my name one night, drunk. I told him Nobody. He wrote it down. Then I disappeared." He reached down slowly and pulled up the left leg of his old trousers. On his thigh, long and white against the black, was a scar. "A marlin," he said. "When I was sixteen, off the reef at Pasil. Your grandfather pulled the bill out with his hands."

Tomas Santos sat very still on Ka Emong's porch for a long time.

Then he put his head in his hands and wept like a child. His father put his arms round him and held him, for the first time in nineteen years, and wept too.

## VII. THE PLAN

They didn't tell anyone. That was Ely's idea, and Tomas, once he understood, agreed.

"If I walk into that store now," said Ely, that night, on Ka Emong's porch, "and tell your mother who I am, what happens? Antonio Lim laughs. He says I'm an old beggar off the ferry who's heard the story and wants the land. He says I'm a fraud. He has the barangay captain and a judge in Cebu. I have no ID except a travel document from Fiji that anyone could fake. No birth certificate, no marriage certificate. The church burned down in '09, Ka Emong says, with all the records. I have a scar, and nineteen years of stories nobody can check." He shook his head. "They'll throw me off the island in a day, son. And your mother will have to watch it."

"So what do we do?"

Ely looked out across the dark bay, towards the store under its Pepsi umbrella, where a single kerosene lamp was burning in an upstairs window.

"The fiesta," he said. "In eight days. Antonio Lim wants her to sign at the fiesta, in front of everyone, Ka Emong says. Make a show of it. He'll make a speech. He'll give money to the church." He was quiet for a while. "Let him. Let him have his show. And we'll give him one he won't forget."

---

So for eight days, Eliseo Santos lived as a beggar in his own village.

He slept on Ka Emong's porch. He helped with the pigs. He sat on the beach in the mornings with the old men, mending nets, and listened to everything. He went to his own wife's store every afternoon and bought a single cigarette with the coins Tomas gave him, and stood at the counter under the Pepsi umbrella, a few feet from her, while she tied her knots. He watched her hands moving, quick and sure, as they always had. He looked at the grey in her hair and the lines round her eyes, and saw that she was still the most beautiful woman he had ever seen. She didn't recognise him. She sold him a cigarette and gave him his change and smiled politely, the way she smiled at strangers, and went back to her net.

And every evening, he watched Antonio Lim come in his white Hilux, and sit on the plastic chair by her counter, drinking her Coke without paying, telling her she was still a beautiful woman, and that it was time. He watched the other six come and go. They ate at her table and drank her rum and laughed in his father's house until two in the morning. He heard one of them, a young man from the barangay captain's office called Melchor, call his wife *ang biyuda'ng buang*, the crazy widow, and laugh about the net. And he said nothing. He sat at the edge of the lamplight with his cigarette, an old beggar off the ferry, invisible, and waited.

Once, on the third evening, Melchor saw him there and threw a fish head at him, for fun. It hit him on the shoulder. Ely picked it up, thanked him politely, and put it in his plastic bag.

Tomas, watching from the shadows by the pigpen, had to bite his own hand to stop himself shouting.

"Not yet," said his father quietly, later, on the porch. "Not yet. A man who loses his temper loses everything. I learned that on the boat."

## VIII. THE DOG

On the fifth day, something happened that nearly gave him away.

Under the steps of the store, in the shade, there was an old dog. He was very old, grey round the muzzle and blind in one eye, so thin you could count his ribs, lying in the dust with the flies on him. Nobody had fed him properly in years. His name was Bantay. Ely had found him as a puppy on the beach in 2004, a year before he left, half drowned, and brought him home in his shirt. Bantay had slept under the steps of the store every night for nineteen years, Ka Emong said, waiting.

On the fifth afternoon, Ely came up the beach to buy his cigarette. As he passed the steps of the store, the old dog lifted his grey head out of the dust and looked at him with his one good eye.

He didn't bark or growl. He looked at the old stranger for a long time. Then, very slowly, his tail began to move in the dust. Back and forth, back and forth, very weakly, the way a dog's tail moves when it sees someone it knows. He tried to get up and couldn't. He lay there in the dust with his tail moving, looking at Ely with his one good eye. He made a small sound in his throat, a whine, very soft.

Ely stood very still by the steps of the store.

He couldn't go to him. Pilar was behind the counter, three metres away, and Antonio Lim was sitting on the plastic chair, watching. If an old beggar off the ferry knelt down in the dust and took a dying dog in his arms and wept, people would start asking questions. So he stood there and looked at Bantay, and Bantay looked at him, and the tail moved in the dust. Then Ely turned away, bought his cigarette, and walked back down the beach without looking back. Tears were running down his face, and he let them, because nobody looks at an old beggar's face.

Bantay died that night, under the steps of the store, in the dust. Pilar found him in the morning and buried him at the top of the beach under a coconut palm. She sat by the grave for a long time, Ka Emong said, and cried, though nobody knew why she'd cry so much for an old dog.

Ely knew why. He'd waited nineteen years, Bantay had, and seen his master come home, and that was enough.

## IX. THE NET AND THE WIFE

On the sixth night, Pilar Santos came to Ka Emong's porch.

She'd never done that before. She came at midnight, alone, with a kerosene lamp, up the dark path from the store. She stood at the foot of the porch steps and looked at the old beggar sitting there in the dark, mending a fishing line with his fingers.

"Ka Emong says you've come from Fiji," she said. "He says you worked on the tuna boats. Out of Taiwan." Her voice was very steady. "My husband went on the tuna boats. In 2005. A boat called the *Hai Feng 7*. Did you ever meet him? Eliseo Santos? Ely? A thin man with a laugh you could hear across the bay?"

Ely looked at her in the lamplight for a long time.

"I knew him," he said. "On the *Hai Feng 7*. For three years."

She sat down suddenly on the bottom step, as if her legs had gone.

"Is he dead?" she said. "Please. Just tell me. I've waited nineteen years. I just want to know."

Ely didn't answer for a long time. He looked at her, at her grey hair and the lines round her eyes in the lamplight, and her hands, quick and sure, folded in her lap. He thought about telling her. He wanted to more than he'd ever wanted anything. But the fiesta was in two days, and Antonio Lim had the barangay captain and a judge in Cebu. And he'd learned on the boat that a man who loses his temper loses everything, and that a man who tells the truth too soon is a fool.

"He talked about you," he said instead. "Every night. On the boat. He talked about you and the boy and the net he told you to make. He said, *She'll make it. She'll finish it. She's the most stubborn woman in the Visayas.*" He paused. "Have you finished it?"

Pilar Santos looked up at him in the lamplight. Then she began, very quietly, to laugh, and the laugh turned into something else.

"No," she said. "No. I've never finished it. I unpick it, every night. Did Ka Emong tell you? Every night, after I close the store, I sit by the window and cut the knots I tied that day. Nineteen years." She wiped her eyes with the back of her hand. "I told them I'd sign the papers when the net was finished. So I never finish it. That's all. It's the only way I know to wait."

She stood up and picked up her lamp.

"They're making me sign at the fiesta," she said. "On Saturday. Antonio Lim says if I don't, they'll go to court and declare Ely dead anyway, and the land will be auctioned, and he'll get it for nothing. So I'll sign. On Saturday. In front of everyone. And I'll finish the net. Tonight." She looked at him in the lamplight. "Is that what he'd want, do you think? Your friend Ely? For me to stop waiting?"

Ely looked at her for a long moment.

"He'd want you to bring the net to the fiesta," he said. "Finished. And let them see it."

## X. THE FIESTA

The fiesta of Kalubihan is held every year on the first of June, the feast of the village's patron, San Pedro the Fisherman. There's a Mass in the morning in the new church, built in 2011 after the old one burned. There's a procession of the saint's statue down to the beach, the fishing boats are blessed, and in the afternoon there's food, music, cockfights, basketball, and the old contest of the net-cast.

The net-cast is very old, older than the church. In the old days, every man on Lunhaw who called himself a fisherman had to compete in it once a year. You stood waist-deep in the bay with a *laya*, a heavy circular cast net, three metres across, weighted all round its rim with lead, and you threw it. If you threw it well, with the right twist of the hips and the right flick of the wrists, the net spun out flat across the water in a perfect circle. It landed like a flower opening and sank, trapping whatever was under it. If you threw it badly, it went up in a tangled lump and came down in a heap, and the whole village laughed. Nobody on Lunhaw had thrown a perfect circle with the old *laya* since Ely Santos left. It hung on the wall of the barangay hall, his father's net, heavy and old and stiff with salt, and the young men took turns trying every fiesta, and failed.

At four o'clock on the afternoon of the fiesta, before the whole village, gathered on the beach under the palms in their best clothes, Antonio Lim stood up on a plastic chair with a microphone and made his speech.

He spoke about progress, development, jobs, tourism, and the future of Kalubihan. He spoke about the hundred-room resort and the marina that would bring prosperity to every family on the island. He spoke, with a hand on his heart, about poor Ely Santos, a good man, a great fisherman, lost at sea, God rest his soul. He spoke about poor Pilar, who'd waited so long, so faithfully, and who had at last agreed, today, before the saint and the whole village, to let her husband go. He gave a cheque for a hundred thousand pesos to the parish priest for the church roof. He held up a folder of papers and a pen, and invited Pilar Santos to come forward.

She came forward through the crowd. She was carrying the net.

It was finished. Nineteen years of knots, a hundred metres of nylon gill net, every mesh perfect, folded in her arms. She laid it on the sand at Antonio Lim's feet, and the whole village went quiet.

"It's finished," she said. "I said I'd sign when it was finished."

Antonio Lim smiled and held out the pen.

And from the back of the crowd, an old beggar's voice said, quite loudly, in Cebuano with a strange accent, "Wait."

## XI. THE CAST

Everyone turned.

The old beggar off the ferry was standing at the back of the crowd, thin and stooped and burned black, in his cheap shirt. Tomas Santos was standing beside him.

"Before she signs," said the old man, "it's the fiesta of San Pedro. And there's the net-cast. Nobody's thrown the old *laya* in a perfect circle for nineteen years, they tell me." He limped forward through the crowd towards the barangay hall, where the old cast net hung on the wall. "I used to fish, when I was young. Let an old man try, before the papers are signed. For luck. For San Pedro." He looked at Antonio Lim. "Or are you afraid of an old beggar, sir?"

The crowd laughed. Antonio Lim laughed too, and spread his hands.

"Go on, *lolo*," he said. "Try. Make a fool of yourself. Then we'll sign."

The old man took the heavy *laya* down from the wall of the barangay hall. It was stiff with salt, heavy with lead, and had been made by his father in 1971. He carried it down the beach to the water's edge, limping, and waded out into the bay until he was waist-deep, with the whole village watching from the sand. The sun was low over Leyte, gold on the water.

He gathered the net in his hands the old way, with the lead line in his teeth and the bulk of the net over his left shoulder. He had done this ten thousand times as a boy and a young man, off the reef at Pasil and in the bay at Kalubihan. He hadn't done it in nineteen years. Nineteen years of longlines and cane fields and copra plantations. He stood very still in the water for a long moment, feeling the weight of his father's net, and the weight of everything else.

Then he turned his hips and flicked his wrists and let go.

The old *laya* went up into the gold light, spinning, and opened. It opened like a flower, a perfect circle, three metres across, every lead weight on its rim spinning out in an exact ring, and came down on the water flat and silent and whole. It sank, with a soft hiss, gathering the light.

There was absolute silence on the beach.

Then old Ka Emong, at the front of the crowd, half blind, said in a cracked voice, "Only one man on this island ever threw it like that."

The old beggar waded back up out of the bay with his father's net dripping in his hands. He walked up the beach, through the silent crowd, to where his wife was standing by the finished gill net with her hand over her mouth. He stopped in front of Antonio Lim and pulled up the left leg of his old trousers.

"A marlin," said Eliseo Santos, to the whole village. "Off the reef at Pasil. When I was sixteen. My father pulled the bill out with his hands." He let the trouser leg fall. "And my name is not Walang Tao."

## XII. THE RECKONING

What happened next has been told so many times on Lunhaw, and in so many versions, that nobody's sure any more of the truth.

Some say Antonio Lim tried to laugh it off and called Ely a fraud and a beggar. They say old Ka Emong and every old fisherman on the beach came forward one after another, and looked at the scar and the face and the eyes, and said *yes, it's Ely, it's Ely Santos, he's come home*. Some say the parish priest tore up the cheque for a hundred thousand pesos then and there. Some say Melchor from the barangay captain's office tried to slip away down the beach. Tomas Santos caught him by the collar and handed him back the fish head his father had kept in a plastic bag for five days, and the whole village laughed until they cried. Some say there was a fight. Most say there wasn't.

What's certain is that Antonio Lim got into his white Hilux that evening and drove to the ferry. He never came back to Lunhaw. A journalist from the *Cebu Daily News*, alerted by Tomas, discovered over the following month that Lim's company had been forging land titles all over the Camotes islands for a decade, with the help of a judge in Cebu City and the barangay captain of Kalubihan. All three were charged. The case is still going.

What's certain, too, is that Eliseo Santos was no longer a beggar by the end of that evening. He was a story, the one people on Lunhaw will tell for a hundred years: about the fisherman who went away to the tuna boats and came home after nineteen years as Nobody, and threw his father's net in a perfect circle at the fiesta of San Pedro.

## XIII. THE BED

But there was one person on the beach who didn't come forward to look at the scar.

Pilar Santos stood by her finished net, very still, with her hand over her mouth. She watched the old fishermen embrace her husband one after another, and the priest bless him, and Tomas weep on his shoulder, and she didn't move.

When the crowd had begun at last to drift away up the beach towards the food and the music and the cockfights, and it was dusk, and the first stars were coming out over Leyte, he came and stood in front of her.

"Pilar," he said.

She looked at him for a long time in the dusk. At the white hair, the burned black face, the dried-riverbed lines, the limp. At the eyes, which had seen things she would never know about.

"Everyone on this beach has known you since you were a boy," she said quietly. "Ka Emong, the old men, the priest. They looked at your scar and your face and the way you threw that net, and they believed you." She paused. "I was married to Ely Santos for six years. I've waited for him for nineteen. I'm not going to believe a scar."

He nodded slowly. He'd expected that. She was the most stubborn woman in the Visayas.

"Then ask me something," he said. "Something only he'd know."

Pilar was quiet for a long time.

"The bed," she said at last. "Our bed, in the house. The one we slept in. Tell me about it. If you're Ely, you know."

He smiled, for the first time in nineteen years, the old laugh almost in it.

"It's not a bed you can move," he said. "Nobody can. When we got married, in 1999, I built the house round a mango tree at the top of the beach, my grandfather's tree, the biggest on the island. I cut the trunk off at the height of a table and built the bedroom round it. I carved the bed out of the living stump, with the roots still in the ground. It's still alive. It still puts out shoots every rainy season, and you used to cut them off with your kitchen knife and complain." He looked at her. "Unless someone's cut it down. Unless one of those men who slept in my father's house went into ours and took a saw to my grandfather's tree, to move the bed. Has someone?"

Pilar Santos made a sound he'd never heard her make, something between a laugh and a cry. Then she crossed the space between them on the sand in two steps and put her arms round him, hard, the way she'd held him on the pier in April 2005 with Tomas on her hip. She held on as if she would never let go again.

"Nobody," she said into his shirt. "Nobody's touched it. Nobody was ever allowed in that room. Nineteen years."

They stood there on the beach in the dusk for a long time, with the finished net folded at their feet, while the music started up under the palms and the stars came out over Leyte, one by one.

## XIV. AFTERWARDS

Eliseo and Pilar Santos live in the house at the top of the beach at Kalubihan, round the mango tree. Every rainy season, it still puts out shoots from the bed, and Pilar still cuts them off with her kitchen knife, and complains.

Ely doesn't fish much any more. His leg is bad, and the reef is still dying, though slower now; the island has set up a marine sanctuary off Pasil, and some of the fish are coming back. He mends nets, sitting under the Pepsi umbrella by his wife's store. He tells stories to the children who gather round him: about the One-Eyed and the *Hai Feng 7*, about Nobody and the police station in Suva, about the island in Fiji where the reef was still alive. He tells them that a man who loses his temper loses everything, and a man who tells the truth too soon is a fool. And he tells them that a man who never comes home at all is the biggest fool of the lot, because everything he ever wanted was waiting for him the whole time, tying knots.

Every year, at the fiesta of San Pedro, he throws his father's *laya* in the bay at sunset. And every year it opens in a perfect circle, like a flower, and the whole village watches from the beach in silence.

Tomas Santos went back to Manila in the autumn of 2024 and found the NGO that had written the report on the *Hai Feng 7*. He works for them now, travelling the ports of Taiwan and Fiji and Indonesia, finding men like his father: men who went to sea and never came home, men who don't exist. Last year he found eleven. Six of them have gone home.

He still has the photograph: a thin, laughing man with a moustache, squinting into the sun on the prow of a banca, holding up a grouper. He keeps it in his wallet. Beside it now he keeps another, taken by a journalist from the *Cebu Daily News* on the first of June 2024. It shows a thin, stooped old man, burned black, with white hair, standing waist-deep in the bay at sunset with his arms outstretched. Above him in the gold light, spinning, opening, is a perfect circle of net.

And Pilar Santos?

She still sits under the Pepsi umbrella every morning, behind the counter of her store, with a heap of nylon twine in her lap, tying knots. She's making a new net, a hundred metres of gill net, every mesh perfect.

She finished it last month. Then she started another.

She doesn't unpick them any more. She gives them away to the young fishermen of Kalubihan, one by one, as they finish. She says she got into the habit, in nineteen years, and can't stop. She says her hands don't know what else to do.

But Ely knows the truth. He sits beside her under the umbrella in the mornings, mending his own nets, watching her hands. She's not waiting any more. She's tying the knots now for the pleasure of finishing them.

2. The Odyssey
Title of the Work The Rooted Cedar


Creative Work


I. The Unfinished Ledger

For eleven years, the creditors and timber brokers of the lower Columbia River had been eating the salt salmon and drinking the rye whiskey at Corban’s Landing, waiting for Mara Corban to sign over the logging rights to the upper watershed.

They came up from Astoria and Portland on the sternwheelers every spring and autumn, boots muddy, pockets full of options and foreclosure notices, settling onto the wide cedar porch of the main house as if the boards were already theirs. After the brig Albatross had gone down—or vanished, for no spar had ever washed ashore—in the fog off the Kuril Islands eleven winters back, every man along the river had declared Elias Corban dead. Every man except his son, Jude, who was nineteen now and had his father’s deep-set, calculating grey eyes, though none of his bulk, and Mara herself, who sat in the counting-house behind the kitchen every afternoon with the great leather-bound timber survey spread open across her knees.

"A widow can’t cruising-mark forty thousand acres of old-growth fir by herself, Mrs. Corban," said Harmon Vance, the loudest of the syndicate buyers, leaning his chair back against the porch rail while he carved a slice of smoked venison from the platter on the trestle table. "The taxes are three years in arrears. Pick a partner from among us, sign the deed of trust, and your boy keeps the lower pasture and the mill-pond. Hold out another winter, and the county sheriff will auction the roof off over your heads."

Mara stood in the doorway with a shawl pulled tight around her shoulders. She was forty, her dark hair silvered at the temples like wet slate, her face calm and unreadable. "You speak fairly, Mr. Vance, as you have every October since the year of the high water. And as I told you in the spring, the boundaries on the north fork were never properly plotted before Elias sailed. A woman cannot sign a transfer on unsurveyed timber without defrauding her husband’s father, who cleared that valley with his own hands. When I have finished reconciling my husband’s field notes into a clean plat for the magistrate, I will name the man who takes the deed."

What none of the brokers knew—until a bribed kitchen girl let it slip in the tavern down at the landing—was that every night after the lamps were blown out in the bunkhouse, Mara took a steel eraser and a bottle of turpentine to the parchment map, scraping away the ink lines she had drawn by daylight, dissolving the township lines back into blank vellum so the forest remained unmeasured and untouchable for another dawn.

Now they knew. Vance and six of his partners had refused to leave the dining hall since Tuesday, slaughtering two of the spring steers from the home pasture and setting a watch on the skiff dock so Jude could not row downriver to the circuit court at Oregon City.

Yet Jude had slipped past them before the morning fog lifted, taking the sixteen-foot Whitehall boat and two Chinook oarsmen down the cold, grease-grey current of the Columbia. He had gone looking for Captain Severin, the only master mariner on the coast who had sailed with Elias in the northern sealing grounds, needing either a witness who had seen his father’s ship go under or a word strong enough to make him stand and fight the syndicate men alone.

II. The Fog on the Bar

Two hundred miles north, in a sheltered cove on Vancouver Island where the cedar smoke hung low over the drying racks and the salmon ran thick enough to walk across, Elias Corban sat on a drift log mending a gillnet and staring southward into the rain.

He could have stayed there until he died without another scar. Three years after the Albatross was crushed in the Bering pack ice—after he had watched his crew perish one by one on the Aleutian shingle, some from the red madness of bad shellfish that made men forget their own names and sit smiling in the surf until the tide took them, others torn from the rigging by sixty-foot rollers in the Unimak Pass—he had washed ashore half-dead at the trading post of a wealthy widow named Claire Duchesne.

Claire owned three schooners, a fur warehouse, and an orchard of Gravenstein apples that never froze in the mild Pacific current. She had pulled the frostbitten stranger into her warm cedar house, fed him marrow broth and French brandy, and offered him half her fleet if he would stay and let the south go.

"You are forty-five, Elias," she told him on the fifth autumn, coming down to the shingle beach where he sat every afternoon watching the south-bound mail packets pass Hull Point. She laid a hand on his weathered neck, her fingers warm and smelling of dried lavender and beeswax. "Your hair is iron-grey. The river you came from is full of lawyers and fog, and the woman you left behind is either married to a banker by now or worn as thin as an old oar. Stay here. Nobody grows old in this cove unless they choose to."

"She is ten years older than when I left, and her hands are probably rough from the lye soap," Elias said without turning his head from the gray water. "And I know what you offer me, Claire, is softer than anything waiting for me on the Columbia. A man would be a fool to leave this fire for a house full of strangers." He looked up at her then, his salt-bleached eyes steady and terrible in their homesickness. "Give me the sixteen-foot dory you keep under the boathouse tarpaulin and four kegs of fresh water. If the bar at the river’s mouth drowns me, let it drown me within sight of Cape Disappointment."

She let him go on the first morning of November, watching from the headland as he stepped the small lugsail alone and steered out into the long, lead-colored swell of the Pacific.

For twelve days the northwester held, driving the small boat down the coast past the jagged basalt needles of Tillamook, where the surf boiled white over sunken reefs like the teeth of submerged beasts waiting to strip the planks from his ribs. On the thirteenth night, crossing the Columbia bar in a black squall, a cross-sea caught the dory broadside and snapped the spruce mast at the thwart. Elias went over into the freezing brackish churn, his wool coat dragging him down like lead until he cut the brass buttons free with his belt knife. He clung to the overturned gunwale for six hours while the flood tide carried him up the estuary, finally rolling him onto the mudflats below his own lower alder bottom just as the false dawn turned the mist the color of pewter.

He crawled into a hollow beneath the roots of a wind-thrown spruce, pulling a drift of wet bracken over his shivering ribs like an ember banked in grey ash, and slept while the river rain washed the salt from his beard.

III. The Herdsman’s Shack

When Elias walked up the skid road toward the high pasture at noon, no man on the river would have given him a second glance except to set the dogs on him. He wore a cast-off canvas slicker stiff with tar, split cowhide boots tied with twine, and a wool cap pulled low over the old scar above his left eyebrow—a jagged white crescent where a snapped logging chain had laid his skull open to the bone when he was twenty.

At the edge of the upper clearing stood the shake-roofed cabin of Tam, the old Scotch-Irish herdsman who had tended the Corban cattle since Elias’s father first filed the donation land claim. Three brindle curs burst from under the porch, hackles up and teeth bared, lunging through the mud at the stranger’s throat. Elias didn't run or swing his alder staff; he dropped flat onto one knee in the wet grass and lowered his chin. Before the lead hound could close its jaws on his sleeve, Tam came out of the shed with a split-oak stave, roaring at the dogs and pelting them back under the steps with clods of turf.

"You’d have been rags in another heartbeat, old man," Tam said, breathing hard as he leaned on his stave. "And I’ve grief enough on this place without burying a peddler in the rain. Come in by the stove and dry your shins."

The cabin smelled of woodsmoke, boiled potatoes, and tallow. Tam set a tin plate of salt pork and dark bread on the oilcloth table and poured two mugs of hot cider.

"You’ve a fine herd in the lower meadow," Elias said, warming his cracked hands around the tin mug, his voice roughened by salt and smoke into a low rasp. "Fifty head of Durham, by the look of them. Whoever owns this claim must be a rich man."

Tam spat into the woodbox. "He was, before the north sea swallowed him. Now I fatten his steers for seven land-sharks from Portland who sit in his parlor every night drinking his French brandy and waiting for the missus to break. If the master walked through that door tomorrow, he’d make cordwood of their bones. But his ribs are down among the crabs off Kamchatka, and every lying tramp who comes up the river with a tale of having seen him in Sitka or Victoria only makes the mistress weep the harder after she’s given him a silver dollar and a clean shirt."

"I don’t want a shirt or a dollar," Elias said quietly. "I worked a season on a sealing schooner out of Victoria three years back. There was a mate aboard from the Columbia—walked with a slight roll in his right shoulder, carried a white scar like a sickle-moon over his left eye. He told me he had forty weight of seal pelts cached in the north and was working his passage down the coast before the winter solstice."

Tam shook his head, not even looking up from his knife as he pared a plug of tobacco. "Eat your pork, friend, and leave the dead in the water. Hope is a cruel thing to bring into a house that’s already bleeding to death."

Before Elias could answer, the hounds outside gave a low, eager whimper—no bark this time, only the thumping of wet tails against the porch boards. The plank door swung open, and Jude stepped in out of the rain, his rifle cradled in the crook of his arm, his oilskin streaming water onto the puncheon floor.

Elias’s breath caught in his throat. When he had sailed down the river, his son had been an eight-year-old boy crying on the wharf with a wooden toy boat in his fist. The young man standing by the door had his mother’s straight dark brows and his own long, stubborn jaw.

"Tam," Jude said, pulling off his wet hat as the old herdsman hurried to take his rifle. "Did the men from the landing come up the ridge while I was gone? I rowed past their watch-skiff in the fog before daylight."

"Your mother’s still shut in the upper rooms, lad, and the brokers are still down in the hall," Tam said, gesturing toward the corner by the stove. "This old drifter came up from the slough an hour back. Claims he’s off the coasters."

Elias stood up out of the shadow by the woodbox so the boy could take his seat, bowing his head like a vagabond.

"Keep your stool, old man," Jude said gently, though his face was drawn with fatigue. "No guest gets turned out of his chair under my father’s roof while I still have two hands, even if I can only offer you a herdsman’s fire. Don’t go down to the main house tonight. The men drinking in our hall have no decency left in them, and I’m only one rifle against seven."

Tam went out to pen the calves before the squall worsened, pulling the door shut behind him.

The moment the latch clicked, Elias straightened his back. He took off the sodden wool cap, letting the firelight strike the high, gaunt planes of his cheekbones and the white crescent scar above his left eye.

"A man doesn't count the rifles in his own kitchen, Jude," Elias said, his voice dropping the drifter’s wheeze and ringing out with the flat, iron cadence that had once carried over a gale from the quarterdeck.

Jude stepped back against the wall, his hand dropping toward his belt knife, the blood draining from his face. "Who are you? Who told you to use that voice?"

"Look at my brow, boy. Look at the scar your grandfather stitched with horsehair the year the big spruce rolled on the skidway." Elias took two steps across the small room and caught his son by both shoulders, his grip hard enough to bruise through the wool coat. "It’s me, Jude. No other Elias Corban is ever coming up that river."

For five seconds the boy stared into the weathered, salt-scored face—seeing through the grey beard and the sunken cheeks to the fierce, unmistakable light in the grey eyes—and then his knees gave way. He caught his father around the ribs, pressing his forehead into the tar-stained canvas slicker, sobbing with the raw, choked fury of eleven years spent guarding an empty house.

They stood holding each other by the stove until the rain slackened on the shakes, and then Elias held his son at arm’s length.

"Listen to me now, and keep your face cold when you walk into that hall tonight," Elias said. "If a single kitchen girl guesses who I am before the doors are barred, Vance and his men will shoot us through the windows and burn the house to hide the bodies. Go down now. Tell your mother you’re back from Oregon City. In an hour, Tam will bring me down to the porch begging for scraps. Even if you see them kick me into the mud or break a chair across my back, do not touch your rifle until I give you the word. Tonight, when they’ve drunk themselves heavy, take every Winchester and revolver out of the gun rack in the hall and lock them in the root cellar—tell them the damp is rusting the actions. Leave only two carbines and the old heavy-bore Sharps buffalo gun behind the pantry door."

IV. The Ashes and the Iron

The dining hall of Corban’s Landing was forty feet of squared Douglas fir timbers, lit by whale-oil lamps and a roaring hearth at the far end. When Elias limped onto the threshold at dusk behind Tam, leaning on his alder staff, the seven timber brokers were already three bottles deep into the last case of Elias’s Monongahela rye.

At the sight of the old hound, Ranger—blind in both milky eyes and too arthritic to lift his hindquarters off the cedar shavings by the woodshed outside—Elias had nearly broken his own rule. The dog, eighteen years old and forgotten by the stable hands, had caught the scent on the wet wind as Elias passed the gate; the gaunt tail had thumped twice against the mud, the grey muzzle lifting once toward the master he had waited eleven winters to smell again, before the old heart simply stopped and the head settled down between his paws for good. Elias had wiped his cheek with the back of his sleeve in the dark and walked inside.

"What have you dragged in from the swamp, hog-keeper?" Harmon Vance laughed from the head of the oak table, where he sat in Elias’s own high-backed armchair. "We’ve enough mouths on this place without feeding every wharf-rat between here and Astoria."

"A house that turns a wet man from its fire on a November night has forgotten whose timber built the walls," Jude said from the sideboard, his voice steady as he set a trencher of beef and bread on the lower step near the door for the beggar.

Vance’s eyes narrowed. He picked up a heavy pewter tankard from the table and hurled it across the room. Elias tilted his head an inch to the left; the tankard grazed his shoulder and smashed against the fir planking behind him, spilling stale beer over his coat. Elias did not flinch, nor did he look up from his bread. He simply chewed, his grey eyes travelling slowly from face to face around the table, counting their holsters and noting that the gun rack by the hall door was already bare, just as he had ordered.

At nine o'clock, when the brokers finally stumbled out across the dogtrot to the guest bunkhouse to sleep off their liquor, the hall grew quiet save for the popping of the fir logs.

Then the inner door opened, and Mara came down the stairs with a candle in her hand, followed by old Martha, the housekeeper who had nursed Elias when he was born in the original log cabin upriver.

Mara stopped ten feet from the hearth, where the ragged stranger sat on a low bench warming his boots. Even in the dim light, her posture was straight as a plumb line, though the dark hollows beneath her eyes told what the last four years had cost her.

"My son tells me you claim to have sailed with a man from this river in the north," she said, setting her candle on the mantel. "I have listened to twenty men sit on that bench and lie to me for a warm coat. If you knew Elias Corban, tell me what he carried in his pocket when he left this landing, or eat your supper in peace and do not speak his name."

Elias kept his gaze fixed on the floorboards so the firelight would not catch his eyes. "It is a long time to remember another man’s kit, ma'am. Eleven years in the northern ice washes most things out of a man’s head. Calling it back only brings the cold with it."

"Try," Mara said softly.

"When he came aboard the Albatross at Astoria," Elias said in his low, gravelly rasp, "he wore a double-breasted Mackinaw coat of dark blue wool that had been woven on a hand-loom—tight enough to turn three days of sleet. And pinned to the inside pocket, where no salt could reach it, he carried a silver compass case his wife had given him the day they were wed. The lid was engraved with a kingfisher diving into a salmon eddy, and the hinge had been mended with a pin of soft copper because he’d dropped it on the rocks at Celilo Falls."

A sound came from Mara’s throat—half a gasp, half a sob that she bit back with her teeth. She sat down hard on the settle by the fire, her hands gripping the wooden armrests until her knuckles turned white, tears spilling silently down her cheeks. "I mended that hinge myself with a piece of copper wire from the seine loft," she whispered. "And what did he tell you of his coming back?"

"He told me," Elias said, "that a man who has lost his ship and his crew does not come home empty-handed to a house full of wolves, and that before this November moon is dark, he will stand on his own hearth and settle every ledger on the Columbia."

"You speak kind words for an old man," Mara said, wiping her eyes with the corner of her shawl, her voice hardening again with the terrible, protective exhaustion of a woman who could not afford another false dawn. "Martha, bring the cedar tub and hot water from the kettle. Wash this traveller’s feet and give him a dry blanket by the hearth. Tomorrow morning, before the sun clears the ridge, I am bringing out my husband’s surveying transit and his heavy Kentucky target rifle. The man among those seven who can sight the transit true from the porch and drive a lead ball through the eye of the five-Hundred-yard iron surveying ring down by the river-bend—a shot only Elias could ever make off-hand—will have my signature on the timber deed before noon. I cannot hold the roof up any longer alone."

"Do not put off your trial by an hour, ma'am," the beggar said from the shadows. "Elias Corban will be in this room before any man among them can draw a bead through that ring."

Mara turned away toward the stairs, unable to bear the ache in her chest any longer. Old Martha knelt by the hearth with the wooden tub of steaming water, lifting the stranger’s mud-caked boot and rolling up the frayed hem of his canvas trousers to wash his shin.

Her gnarled fingers ran up the calf toward the knee—and stopped dead against the thick, ridged welt of an old wound where a logging chain had torn the muscle forty years ago, a scar she had poulticed with pitch and comfrey with her own hands when he was a boy of twenty.

The tin dipper dropped from Martha’s hand, clattering against the rim of the tub and splashing warm water across the hearthstones. Her mouth opened, her old eyes wide with terror and joy as she looked up into his face. "Elias—"

Before the name could carry to the stairwell, Elias’s iron hand closed gently but immovably over her mouth, his other arm drawing her gray head against his knee.

"Not a breath, Martha," he whispered into her ear. "If you love me and the boy, be as dumb as the hearthstone until tomorrow’s work is done."

The old woman nodded fiercely against his palm, her tears wetting his wrist.

V. The Five-Hundred-Yard Ring

Dawn came clear and bitter cold, with a skim of white frost on the porch rails and the river steaming below the bluff.

By nine o'clock, Vance and the six syndicate men were gathered on the wide veranda, stamping their boots and laughing over their coffee as Jude brought out the long, octagonal-barreled Kentucky rifle and the brass-bound surveyor’s transit, setting them on the oak table by the steps. Down by the water’s edge, five hundred yards out through a narrow lane cut in the alders, an iron mooring ring four inches across hung from a whitewashed cedar post.

"A fair enough game to settle four years of waiting," Vance grinned, stripping off his buckskin gloves. "Though why a woman wants a sharpshooter for a business partner is beyond me."

He stepped to the transit first. The vernier screws had been set by Elias himself twelve years ago to a private zero-mark known only to him; Vance squinted through the brass tube, cursed the crosshairs, and turned to the long rifle. The double-set trigger and the heavy forty-pound barrel were built for a man with the shoulders of a sawyer. Vance raised the stock, wavered in the cold breeze coming off the water, and fired. The lead ball kicked up a spray of mud thirty feet short of the whitewashed post.

One by one the others tried. Two couldn't even set the hair-trigger without misfiring into the gravel; another grazed the cedar post a foot below the iron ring.

From the doorway behind them, Elias stepped out onto the porch with his alder staff in his hand, while Tam and Jude quietly slipped the heavy oak bar through the outer courtyard gate behind the brokers’ backs.

"Let an old deckhand feel the balance of that iron, gentlemen," Elias said, setting his staff against the wall. "I used to shoot sea-otters off the taffrail in a cross-swell when my eyes were younger. I’d like to see if the river fog has rusted my arms."

"Get back by the kitchen, you old fraud, before I have you whipped off the claim," Vance snarled, his pride raw from his miss.

"Let him lift it," Jude said coldly from the top step, his hand resting inside the pantry door where the two loaded Winchester carbines leaned in the dark. "The rifle belongs to my father’s house, not to you, Vance. If a beggar can shoot straighter than the men who want to own this valley, I’d like to see it."

Elias picked up the long rifle. The moment his calloused fingers closed around the curly-maple stock, the stooped, shuffling hesitation vanished from his spine. He didn't even use the brass transit. With the easy, practiced grace of a fiddler tuning his own instrument, he thumbed back the heavy hammer, seated a patched ball and percussion cap from the pouch on the table, and brought the octagonal barrel to his shoulder in a single fluid motion.

The rifle cracked like a dry fir snapping in a hard freeze.

Down by the river-bend, five hundred yards through the morning mist, a clean blue puff of lead dust rang sharp as a church bell from the center of the iron ring, and the target post behind it splintered dead in the bull's-eye.

The brokers went very still on the porch.

Elias lowered the smoking muzzle of the Kentucky rifle, reached into the open pantry door behind him, and drew out the heavy-bore Sharps repeater, working the lever with a loud, metallic clack as he threw off his wool cap.

"That trial is finished," Elias Corban said, his voice rolling across the frost-whitened yard. "Now let’s see how well you gentlemen settle an eleven-year bill for my cattle, my timber, and my roof."

Vance reached for the Colt under his coat-tail; before the barrel cleared the leather, the Sharps roared from Elias’s hip, taking Vance cleanly through the breastbone and knocking him backward over the porch rail into the frozen mud.

The remaining six men lunged for the hall door, drawing their pocket pistols and Bowie knives, only to find Jude stepping out of the doorway with a Winchester leveled at their chests and Tam flanking them from the woodshed with a double-barreled ten-gauge loaded with buckshot. It was over in less than four minutes of acrid black-powder smoke and shouting on the frosty planks—a short, merciless reckoning in which no quarter was asked or given by men who had spent four years preying on a house they believed had no master.

VI. The Stump in the Bedroom

When the yard had been washed down with buckets from the well and the sheriff’s deputy from the lower landing had been sent downriver to fetch the coroner and the magistrate, the house fell into a silence deeper than any it had known in a decade.

Elias washed the powder grime and salt from his skin in the warm room off the kitchen, shaved the tangled grey beard from his jaw, and put on a clean wool shirt and trousers of dark broadcloth that Martha laid out for him. When he walked back into the great hall, Mara was sitting alone on the settle opposite the fire, her hands folded in her lap.

She looked at him for a long time without speaking. Without the beard, with the lamplight falling across the high, lean bones of his face and the white crescent scar above his eye, he looked terribly like the man who had kissed her on the wharf eleven years ago—and yet like a stranger carved out of harder, older wood.

"Mother," Jude said from the doorway, his voice tight with bewilderment. "What is wrong with you? He’s come back from the bottom of the sea and cleared our house, and you sit ten feet away from him as if he were a tax collector."

"Leave us alone, Jude," Mara said softly, never taking her eyes off the man by the hearth. "If this is Elias Corban standing under his own roof, he and I have ways of knowing each other that do not need a boy’s word."

Elias smiled—a slow, tired creasing of the corners of his eyes—and nodded to his son. "Go down and see to the stock with Tam, lad. Your mother was never a woman to be hurried, or those seven men out by the gate would have owned this valley three years ago."

When the door closed behind Jude, Elias sat down on the bench across from her. "You’re harder than the basalt at Celilo, Mara. Any other wife on this river would have had her arms around my neck before the smoke cleared the porch. Martha, go upstairs and make up the spare cot for me on the landing; it seems the mistress of this house has forgotten who built it."

"I am not proud, Elias, nor am I cold," Mara said, her voice trembling for the first time as she tested him with the one secret no sailor in Victoria could ever have heard. "I remember every line of the man who sailed out of Astoria on the Albatross. Go up, Martha, and pull our big four-poster bed out from the corner of the master bedroom into the hallway, and lay fresh blankets on it for him there."

Elias’s grey eyes flashed with sudden, genuine heat. He leaned forward on his knees. "And what team of oxen did you bring into my bedroom to move that bedstead, woman? Unless a logger came in here with a crosscut saw while I was gone, no four men on the Columbia could shift that frame an inch from the north wall!"

His voice rose, rough with the pride of a craftsman whose work had been questioned. "When I cleared this knoll twenty-two years ago, there was a four-foot red cedar growing straight and sound right where the corner of the house was to stand. I built the log walls around that living trunk, topped it off four feet above the floorboards with my own broadaxe, and adzed the rooted stump square to form the head-post of our bed! I mortised the rails straight into the heartwood and pegged them with seasoned oak while the roots were still deep in the river clay underneath the foundation. Tell me right now—who took an axe to my cedar tree?"

Mara didn't answer him with words. The last iron bar that had held her upright for four thousand nights snapped clean in two. She was across the hearthstones before he could rise, dropping to her knees between his boots, throwing her arms around his neck and burying her face against the clean wool of his shoulder while her whole frame shook with eleven years of unshed tears.

"Nobody touched the cedar, Elias," she sobbed against his throat, her fingers tangling in his iron-grey hair as if she were drowning and he were the only timber left afloat on the river. "Forgive me. Every man who came up that path for eleven years wanted to take something from this house with a lie. I couldn't let my heart open the door until I knew it was your hand on the latch."

Elias wrapped his scarred arms around her waist, pulling her up onto the bench against his chest, his own face buried in her silvered hair while the tall clock in the corner measured out the quiet, reclaimed minutes of their life. Outside, the November wind came off the Pacific, rattling the shingles and driving the cold rain against the glass, but the house stood fast around the living root that anchored it to the earth.
