27. Title The Turn of the Screw

# The Feed

## A FOREWORD, OF SORTS

It was New Year's Eve, and there were eight of us in the old farmhouse in the Borders, snowed in, with the power off and candles on the kitchen table. We'd spent the evening telling ghost stories, as you do. Somebody's aunt's house in Wales, a hotel in the Highlands, a nursery monitor that picked up a voice nobody could account for. That one got a laugh, then a silence.

And then Douglas Ferrier, who was seventy-four and a retired consultant psychiatrist, and who hadn't told a story all evening, said quietly from the end of the table, "I have one. About a monitor, as it happens. And two children. It's not mine. It was written by someone I treated, a long time ago." He paused. "I've never shown it to anyone. I've had it in a drawer for nineteen years."

We asked him to fetch it. He said he couldn't; it was in his house in Edinburgh. But he said that if the roads were open in the morning, he'd drive home and bring it back the following night. He did. It was a cardboard folder with about sixty pages of printed A4, closely typed, with a few handwritten corrections. He read it aloud to us at the kitchen table by candlelight on the second of January, over about four hours. Nobody moved.

Before he began, he told us three things.

The woman who wrote it was twenty-four at the time. She was intelligent, sensitive, highly educated, and the youngest of five children of a Free Church minister in Lewis. She'd been his patient for about two years afterwards. She was, he said, one of the most remarkable people he'd ever met.

The events took place in 2005, on an island off the west coast of Scotland.

And, he said, looking round the table at us in the candlelight, "I've thought about it for nineteen years, and I still don't know what happened. I want you to know that before I begin. I don't know. Make of it what you will."

Then he opened the folder and began to read.

---

## THE ACCOUNT

### I.

I'm writing this because Dr Ferrier asked me to, and because I think if I don't set it down in order, I'll lose the order of it. I'm already losing it. Things come back to me in the wrong sequence, in the middle of the night. I'll write it as it happened, as truthfully as I can. I won't explain anything I can't explain. I'll leave that to whoever reads it.

---

I answered an advertisement in the *Times Educational Supplement* in the spring of 2005: *Live-in tutor and companion required for two children, aged 8 and 10, on private island estate, Inner Hebrides. Excellent salary. Discretion essential. Interviews in London.*

I'd just finished a postgraduate certificate in education at Edinburgh and hadn't found a post. I'd never been further south than Glasgow. I'd never met a rich person. I went to London on the overnight bus for the interview, in my one good suit, because the salary was three times what any school in Scotland would pay me. I'd decided, at twenty-four, that I wanted something to happen to me.

The interview was in an office on the thirtieth floor of a glass tower in the City. The man who interviewed me was the children's uncle and guardian, Mr Alexander Grant. He was about forty-five, tall and handsome and charming, with the easy, careless, generous manner of a man who's never been told no. He ran a hedge fund. He'd inherited the children, he explained, cheerfully, three years before, when his brother and sister-in-law were killed in a helicopter crash in the Alps. He'd inherited the island too, Inverlaig, off the coast of Mull. It was a family estate, a big Victorian house, eleven hundred acres of moor and loch and sea, and he had no idea what to do with any of it.

"I'm hopeless with children," he said, smiling at me across his enormous desk. "Absolutely hopeless. I love them, of course, but I haven't the faintest idea how to talk to them. So I've left them up there with Mrs MacLeod, the housekeeper, who's marvellous. What they need is someone young and clever and kind to teach them, and look after them, and be with them. Someone who'll take it all off my hands."

He leaned forward.

"There's one condition," he said. "It's important. Once you're there, you deal with everything yourself. Everything. You don't ring me. You don't email me. You don't write to me about problems. If something goes wrong, you sort it out. I trust you completely. I'm paying you very well precisely so that I never have to think about it. Do you understand?"

I said I understood. I didn't, of course. I was twenty-four and in a glass tower in London, and a handsome, charming man was smiling at me and saying *I trust you completely*. I'd have agreed to anything.

"Splendid," said Mr Grant. "When can you start?"

---

He told me one more thing, at the door, almost as an afterthought.

"There was a tutor before you," he said. "A young woman, Miss Jessop, Emma Jessop. She left last year, rather suddenly. And then she died." He looked briefly uncomfortable. "Nothing to do with Inverlaig, I'm sure. Some private trouble. She drowned. In Oban harbour." He held out his hand. "The children were very fond of her. You might find them a little unsettled. But I'm sure you'll manage beautifully."

### II.

Inverlaig is two miles long and a mile wide, a long low hump of heather and rock in the sea off the west coast of Mull, with a single house on it. There's no ferry. A man called Duncan brings the post and the supplies across from Mull twice a week in an open boat, weather permitting, and it often doesn't. There's no mobile signal. There's a landline that works when the wind isn't too strong, and a satellite internet connection in the estate office that works when the clouds aren't too thick. And there's the house.

It's a big grey Victorian mansion, built in 1872 by a shipping magnate from Glasgow, with turrets and gables and fifty-two rooms. Most of them are shut up, with dust sheets on the furniture. It stands at the head of a sea loch on the east side of the island, looking across the water to the mountains of Mull. Behind it there's a walled garden, a ruined chapel, a little graveyard, and a long, dark loch in the hills called Loch nan Eun, the loch of the birds. And around it, on every side, there's the sea.

I arrived on the first of May, on a day of such extraordinary beauty that I wept on Duncan's boat. The sea was dead calm and blue as glass. The mountains of Mull were purple with heather, and there were seals on the rocks, and an eagle, a sea eagle, circling over the island on wings like a door.

And the children were waiting for me on the jetty, holding hands. I'll never forget them.

Flora was eight. She was small and fair, with grave grey eyes and a stillness about her that I'd never seen in a child. She held out her hand to me on the jetty as if she were a duchess, and said, "How do you do. I'm Flora. You're very welcome to Inverlaig." Then, after a pause, without smiling: "We hope you'll stay longer than the last one."

Miles was ten, and he was the most beautiful child I've ever seen. I don't know how else to say it. He was dark and slender and quick, with a face like a Renaissance angel and a smile that went straight through you. He took my bag from Duncan without being asked and carried it up the jetty, chattering. He told me about the seals and the eagle and the house and the loch, and asked me a hundred questions about Edinburgh and about myself, and by the time we reached the front door he had me laughing.

Mrs MacLeod was waiting in the doorway, a stout, kind, red-faced woman of sixty from Tobermory. She'd been housekeeper at Inverlaig for thirty years. She took one look at my face and said, "Och, you're just a lassie yourself. Come in, come in, you'll be wanting your tea."

That first evening, sitting in the big warm kitchen with the children and Mrs MacLeod, with the sun going down over Mull and the sea turning gold, I thought I'd never been so happy in my life.

### III.

The house had a security system. I should mention that, because it matters.

Mr Grant had had it installed after the children came to Inverlaig, at enormous expense. There were cameras everywhere, eighteen of them, on the jetty, on the drive, in the garden, at every door, in every corridor of the house except the bedrooms and bathrooms. They fed into a bank of monitors in a small room off the estate office. There was also a monitor on the wall of my bedroom, a small screen that cycled through all eighteen camera feeds, ten seconds each, day and night. Mrs MacLeod had one in her room too. It was for the children's safety, Mr Grant had said. On an island, with the sea all round, you couldn't be too careful.

I didn't like it at first. It felt like being watched. But after a week I stopped noticing it. It was just there on the wall by my bed, cycling silently through the empty corridors and the dark garden and the jetty at night: corridor, stairs, garden, jetty, drive, corridor.

And then, on the night of the nineteenth of May, I saw the man on the tower.

### IV.

It was about eleven o'clock. I was in bed, reading, with the lamp on. The monitor on the wall was cycling through its feeds as usual, and I glanced up at it, the way you do.

It was showing camera eleven. Camera eleven was on the roof of the east wing, pointing across the slates at the old tower on the north-east corner of the house. It was a round turret with a crenellated top, part of the original Victorian folly. It had been closed for years because the stairs were unsafe.

There was a man standing on top of the tower.

He was standing quite still, against the parapet, in the faint blue light of the May night. It never gets fully dark in the Hebrides in summer. He was tall and thin. I couldn't see his face; the camera was too far away, and the image was grainy. He wasn't wearing a hat. His hair was red, I thought, or at least light. And he was looking at the camera, straight at it, with his face turned towards me, as if he knew it was there, and knew I was watching.

Ten seconds. Then the monitor cycled to camera twelve, the back door, empty.

I sat up in bed with my heart pounding. I waited. Seventeen feeds later, camera eleven came round again. The top of the tower was empty.

I told myself it was a glitch. A shadow, a trick of the light, a reflection. Then I told myself it was Duncan, or a fisherman who'd landed on the island, or a birdwatcher. Then I told myself I'd been reading too late and imagined it. I lay awake until three, watching the monitor cycle round, waiting for camera eleven.

He didn't come back that night.

---

In the morning I asked Mrs MacLeod, as casually as I could, whether anyone else lived on the island, or visited it. A shepherd, perhaps, or a gamekeeper.

She looked at me. "There's nobody, hen. There's been nobody since—" She stopped. "Since Peter."

"Peter?"

Mrs MacLeod put down the teapot very carefully.

"Peter Quinn," she said. "The groundsman. He was here when Mr Grant's brother had the place, and stayed on after the accident. A big red-headed Irishman from Donegal. He looked after the boats, and the garden, and the generator." Her mouth tightened. "He drank. And he wasn't a good man. Mr Grant never knew. He was never here. But I knew. And the lassie knew. Miss Jessop."

"What did he do?"

Mrs MacLeod looked at me for a long time across the kitchen table.

"He was too much with the children," she said at last. "Especially the boy. He took him out on the boat, on the loch, for hours. He taught him things. Swearing, and lying, and keeping secrets. He told him terrible stories, about the sea and drowned men and what happens after you die. And Miss Jessop, God forgive her, she was a lonely young lassie on an island at the end of the world, and he was a big handsome man, and she—" She stopped again, and shook her head. "They were very close, the two of them. Too close. And the children saw everything. They were always with them."

"What happened to him?"

"He fell," said Mrs MacLeod. "Off the tower. Last February. Drunk, at night, in a gale. He used to go up there to drink, on his own, though it was forbidden. They found him on the slates of the east wing in the morning with his neck broken." She crossed herself, though she was Church of Scotland. "Miss Jessop left the island a fortnight after. She wouldn't say why. She just packed her bag and went with Duncan on the boat, and didn't say goodbye to the children. Three weeks later they found her in Oban harbour."

I sat very still at the kitchen table.

"What did he look like?" I said. "Peter Quinn?"

Mrs MacLeod looked at me strangely.

"Tall," she said. "Thin. Red hair. He never wore a hat, even in winter." She paused. "Why are you asking, hen?"

I didn't answer.

### V.

I saw him again on the second of June, in the afternoon, in daylight.

The children were at their lessons in the old schoolroom on the first floor, which looked out over the walled garden. I'd stepped out to fetch a book from the library. As I came back along the corridor, I glanced, as I always did now, at the small monitor screen fixed to the wall at the top of the stairs. There was one on every floor. It was showing camera four: the walled garden, from the gate, looking towards the house.

He was standing in the middle of the garden, on the path between the rosebeds, looking up at the schoolroom window.

He was closer this time. I could see him much more clearly: a tall, thin man in an old waxed jacket, with no hat, red hair, a long pale face, stubbled. He was looking up at the window of the schoolroom, where the children were. He was absolutely still. And there was something in his face, even on the grainy screen, that I can't describe. It was a kind of hunger.

I ran. I ran into the schoolroom, to the window, and looked down into the walled garden.

It was empty. The roses, the path, the sundial, the gate. There was nobody there. I stood at the window with my heart hammering and looked down at the empty garden for a long time.

Behind me, very calmly, Flora said, "What are you looking at?"

I turned round. Both children were sitting at the schoolroom table with their books open, looking up at me. Flora's grave grey eyes, and Miles's beautiful dark ones. Miles was smiling.

"Nothing," I said. "I thought I saw a bird."

"What kind of bird?" said Miles.

I looked at him. He was still smiling, very sweetly, with his angel's face.

"A big one," I said.

### VI.

I didn't sleep after that. Not properly. I sat up every night in my bedroom with the lamp off and watched the monitor on the wall cycle through its eighteen feeds, over and over, until dawn.

I saw him three more times in June, always on the screen, never in person. Once he was on the jetty at midnight, standing at the end, looking out to sea. Once he was in the corridor outside the children's bedrooms, at about two in the morning, standing quite still with his back to the camera, facing their doors. That time I ran out into the corridor in my nightdress with a poker from the fireplace. The corridor was empty. Both children were asleep in their beds. And once he was on the shore of Loch nan Eun, the dark loch in the hills behind the house, at dusk, standing at the water's edge, and he wasn't alone.

There was a woman with him. She was standing a little way off, among the reeds, in a dark coat, with long dark hair hanging wet over her face. She was looking down into the water. She didn't move at all.

I told Mrs MacLeod about the woman at the loch. I hadn't told her about the others. She went very white.

"Miss Jessop had long dark hair," she said quietly. "Down to her waist. And she used to walk up to Loch nan Eun in the evenings, with him." She looked at me. "Hen, there's nobody on this island but us. You know that. Duncan hasn't brought anyone over since March."

"I saw them."

"On the screen," said Mrs MacLeod. "You saw them on the screen." She took my hand across the kitchen table. Hers was warm and rough. "Those cameras are old, hen. They play tricks. Shadows, reflections, interference from the generator. Peter used to say he saw all sorts on them." She squeezed my hand. "You're tired. You're not sleeping. You're a long way from home, all on your own, on an island at the end of the world, with two wee bairns to look after and no one to talk to. It's no wonder you're seeing things."

I looked at her.

"Have you never seen them?" I said. "On your monitor? In your room?"

Mrs MacLeod didn't answer for a long time.

"No," she said finally. "I've never seen anything."

But she didn't meet my eyes.

### VII.

It was then that I began to understand.

It came to me slowly, over the last weeks of June, in the long white nights, sitting in my bedroom watching the screen. They weren't coming for me. I was nothing to them. I'd never met them. They were coming for the children.

Peter Quinn and Emma Jessop had been with Miles and Flora every day for two years. They'd taught them things: swearing and lying and secrets, terrible stories about the sea and drowned men and what happens after you die. The children had seen everything that passed between them. And now the two of them were dead, and something of them hadn't gone. They were still here, on the island, on the tower and in the garden and at the loch and outside the children's bedroom doors at two in the morning. They were waiting. Watching. Wanting the children back.

And the children knew.

I was sure of it. I couldn't prove it. I never saw them look at the screens, or speak of Peter or Miss Jessop. When I tried, very carefully, to raise the names, they changed the subject so smoothly that I hardly noticed until afterwards. But there was something about them, about both of them, that I'd been too dazzled to see at first. It was a kind of perfection. They were too good, too charming and obedient, too beautiful. They never quarrelled, never cried, never sulked or lost their tempers or behaved, ever, like ordinary children. It was as if they were acting, beautifully, all the time, for my benefit, while underneath, they were somewhere else entirely. They were with someone else, in a secret world I couldn't see.

I decided I would save them.

I want to be clear about that. Dr Ferrier says I should be honest about my own part in this, and I'm trying to be. I decided, quite consciously, in the last week of June, sitting in my bedroom at three in the morning watching the monitor, that I would stand between those two children and whatever was on the tower and at the loch. I'd protect them, whatever it cost. I was the only person in the world who could see it, and the only one who could save them. And if Mr Grant in his glass tower in London didn't want to know, and Mrs MacLeod wouldn't admit what she'd seen, then I'd do it alone.

I've thought since about that word, *alone*. It's a dangerous word for a young woman on an island at the end of the world.

### VIII.

On the second of July, Flora disappeared.

It was afternoon, hot and still. I'd been sitting with both children in the walled garden, reading aloud. I'd looked down at the book for a moment, and when I looked up, she was gone. Her chair was empty, and the gate was open.

Miles was sitting in his chair across from me, smiling.

"Where's Flora?" I said.

"I don't know," he said sweetly. "She was here a minute ago." He stood up. "Shall I play the piano for you? I've been practising."

He went into the house. A moment later I heard him begin to play in the drawing room: Chopin, a nocturne, very beautifully, much better than any ten-year-old should.

I ran. I ran out of the gate and up the path behind the house into the hills. I knew where she'd gone, though I couldn't have said how. I ran up through the heather to the shore of Loch nan Eun, the dark loch, and there she was.

She was standing on a rock at the water's edge, in her blue summer dress, with her back to me, quite still, looking out across the black water.

And on the far side of the loch, among the reeds, in a dark coat, with long dark hair hanging wet over her face, the woman was standing, looking back at her.

I saw her. Not on a screen. With my own eyes, in daylight, across a hundred yards of black water, as clearly as I've ever seen anything in my life.

"Flora," I said.

The child turned round slowly on the rock and looked at me with her grave grey eyes.

"She's there," I said. My voice was shaking. "Isn't she? On the other side. You can see her. You came up here to see her. Miss Jessop."

Flora looked at me for a long, long time.

Then she looked across the loch, at the reeds on the far shore, where the woman was standing, and back at me. And her face changed. It wasn't the grave, still, perfect face of the duchess on the jetty. It was a child's face, eight years old, frightened, bewildered, crumpling.

"There's nobody there," she said. "I came to look at the ducks." Her voice rose. "There's nobody there! Why do you keep looking at things? Why do you keep looking at things that aren't there?"

I looked across the loch.

The far shore was empty: reeds, rocks, black water, the hills going up behind into the blue afternoon sky. There was nobody there at all.

Flora burst into tears. She stood on the rock at the edge of the loch and screamed at me, sobbing, her face red and wet, that she hated me. She said I was mad, I frightened her, I watched them all the time, I was always looking at the screens and always looking at things. She wanted Mrs MacLeod. She wanted to go home. She wanted her mummy.

I tried to hold her, and she fought me off and ran down the hill towards the house, screaming. I stood alone on the shore of the black loch for a long time. When I looked across the water again, the woman was standing in the reeds, quite still, with her wet hair over her face. She was looking at me.

### IX.

Mrs MacLeod took Flora to Mull the next morning on Duncan's boat. She said the child was ill: a fever, nightmares, screaming in her sleep. She was taking her to her sister in Tobermory, to the doctor. She'd ring Mr Grant from there.

She stood on the jetty with Flora in her arms, wrapped in a blanket, and looked at me. Her kind red face was full of something I didn't want to see. It was pity, and fear.

"Come with us, hen," she said quietly. "Please. Leave the boy with Duncan for a day or two. Come to Tobermory. See a doctor yourself. You're not well."

"I can't leave Miles," I said. "Not alone. Not here. Not with them."

Mrs MacLeod looked at me for a long moment.

"There's no *them*, hen," she said. "There's just you, and a wee boy, and an old house, and a lot of cameras." She shifted Flora in her arms. "Please."

I shook my head.

Duncan started the engine. The boat pulled away from the jetty and out across the blue water towards Mull. Flora's small white face looked back at me over Mrs MacLeod's shoulder, and then the boat went round the point, and I was alone on the island with Miles.

### X.

I'll set down what happened next as plainly as I can. I don't want to make it more than it was, or less.

It was the evening of the third of July, still and golden, with the sea like glass and the light lasting until nearly midnight. Miles and I had supper alone in the big dining room. He was charming, as always. He talked about books and music and the eagle he'd seen that morning over the cliffs, and asked me questions about Edinburgh and my family in Lewis. He was so sweet and so clever and so beautiful that for an hour I almost forgot. Almost.

After supper we sat in the drawing room. The long windows were open onto the terrace and the sea. He played the piano for me, the Chopin nocturne again, and when he'd finished he sat on the piano stool with his hands in his lap and looked at me.

"Are you going to make me go away?" he said. "Like Flora?"

"No," I said. "I'm going to keep you safe."

"Safe from what?"

I looked at him. And I decided, God forgive me, that it was time.

"Miles," I said, very gently, "I know about Peter Quinn. And Miss Jessop. I know what they were to you. I know they're still here. I've seen them. On the tower, and in the garden, and at the loch, and outside your bedroom door at night. I've seen them on the cameras, and I've seen them with my own eyes." I leaned forward. "You don't have to pretend any more. You don't have to be perfect for me. I know. And I'm not afraid of them. I'll stand between you and them for as long as it takes. But you have to tell me the truth. You have to tell me you see them too. Then they'll have no power over you. Then you'll be free."

Miles stared at me from the piano stool. His beautiful face had gone very white.

"I don't—" he began.

And over his shoulder, through the long open window, on the terrace in the golden evening light, not on a screen, not on a camera, but there, ten feet away, real, with the sea behind him, stood Peter Quinn.

He was tall and thin, in his old waxed jacket, with no hat and red hair and a long pale stubbled face. He was looking past me, straight at the boy on the piano stool, with that hunger in his face.

"He's there," I said. My voice cracked. "Miles, he's there. Behind you. On the terrace. Turn round. Tell me you see him. Say his name."

Miles's face convulsed. He looked at me, at my face, at whatever was in my face. He began to shake.

"Peter," he whispered. "Peter Quinn. Is it him? Where? *Where?*"

"There!" I cried. "There, on the terrace! You see him, don't you? Say you see him! Say it, and he'll lose you forever!"

Miles twisted round on the piano stool to look at the open window, at the terrace, at the golden evening and the glass-calm sea. He looked for a long, long moment.

Then he made a sound I'll hear for the rest of my life. It was a cry, very high, like a creature falling from a great height, and he crumpled sideways off the piano stool. I caught him. I caught him in my arms as he fell, and held him, and called his name, and held him tighter, and called again.

On the terrace, there was nobody. There was only the golden evening, and the sea, and the mountains of Mull.

It was several minutes, I think, before I understood that the boy in my arms wasn't breathing.

### XI.

Duncan came back across from Mull at ten that night, because Mrs MacLeod had made him. She'd had a feeling, she said. He found me on the floor of the drawing room with the boy in my arms. I'd been doing CPR for nearly two hours, and I wouldn't stop, and he had to take my hands away by force.

The coastguard helicopter came from Prestwick at midnight.

The post-mortem said that Miles Grant, aged ten, had died of a cardiac arrhythmia, a rare congenital heart condition called long QT syndrome. It had never been diagnosed. It can cause sudden death in children, the pathologist said, usually triggered by extreme fright or stress. Nobody had known he had it. His father had had it too, as it turned out. It had probably caused the helicopter crash in the Alps; he'd been the pilot.

There was a fatal accident inquiry in Oban in the autumn. I gave evidence. I told them everything, all of it, exactly as I've written it here. I watched their faces. The sheriff was kind. He recorded that the death was natural, and that nobody could have foreseen it.

He didn't say anything about the cameras. Nobody did. Mr Grant's lawyers had had the whole security system removed from Inverlaig within a week of the death, and the recordings destroyed. They said it was routine. They said the system had been faulty for months, and that Peter Quinn had complained about it constantly, about glitches and shadows and figures on the screens that weren't there.

---

That's all.

I don't know what I saw. I've had two years with Dr Ferrier to think about it, and I still don't know. Some days I'm absolutely certain. They were there, Peter Quinn and Emma Jessop, on the tower and in the garden and at the loch and on the terrace. They were real, and they wanted the children. I was the only one who could see them, and I tried to save the children, and I failed. Other days I lie awake at three in the morning and see Flora's face on the rock by the loch, crumpling, screaming *why do you keep looking at things that aren't there?* And I think: *it was me. There was nothing there but me.*

There was a lonely young woman a long way from home, who'd been told that two people had been too much with the children and then died, and who wanted something to happen to her. She was sitting up every night watching a faulty screen until three in the morning. She decided she was the only one in the world who could see the truth, and she wouldn't let anyone tell her otherwise. And a frightened ten-year-old boy with a bad heart, whom she loved more than anyone she'd ever loved, turned round on a piano stool on a golden evening to look at what she was pointing at, and saw nothing. And all the fear she'd been pouring into him for weeks went into his heart at once, and it stopped.

I don't know which is true. I don't think I ever will. Perhaps they're both true. Perhaps that's the worst of it.

---

## AFTERWORD

Douglas Ferrier closed the folder and sat for a long time at the end of the kitchen table, in the candlelight, without speaking.

"What happened to her?" somebody said at last. "The writer?"

"She got better," said Douglas. "Mostly. She went back to Lewis, and then to Glasgow. She retrained as a social worker. She worked for twenty years with children in care: children nobody believed, children who saw things, children who'd been too much with the wrong adults." He paused. "She was extraordinary at it. Better than anyone I ever knew. She had a way of looking at a child and seeing exactly what was there, and nothing else. She said she'd learned it the hard way."

"And the little girl? Flora?"

Douglas was quiet for a moment.

"I met her once," he said. "About ten years ago. She was twenty-something by then, a doctor, a paediatric cardiologist, at the Sick Kids in Edinburgh. She came to see me. She wanted to know about her brother, and about her old tutor, whom she'd never seen again after the jetty." He looked down at the folder on the table. "I didn't show her this. But I asked her one question. I'd always wanted to ask it."

"What?"

"I asked her whether she'd ever seen anything on Inverlaig. On the cameras, or at the loch, or anywhere." He was quiet for a long time. "She looked at me with those grave grey eyes, and said, *Dr Ferrier, I was eight. I saw everything.*"

"What does that mean?"

Douglas Ferrier picked up the folder and held it for a moment in his hands. Then he stood up from the table.

"I don't know," he said. "That's the point. I've never known. I told you that at the beginning."

He went upstairs to bed. The rest of us sat at the kitchen table for a long time without speaking. The candles burned down, and the snow fell outside on the dark hills of the Borders. None of us, I noticed, looked out of the window.

## 1. Title of the Work

## 2. Creative Work

It was an architecture of suffocating transparency. When I first arrived at the Solitude Observatory, perched on the jagged, wind-battered cliffs of the northern coast, I believed the great glass dome would let in all the truth of the world. I had been commissioned by the reclusive benefactor of the estate to oversee the botanical archives and, more importantly, to take over the tutelage of his nephew, Julian. Julian was ten years old, a creature of such pale, luminous fragility that I felt an immediate, overwhelming mandate to shield him from the encroaching rot of the world.

His previous guardian, a brilliant but disgraced botanist named Dr. Aris, had died under circumstances the estate lawyers refused to clarify. They spoke only of a "sickness of the mind" that had led Aris to wander into the freezing tides. From my very first week, I sensed the lingering contagion of Aris’s intellect in the observatory's shadowed corridors, but most acutely, I feared its invisible spores had settled into the pristine soil of Julian’s mind.

Julian was a child of unsettling perfection. He moved through the humid, overgrown aisles of the great glasshouse with a silent grace, his small fingers tracing the veins of exotic orchids and carnivorous pitchers with a familiarity that chilled me. He never spoke of Aris. When I asked him about his former lessons, his eyes—wide, dark, and fathomless—would fix upon me with a terrifyingly blank innocence. He would simply smile, a gesture so sweet it broke my heart, and redirect my attention to the blooming nightshade.

The obsession took root in me slowly, like a creeping ivy. I began to watch Julian not as a tutor, but as a sentinel. I was convinced that Aris had left something behind—a philosophy, a dark communion, a secret language—that he was still transmitting to the boy from beyond the grave.

The first manifestation occurred in the dead of winter. The glass dome was lashed with sleet, isolating us in a world of humid greenery and roaring white noise. I had been reading in the archive when a sudden chill, entirely distinct from the drafts of the old ironwork, seized the back of my neck. I looked up, through the tangled canopy of the hanging ferns, toward the upper gantry.

He was standing there.

It was a man, gaunt and impossibly tall, his face obscured by the heavy shadows of the foliage, but his posture reeked of ownership. He was looking down not at me, but at the potting benches below. I leapt from my chair, my heart hammering a frantic rhythm against my ribs, and rushed to the iron spiral staircase. By the time I reached the gantry, the catwalk was empty. Only the faint, metallic sway of the grated floor remained. I looked down. There, perfectly centered beneath the spot where the figure had stood, was Julian, quietly repotting a highly toxic belladonna plant. He did not look up. He did not need to.

From that evening, my purpose crystallized into a holy terror. I was the shield. I was the screen between Julian and the phantom of Aris’s influence. I began to intercept Julian’s every glance, parse his every silence, and hover over his bed at night, waiting to catch him communing with the ghost I knew walked the aisles of the glasshouse. Julian bore my suffocating presence with a tragic, angelic patience that only fueled my paranoia. If he was truly innocent, my surveillance would keep him so. If he was already corrupted, I would force the poison to the surface.

The pressure inside the dome became intolerable. The air felt thick, breathable only as water is breathable to the drowning.

The climax of our silent, desperate war came on a twilight evening in late March. The dome was painted in bruised purples and dying golds. I had found Julian alone in the deepest section of the conservatory, standing before a massive, ancient cycad. He was entirely still, his back to me, staring out through the glass into the darkening mist over the cliffs.

I approached him silently. The air was heavy with the scent of damp earth and decaying orchids. As I drew close, my eyes instinctively followed his gaze out into the gray void beyond the glass.

My breath caught. Outside, standing on the narrow, precarious ledge between the glass and the sheer drop to the sea, was Aris. His face was pressed near the pane, pallid, wet, and warped by the condensation, his hollow eyes fixed with a ravenous hunger upon the boy.

A surge of protective violence erupted within me. I lunged forward and grabbed Julian by the shoulders, spinning him away from the glass and pulling his small, frail body flush against my chest.

"Don't look at him!" I shrieked, the sound tearing my throat. "I am here! I have you!"

Julian struggled against my grip, his hands pushing weakly against my coat. He was panting, his eyes darting frantically around the humid enclosure. "What?" he cried out, his voice cracking with a pure, unadulterated panic. "Who? Let me go!"

"You know who it is!" I demanded, my hands tightening like iron bands around his narrow shoulders. I shook him, desperate to break the seal of his secrecy, desperate to drag him into the light of my own salvation. "Confess it, Julian! Look at the glass and tell me you see him! Say his name!"

"There is no one!" Julian screamed, a sound of such profound, agonizing terror that it echoed off the glass panels like shattering crystal. He writhed, his face pale and slick with sweat. "You're hurting me! There's nothing there! Only you!"

"Liar!" I wept, burying my face in his hair, shielding his eyes from the window while simultaneously demanding he acknowledge the monster outside. "He wants to take you, but I won't let him! Say you see him, Julian! Surrender him to me, and you will be free!"

"No more, please, no more!" Julian gasped, his struggles growing frantic, then erratic, like a bird caught in a snare.

I looked up, over his head, glaring in defiance at the window. The mist swirled against the glass. The ledge was empty. The phantom had vanished, defeated by my fierce, uncompromising love.

A profound, triumphant silence fell over the conservatory. I had won. I had driven the shadow away. I loosened my grip, smiling, waiting for the boy to sag against me in gratitude and relief.

But as I stepped back, Julian did not look at me. His head lolled forward on his chest. The unnatural tension that had animated his small frame evaporated all at once. I caught him as he slipped toward the damp stone floor, sinking to my knees to cradle him.

I called his name, smoothing the damp hair from his forehead, waiting for his dark eyes to open and reflect the clarity of the world I had just cleansed for him. But the glasshouse was quiet, and the boy in my arms was perfectly, infinitely still.

That afternoon, Mara visited the municipal records commissioner, Adrian Sorel.

He was a polished man of sixty who had inherited both his father's political connections and his confidence that every difficult problem could be solved by appropriate filing.

He listened to Mara's discoveries with an expression of professional sympathy.

"These are very old matters," he said.

"They concern people who may never have been counted among the dead."

"Historical records are often incomplete."

"Someone altered the inspection reports."

"That is a serious accusation."

"I have the documents."

"Then submit them through the proper channels."

Mara placed the forged statement on his desk.

"Your father was director of municipal engineering when the accident occurred."

Sorel glanced at the document.

"I was aware."

"His signature appears on the authorization."

"Many decisions were made during that emergency."

"Was he aware of the workers in the lower chamber?"

Sorel folded his hands.

"Miss Venn, I understand that your father's disappearance makes this a deeply personal subject."

"It is personal to everyone who died."

"Speculation will not bring them back."

"No. But it may tell us who they were."

His pleasant expression disappeared.

"Some doors are closed because opening them serves no useful purpose."

Mara collected her papers.

"Doors are made to be opened."

"Not when there is water behind them."

The words were spoken quietly.

Nevertheless, Mara felt as though someone had struck her.

She turned toward him.

"What did you say?"

Sorel stood.

"Our meeting is concluded."

Outside the municipal building, rain had begun to fall.

At the foot of the steps, an old woman was sitting beneath a dark umbrella, selling little bundles of autumn flowers.

Mara had seen her there many times.

The woman watched her with unusual attention.

"You're the engineer's daughter," she said.

Mara stopped.

"Did you know him?"

"My husband worked below the streets."

"Was he part of the night crew?"

The woman's eyes filled.

"That's what they called them, wasn't it? A crew. As though they were machinery."

She took a photograph from her coat.

It showed five men and a young boy standing beside a drainage entrance.

"My husband was thirty-seven. The boy was his nephew. They went down together."

Mara studied the photograph.

"Do you remember their names?"

"Of course."

"Would you tell me?"

The woman looked surprised.

Then she began.

As the rain fell around them, Mara wrote down every name.

## Chapter Five: The Room Beneath the River

The city announced the demolition of the old telephone exchange on the first Monday in November.

The building stood above Section Nine.

Its foundations had been declared unstable, and the government intended to replace it with a modern civic plaza.

Mara understood what that meant.

Once the foundations were removed and the lower tunnels filled with concrete, whatever remained beneath the exchange would become unreachable.

She had six days.

Tomas agreed to help her.

"Why?" she asked when he accepted.

He looked down at his hands.

"Because I've spent fifty-four years hearing a bell whenever the house gets quiet."

They entered the exchange through a maintenance door shortly after sunset.

The building had been abandoned for decades. Its windows were opaque with dust, and ivy climbed through the empty frames.

Inside, ranks of telephone switches stood like a congregation of rusted skeletons.

Hundreds of disconnected wires hung from the ceiling.

Mara carried a lantern and the original survey map.

Tomas carried a small toolkit and a length of rope.

They found the stairway behind a locked iron door.

The first flight descended into a chamber lined with green tiles.

The second led beneath the old reservoir wall.

At the third landing, Mara heard a bell.

One slow note.

Then another.

Tomas stopped.

"That's impossible."

"Why?"

"The bell was removed after the accident."

The sound came again.

They followed it into a passage where mineral deposits glittered on the walls.

At the far end stood an iron gate.

Its surface was coated with rust, but a newer chain had been drawn tightly across its bars.

Mara examined the lock.

"Someone has been here recently."

Tomas touched the masonry.

"Look."

There were marks where a plaque had once been attached.

A faint rectangle of cleaner stone remained.

Above it, scratched into the wall, were several numbers.

Mara counted them.

Eleven.

The last three had been carved so deeply that the stone had fractured.

From somewhere beyond the gate, a child began to hum.

Mara turned.

"Did you hear that?"

Tomas nodded.

For several seconds neither moved.

Then a man's voice spoke from the darkness.

"Don't open it."

Mara lifted the lantern.

The passage was empty.

"Who's there?"

"Not while the river is high."

She recognized the voice.

It belonged to her father.

Or to the memory of him that she had carried for thirty-four years.

She could not tell which.

Tomas grasped her arm.

"He's right."

Water was seeping through the mortar near the ceiling.

The old reservoir had filled during the recent rains.

If they broke the gate or disturbed the wall, the pressure might send a sudden flood through the passage.

They retreated to a dry landing.

There Tomas examined the survey map.

"The chamber has another entrance," he said.

Mara leaned closer.

"Where?"

"Through the inspection vault."

"But the staircase ends."

"The staircase they left on the public plans ends."

He pointed to a narrow service passage marked in blue pencil.

"Your father drew this. He must have wanted someone to find it."

The passage began behind a low brick partition.

Its entrance had been concealed by a rusted electrical cabinet.

Together they pushed the cabinet aside and removed several loose bricks.

Beyond them lay a narrow tunnel.

Mara entered first.

The air smelled of wet iron and old earth.

After several yards, the passage opened into a vaulted room.

Their lantern illuminated a table, two overturned chairs, a broken clock, and an emergency telephone fixed to the wall.

The room had remained untouched for decades.

Against the far wall stood a metal cabinet.

Mara opened it.

Inside were a ledger, several inspection notebooks, and a bundle of letters wrapped in oilcloth.

The first notebook bore her father's name.

She opened it with trembling fingers.

The final entry was dated the night of the disaster.

Upper gate opened at 11:42.

Lower chamber occupied.

Emergency closure attempted.

Control refuses reversal.

I am going down.

Mara read the last sentence again.

There was no further entry.

Beside the notebook lay a small child's shoe.

Its laces had been carefully tied together.

And beneath the shoe, someone had placed eleven stones in a row.

## Chapter Six: The Eleventh Name

They carried the papers back to the surface before midnight.

Tomas was silent throughout the return journey.

Only when they reached his cottage did Mara begin examining the ledger.

It contained wage records for the night crew.

Eleven workers had entered Section Nine on the evening of the flood.

Seven were adults employed through a private contractor.

Three were temporary laborers who had come to Bellwether looking for work.

The eleventh was a boy of fourteen.

His name was Daniel Arlen.

He had been hired to carry tools and relay messages between the underground chambers.

Mara recognized him from the old woman's photograph.

The official accident report mentioned none of these people.

But the ledger contained something even more disturbing.

The wages for the entire crew had been paid out three days after the accident.

Each entry bore a signature acknowledging receipt.

Mara inspected the signatures.

They had been written by the same hand.

The city had not merely neglected to record the deaths.

It had created documents suggesting that the workers had survived.

"Why?" she whispered.

Tomas sat beside the cold fireplace.

"Compensation."

Mara looked up.

"Families of employees killed during municipal work were entitled to payments. Families of casual laborers received less. Families of people who were never officially employed received nothing."

"And the contractor?"

"He was paid for completed work."

Mara turned another page.

Attached to the ledger was a receipt for the closure of the lower chamber.

The date was four days after the flood.

The contractor had billed the city for sealing the entrances.

"Someone knew they were down there," Mara said.

Tomas did not answer.

She lifted the last document from the bundle.

It was a letter written by her father to the municipal engineering director.

I entered the lower level after the diversion began. The southern passage had collapsed, and the principal exit was already impassable. I reached the inspection vault but could not open the chamber gate against the pressure.

I heard the emergency bell continuously for seventeen minutes.

I attempted communication with the control station. My warnings were acknowledged, but the diversion was not reversed.

There were eleven persons in the chamber. I am recording their names so there can be no uncertainty later.

The letter continued with a list.

At the bottom, in smaller writing, was a final paragraph.

I do not know whether any of them remain alive. I will attempt to reach the chamber from the eastern service tunnel.

Mara turned the page.

There was nothing more.

Her father had not written a farewell.

He had not explained himself.

He had simply gone back into the dark.

Mara closed the letter.

For the first time since childhood, she began to cry without trying to stop herself.

Tomas moved toward her but remained at a respectful distance.

After a while she said, "They knew he was there."

"Yes."

"They knew about the others."

"Yes."

"And afterward they made the records disappear."

Tomas lowered his head.

"I helped."

Mara looked at him.

He seemed suddenly much older.

"I was ordered to remove the emergency bell. I took down the telephone connections. I signed a statement that the lower chamber had been empty."

"Why are you telling me now?"

"Because you have the proof."

"You had it then."

His hands trembled.

"Yes."

Mara rose from the table.

For a moment she wanted to shout at him, to demand the return of her father, to force him to account for thirty-four years of silence.

Instead she asked, "Was the bell still ringing when you removed it?"

Tomas stared at the floor.

"No."

She waited.

He swallowed.

"By then it was under water."

## Chapter Seven: The Man at the Window

Three nights before the scheduled demolition, someone broke into Mara's office.

The archive drawers were emptied, and the documents she had left there were scattered across the floor.

A cupboard had been forced open.

But the intruder had overlooked the most important papers, which Mara had taken home.

The black telephone remained on her desk.

Beside it lay an envelope.

Inside was a single sheet of paper.

Your father made mistakes. Do not make another.

Mara carried the letter to the police.

The officer who received it was courteous and entirely unhelpful.

Without evidence identifying the sender, he explained, there was little they could do.

When Mara returned home, she found Adrian Sorel waiting outside her apartment.

He stood beneath the streetlamp, bareheaded in the rain.

"I hoped we could speak privately," he said.

"About the break-in?"

He seemed genuinely surprised.

"What break-in?"

Mara studied him.

"Then why are you here?"

Sorel looked toward the dark windows of the neighboring houses.

"My father died twelve years ago. I inherited his papers, his property, and a considerable number of things he never explained."

"Such as?"

"A sealed account of the Section Nine accident."

Mara remained silent.

Sorel continued.

"I knew there had been an irregularity. I knew workers had been omitted from the report. But I believed the omission concerned four men."

"There were eleven."

He closed his eyes.

"Eleven."

"And my father."

Sorel looked at her sharply.

"Your father was not in that chamber."

"How do you know?"

"Because my father received a message from him after the flood."

Mara felt the pavement shift beneath her feet.

"What message?"

Sorel reached into his coat and produced a folded letter.

It was written in the hand she recognized.

The eastern passage remains accessible. I intend to return to the lower chamber once the water falls. Please prevent further sealing operations until the site is examined.

The letter was dated two days after the disaster.

"He survived," Mara whispered.

"For at least two days."

"Then why was he declared missing?"

"I don't know."

"Where is the rest of the correspondence?"

"My father destroyed most of it."

"And you?"

"I found this among his private papers."

Mara looked at the letter, then at Sorel.

"Why give it to me now?"

He drew a long breath.

"Because something has been happening in my house."

She waited.

"For three weeks, my telephone has rung every night. It isn't connected to the old system. At first I thought it was an electrical fault."

"What did you hear?"

"Water."

"And?"

Sorel's composure failed.

"A boy asking whether his mother had been told."

Mara said nothing.

"He asks the same question every night."

"Have you answered?"

"What could I say?"

"You could tell her."

Sorel looked away.

"She died twenty years ago."

"Then tell someone else."

The rain thickened.

At last he said, "What do you want me to do?"

Mara folded the letter.

"Help me open the chamber."

## Chapter Eight: The Last Door

The municipal council granted an emergency suspension of demolition after Sorel produced the documents from his father's estate.

It was an unusual proceeding.

Some officials protested that the evidence was insufficient. Others argued that the cost of reopening the underground chamber would be excessive.

The mayor spoke of public confidence.

The city solicitor spoke of legal responsibility.

Mara listened to them all.

Then she placed the photograph of the night crew on the council table.

"These people had names," she said.

The room became quiet.

"Before we discuss the city's reputation, perhaps we should acknowledge that."

The vote was narrow.

But the chamber would be examined.

A specialist engineering team entered Section Nine the following morning. They used temporary supports, pumps, and reinforced barriers to stabilize the flooded passage.

Mara waited aboveground with Tomas, Sorel, and the families who had gathered after hearing the news.

Some were elderly.

Others were grandchildren of people they had never met.

One woman brought a faded photograph of her brother.

A man carried a letter his father had written before leaving home to seek work in Bellwether.

By afternoon, the engineers had reached the lower chamber.

They found remains.

They found tools, clothing, and an iron emergency bell still attached to the wall.

They found the names of several workers scratched into the stone.

Near the entrance stood a narrow wooden shelf.

On it were eleven small stones.

The engineers photographed everything.

But they found no trace of Elias Venn.

Mara received the news without surprise.

By then she understood that her father had escaped the original flood and returned afterward.

What had happened to him next remained uncertain.

An engineer brought her one final discovery.

Behind the emergency telephone, concealed in a shallow recess, lay a sealed metal cylinder.

Inside was a carefully folded letter.

It was addressed to whoever might eventually enter the chamber.

Mara opened it.

The writing was unmistakably her father's.

I returned because I had been told to leave.

I had seen the dangerous conditions. I had signed the amended inspection certificate. I told myself the work would be completed quickly and that no disaster would occur.

When the storm came, I knew the risk before the order was given.

I protested, but I did not stop them.

The others paid for that failure.

Mara stopped reading.

The words seemed to rearrange the father she had remembered.

He had not been entirely innocent.

He had known.

He had signed.

He had tried to correct his mistake only after the danger had become unavoidable.

For a moment, Mara felt the old childish longing to defend him.

Then she continued.

There is a difference between fearing a wrong and refusing to take part in it. I understood that difference too late.

If these pages are found, please record the names of the people in this chamber. Do not make heroes of them. Do not make a hero of me.

Tell their families what happened.

And if there is a bell aboveground, ring it.

The letter ended there.

Mara lowered the paper.

Beyond the barrier, pumps continued to draw water from the ancient passages.

For an instant she thought she heard someone walking beneath the floor.

Not hurriedly.

Not angrily.

Simply walking away.

## Chapter Nine: The Ceremony of Names

Winter arrived early that year.

The first snow fell on the morning the city held its memorial ceremony.

The cathedral square filled with people.

The names of the eleven workers were engraved on a stone monument beside the names of the seven men officially acknowledged decades earlier.

Elias Venn's name was added to a separate inscription explaining his disappearance and his role in the disaster.

The investigation had established that the city had concealed the presence of the lower crew, falsified employment records, and suppressed safety objections.

The identities of several individuals responsible were known, though most had died before they could be held accountable.

The city established compensation arrangements for surviving families.

It also opened its historical records to public inspection.

These actions could not restore the dead.

They could not return childhoods, marriages, or years of grief.

But they did give shape to something that had previously been allowed to vanish.

Mara stood beside Tomas as the mayor approached the monument.

He gave a speech.

It was brief, solemn, and somewhat awkward.

For once, Mara found herself grateful for the awkwardness.

Perfect words would have seemed dishonest.

When the mayor finished, a cathedral attendant approached the bell tower.

The great bronze bell had not been used for a funeral in more than twenty years.

Its mechanism was old, and there was some concern that the clapper might not move properly.

The attendant pulled the rope.

Nothing happened.

He pulled again.

A small murmur passed through the crowd.

Then, deep inside the tower, a dull vibration began.

The first note emerged uncertainly.

The second was stronger.

By the third, the bell was ringing across the entire city.

Its sound travelled over rooftops, through marketplaces, and along the riverbanks where the winter ice had begun to form.

People lowered their heads.

Some wept.

Others listened in silence.

Mara counted the tolls.

One for each of the eleven workers.

One for each of the seven men.

One for her father.

Nineteen.

When the final sound faded, she felt Tomas take her hand.

"I wish I'd spoken sooner," he said.

"So do I."

He looked at her, surprised by the firmness of her answer.

Mara continued.

"But you spoke."

He nodded, though the words did not entirely comfort him.

Perhaps they were not meant to.

## Chapter Ten: What the Water Keeps

The black telephone remained in Mara's office.

After the memorial, it no longer rang at midnight.

She examined it carefully.

Its interior wiring was badly corroded. The receiver contained an old magnetic diaphragm. The instrument had been disconnected from the exchange long before it reached her desk.

A technician declared that it could not possibly have received a call.

Another suggested that some internal mechanism might have produced sounds resembling speech.

A third proposed that Mara's grief had influenced her perception of ordinary noises.

She considered each explanation seriously.

None completely satisfied her.

But she was no longer certain that satisfaction mattered.

The important things had been recovered.

The names.

The documents.

The knowledge of what had happened.

The living had finally taken responsibility for the dead.

In December, Mara received a parcel from the engineers completing the restoration of Section Nine.

Inside was a small brass object.

It was the clapper from the emergency bell.

An accompanying note explained that the bell itself would be preserved in the municipal museum, but the clapper had been replaced during conservation.

Mara placed it beside the black telephone.

That evening, snow gathered against the archive windows.

She remained at her desk long after the other employees had left.

At eleven minutes past midnight, she heard a sound.

It was not the telephone.

It came from the brass clapper.

A delicate metallic note, almost too soft to distinguish from the settling of the building.

Mara looked at it.

"Who is there?" she whispered.

There was no reply.

She rose and approached the window.

Far below, Saint Oran's Square lay beneath a quiet covering of snow.

Near the fountain stood a man in a dark coat.

His features were indistinct.

He was looking toward the clock tower.

Mara pressed her hand against the glass.

The man lifted one arm.

For an instant she saw something familiar in the gesture.

Then a tram passed through the square, its windows casting yellow rectangles across the snow.

When it had gone, the man was no longer there.

Mara remained at the window.

She could have run downstairs.

She could have searched the square, questioned the tram driver, or followed the footprints that might or might not exist.

Instead she returned to her desk.

She opened a fresh ledger.

At the top of the first page she wrote:

Persons Missing from the Historical Record

Then she began to work.

There were other disappearances in Bellwether.

Other accidents that had never been properly investigated.

Other families who had accepted silence because no one had offered them anything else.

She would not be able to resolve every mystery.

Some stories had already lost their witnesses. Some records had been destroyed. Some truths would remain buried beneath the weight of years.

But she could begin.

Outside, the snow continued falling.

The black telephone stood silent.

And somewhere beneath the streets, beyond the sealed gates and forgotten passageways, water travelled patiently through the darkness.

It had carried secrets for generations.

It had worn away stone, swallowed footsteps, and erased the traces of countless lives.

Yet Mara had learned something the city had failed to understand.

Water could hide the dead, but it could not absolve the living.

And memory, once awakened, could become more enduring than stone.

She wrote until morning.

When the first pale sunlight entered the archive, the brass clapper moved once upon the desk.

There was no wind.

No passing train.

No vibration from the clock tower.

Only a small, clear sound.

Like a bell being answered.

The End.
