29. UNDER THE RED DRAGON.

# The Dragon's Return

## PART ONE: TWO SUMMERS

### I.

The letter came in June 1981, when I was twenty-three and a second lieutenant in the Welsh Guards, stationed at Pirbright. It was from Sir Emrys Pryce, my late father's oldest friend, inviting me to spend a fortnight's leave at Plas Eryri in August "as you always used to, boy, before the Army got its claws into you."

"And who's this Sir Emrys when he's at home?" said Tom Caradog, my fellow subaltern, reading over my shoulder in the mess.

"An old man with a big house in Snowdonia," I said. "My father's friend. I spent every summer there till I was eighteen."

"And?"

"And nothing."

Tom grinned. He was a farmer's son from Carmarthen with a face like a cheerful potato, and he could read me like a book.

"There's a girl," he said. "Isn't there?"

There was, though not the one he meant, and not the one I meant either. I didn't know that yet.

---

Plas Eryri stands at the head of a long valley in the mountains above Betws-y-Coed, a grey slate house with too many chimneys, half-covered in ivy, with a view straight up the valley to the great dark wall of the Carneddau. My father had been Sir Emrys's estate manager for twenty years, until he died. I'd grown up in the lodge at the bottom of the drive, and spent my childhood running wild on the mountain with the old man's granddaughter.

Her name was Ffion Pryce. She was a year younger than me: small and dark and quiet, with grey eyes and her grandfather's stubbornness. Through every summer of our childhood we'd been inseparable. We built dams in the stream, climbed Tryfan, fished Llyn Cowlyd, and argued about everything. She was the nearest thing I had to a sister. When I left for Sandhurst at eighteen, she stood at the bottom of the drive and didn't wave, and didn't write, and I didn't think about it.

She was there when I arrived in August, at the top of the steps, in jeans and a jumper, with mud on her boots. She was a staff nurse now at Ysbyty Gwynedd in Bangor. She shook my hand, very formally, and said, "Hello, Rhys," and went back inside.

And there was someone else there.

### II.

Her name was Arabella Cressington. She was twenty-two, the daughter of a Conservative MP, and a friend of Sir Emrys's London niece, who'd brought her up to Snowdonia for the fortnight "to get some air." She was tall and fair, with the kind of beauty that makes rooms go quiet, and a laugh like breaking glass. Within an hour of meeting her, at dinner on the first night, I'd forgotten everything else in the world.

I won't pretend it was anything but what it was. I was twenty-three, a farm manager's son from a lodge at the bottom of a drive. She was everything I'd ever been told I couldn't have: London, money, glamour, a father in the House of Commons. She seemed, impossibly, to find me interesting. She asked about the Army and listened to the answers. She laughed at my jokes. She took my arm on the terrace after dinner and asked me to show her the stars. And when I did, she looked at me instead.

I spent the fortnight following her about like a dog. Ffion, I barely noticed. She was there at breakfast, gone to the hospital by eight, home again for dinner, quiet, watching. Once, on the fourth day, she asked if I'd like to climb Tryfan with her on her day off, as we used to. I said I'd promised to take Bella to Portmeirion. Ffion said, "Of course," and went up the mountain alone.

---

On the tenth day, Bella and I took a boat out from Abersoch into Cardigan Bay. It was her idea, and a stupid one. The sky was blue when we left, and there was a storm by four. A squall came in off the sea like a wall and capsized the dinghy a mile off Porth Ceiriad. We were in the water for an hour. I held her up, both of us half drowned, until the tide threw us onto the rocks at the foot of the cliffs at dusk.

A farmer found us at dawn, washed up among the weed and the wreckage, soaked and freezing and alive. Bella was clinging to me as if she would never let go.

That night, in the farmer's kitchen in Aberdaron, with blankets round us and tea laced with whisky, she took my face in her cold hands and said, "You saved my life, Rhys Wynne. I'll never forget it. Never." And she kissed me.

We were engaged by the end of the week, secretly. Her father would never allow it, she said, not yet, not a second lieutenant with no money and no family. We'd wait. When I was a captain, when I'd made my name, she'd tell him, and we'd be married in St Margaret's, Westminster, with the whole regiment in scarlet. Until then, it would be our secret. She gave me a ring, a thin gold band that had been her grandmother's, to wear on a chain round my neck. I gave her my father's signet ring.

I told nobody except Tom Caradog.

And Ffion, I think, knew anyway. On the morning I left Plas Eryri at the end of the fortnight, she was standing at the bottom of the drive by the lodge, as she had been when I left for Sandhurst. She didn't wave. But as the car went past she looked at me, and there was something in her face I didn't understand. I didn't think about it again for a long time.

### III.

There was a man called Giles Fanshawe.

I met him at Bella's parents' house in Chelsea that autumn, at a drinks party to which she'd smuggled me as "a friend of a friend." He was thirty, a stockbroker, beautifully dressed, beautifully spoken, very rich, with a thin, clever face and a way of looking at Bella across a room that made my fists clench. He was, Bella said, laughing, an old family friend, a bore, harmless. He sent her flowers every week. Her father adored him.

"He's a crook," said Tom Caradog, who'd come with me to the party. He'd watched Fanshawe for an hour with his farmer's eye. "Mark my words, Rhys. That man owes money to half of London. Look at his shoes, then look at his eyes. The shoes are new. The eyes are counting."

I didn't listen. I was in love, and a man in love doesn't listen to anyone.

## PART TWO: THE SOUTH ATLANTIC

### IV.

On the second of April 1982, Argentina invaded the Falkland Islands.

I'll not write a history of that war. Better men than me have done it. I'll say only that on the twelfth of May, the 1st Battalion, Welsh Guards, sailed from Southampton on the *Queen Elizabeth 2*. Eight thousand miles south, through the tropics and into the Southern Ocean, to a place most of us had never heard of six weeks before. Tom Caradog and I stood at the rail as she pulled away from the quay in Southampton with the band playing "Men of Harlech," and the whole of the dock was a sea of waving flags, red dragons on green and white.

Bella wasn't there. She'd written to say she couldn't bear to see me go. She'd sent a photograph and a lock of her hair and a letter, three pages, beautiful and passionate, promising to wait forever.

Ffion was there.

I didn't see her until the last moment. The great ship was already moving, the gap of black water widening between the hull and the quay. And there she was, at the edge of the crowd, small and dark in a navy coat, not waving, looking up at the rail. She'd driven down overnight from Bangor, I found out later, three hundred miles, after a twelve-hour shift, to stand on a quay for ten minutes and watch me go. She didn't wave. She just stood there, looking up, until the ship was too far away for me to see her face.

I thought it was kind of her. That's all I thought.

### V.

Bella wrote every week at first. Long letters, scented, full of London and parties and how much she missed me. I read them by torchlight in my bunk on the *QE2*, and later on the *Canberra*, and later still in a slit trench on East Falkland in the rain, and kept them in a plastic bag inside my smock, against my heart.

Then they came every fortnight. Then less. Shorter. She'd been to Henley, she wrote. And Ascot. Giles had taken her. He was being very kind. Daddy said it was good for her to be seen out and about. Everyone was so worried about the war. It was all so horrid. She hoped I was keeping warm.

Ffion wrote too.

She wrote every week, without fail, the whole time I was away, eleven letters, on lined paper from a hospital notepad, in a small, neat, sloping hand. They weren't scented or passionate, and they didn't say anything at all, really. They were about Plas Eryri, and the mountain, and her grandfather's health, and the weather in the valley. The heather was coming out on the Carneddau. A pair of ravens were nesting on the crag above Llyn Cowlyd, where we'd watched them as children. She'd climbed Tryfan on her day off, alone, and sat on the summit between Adam and Eve, the two great stones on top, and thought about the time I'd dared her to jump from one to the other when she was nine, and she had, and nearly broken her neck.

I read them quickly, in the trench, and smiled, and put them in my pack, not my smock. They were from home. They were a comfort, the way a cup of tea is a comfort. I didn't think about them any more than that.

I was a fool, of course. Tom Caradog told me so, in so many words, in a slit trench near Fitzroy at the beginning of June, in the rain, reading over my shoulder as I tossed Ffion's tenth letter into my pack and took out Bella's latest, two pages, from Ascot.

"You're an idiot, Rhys Wynne," he said cheerfully. "A great Welsh idiot. You'll realise one day. I just hope it's not too late."

"Realise what?"

But he only shook his head and went back to cleaning his rifle.

### VI.

On the night of the sixth of June, my platoon was sent forward on a patrol towards the Argentine positions on Mount Harriet. We were to find a route and come back. We found it, and on the way back, at about two in the morning, in the dark, in the rocks below the mountain, we found a boy.

He was lying in a hollow between two boulders, in the freezing rain. He was an Argentine conscript, eighteen or nineteen, in a thin green parka two sizes too big, with no gloves, and a wound in his stomach from a mortar fragment. He'd been there for a day and a night, I think, left behind when his unit pulled back. He was very cold and very frightened and dying, and he knew it.

He looked up at me in the dark, at the barrel of my rifle and my blackened face, and said something in Spanish I didn't understand.

I knelt beside him in the rain. I didn't think. I took off my own gloves and put them on his hands. Then I took his head in my lap, out of the mud. I'd done a first-aid course at Sandhurst, so I looked at his wound, and knew there was nothing to be done.

"*Mamá*," he said. "*Mamá.*"

I understood that.

My sergeant, an old Rhondda man called Davies the Bomb, crouched beside me in the dark. "Sir," he said quietly. "We've got to move. We'll be seen at first light."

"Five minutes," I said.

The boy's hand found mine. He was holding something in it: a rosary, cheap wooden beads on a string, with a small tin crucifix. He pressed it into my palm and closed my fingers round it, and said something in Spanish, over and over. I think it was a name and a place. *Lucas Benítez. Corrientes. Corrientes.*

He died about four minutes later, with his head in my lap, in the rain, in the dark, under Mount Harriet, eight thousand miles from Corrientes. I closed his eyes. We left him there, under a groundsheet, with a stone on it and his name written on a scrap of paper. I told the battalion HQ where he was in the morning. Months later I found out that the Argentines had buried him with their own dead at Darwin.

I kept the rosary. I wore it round my neck, on the same chain as Bella's grandmother's ring.

I don't know why I'm telling you this. It has nothing to do with the rest of the story, except that it has everything to do with it.

### VII.

On the morning of the eighth of June, the 1st Battalion, Welsh Guards, was waiting on board the landing ship *Sir Lamorak* in the anchorage at Port Pleasant, near Fitzroy, to be put ashore.

We'd been waiting for hours. Something had gone wrong with the landing craft. Nobody seemed to know what. The ship was packed with men and ammunition and fuel, and we sat in the tank deck and on the vehicle deck and in the passageways, waiting. It was a clear, bright, cold day, the first clear day in weeks. Tom Caradog was sitting beside me on an ammunition box, eating a Mars bar and reading a letter from his mother.

At about ten past two in the afternoon, the Argentine air force came.

I remember a sound like the sky tearing open. I remember Tom Caradog looking up from his letter. I remember a white light and a great blow of heat. And then nothing, for a long time.

---

They told me afterwards what happened. I don't remember any of it. Two bombs hit the *Sir Lamorak*, and the tank deck became a furnace. Men came up the ladders on fire. The lifeboats and helicopters went in under the smoke, and the rescue went on for hours. Davies the Bomb carried me up a ladder from the tank deck on his back, through the fire, with my clothes burning. He went back down for another man and didn't come up again.

Thirty-two Welsh Guardsmen died on the *Sir Lamorak* that afternoon.

Tom Caradog was one of them. They found him on the tank deck, still sitting on the ammunition box, with his mother's letter in his hand.

I woke up four days later on the hospital ship *Uganda*, in the South Atlantic, with burns to my face and neck and chest. My left hand was gone, taken off at the wrist by a surgeon in a field hospital in Ajax Bay the night of the bombing. There was a nurse beside me, a young Navy nurse with a kind tired face. She told me, very gently, about Tom, and Davies, and the others.

I asked for the plastic bag inside my smock, with Bella's letters in it. It had burned, she said. Everything had burned.

But she gave me the chain from round my neck. They'd cut it off me in the field hospital and kept it. It had two things on it. One was a wooden rosary, scorched black, with a small tin crucifix, melted slightly at one corner. The other was a thin gold band that had been Bella Cressington's grandmother's.

## PART THREE: THE PARADE

### VIII.

I came home in July, on a stretcher, to the military hospital at Woolwich. Then I was moved to the burns unit at Queen Mary's, Roehampton, where they began the long business of grafting new skin onto my face and fitting me with a hook.

Bella came to see me once.

It was in August, a year almost to the day since the storm in Cardigan Bay. She came into the ward at Roehampton in a cream linen dress, with flowers. She stopped at the end of my bed and looked at me: at the bandages and the grafts and the raw red skin on my face and neck, at the empty place at the end of my left arm where my hand had been. I saw her face.

I'll not describe what I saw in her face. I'll say only that it lasted perhaps two seconds, and then she smiled, beautifully, and came and sat beside the bed and took my right hand and talked for twenty minutes about London, and Henley, and Daddy. She said how brave I'd been, how proud she was, how dreadful it all was. She didn't once look at my face again. And when she left, she kissed me on the forehead, on the one place that wasn't bandaged, and said she'd come again soon.

The letter came three weeks later. Two pages, in her beautiful round hand. She'd been thinking so much, she wrote. She was so young. We'd both been so young, last summer, after the storm. It had been so romantic, but perhaps it hadn't been quite real. Perhaps we'd mistaken gratitude for something else. She would always, always be so grateful to me for saving her life. But she thought it would be kinder to us both if we were honest. She hoped I'd understand. She enclosed my father's signet ring.

She didn't mention Giles Fanshawe. She didn't need to. It was in the *Telegraph* a month later. *The engagement is announced between Giles, son of Sir Peregrine and Lady Fanshawe, and Arabella, daughter of Mr and Mrs Hugo Cressington MP.*

---

I took her grandmother's ring off the chain round my neck that night, alone in the ward at Roehampton, and put it in an envelope, and sent it back to her without a letter.

I kept the rosary.

### IX.

In October there was a victory parade in the City of London: the Falklands Task Force, marching through the streets past the Mansion House, with the Prime Minister on the steps of the Guildhall taking the salute, and a quarter of a million people cheering. I was given leave from Roehampton to watch from a stand reserved for the wounded. I went in my uniform, with my face half-grafted, and my empty left sleeve pinned up, and a black glove on my right hand.

I saw them from the stand. Bella, in a fur coat, in the VIP enclosure on the other side of the street, with Giles Fanshawe beside her, laughing at something he'd said. She glanced across at the stand of wounded men, at the empty sleeves, the burned faces and the wheelchairs, for about two seconds. Then she looked away and laughed again.

I don't think she recognised me. I don't think I'd have recognised myself.

I found out later that Giles Fanshawe was arrested in 1984 for fraud. There'd been a Ponzi scheme involving the pension funds of three Lloyd's syndicates, eleven million pounds. He served four years in Ford Open Prison. Bella divorced him in 1985 and married a Swiss banker. Tom Caradog had been right about the shoes and the eyes. He usually was.

I wish he'd been there to tell me so.

## PART FOUR: THE MOUNTAIN

### X.

I went home to Wales in the spring of 1983, discharged from the Army on medical grounds, twenty-five years old, with a face that made children stare in the street and a hook where my left hand had been. I had nowhere else to go. My mother had died when I was at Sandhurst. The lodge at the bottom of the drive at Plas Eryri had been let to a family from Liverpool. Sir Emrys had written to me in hospital, in his shaky old-man's hand: *Come home, boy. There's a room for you here. There always will be.*

So I went home.

The old man met me at the top of the steps, leaning on his stick, as he had when I was a boy. He looked at my face for a long moment, and at the hook, and then he put his arms round me and held me, which he'd never done before, and said nothing at all. Then he took me inside and gave me a whisky.

Ffion wasn't there. She was at the hospital, he said. She'd be home later.

I went up to my old room at the top of the house, overlooking the valley and the dark wall of the Carneddau, and lay on the bed in my clothes, and slept.

---

I dreamed about Ffion.

It was a strange dream. I knew it was a dream even while I was dreaming it. She was sitting on the edge of my bed in the dark, in the room at the top of the house, as she used to when we were children and I had nightmares. Her small cool hand was on my forehead, on the burned skin. She was crying, very quietly, the way she always cried, without making a sound.

"You stupid boy," she was saying in Welsh, over and over, so softly I could hardly hear. "You stupid, stupid boy. I told you. I told you not to go."

Then she was gone, and I woke up, and the room was dark and empty.

But the pillow beside my head was damp, as if someone had been crying on it.

### XI.

She was in the kitchen in the morning, in her nurse's uniform, making toast, as if I'd never been away. She looked at my face across the kitchen table for a long moment, quite steadily, without flinching, with her grey eyes. It was the first time anyone had looked at my face like that since Ajax Bay. She looked at it the way a nurse looks at a wound, or the way you look at a mountain you know well after a storm, to see what's changed.

"It's healing well," she said. "The grafts. They've done a good job at Roehampton." She put a plate of toast in front of me. "Eat."

I ate.

Afterwards, when she'd gone to the hospital, I went up to my old room and sat by the window looking at the mountain, and found I was thinking about her letters. Eleven of them, on lined hospital paper, in a small neat sloping hand. They'd been in my pack, not my smock. They'd come home with my kit from the *Sir Lamorak*, in a cardboard box the Army sent to Roehampton, smelling of smoke, and I'd never opened it.

I opened it that afternoon.

They were all there, at the bottom of the box, under my burned boots and my spare socks: eleven letters, smoke-stained, in their envelopes. I read them, properly, for the first time, sitting by the window at Plas Eryri with the mountain outside.

They weren't about the weather. I'd been too stupid to see it. They were about the weather the way a love song is about the moon. Every one of them was about the mountain, and the valley, and the places we'd been as children. The ravens on the crag above Llyn Cowlyd. The stream where we'd built dams. The summit of Tryfan, between Adam and Eve, where I'd dared her to jump at nine years old and she had, and nearly broken her neck. Every one of them said, on every line, without ever once saying it: *come home. Come home. I'm waiting. I've always been waiting. Come home.*

And the last one, the eleventh, dated the fourth of June 1982, four days before the *Sir Lamorak*, ended with a line I'd skimmed past in a slit trench near Fitzroy in the rain without really reading it:

*I climbed Tryfan again on Sunday and sat between Adam and Eve and jumped, as you dared me to when I was nine. I didn't fall this time. I don't think you know why I did it then, Rhys. I don't think you've ever known. But I hope one day you will. — F.*

### XII.

I climbed Tryfan the next Sunday.

It took me five hours, with one hand and lungs still scarred from the smoke, and I fell twice on the north ridge and cut my face on the rock. But I got to the top. I sat on the summit in the wind with the whole of Snowdonia spread out below me, the valleys and lakes, and the sea in the distance, silver, beyond Anglesey. I looked at the two great stones on the summit, Adam and Eve, standing side by side, with a gap between them of about four feet and a drop of a hundred on either side.

She was already there.

She was sitting on the far side of Eve, in her old walking jacket, with her knees under her chin, looking out at the sea. She'd come up by the south ridge, I found out later, two hours before me. She'd known I would come. She didn't turn round when I came up onto the summit. She just said, in Welsh, very quietly, without looking at me, "You read them, then."

"Yes," I said.

"All of them?"

"All eleven."

She was quiet for a long time, looking at the sea.

"I jumped when I was nine," she said, "because I'd decided that day, on the way up, that I was going to marry you. And I thought, if I'm brave enough to jump, he'll notice." She laughed, a small unsteady laugh. "You didn't. You said I was mad, and went home for your tea."

"I'm sorry," I said.

"I've been waiting sixteen years, Rhys Wynne. I watched you go to Sandhurst and didn't write, because I thought if you wanted me you'd write first. I watched you fall in love with a girl from London who looked at you like a new handbag. I drove three hundred miles to Southampton after a twelve-hour shift to stand on a quay and watch you sail away to a war. And I wrote you eleven letters about the weather because I couldn't bear to write you one about anything else." She turned round at last and looked at me, at my burned face and my hook, with her steady grey eyes. "And then they rang Taid from the Ministry, and said there'd been a bomb, and you were badly burned, and might not live. I sat in the hospital chapel at Bangor on a night shift and made a bargain with God. I said, *let him come home, and I'll never ask for anything else. I won't even ask him to love me. Just let him come home.*"

She stopped. Her eyes were wet.

"And you came home," she said. "So I'm not asking for anything. I promised."

I looked at her for a long time across the gap between Adam and Eve, with the wind blowing and the whole of Wales spread out below us in the sun.

Then I stood up and jumped.

It's four feet, with a drop of a hundred on either side. I had one hand, burned lungs, and a bad leg from the fall on the north ridge. I landed badly on the far side and nearly went over, and she caught me by my jacket with both hands, and held on. We stood there on top of Eve, in the wind, holding on to each other, both of us crying, both of us laughing.

"You're mad," she said, into my chest. "You're completely mad."

"I know," I said. "I've been mad for sixteen years. I've only just noticed."

## EPILOGUE

### XIII.

We were married at the little chapel in the valley below Plas Eryri in the summer of 1984, with Sir Emrys giving her away in a wheelchair and the whole village crammed into the pews. Davies the Bomb's widow, Glenys, came up from the Rhondda. Tom Caradog's mother came from Carmarthen. She brought a Mars bar, and put it in my hand at the chapel door without a word, and I had to go and stand behind the vestry for ten minutes before I could go on. The minister was the curate from Betws, a tall pale young man in a long coat. He'd been in love with Ffion for three years, she told me afterwards, and had never said a word. He married us anyway, very beautifully, which I've always thought was the bravest thing I saw anyone do in all of 1982 and 1983.

We still live at Plas Eryri. Sir Emrys died in 1990 and left it to Ffion. I manage the estate, as my father did, with one hand and a hook, and I'm good at it. Ffion was a ward sister at Ysbyty Gwynedd until she retired. We have two sons and a daughter, and five grandchildren. They've all climbed Tryfan, and all jumped from Adam to Eve, and their grandmother has had to look away every time.

### XIV.

There's one more thing.

In March 2007, twenty-five years after the war, Ffion and I flew to Buenos Aires. Then we took a bus nine hundred kilometres north to the city of Corrientes, on the Paraná River, near the border with Paraguay. I had a scorched wooden rosary in my pocket, with a small tin crucifix melted slightly at one corner.

It had taken me three years to find her, through the Argentine veterans' associations, the Red Cross, and a priest in Corrientes who'd written to me in careful English.

Her name was Rosa Benítez. She was seventy-one. She lived alone in a small blue house on a dusty street near the river. Her only son, Lucas, a student at the teacher-training college, had been conscripted in March 1982 at eighteen, sent to the Malvinas in April, and never came home. She'd been told he was buried at Darwin, in the Argentine cemetery. She'd never been allowed to visit. She'd never known how he died.

She opened the door of the blue house and looked at me: a sixty-year-old Welshman with a scarred face, a hook, and a British accent, standing on her doorstep beside a small grey-haired Welshwoman. For a moment I saw fear in her face, and then anger, and then something else.

The priest from Corrientes was with us, to translate. I told her. I told her about the night of the sixth of June, under Mount Harriet, in the rain, in the dark. I told her about the boy in the hollow between the boulders, in a thin green parka two sizes too big, with no gloves. And that he hadn't been alone at the end. A stranger had put his own gloves on his hands and held his head in his lap, out of the mud. He'd said her name, *mamá*, over and over, and given me this, and told me his name and his city, so that one day someone would come and tell her.

I took the rosary out of my pocket and put it in her hand.

She stood in the doorway of the blue house for a long time, looking down at the scorched wooden beads in her palm, and the small tin crucifix, melted slightly at one corner. Then she began to weep. She wept the way Ffion weeps, without making a sound. And then, to my astonishment, she put her arms round me, a stranger, an enemy, a man from the army that had killed her son, and held me on her doorstep in the dusty street, for a long time.

"*Gracias*," she said. "*Gracias por no dejarlo solo.*"

The priest translated, quietly. *Thank you for not leaving him alone.*

---

We stayed in Corrientes a week. Rosa Benítez cooked for us every night in the blue house: *chipá*, and fish from the Paraná, and a stew whose name I never learned. She showed us photographs of Lucas as a baby, as a schoolboy, playing football, on the day he left for the war. She asked about Wales, and Ffion showed her photographs of Tryfan, and Adam and Eve, and our grandchildren, and the two women sat at Rosa's kitchen table and laughed and cried together without a word of language in common between them.

On the last night, Rosa gave me something wrapped in tissue paper. It was a pair of woollen gloves, hand-knitted, thick and dark green, and she'd made them that week.

"*Para usted*," she said, and touched my right hand. *For you.* Then she touched the hook, very gently, on the left. "*Y uno para Lucas.*"

And one for Lucas.

---

I wear them every winter, on the mountain. The left one doesn't fit my hook, of course. I carry it in my pocket instead.

3. UNDER THE RED DRAGON.

1. Title of the Work

The Gilded Anchor

2. Creative Work

The waltz drifting from the grand ballroom of the Breakers mingled with the rhythmic crashing of the Atlantic against the Newport cliffs, a stark contrast between the fragile orchestrations of high society and the unstoppable forces of nature. Julian stood on the marble terrace, the brass buttons of his naval dress uniform cold against the sea fog. By dawn, his cruiser would weigh anchor for the blockade of Santiago. Tonight, however, the battlefield was a gilded one, and the enemy wore a tailored tuxedo and a smile of practiced venom.

Through the glass doors, Julian watched her. Isabella’s beauty was of a severe, statuesque quality that made the diamonds at her throat seem redundant. She moved through the crowd with the mechanical grace demanded by her mother, Mrs. Van Alen, a matriarch whose ambition was as vast and unforgiving as the ocean. Isabella was destined, if her mother’s relentless maneuvering proved successful, to marry Elias Thorne, a man whose railroad empire obscured a past whispered to be built on ruin and deceit.

Thorne was currently beside her, leaning in with a proprietary air, the magnificent ruby on his hand catching the chandelier’s light. It was the same ruby, Julian knew, that a weeping woman in a faded boarding house had described to him only yesterday—a woman Thorne had married in secret, drained of her inheritance, and abandoned in a foreign port.

Julian’s jaw tightened. The societal cage closing around Isabella was forged of lies, yet she was dangerously close to accepting it, driven by a profound sense of familial duty and a recent, engineered misunderstanding.

Only that morning, Julian had been confronted at the estate gates by a hysterical woman. Seeking to help her, he had supported her as she collapsed. Isabella’s carriage had rolled past at that precise moment. Thorne, riding beside the carriage, had masterfully spun the tableau, planting the venomous seed that the woman was a discarded liaison of Julian’s. The truth—that the woman was Thorne’s own desperate, abandoned wife seeking her husband—was a reality too melodramatic for the insulated Mrs. Van Alen to believe, even if Julian had the proof, which had been efficiently stolen and destroyed by Thorne’s attorneys.

A rustle of silk announced Beatrice, Isabella’s cousin, who stepped onto the terrace with a sympathetic sigh. Beatrice possessed a gentle, observant nature, free from the crushing expectations placed upon Isabella.

"She is looking for you," Beatrice said softly, her dark eyes reflecting a mixture of sorrow and encouragement. "Though she would sooner walk into the sea than admit it to my aunt."

"Her pride is a fortress, Beatrice. Thorne has managed to raise the drawbridge," Julian replied, his voice barely rising above the surf. "I sail at first light. I cannot leave her to a life anchored to a fraud, even if she will not have me."

"Then do not let her go," Beatrice urged, touching his sleeve. "The music is ending. She is retreating to the conservatory. Go to her, Julian. We owe nothing to the lies of society, and everything to the truth of the heart."

Julian navigated the labyrinth of potted palms and trailing orchids until he found Isabella standing by a marble fountain, the water reflecting the pallor of her face. When she saw him, her spine stiffened, though her hands trembled as they clutched her ivory fan.

"I did not think the Navy allowed its officers to abandon their posts so easily, Lieutenant," she said, her voice a fragile weapon. "Or perhaps your obligations at the estate gates were concluded early?"

"I have only one obligation tonight, Isabella," Julian stepped closer, refusing to let the chill of her demeanor deter him. The scent of gardenias hung heavy in the damp air. "And that is to the truth. The woman you saw today was not mine. She is Elias Thorne’s wife."

Isabella’s eyes widened, a flash of vulnerability breaking through her aristocratic mask. "Mr. Thorne assured my mother—"

"Mr. Thorne is a master of assurances," Julian interrupted gently but firmly. "He has built his fortune on them, and he builds his alibis just as smoothly. He married her in Havana three years ago, squandered her estate, and left her to the mercy of strangers. I was trying to direct her to a magistrate when your carriage passed."

She looked away, staring into the dark water of the fountain. "Why should I believe you? My mother says you are a romantic with a sword and no inheritance. She says Mr. Thorne offers security."

"Security built on a foundation of sand and theft," Julian said, closing the distance between them until he could see the rapid pulse at the base of her throat. He reached into his tunic and withdrew a small, battered silver locket. "The woman dropped this when she fainted. Look inside."

Isabella took the locket. Her trembling fingers pried it open. Inside was a miniature portrait of a younger Elias Thorne, and an inscription: *To my husband, forever. Havana, 1895.*

The ivory fan slipped from Isabella’s grasp, shattering on the marble floor. The sound was sharp, final. The icy facade crumbled, leaving only the woman he loved—bewildered, betrayed by her world, but finally seeing clearly.

"He lied," she whispered, the horror dawning in her eyes as she realized the depth of the precipice she had been standing upon. "My mother... she was so certain."

"Society values the illusion of wealth over the reality of honor," Julian said, taking her hands. They were cold as the marble surrounding them, but he held them tightly. "I leave for the blockade in six hours. I have no railroad empire to offer you, Isabella. I have only my commission, my name, and a heart that has been entirely yours since the day we met."

Tears, long held back by pride and propriety, spilled over her lashes. The rigid posture instilled by a lifetime of wealthy expectations melted away as she stepped into his arms.

"I do not want an empire," she murmured against his shoulder, her voice fierce and sudden. "I want you to come back to me. Let Mr. Thorne keep his illusions and his stolen rubies. I will face my mother. I will face them all."

Julian held her close, the distant sound of the waltz now entirely drowned out by the roaring, authentic truth of the ocean. The battle ahead on the Spanish seas would be fraught with peril, but as he kissed her beneath the shadows of the orchids, he knew the greatest victory of his life had already been won.

# The Garden of Unfinished Goodbyes

## Creative Work

### Chapter One: The City That Kept the Rain

In the city of Bellweather, every house had a rain bell.

They hung beneath the eaves, small instruments of copper and glass that chimed whenever the wind carried moisture from the sea. Some rang with a bright, impatient music; others answered the weather in low, melancholy notes. The oldest bells were said to remember every storm that had passed over the city, though no one had ever discovered how to persuade them to speak of the past.

Mara Vale repaired these bells for a living.

She was thirty-four, with restless hands, an unruly collection of books, and a particular dislike of silence. Her workshop occupied the ground floor of a narrow house overlooking the eastern harbor. Behind it grew a garden of flowers that had no business flourishing so close to the salt water.

Mara had inherited the garden from her mother, along with a curious instruction written on the back of a faded photograph:

Nothing beautiful belongs to us merely because we have loved it.

For years she had considered the sentence unnecessarily severe.

She understood its meaning only after she met Julian Ash.

He arrived one October morning carrying a broken rain bell wrapped in a sailor's coat. The bell was old and blackened, its glass chamber cracked in three places.

"Can you make it sing again?" he asked.

Mara examined the instrument.

"Perhaps. Where did you find it?"

"On a ship that hasn't sailed in forty years."

"Then its silence may be deliberate."

He smiled, and Mara discovered that a stranger's smile could alter the atmosphere of an entire room.

Julian was a mapmaker who worked for the coastal survey. He traveled among the islands beyond Bellweather, recording disappearing shorelines, forgotten passages, and reefs that shifted beneath the waves. His profession required long absences, dangerous crossings, and an unusual willingness to trust things that could not be seen.

He was twenty-nine, though there was something timeless about his expression. His eyes were the gray-green of shallow water beneath cloud, and he spoke with the quiet certainty of someone who had learned that the world was not obliged to explain itself.

When Mara told him the repair would require several days, he seemed pleased.

"I'll come back on Thursday."

"You might find the bell finished before then."

"Then I'll come back to admire your efficiency."

She watched him leave, his coat moving in the wind like the wing of a dark bird.

That evening, the rain bells throughout Bellweather began to ring.

Mara remained in her workshop long after sunset, holding Julian's broken instrument against the lamplight. She had repaired hundreds of such bells, but never before had she wondered who might be listening when one finally sang.

### Chapter Two: A Map Without Borders

Julian returned on Thursday, and then again the following week.

Soon he was coming not because the bell required attention but because Mara invited him to tea. They sat in her garden beneath the crooked branches of a pear tree, discussing everything from ancient navigation to the habits of gulls.

Julian spoke of islands where the beaches glowed at night, of fishing villages abandoned so slowly that their streets had become forests, and of a distant stretch of coast where the sea withdrew for miles during certain tides, exposing the foundations of a drowned town.

Mara listened with growing fascination.

"Doesn't it frighten you?" she asked one afternoon. "To go so far from everything familiar?"

"Sometimes."

"Then why continue?"

"Because I would rather know the world is larger than my fear."

She considered this.

"Perhaps your fear is simply smaller than other people's."

"Perhaps," he said. "Or perhaps I have learned to travel with it."

Mara had never traveled beyond the eastern provinces. Her life had been built around permanence: the workshop, the garden, the familiar streets, the reassuring persistence of objects that could be repaired.

Julian regarded permanence differently.

"Nothing stays where we put it," he told her. "Not even the land. The coast is moving every day. We call something a boundary because we happen to be standing there when we draw the line."

"That sounds like a lonely philosophy."

"It can be. But it leaves room for surprise."

She began to anticipate his visits with an intensity that embarrassed her.

She planted winter roses because he had once mentioned admiring them. She learned the names of distant islands from his maps. She kept his favorite tea in a blue tin beside the stove.

In time, affection became longing, and longing developed the dangerous habit of making decisions without consulting reason.

One evening, as rain struck the workshop windows, Mara asked him to stay for supper.

He accepted.

They ate bread, roasted vegetables, and pears preserved in honey. Afterward, Julian helped her carry the dishes to the kitchen.

"You've made a place for me here," he observed.

Mara laughed nervously.

"Is that a complaint?"

"No."

"Then what is it?"

He looked toward the open door, beyond which the rain was transforming the garden into a trembling darkness.

"A thing I ought to understand before it becomes something else."

She felt a sharp disappointment.

"Must everything be examined so carefully?"

"Only the things I might hurt."

The words seemed tender enough to be a promise.

Mara mistook them for one.

### Chapter Three: The Language of Wanting

Winter entered Bellweather on a wind that scattered the harbor birds inland.

Julian's visits grew more frequent. Sometimes he arrived with books, sometimes with drawings, sometimes with nothing except the desire for company. They walked along the seawall and watched the waves dissolve into white spray.

Mara fell in love with him completely.

It was not a quiet transformation.

She loved his patience, his curiosity, the absentminded way he touched a map while thinking. She loved his capacity for wonder and the seriousness with which he listened to people whose opinions he did not share.

But she also loved what he made possible in her imagination.

With Julian, the workshop no longer seemed a place of confinement. The garden became the beginning of a larger world. She pictured journeys they would make together, rooms they would inhabit, ordinary mornings arranged around the astonishing fact of his presence.

The future filled with him before he had agreed to enter it.

One night, beneath the pear tree's bare branches, she finally spoke.

"I want you to stay."

Julian looked at her.

"For how long?"

She tried to smile.

"Long enough that I stop wondering when you'll leave."

He said nothing.

"Perhaps forever," she added.

The wind moved through the branches above them.

"Mara."

She disliked the gentleness in his voice. It sounded too much like an apology.

"You know how I feel," she said.

"I do."

"And?"

"I care for you deeply."

"But not enough."

He shook his head.

"Not in the way you want."

She turned away.

"How can you know? Perhaps you have never allowed yourself to love anyone."

"That isn't the problem."

"Then tell me what is."

Julian was silent for so long that she nearly walked away.

At last he said, "You have begun to love a future in which I have already promised to remain. I haven't made that promise."

Mara felt as though he had accused her of dishonesty.

"I wouldn't imprison you."

"I know you wouldn't intend to."

"Then why speak as though my love were a trap?"

"Because even a beautiful room becomes a prison if the door cannot be opened."

She wanted to contradict him, but something in his expression restrained her.

The worst part was that he looked sorrowful rather than angry.

"I don't ask you to stop loving me," he said. "I only ask that you believe me when I tell you who I am."

That night Mara lay awake listening to the rain bells.

For the first time, their music sounded less like a celebration of the weather than an argument with it.

### Chapter Four: The Northern Passage

In February, Julian received an assignment to survey the northern passage beyond the island of Vey.

The region was notorious for violent currents and sudden fog. Several ships had been lost there during the previous century, and the charts remained dangerously incomplete.

He came to Mara's workshop carrying his traveling case.

"I leave in six days."

She stared at him.

"Surely someone else can go."

"Someone else could. But I know that coast."

"Knowing it doesn't make it safe."

"No."

"Then refuse."

Julian placed his case on the floor.

"The survey could prevent other ships from being lost."

"And if you are lost?"

"Then the work will have cost more than I hoped."

His calmness infuriated her.

"You speak as though your life were an ordinary price to pay."

"It is the only life I have. I know its value."

"Do you?"

He looked wounded.

Mara wished instantly that she could recall the question.

She tried again.

"Stay until spring. The weather will improve."

"The passage must be measured during the winter currents."

"Then wait another year."

"Another year won't make the sea harmless."

Every answer seemed to close another door.

At last she seized his hand.

"Please. I am asking you because I love you."

Julian held her gaze.

"And I am answering you because I respect you."

She released him.

He stood there, uncertain whether he had permission to approach.

For one terrible moment, Mara understood that she wanted to use his kindness against him. She wanted to show him her tears, her fear, the future she had imagined, and ask whether he could bear to destroy them.

Instead, she opened the workshop door.

"I hope your maps are worth the trouble."

He flinched.

She had meant to hurt him.

The knowledge made her feel suddenly ashamed, but pride held her silent.

Julian lifted his case.

"Goodbye, Mara."

He was halfway down the street when she called after him.

"Wait."

He stopped.

She walked toward him, the cold air burning her face.

"I am afraid," she said. "That is what I should have told you."

His expression softened.

"I know."

"I don't want you to go."

"I know that too."

She looked at the case in his hand.

"Will you write?"

"Whenever I can."

They embraced briefly.

Then she stepped aside.

He left without looking back, not because he was indifferent, but because he understood that another farewell might become an argument neither of them could bear.

Mara watched until his figure disappeared beyond the harbor warehouses.

Only afterward did she understand that she had never truly believed he would go.

### Chapter Five: The Weight of Silence

For three weeks, letters arrived from the north.

Julian described islands of black stone, fishermen who navigated by the flight of seabirds, and a peculiar blue light that appeared beneath the ice during the longest nights.

His final letter contained a drawing of a small coastal flower.

It had five narrow petals and a dark center.

I found these growing above a cliff where almost nothing survives, he wrote. They bend nearly flat in the wind and straighten afterward. I thought you would like them.

Beneath the drawing he added:

The world is full of things that do not last, and that is no reason to love them less.

Mara read the sentence many times.

She wanted to write back immediately, but she found herself unable to choose the right words.

She began several letters.

In one she apologized for trying to persuade him to abandon his work.

In another she confessed that the workshop felt uninhabitable without him.

In a third she wrote simply that she missed him.

None seemed adequate.

She finally sent a short message describing the pear tree's first buds and asking whether he was eating properly.

The reply never came.

Instead, on the first morning of March, a government vessel entered Bellweather harbor flying its flag at half-mast.

The survey ship Northward had been caught in a sudden storm near the passage. Its navigation mast had failed, and the ship had struck a submerged ridge. Several crew members survived in the emergency boats.

Julian was not among them.

The captain's report stated that he had remained on deck helping two younger sailors secure the final boat.

Afterward, no one had seen him.

There were searches.

There were official letters.

There were conversations in which people spoke carefully, as though selecting words from a table covered with broken glass.

His body was never recovered.

Mara found herself unable to accept the phrase lost at sea.

It seemed offensively imprecise.

A coin could be lost. A key could be misplaced. A book could disappear behind a cabinet.

Julian had been alive, and now the world could offer no place where she might find him.

She returned to her workshop and locked the door.

Outside, the rain bells rang without interruption.

### Chapter Six: The House of Unanswered Questions

Grief did not come to Mara as she had imagined.

There was no single great collapse.

Instead, it entered her daily life through small and humiliating discoveries.

She set out two cups for tea.

She turned toward the door whenever footsteps passed.

She bought a newspaper because it contained an article about the northern islands, then could not bear to read it.

She grew angry with people who laughed in the street.

She grew angrier with those who lowered their voices when she entered a room.

At night she replayed her final conversation with Julian, altering it in her mind until the words seemed capable of producing a different ending.

If she had pleaded more gently, perhaps he would have stayed.

If she had argued more forcefully, perhaps he would have refused the assignment.

If she had confessed her love earlier, perhaps the future would have arranged itself differently.

These thoughts became a private ritual.

They gave suffering the appearance of purpose.

One afternoon, her oldest friend, Elian, found her sitting on the workshop floor surrounded by Julian's letters.

"You need to eat," he said.

"I ate yesterday."

"It is Thursday."

She shrugged.

Elian sat beside her.

After a while he asked, "What are you trying to discover?"

Mara held up one of the letters.

"Why he went."

"You know why."

"No. I know what he told me."

"Wasn't that enough?"

She looked at him angrily.

"He could have lived."

"Yes."

"He could have stayed."

"Yes."

"Then how am I supposed to forgive him?"

Elian considered her.

"Perhaps forgiveness isn't what he needs from you."

The words made her cry with a violence that startled them both.

She covered her face.

"I wanted him to choose me."

Elian waited.

"I wanted to be more important than the sea."

"You were important."

"Not enough."

"Those are not the same thing."

She began to protest, then stopped.

The silence between them deepened.

At last Elian said, "You keep imagining that love should have made him someone else."

Mara lowered her hands.

The statement was painful because it described something she had known without admitting.

She had loved Julian's curiosity, yet resented the journeys it demanded. She had admired his courage, yet wished it could be exchanged for caution. She had fallen in love with the freedom in him, then hoped that freedom would eventually become devotion to her.

She had wanted the whole man, except for the parts that might take him away.

That evening she opened the workshop windows for the first time in weeks.

The air smelled of rain and thawing earth.

She did not feel better.

But she began, very slowly, to feel honest.

### Chapter Seven: The Garden of Names

Spring arrived with unusual warmth.

The pear tree flowered early, and the first bees appeared among the roses.

Mara returned to work, repairing bells for neighbors who tactfully avoided mentioning Julian.

She found comfort in the physical demands of her craft. Cracked glass could be replaced. Corroded copper could be cleaned. Bent mechanisms could be restored.

There was something merciful about damage that obeyed the laws of repair.

One morning, an elderly woman named Mrs. Fen brought her a bell that had belonged to her husband.

"He made it himself," she explained. "It hasn't rung since he died."

Mara examined the mechanism.

A small bronze weight had slipped from its fastening.

"This is easily repaired."

Mrs. Fen smiled faintly.

"That's good."

As Mara worked, the woman wandered into the garden.

When she returned, she was carrying a fallen pear blossom.

"Your mother used to let me sit out there," she said.

"You knew her?"

"For nearly forty years."

Mara looked up.

"She never mentioned you."

"Oh, we weren't close when you were little. We had a disagreement."

"About what?"

Mrs. Fen hesitated.

"Your father."

Mara's father had died before she was born. She knew him only through photographs and the occasional story her mother told on winter evenings.

"He wanted to travel," Mrs. Fen continued. "Your mother wanted him home. They fought about it for years."

Mara set down her tools.

"What happened?"

"He took a position overseas. She refused to go."

"Did he come back?"

"For visits, at first. Then he fell ill and died."

Mara felt the familiar pressure of grief, though this loss belonged to another lifetime.

"She must have hated him."

"No," Mrs. Fen replied. "She hated that loving him did not give her the power to keep him safe."

The elderly woman turned the pear blossom between her fingers.

"Near the end of her life, your mother told me something I never forgot. She said the hardest part of loving another person was discovering that their life continued beyond the boundaries of your own hopes."

Mara thought of the instruction written behind the photograph.

Nothing beautiful belongs to us merely because we have loved it.

For years she had mistaken it for a warning against affection.

Now she understood it as an invitation to love without possession.

When Mrs. Fen departed, Mara went into the garden and stood beneath the pear tree.

She realized that she had been using grief as a final claim upon Julian.

By keeping herself unhappy, she had imagined she was remaining faithful.

By refusing to change, she had tried to preserve the world in which he was still alive.

But time had continued without asking her permission.

The flowers had opened.

The bells still rang.

And somewhere beyond the harbor, ships were sailing across waters that had not become less dangerous because she had suffered.

### Chapter Eight: The Last Map

In early summer, a parcel arrived from the coastal survey office.

It contained Julian's field notebooks, a damaged compass, and several maps recovered from the captain's cabin.

A letter explained that the documents had been inspected and copied. Because Julian had named Mara as a personal contact, the originals were being entrusted to her.

She spread them across the workshop table.

There were sketches of reefs, notes on tidal movement, and rough drawings of the coastal settlements.

One chart was marked with corrections in Julian's careful handwriting.

Another contained observations about the northern passage, including a previously unrecorded channel that might offer safer navigation during winter storms.

Mara studied the chart for hours.

It was unfinished.

The soundings stopped abruptly near the ridge where the Northward had been wrecked.

A blank space stretched between two clusters of measurements.

For several days, Mara could not look at it without imagining Julian's final hours.

Then she noticed a note written near the margin:

The passage should be named for the harbor, not the person who charts it. A map ought to serve those who come after.

She sat back.

All winter she had imagined Julian's work as a rival that had stolen him from her.

Now, looking at the unfinished chart, she saw the people who might someday travel through those waters.

Fishermen returning to their children.

Merchants carrying supplies.

Travelers who had never heard of Julian Ash and would never know the danger he had faced.

The map was not evidence that he had loved the sea more than her.

It was evidence that he had cared about a world larger than either of them.

Mara took the damaged compass from its wrapping.

Its needle trembled uncertainly.

She placed it beside the window, where the afternoon light touched the brass.

For the first time since his death, she was able to remember Julian without immediately wishing he had been different.

### Chapter Nine: A Flower Against the Wind

The following autumn, Mara traveled north.

She went aboard a small coastal vessel carrying surveyors, merchants, and a family returning to their island home.

The journey frightened her.

At night the ship creaked beneath unfamiliar stars, and the sea moved with a power that made the buildings of Bellweather seem temporary and absurd.

She often stood at the rail, gripping it until her fingers ached.

On the third day, the captain pointed toward a distant coast.

"That's where Ash made his observations."

Mara followed his gesture.

The land rose from the water in dark cliffs broken by narrow inlets. Waves shattered against the rocks, sending white spray high into the air.

The captain said, "His chart has already helped us avoid two dangerous approaches."

Mara looked toward the headland.

She wanted to feel proud.

Instead, she felt grief return with such force that she had to turn away.

Later, when the ship reached a sheltered harbor, she went ashore alone.

A narrow path climbed the cliffs beyond the village. She followed it through grass flattened by the wind.

Near the summit she found the flowers Julian had drawn.

They grew in small clusters among the stones, their pale petals surrounding dark blue centers. Each stem bent toward the earth when the wind strengthened, then slowly lifted when it passed.

Mara knelt beside them.

They were smaller than she had imagined.

She thought of taking one home.

Her hand reached toward the nearest flower and stopped.

She imagined pressing it between the pages of a book, preserving its shape and color while its living substance dried away.

The old impulse was still there.

To possess what she loved.

To protect it by removing it from the dangers of the world.

To make permanence out of something that had never promised to endure.

She withdrew her hand.

Instead, she opened her notebook and drew the flower where it grew.

Her first attempt was awkward.

Her second was better.

By the third, she had begun to notice things she would otherwise have missed: the fine hairs along the stem, the slight asymmetry of the petals, the pale dust gathered near the center.

The wind lifted her hair.

For a moment she remembered Julian sitting beneath the pear tree, talking about coastlines that moved beyond the boundaries of maps.

She spoke his name aloud.

The sea answered with the sound of waves breaking below.

There was no revelation.

No sudden peace.

Only the cliff, the flowers, and the great unsettled weather of the world.

Mara closed her notebook.

She remained until evening.

### Chapter Ten: What the Living Owe the Dead

When Mara returned to Bellweather, she began a project that surprised everyone who knew her.

She transformed the rear portion of her property into a public garden.

She removed the old boundary wall, replaced the narrow gate with a wide entrance, and built wooden benches beneath the pear tree.

She planted flowers from different coastal regions, selecting varieties that could survive the salt air and changing seasons.

At the entrance she hung Julian's repaired rain bell.

It was the instrument he had brought into her workshop on the morning they met.

Its glass chamber was clear now, and the copper had been polished until it reflected the shifting light.

Mara did not dedicate the garden to Julian.

She named it the Garden of Unfinished Goodbyes.

At first the neighbors were puzzled.

Then people began to come.

An elderly man brought a photograph of his wife and sat beneath the pear tree every Sunday.

A young woman who had lost her brother planted a row of white flowers near the eastern fence.

A fisherman who had survived a wreck left a smooth stone beside the path.

Children came to chase butterflies.

Travelers stopped to rest.

People who were lonely found a place where loneliness did not require explanation.

Mara made only one rule.

Nothing living was to be taken from the garden without permission.

"You can take seeds," she told the children. "And you may take drawings or photographs. But let the flowers finish their own lives."

In winter, she began teaching young apprentices to repair rain bells.

In spring, she traveled to neighboring towns to collect native seeds.

She discovered that her world could expand without the destruction of everything she had once called home.

The workshop remained.

The pear tree remained.

Julian remained too, though not in the manner she had once desired.

He was present in the maps that guided ships safely through the northern passage. He was present in her willingness to travel, in the drawings she made, and in the garden that welcomed people she had never met.

His absence had not become smaller.

Her life had grown around it.

### Chapter Eleven: The Storm at Bellweather

Seven years after Julian's death, a violent storm approached the city.

The harbor authorities ordered residents near the waterfront to prepare for flooding. Boats were secured, shutters fastened, and the old seawall reinforced with sacks of sand.

Mara spent the afternoon helping her neighbors move furniture to higher ground.

By sunset the streets were empty.

Wind struck the houses with such force that the rain bells rang continuously, their individual voices merging into a wild, disordered music.

Mara stood at her workshop window.

Beyond the garden, the pear tree thrashed beneath the storm.

A tremendous gust tore several branches from its crown.

Then the eastern fence collapsed.

Mara watched helplessly as the wind stripped petals from the late-blooming flowers and scattered them across the flooded path.

For an instant she felt the old terror rising.

Everything she loved was being destroyed.

She seized her coat and hurried toward the door.

But as she reached it, she stopped.

Outside, the storm was still gaining strength. The garden could not be saved by her presence, and entering it would only place her in danger.

She stood with her hand on the latch.

The memory came to her with painful clarity: Julian, carrying his traveling case, explaining that the sea could not be made harmless.

She had once believed love required her to prevent every possible loss.

Now she understood that sometimes love required the courage to remain still.

Mara stepped away from the door.

She went upstairs and waited through the night.

By morning, the storm had passed.

The garden was devastated.

Branches covered the paths. Several flower beds had been washed away. The rain bell lay shattered beneath the ruined entrance.

Mara walked through the wreckage in silence.

She found the pear tree split down its center, one half fallen, the other still rooted in the earth.

For a long time she stood before it.

Then she noticed something.

Near the base of the broken trunk, protected by its roots, a cluster of small green shoots had survived.

They were pear seedlings, grown from fruit that had fallen the previous autumn.

Mara crouched beside them.

She felt neither triumph nor consolation.

The broken tree was still broken.

The lost flowers remained lost.

But here was life continuing without consulting sorrow.

She touched the earth beside the seedlings and began to laugh.

Then she cried.

And for the first time in many years, she found no contradiction in doing both.

### Chapter Twelve: The Music of Things That Pass

By the following spring, the garden had been rebuilt.

The pear tree's surviving half produced a modest crown of leaves, and the young seedlings were transplanted into a sheltered corner.

A new rain bell hung above the entrance.

Mara had made it herself.

Its body was formed from the metal of the old bell Julian had brought her, melted and recast into a different shape. She had added a small silver weight from her mother's collection and a glass chamber made by one of her apprentices.

When rain approached, the bell sounded a clear, resonant note that carried across the garden.

Visitors sometimes asked why it was unlike the other bells in Bellweather.

Mara told them that it had been made from several broken things.

"Does that make it special?" a little girl asked one afternoon.

Mara considered the question.

"Not necessarily," she said. "But it gives it a history."

The child thought about this.

"Will it break again?"

"Probably, one day."

"Then why make it?"

Mara smiled.

"Because it can sing until then."

Years passed.

Mara grew older.

Her hands became less steady, and she began entrusting the finest repairs to her apprentices. She traveled less often, but the garden continued to flourish under the care of neighbors and friends.

People came and went.

Some fell in love beneath the pear tree.

Some said farewell there.

Some returned after many years, astonished to discover how much had changed and how much remained recognizable.

The garden became a place where the passage of time was neither celebrated nor denied.

It was simply witnessed.

On a quiet evening near the end of Mara's life, she sat beneath the rebuilt pear tree with Julian's final letter resting in her lap.

The paper had yellowed.

The ink had faded.

She knew every word.

For years she had believed the letter contained an unfinished conversation, something she was obliged to answer before she could be free.

Now she understood that some conversations were completed by the lives that followed them.

She thought of the young woman who had once sat in this same garden, certain that love must be rewarded with permanence.

She felt tenderness for that woman.

She also felt sadness for the pain she had caused herself by confusing longing with entitlement and fear with devotion.

She had learned that love could be generous and selfish in the same instant.

That desire could reveal beauty while obscuring the beloved's freedom.

That grief could become a shelter or a prison.

And that death, though it ended a life, could not entirely determine what that life would mean to those who remained.

The wind shifted.

Far beyond the garden, the sea reflected the last light of the afternoon.

Mara closed her eyes.

For a moment she imagined Julian sitting beside her, his notebooks spread across his knees, his expression bright with some new discovery.

She did not ask him to stay.

She did not ask where he had been.

In her imagination, he looked toward the western horizon.

Then he smiled.

And Mara, who had spent so much of her life learning how to say goodbye, finally understood that farewell was not always the opposite of love.

Sometimes it was the form love took when it had ceased asking for possession.

Above her, the rain bell began to ring.

Its music drifted through the branches, over the garden paths, and into the streets of Bellweather, where people lifted their heads and listened for the coming rain.

The sound did not endure.

Each note arose, trembled briefly in the air, and disappeared.

Yet before the silence could settle, another followed.

And another.

And another.

Until the entire garden seemed filled with the fragile, inexhaustible music of things that could not remain forever, but had been beautiful while they were here.

The End
