30. VENUS AND ADONIS

Fritillary
I. THE FIRST DAY

Vera Salt had been the most desired woman in Britain for thirty years, and she had never once been told no.

That isn’t quite true. She’d been told no by directors, producers, critics, and the occasional husband (she’d had three). But never by a man she’d chosen. Never, not once since she was nineteen and a drama student at RADA, had she looked across a room at someone and wanted them and not had them. It wasn’t vanity. Or not only vanity. It was simply how the world had always arranged itself around her, like iron filings round a magnet. She’d stopped noticing, years ago, that it was happening.

She was fifty-one that summer. She had two Oscars, four BAFTAs, a damehood, a house in Primrose Hill, a farmhouse in Provence, and a face that had been on the cover of Vogue eleven times. Critics said it had got more beautiful with age, not less. She’d come to the Isle of Skye in June 2019 to make a film, a big, expensive, romantic period drama about the Jacobite rising. She was playing Flora MacDonald, the woman who smuggled Bonnie Prince Charlie over the sea to Skye disguised as her maid. She would be on the island for ten weeks. She was bored within three days.

On the fourth day, she saw him.

The production had hired a team of local climbing instructors as safety staff, to rig ropes on the cliffs and crags for the location shoots, and keep the actors and crew from falling off the island. There were five of them, all from Glenbrittle and Portree, weathered and taciturn and expensive. On the fourth morning, on a ledge high on the sea cliffs at Neist Point, where they were filming a scene of Flora watching for the Prince’s boat, Vera stood in her eighteenth-century costume, waiting for the light. She looked down, idly, at the cliff below her.

There was a young man climbing it.

He had no rope. He was alone, a hundred and fifty feet up a sheer black wall of basalt, above a sea that was smashing itself white on the rocks below. He was moving up the face as if it were a staircase. He was lean, brown, barefoot, with sun-bleached hair tied back, in shorts and a vest, with a chalk bag at his waist and nothing else. He moved with a kind of absolute calm, unhurried, utterly focused, his whole body attending to the rock. It was the most beautiful thing Vera had ever seen.

She stood on the ledge in her costume and watched him climb, and forgot to breathe.

He reached the top of the cliff about twenty feet from where she was standing. He hauled himself over the edge onto the grass, sat down, unlaced a pair of climbing shoes from round his neck, and looked out to sea for a long moment with an expression of complete contentment. Then he noticed her, and the camera crew, and the cables, and the forty people standing about on the clifftop. He looked faintly startled.

“Sorry,” he said, in a soft Skye accent. “Didn’t know you’d started. I’ll get out of your way.”

He stood up and began to walk away along the cliff.

“Wait,” said Vera Salt.

He stopped and turned round.

She looked at him: at the sea-blue eyes, the sun-bleached hair, the chalk on his hands, the face that was, she realised, very young. Twenty-five, twenty-six. Thirty years younger than her. It didn’t matter. It had never mattered.

“What’s your name?” she said.

“Ash,” he said. “Ash Morrow. I’m one of the safety team.” He smiled briefly, politely, the way you smile at a stranger. “You’re Vera Salt. My mum’s a big fan.”

Then he turned and walked away along the cliff into the wind, and didn’t look back.

II. THE PURSUIT

She had him assigned to her the next day. It was easy. She told the first assistant director that she was nervous on the cliffs, and wanted a dedicated safety instructor, and asked for the young one, Morrow, who’d seemed so steady. The first AD rearranged the schedule within the hour. Nobody ever said no to Vera Salt.

So for the next fortnight, Ash Morrow stood beside her on every ledge and clifftop and crag on the Isle of Skye. He clipped her into harnesses and checked her ropes and told her where to put her feet. He was quiet, polite, professional and entirely unmoved.

She tried everything. She was very good at it. She’d had thirty years’ practice, and she’d never once failed.

She asked about his life, and listened to the answers with her famous grey eyes fixed on his face. She found out that he’d grown up in Portree, the only son of a widowed primary school teacher, that he’d been climbing since he was six, and that he’d turned down a place at Edinburgh University to stay on Skye and climb. He worked as an instructor in summer and on the fishing boats in winter, and spent every spare hour alone on the rock. He’d soloed every route on the Cuillin ridge, she was told by the other instructors, half admiring and half disapproving. He didn’t use ropes when he climbed for himself, ever. He said ropes made him lazy.

She laughed at his jokes, which were rare and dry. She touched his arm when he clipped her into the harness. She invited him to dinner at the big hotel in Portree where the cast were staying, and he politely declined. She was given notes by the director about the light in a scene, and turned to Ash instead and asked what he thought. He looked surprised, and said he didn’t know anything about films. She sent him a signed photograph for his mother. He thanked her, gravely, and said his mother would be thrilled.

And at the end of the second week, on a ledge at the top of the Quiraing in a long golden evening, while the crew packed up the cameras below, she took his chalky hand in both of hers, and looked up into his sea-blue eyes, and said, quite simply, “I want you.”

He didn’t pull his hand away. He looked down at her hands holding his, for a long moment. Then he looked at her face, quite steadily, with no embarrassment at all, and no unkindness.

“No,” he said.

Vera Salt stared at him.

“I’m sorry,” said Ash Morrow gently. “I mean that. You’re a lovely woman, and I’m flattered. But no.”

“Why?” She heard her own voice and didn’t recognise it. “Is it my age? Is that it?”

“No.” He shook his head. “It’s not your age. It’s not you. It’s—” He looked out across the Quiraing, at the great broken pinnacles of rock and the green hollows, and the sea and the mountains of the mainland beyond, gold in the evening light. “I don’t want anyone, Ms Salt. Not like that. Not right now. I’ve got this.” He gestured at the rock, the hills, the sea. “It’s enough. It’s everything. I don’t have room for anything else.”

“Everyone has room.”

“No,” he said. “Not everyone.” He took his hand gently out of hers. “I’m sorry. I’ll ask to be reassigned tomorrow. It’ll be easier for you.”

He turned and began to walk away down the path.

“You’ll change your mind,” said Vera Salt behind him. Her voice was shaking. “You’ll see. No one ever says no to me. No one.”

He stopped and turned round on the path and looked back at her for a long moment, with the gold light on his face.

“Then maybe,” he said quietly, “it’s time somebody did.”

III. THE ARGUMENT

He wasn’t reassigned. Vera saw to that. She went to the producer the next morning and said that if Ash Morrow was taken off her safety team she’d walk off the film, and the producer, who had forty million pounds riding on her name, went pale and said of course, of course.

So Ash stood beside her on the cliffs for another week, silent, professional, unmoved. And Vera Salt, who had never in her life been refused, found that she couldn’t stop.

She didn’t understand it. She’d been in love, she thought, a dozen times, and in lust a hundred. She’d been married three times and divorced three times, and had affairs with actors, directors, a Spanish tennis player, a Labour cabinet minister and a French count. None of it had been like this. This was something else, something that had her lying awake in her suite at the hotel at three in the morning, staring at the ceiling, thinking about a barefoot boy on a black cliff above a white sea. She couldn’t eat. She forgot her lines. The director, who’d worked with her four times and adored her, took her aside after a ruined take and asked her, very gently, whether she was ill.

“I’m fine,” she said.

She wasn’t fine. She was fifty-one, and the most desired woman in Britain, and for the first time in her life she wanted something she couldn’t have. The not having was eating her alive.

She went to his house.

It was in the fourth week, on a Sunday, when there was no filming. She drove herself in a hired Land Rover, out of Portree on the Dunvegan road and up a single-track lane to a small white cottage on a hillside above Loch Snizort, with a garden full of washing and a view of the sea. His mother opened the door: a small, tired, grey-haired woman in a cardigan, a primary school teacher, who went white, then red, and stammered that she’d seen every one of Vera Salt’s films.

Ash came out of the kitchen behind her, in jeans and a jumper, holding a mug of tea. He saw Vera on the doorstep and his face changed. It was quite small, the change. Something in it closed, like a door.

“Mum,” he said quietly, “could you give us a minute?”

His mother looked at him, at Vera, at him again, and went into the kitchen.

Ash came out onto the doorstep and pulled the door to behind him.

“You shouldn’t have come here,” he said.

“I had to see you.”

“You see me every day. On the cliffs.”

“Not like that.” Vera took a step towards him. “Ash, please. Just listen. I’ve never felt like this. Never, about anyone. I can’t sleep. I can’t work. I think about you every minute. That must mean something. It must. You can’t just—” Her voice broke. “You can’t just say no, as if it’s nothing.”

Ash looked at her for a long time on the doorstep, in the wind, with the sea grey and white below.

“Ms Salt,” he said at last, quite gently. “Vera. Can I tell you what I think? Honestly?”

She nodded.

“I don’t think you love me,” said Ash Morrow. “I think you want me. That’s different. You saw me on a cliff and you wanted me, the way you’d want a painting, or a house, or a part in a film. And you’ve never not got anything you wanted, so now you can’t stop. It’s not about me at all. It’s about you not being able to bear the word no.” He paused. “If you loved me, you’d have heard me the first time. You’d have let me go. Love doesn’t chase people up hillsides on a Sunday. Love listens.”

Vera Salt stood on the doorstep of the small white cottage in the wind and couldn’t speak.

“I’m sorry,” said Ash. “I don’t want to hurt you. But I’ve said no three times now, as kindly as I know how. I’m not going to change my mind. So please. For both of us. Let me go.”

He went back inside and closed the door.

She sat in the Land Rover at the bottom of the lane for an hour, in the rain, with her hands on the wheel, shaking. She didn’t cry. Vera Salt didn’t cry, except on camera.

She drove back to Portree in the dark.

IV. THE EXECUTIONER

There’s a mountain on the Cuillin ridge on the Isle of Skye called Am Basteir. In Gaelic, it means the Executioner.

It’s a great black fin of gabbro rock, about three thousand feet high, at the northern end of the ridge, above Sligachan. On its western end it has a sharp, overhanging prow of rock called the Basteir Tooth: a sheer black blade, leaning out over a drop of a thousand feet, with almost no holds. The local climbers call it the Tooth. Very few people have ever climbed the direct line up its overhanging north face without a rope, in one push, from the bottom of the corrie to the summit. Two men died trying it in the 1990s. The other instructors told Vera all this, over drinks in the hotel bar, in the fifth week.

Ash Morrow was going to try it.

“He’s been working on it for three years,” said one of them, a grizzled man called Hamish, shaking his head over his whisky. “Every summer. Rehearsing the moves on a rope, over and over, till he knows every hold. He says this is the year. He says the rock’s dry and he’s ready. He says he’ll do it at the end of August, when the filming’s done.” Hamish took a long pull of his whisky. “We’ve all told him he’s mad. His mother’s begged him. He just smiles and says it’s what he’s for.”

Vera went cold all over.

She found him the next morning on the clifftop at Neist Point, coiling ropes after the morning’s shoot, alone. She hadn’t spoken to him since the Sunday at his mother’s house. She stood in front of him in her eighteenth-century costume, with the wind whipping her skirts, and said, “Don’t.”

He looked up from the ropes.

“The Tooth,” said Vera. “Am Basteir. The Executioner. Hamish told me. Don’t do it, Ash. Please.”

He looked at her for a long moment.

“That’s not really your business, Vera,” he said quietly.

“I know. I know it’s not. I know I’ve no right. I know you’ve told me no, and I know I didn’t listen, and I’m sorry, I’m so sorry.” The words were tumbling out of her, unrehearsed, for perhaps the first time in thirty years. “But please. Not that. Two men died on it. I’ve had dreams about it. Every night this week. I see you on that black rock, and a wind comes, and you—” She stopped. “Please. I’ll leave you alone. I’ll never speak to you again. I’ll leave the island. Just don’t climb that mountain.”

Ash Morrow stood on the clifftop with a coil of rope in his hands and looked at her. And for the first time since she’d met him, something in his face softened.

“You’re frightened,” he said. “For me. Not for you. For me.”

“Yes.”

He was quiet for a while, looking out to sea.

“That’s closer to love than anything you’ve said yet,” he said at last. “Thank you.” He looked back at her. “But I’m still going to climb it, Vera. It’s not about being brave, or proving anything. It’s—” He searched for the words. “When I’m on the rock, alone, with no rope, everything else goes away. All the noise. The fear. Everything. There’s just me and the rock and the next hold, and it’s the only time I’m ever completely awake. I can’t explain it better than that. It’s what I’m for.” He paused. “You’ve got your films. When you’re in front of the camera, isn’t it the same? Isn’t that the only time you’re completely yourself?”

Vera Salt opened her mouth to answer and found she couldn’t.

“I’ll be careful,” said Ash. “I’ve rehearsed every move a hundred times. I know that rock better than I know my own face.” He smiled, the first real smile he’d ever given her, quick and warm and young. “And I’m not going to die, Vera. Not on the Tooth. I promise you that.”

V. THE MORNING

The filming finished on the twenty-fourth of August. There was a wrap party at the hotel in Portree that went on until three in the morning. Vera Salt sat in a corner of it with a glass of champagne she didn’t drink, and left at midnight, and lay awake in her suite until dawn.

At five in the morning on the twenty-fifth of August, she got up, dressed in walking clothes she’d bought in Portree and never worn, and drove the hired Land Rover through the grey dawn to Sligachan. She parked by the old bridge at the foot of the Cuillin and began to walk up the long path into Coire a’ Bhasteir, alone.

She was fifty-one and had never climbed anything in her life except the stairs at the Old Vic. It took her four hours. She fell twice on the scree and cut her hands. It began to rain, then stopped, then began again, a fine, cold, drifting mist that hid the tops. She kept going. She didn’t know why. She only knew that if she stayed in her suite in Portree that morning, she’d go mad.

At a little after nine, she came up over the lip of the corrie and saw the Tooth.

It was enormous, a great black blade of rock leaning out over her head into the mist, wet and gleaming, like the prow of a ship made of iron. Water was running down it in thin silver threads. The mist was coming and going across its face in grey veils. And about two-thirds of the way up the overhanging north face, small as a spider against the black rock, a figure in a red vest was climbing it, alone, with no rope.

Vera stood at the bottom of the corrie in the drizzle with her bleeding hands and watched him climb.

He was moving very slowly. She could see that even from four hundred feet below. The rock was wet. He’d meant to climb it dry, the instructors had said, on a dry morning, and it had been dry at dawn, when he started. Then the mist had come in off the sea. He was spreadeagled on the overhanging face, his whole body pressed against the black rock, one hand reaching up, feeling for a hold. She saw his hand find it. She saw him shift his weight. She saw him pull, slowly, up.

And then, for a long moment, he didn’t move at all.

The mist came across the face of the Tooth, and she lost sight of him.

When it cleared, a minute later, there was nobody on the rock.

The mountain rescue team from Glenbrittle found him that afternoon, at the bottom of the Tooth, on the scree. They said he would have died at once. They said the rock had been wet, and a hold had broken; they found the fragment beside him, a flake of gabbro the size of a dinner plate, still chalky from his hand. It was nobody’s fault, they said. It was the mountain. It was always the mountain.

They found Vera Salt beside him.

She’d scrambled down the scree to where he lay, falling and cutting herself, in the drizzle. She’d sat down beside him on the wet stones and lifted his head into her lap and held it. She was still holding it four hours later when the rescue team came up the corrie in the rain. She was talking to him, quietly, in a voice they didn’t recognise as hers. She was asking him why. Over and over: why, why, why.

His hands were still white with chalk.

VI. THE CURSE

She didn’t go back to London.

The film was released the following spring and was a great success. Critics said Vera Salt’s Flora MacDonald was the finest performance of her career: luminous, aching, full of a strange, terrible tenderness. She won her third Oscar for it. She didn’t go to the ceremony. Her agent accepted it for her in Los Angeles and read out a short statement she’d written. Nobody understood it. It said only: For A., who said no.

She bought a small stone cottage on the shore of Loch Snizort, a mile from the white house where Ash Morrow’s mother lived. She lived there alone for a year. She didn’t act. She didn’t give interviews. She walked on the shore in all weathers, and sometimes, on dry days, she went up into the Cuillin and sat at the bottom of Coire a’ Bhasteir, looking up at the Tooth.

And she thought.

She thought about the thirty years in which nobody had said no to her. Every man she’d ever looked across a room at and wanted, and had, and lost interest in. Every husband and lover she’d left, bored, the moment they belonged to her. And she thought about a barefoot boy on a black cliff above a white sea, who’d looked at her quite steadily, without embarrassment or unkindness, and said, If you loved me, you’d have heard me the first time. Love doesn’t chase people up hillsides on a Sunday. Love listens.

She’d never once listened, in thirty years. Not to anyone. She’d only ever wanted.

Ash’s mother came to see her in the spring of 2020, on a cold bright morning, with the daffodils out along the shore of Loch Snizort. Her name was Morag Morrow. She was fifty-four, small and grey and tired, and she’d been crying for eight months. She came up the path to Vera’s cottage and knocked on the door and, when Vera opened it, stood on the doorstep for a long time without speaking.

“He told me about you,” she said at last. “That summer. He told me you’d asked him to dinner and he’d said no. And he told me you came to the house that Sunday, and what he said to you on the step.” She looked at Vera with Ash’s sea-blue eyes. “He felt terrible about it afterwards. He said he’d been too hard. He said you were lonely, and frightened, and didn’t know how to be anything else, and he should have been kinder.” She was quiet for a moment. “And he told me about the clifftop. When you asked him not to climb the Tooth. He came home that night and sat in the kitchen with me for a long time. He said, Mum, she was frightened for me. Not for herself. For me. I think that’s the first time she’s ever been frightened for anyone.”

Vera Salt stood in the doorway of the stone cottage and found that she was crying. Not on camera, not for a scene. She was simply crying, in the cold spring sunshine, with her hand over her mouth.

“I wanted to hate you,” said Morag Morrow. “For a long time. I thought you’d driven him up that mountain. That if you hadn’t chased him all summer, he’d have stayed home.” She shook her head slowly. “But it’s not true. He’d have climbed it anyway. He always would have. It was what he was for.” She paused. “And you were with him at the end. The rescue men told me. You held his head in your lap for four hours in the rain. So he wasn’t alone.” She looked at Vera. “I wasn’t there. You were. So I suppose I wanted to say thank you. For that.”

Vera Salt asked her inside. They sat at the kitchen table in the stone cottage by the loch and drank tea and talked for four hours. Morag talked about Ash as a little boy, climbing the garden wall at three, the kitchen dresser at four, the sea cliffs at Neist at twelve. Vera talked about the first morning she’d seen him, on the black cliff above the white sea, moving up the rock as if it were a staircase, the most beautiful thing she’d ever seen.

At the end of the four hours, Morag Morrow stood up to go. At the door she turned and said:

“He’d have liked you, I think. In the end. If he’d had longer. Not the way you wanted. But he’d have liked you.”

“I don’t think I’d have liked me,” said Vera Salt.

Morag smiled sadly.

“That’s a start,” she said.

VII. THE FLOWER

In the autumn of 2020, Vera Salt planted a bed of bulbs in Morag Morrow’s garden, by the white cottage on the hillside above Loch Snizort. She did it herself, on her knees in the wet earth, on a grey October afternoon, with Morag standing beside her holding the trowel.

They were snake’s-head fritillaries. Wild ones, Fritillaria meleagris, a strange, beautiful, old-fashioned flower that grows in damp English meadows and almost nowhere else. Each one is a single drooping bell on a slender stem, purple, chequered all over with white, like a tiny lantern, or a drop of dark blood on pale skin. They don’t grow on Skye. It’s too wet and too windy and too far north. The man in the nursery in Inverness told Vera they’d never survive the winter.

They survived.

In April 2021, on the hillside above Loch Snizort, in Morag Morrow’s garden, forty-one snake’s-head fritillaries came up and bloomed, purple and white, nodding in the wind off the sea. Morag rang Vera at six in the morning and said, “Come and see.” Vera came and stood in the garden beside her in the cold dawn, and they looked at them for a long time without speaking.

“He’d have laughed,” said Morag. “Flowers. He’d have said, Mum, they’re flowers, they don’t do anything.”

“No,” said Vera. “They don’t. That’s the point. They just come up every spring, whether you’re ready or not. Whether you’ve earned them or not.” She knelt down in the wet grass and touched one of the drooping purple bells very gently with her fingertip. “You can’t own them. You can’t keep them. You can only watch them while they’re here, and then let them go.”

Vera Salt went back to work in 2022. She’s sixty now, and still acting. Critics say she’s better than ever: stranger, deeper, sadder, more alive. She’s never once since 2019 played a romantic lead. Her agent has begged her to, and she always says no. She plays mothers now, and widows, and old women in grief, and queens who’ve lost everything. When she plays them, people in the audience weep, and don’t know why.

She gave one interview, in 2023, to a journalist from The Guardian, the only one in five years. The journalist asked her, at the end, whether she’d ever been in love.

Vera Salt thought about it for a long time.

“Once,” she said. “For about ten weeks, on the Isle of Skye. With someone who didn’t love me back. Who told me no, three times, as kindly as he knew how. And I didn’t listen. I chased him all summer, because I’d never once in my life been told no, and I couldn’t bear it.” She looked out of the window. “And then I lost him. Not to me. To a mountain. To the thing he loved more than anything, which was never going to be me.”

“Do you regret it?”

“Every day.” She was quiet for a moment. “But I learned something from it, at fifty-one, that I should have learned at nineteen. Wanting someone isn’t love. Love is what’s left when you’ve stopped wanting, when you can stand at the bottom of a mountain and watch the person you love do the thing that might kill them, and not try to stop them. Because it’s theirs, not yours. Love listens. Love lets go.” She smiled faintly. “He told me that, on a doorstep, in the rain. I thought he was being cruel. He was the kindest person I ever met.”

The journalist asked one more question. Would she ever fall in love again?

Vera Salt laughed, a short, rueful laugh.

“I’ll tell you what I think love is now,” she said. “I think it’s always going to be like that. For everyone. It’s always going to come with sorrow folded inside it, like a flower inside a bulb. It’s always going to be too much or too little, too early or too late, and the one you love best will always be the one you can’t keep. That’s not a curse. I used to think it was. It’s just what love is.” She paused. “The ones who love best don’t get to keep it. They only get to have been there, at the end, holding its head in their lap in the rain.”

Every spring, on the hillside above Loch Snizort, in a small walled garden beside a white cottage, forty-one snake’s-head fritillaries come up and bloom. They’re purple, chequered with white, and they nod in the wind off the sea. They have no business growing that far north. Every spring, at dawn, two women in their sixties stand in the garden and look at them for a long time without speaking.

Then one of them goes inside and puts the kettle on, and the other stays a little longer, kneeling in the wet grass, touching one of the drooping bells very gently with her fingertip. She doesn’t pick it. She has learned not to pick them.

VENUS AND ADONIS
Title of the Work The Unpicked Fruit of the High Ridges


Creative Work


I. The Orchard at Noon

The heat in the Ojai valley did not merely descend; it ripened, thickening the air with the bruised, sugary scent of fallen apricots and crushed sage. At thirty-four, Clara Vance had come to resemble the valley she owned: lush, generous to the point of excess, and restless under a sun that refused to cool. She stood at the edge of the lower terrace, watching Julian tightening the cinch on his bay gelding, her fingers stained faint amber from the peaches she had been halving on the cedar table.

Julian was nineteen, the son of a late surveyor from up north, hired for the summer to map the limestone ridges above her property. He had the sort of unbothered, self-contained beauty that seemed almost rude in its completeness—skin the color of raw almonds, dark hair that curled damply at his nape, and grey eyes that looked through people toward the tree line. He did not hate women, nor did he fear them; he simply had not yet found a reason to interrupt his mornings for them.

"You're riding out before the shade even reaches the wash," Clara said, stepping down from the stone porch. She didn't bother with a hat. Her linen dress was unbuttoned at the throat, damp where her collarbone caught the glare.

Julian didn't look up from the buckle. "The big cat came down as far as the dry cistern last night. Found tracks in the alkali dust. If I wait till four, the wind shifts up-canyon and he'll smell the horse a mile off."

"Let the state trappers take him," she said, coming close enough that the heat off the gelding's flank mingled with the neroli and salt on her own skin. She reached out—not for the bridle, but for Julian's forearm, where a scratch from a manzanita branch had dried into a thin crimson thread. Her thumb pressed the warm muscle just below it. "Stay on the porch. I had the ice brought up from Ventura. There's figs, and the shade under the pergola holds until six."

Julian shifted his weight, a slight, impatient pull that didn't quite free his arm because she didn't let go. A flush rose up his neck, not the dark heat of desire, but the prickling red of a boy who felt himself being crowded in an open field.

"I have five miles of ridge to clear before dark, Mrs. Vance."

"Clara," she murmured, her fingers sliding down to hook into the damp leather of his gauntlet. With a sudden, laughing strength that caught him off balance, she tugged the stirrup strap before he could mount, stepping between his chest and the saddle. "You hoard yourself like a miser, Julian. Look at you—all sinew and frown, rushing off to chase a beast through the scrub when you haven't even learned what the afternoon is for."

"The afternoon is for work," he said stiffly, looking over her shoulder at the glare on the dry hills.

"Work is for winter. Look at the trees behind you." She gestured with her free hand toward the heavy boughs of the orchard, where the late peaches hung so fat their skins were splitting, weeping clear gum into the dust. "If nobody takes them when the sugar is high, they don't stay whole on the branch out of pride. They drop into the weeds and sour. The wasps hollow them out. You act as if keeping yourself untouched is a kind of armor, when really it's just a slower way of wasting."

She leaned in, pressing her cheek against the rough cotton of his shirt, breathing in the sharp, clean smell of cedar shavings, horse sweat, and young skin. Before he could turn his chin away, she caught his jaw in both hands and kissed him—not tentatively, as a girl from the town might have done, but with a hungry, unhurried certainty that sought to strike a spark from cold flint.

Julian stood rigid for three seconds, his boots planted in the dirt, his hands hovering uselessly near her waist without touching her. When he finally wrenched his head back, his mouth was wet and his breath came short, his brows drawn low over eyes that flashed with genuine anger.

"You have no right to handle me like a stray dog," he said, his voice dropping into a rough register he rarely used.

Wait—just then, from the unfenced pasture beyond the creek bed, came a shrill, ringing whinny. One of the neighbor's unbroken fillies, a glossy chestnut that had jumped the low stone wall to reach the fallen orchard fruit, trotted along the irrigation ditch, her tail flagged high, nostrils wide and red.

Julian's bay gelding threw up his head. The horse didn't care about the saddle on his back or the survey tools strapped to the cantle. With a low, rumbling snort that vibrated through the ground, the gelding lunged backward, snapping the leather tie-rein against the hitching post like dry twine.

"Hey! Stand!" Julian shouted, lunging for the cheek-piece.

He missed by a foot. The bay cleared the low lavender hedge in a single bound, iron shoes striking sparks from the shale, neck arched like a drawn bow as he thundered down the slope toward the chestnut filly. Within moments, the two horses were circling each other in the high mustard grass—feinting, nipping, kicking up clouds of yellow pollen before wheeling together and vanishing into the blue shadow of the live oaks.

II. The Debate in the Dust

Julian stood at the edge of the terrace, his chest heaving, his riding crop hanging limp at his side. Without his mount, the five-mile climb to the high ridge before sundown was impossible. He threw his canvas kit bag onto the stone bench with a curse and sat down hard, pulling his wide-brimmed hat low over his eyes to block out both the sun and the woman standing three paces away.

Clara watched the dust settle over the oaks, a slow, triumphant warmth spreading through her ribs. Even the beasts of the field argued on her side. She walked over and knelt on the flagstones in front of the bench—an absurd posture for the woman who signed his paychecks and owned three thousand acres of the valley, yet she took it without a shred of self-consciousness, resting her forearms on his dusty knees.

"Your horse has more sense than his master," she said softly, tipping the brim of his hat up with one finger. "A half-inch of leather couldn't hold him when the blood called. Why do you fight so hard against what comes naturally to everything that breathes?"

"Because I'm not a horse," Julian said to the flagstones. His jaw was clenched so tight a muscle jumped beneath his ear. "And because what you call nature doesn't look like nature to me. It looks like a trap. My horse will come back tomorrow with his knees scraped and his wind broken, ready for the bit again. I don't want to be broken in before I even know what my own stride is."

"I'm not asking to break you, Julian. I'm asking you to live while the sun is still up." Her voice lost its teasing edge, dropping into something raw and unsteady. The sheer closeness of him—the fine golden down on his cheek, the pulse beating fast and visible in the hollow of his throat—made an ache behind her breastbone so sharp it felt like terror. "Do you think beauty like yours is a deed you hold in perpetuity? One bad fever, one slip on the loose shale up on that ridge, one winter of hard rain, and the world goes grey. Nothing keeps unless it gives itself away."

"You talk about giving," Julian said, finally looking her straight in the eyes with the cruel, clear-sighted honesty of the very young, "but you don't want to give. You want to swallow. You don't care who I am when I'm alone on the mountain; you only care how I look standing in your orchard. That isn't love, Mrs. Vance. Love waits until the season is right. It doesn't tear the green fruit off the bough just because its own throat is dry. What you have is a fever, and you want me to catch it so you don't have to burn by yourself."

The words struck her harder than a slap. For a second, the heat of the afternoon seemed to rush into her head all at once; her vision blurred at the edges, the bright white glare of the limestone terrace tilting under her knees. With a sharp intake of breath that wasn't entirely feigned, she went limp, her head dropping sideways against the rough stone of the bench, her eyes fluttering shut.

Julian froze. "Mrs. Vance?"

She didn't move. Her skin, usually flushed with sun, looked terrifyingly pale against her dark hair.

All his boyish certainty vanished in an instant. He dropped to his knees beside her in the dirt, his hands clumsy with sudden panic as he lifted her shoulders against his chest. "Clara? Did the sun take you? Clara, open your eyes!" He uncorked his canteen with his teeth, spilling lukewarm water over his own fingers to press them to her temples, chafing her wrists, leaning down so close his breath brushed her parted lips. In his fright, wanting only to call the warmth back into her face, he pressed his mouth clumsily, earnestly against hers.

Her eyelashes trembled. Slowly, her fingers curled into the front of his shirt, holding him there for a long, dizzying moment before he realized the trick and tried to pull back.

"Stay until dark," she whispered against his chin, her arms locking around his neck with a desperate, trembling gravity. "Just until the cool comes. Then I'll let you go."

Exhausted by the heat, by his own guilt at having frightened himself, and by the sheer, relentless weight of her devotion, Julian stopped struggling. He let her pull him down into the deep grass beneath the shadow of the fig tree, suffering her hands in his hair and her mouth against his throat like a wild hawk enduring the hood—still untamed, his heart beating elsewhere, waiting only for the latch to lift.

When the first purple shadow of the western ridge finally swallowed the orchard, he stood up, brushing the dry grass from his trousers.

"Come back tomorrow at noon," she pleaded, catching his wrist as he reached for his kit bag. "We'll ride down to the river where the willows are."

"I can't," he said, already stepping backward toward the gate. "Now that I've lost the afternoon, I have to go up after the cougar at first light with the hounds. He killed two yearling calves at the Miller place yesterday. I'm meeting the dogs at the lower spring at four."

The color drained from Clara's face—for real, this time. "Not the ridge cat. Not on foot in the chaparral. Hunt the deer in the lower meadows if you must shoot something, Julian! Follow the jackrabbits through the sage—there's sport enough in watching them double back and trick the dogs on the flat ground. A cornered mountain lion doesn't care how fast you are or how straight you shoot. In the thick brush, you won't even see him before he's on your shoulders."

"A deer doesn't kill stock," Julian said simply. He pulled his wrist free—gently, almost apologetically, now that the gate was behind him. "Good night, Clara."

He turned and walked down the white dust of the lane until the dusk closed over him like deep water.

III. The Chaparral at Dawn

She did not sleep. All night the big house felt like a kiln that had been sealed with the embers still inside. Every time the wind rattled the eucalyptus leaves outside her window, she heard the dry cough of a predator in the rocks; every shadow on the plaster ceiling took the shape of torn linen and dark earth.

Before the sky had turned from black to the color of cold pewter, she was out of the house, running up the steep mule track toward the limestone ridges in thin leather shoes that were ruined within the first mile. The mountain scrub tore at her skirt—greasewood and buckthorn catching at her thighs as if the hillside itself were trying to hold her back—and the sharp morning stones bruised the soles of her feet through the thin soles.

Halfway up the second draw, she heard the dogs.

It was not the long, musical baying of a pack running a deer across open timber. It was a choked, frantic snarling that stayed in one spot, high up near the boxed canyon where the spring seeped out of the shale, punctuated by a high, thin yelp that cut off abruptly.

Her breath tore at her throat like swallowed glass. She scrambled up the loose talus slope on her hands and knees, slipping in the gravel, telling herself aloud that he was up on a boulder with his rifle, that he was already skinning the beast, that in thirty seconds she would hear him laughing at her for climbing the mountain in a house dress.

Then she rounded the outcrop of grey rock and met one of the hounds limping down the trail, its left flank laid open in three parallel furrows, whining low in its throat with its tail tucked tight against its belly. A hundred yards farther, under the twisted shade of a scrub oak where the wild scarlet larkspur grew thick around the seep, the brush had been flattened as if by a threshing machine.

The big cat was gone—driven off or crawled away to die in the rocks—and Julian lay on his side in the crushed larkspur.

For a terrible, suspended moment, her mind refused to put the pieces together. He looked almost as he had under the fig tree the evening before, one arm flung out across the pine needles, his dark curls damp against his forehead. Only when she stumbled into the clearing and dropped to her knees beside him did she see where the animal's hind claws had raked down from his collarbone through his ribs, soaking his canvas shirt in a dark, spreading tide that had already begun to thicken in the cold mountain air.

She pulled his head into her lap, her hands trembling so violently she could barely wipe the grit from his cheek. His eyes were half-open, fixed on the pale morning sky above the oak branches, but the fierce, guarded light that had kept her at bay was gone—replaced by a flat, glassy stillness that reflected nothing at all.

"Julian," she whispered, pressing her forehead against his cold temple, rocking him back and forth in the quiet canyon while the blood from his chest soaked through the linen of her dress, binding them together in death as he had never allowed in life. "You wouldn't let me keep you, and look what the mountain did. It didn't even know what it was breaking."

No one answered from the ridge. Above them, the sun cleared the eastern peaks, pouring indifferent gold over the chaparral, warming the stone and the blood-darkened wildflowers alike.

She stayed there until the sun was high, speaking to ears that could no longer refuse her, before her fingers brushed a single stem of wild white campion growing beside his shoulder, its pale petals speckled and streaked with the bright crimson that had run from his side. With steady, hollow deliberation, she snapped the stem near the root—where a tiny bead of clear green sap welled up like a tear—and tucked the stained blossom inside the breast of her dress, directly over her heart.

When the men from the valley finally came up the trail with the mules an hour later, they passed her walking down alone. She did not look at them, nor did she weep. Her face was set like weathered marble, and she walked with one hand pressed flat against her chest, carrying the small, bruised flower back down to the shuttered house where, for the rest of her years, the orchard fruit would fall in the grass and rot untouched.

IV. The Bitter Prophecy

In the weeks that followed, as she sat behind drawn blinds listening to the wind move through the dry valley, the grief inside her hardened into a cold, clear conviction about the world outside her gates. Because the purest thing she had ever reached for had been torn apart before it could bloom, nothing that came after would ever be whole.

Desire, she knew now, would never again walk in step with peace. From this season onward, those who loved most fiercely would always be the ones left begging at a locked gate, while the cold and the careless held the keys. Passion would be a fever that promised spring and delivered drought—making fools of the wise, cowards of the brave, and strangers of those who lay in the same bed—so that no heart on earth would ever taste sweetness without the shadow of the claw waiting in the brush.
